deep.opt-001:
### Context / why they ask this
It is the warm-up question. The interviewer checks that you speak precisely: *right vs obligation*, *strike*, *expiry*, *premium*, *payoff*. On a Sales & Trading desk you will use these words hundreds of times a day, so a crisp, jargon-correct answer immediately signals that you are comfortable.

### Key concepts
- **Underlying**: the asset the option is written on (a stock, an index like the CAC 40 or Euro Stoxx 50, an FX rate like EURUSD, a future, a rate).
- **Strike $K$**: the fixed price at which you can buy (call) or sell (put).
- **Expiry / maturity $T$**: the last date the right can be used.
- **Premium**: the price of the option, paid upfront by the buyer to the seller.
- **Long / short**: long = you bought it (you own the right); short = you sold/wrote it (you have the obligation if the buyer exercises).
- **Exercise**: using the right. **Physical settlement**: you actually receive/deliver the shares. **Cash settlement**: you just receive the payoff in cash (standard for index options).
- **Notional**: number of units times the spot or strike, i.e. the size of the exposure.

### Intuition
- A **call** is like a *reservation* on a flat: you pay a deposit today to have the right to buy at a fixed price later. If prices rise, you exercise and gain; if they fall, you walk away and lose only the deposit.
- A **put** is like *insurance* on your car: you pay a premium, and if the value collapses you can "sell" it to the insurer at the agreed value.
- The asymmetry is the whole point: the buyer has **convex** exposure (gains big on one side, loses a bounded amount on the other). The seller is paid a premium to carry the opposite, **concave** exposure.

### The maths
Payoffs at expiry:
$$\text{Call: } (S_T-K)^+ = \max(S_T-K,0), \qquad \text{Put: } (K-S_T)^+ = \max(K-S_T,0).$$
Both are non-negative, which is why an option premium can never be negative: you never pay anything at expiry by holding an option.
Key identity: $(S_T-K)^+ - (K-S_T)^+ = S_T - K$. A long call plus a short put with the same strike is a forward contract; this is the seed of put-call parity.

### Worked example with numbers
Stock at 100. You buy a 3-month call with strike 105 for a premium of 2.
- If at expiry $S_T = 115$: payoff $=10$, profit $=10-2 = 8$.
- If $S_T = 104$: payoff $=0$, you lose the premium, profit $=-2$.
- Breakeven: $S_T = K + \text{premium} = 107$.
You buy a 3-month put, strike 95, premium 1.5.
- $S_T = 85$: payoff $10$, profit $8.5$. $S_T = 100$: profit $-1.5$. Breakeven $95-1.5 = 93.5$.
Real contracts cover many units (e.g. 100 shares per listed US equity option, EUR 10 per index point for Euro Stoxx 50 options), so multiply by the contract multiplier.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "the obligation to buy": the **holder** has a right; only the **seller** has an obligation.
- Confusing payoff (what the option pays at expiry) with profit (payoff minus premium).
- Thinking a put buyer must own the stock. No: a put can be bought naked, purely as a bearish bet.
- Forgetting the seller's risk: a short call has theoretically unlimited loss.

### How to deliver it
Give the definition in one sentence each, write the two payoff formulas, then add one line of *use case*: "clients buy calls for leveraged upside, buy puts to protect a portfolio, and sell options to earn premium." That link to client use is exactly what a sales desk wants to hear. Offer naturally to draw the hockey-stick payoff diagrams.
deep.opt-002:
### Context / why they ask this
They want to see that you distinguish *what the contract pays* from *what you made*. On a trading desk everything is P&L, and daily P&L comes from mark-to-market, not only from expiry payoffs. It also tests whether you can sketch diagrams quickly, a very common whiteboard task.

### Key concepts
- **Payoff**: contractual cash flow at expiry, always $\ge 0$ for the option holder.
- **Premium**: price paid upfront.
- **P&L**: gain or loss of the position. At expiry: payoff minus premium. Before expiry: current value minus purchase price ("mark-to-market", MtM).
- **Breakeven**: the underlying level at which P&L at expiry is zero.
- **Convex / concave**: a long option's P&L curve bends upward (convex) - good for the holder when the market moves a lot. A short option is concave.

### Intuition
Picture the "hockey stick". The payoff line is flat at zero then rises with slope 1 (call) or falls with slope $-1$ (put) through the strike. The P&L line is the same shape **shifted down by the premium** for the buyer (shifted up for the seller, then flipped). The four diagrams are just reflections of each other:
- Long call: flat at $-c$, kink at $K$, slope $+1$ afterwards. Unlimited upside.
- Short call: flat at $+c$, kink at $K$, slope $-1$. Unlimited downside - this is the scary one.
- Long put: slope $-1$ down to $K$, flat at $-p$ beyond. Max gain $K-p$ (stock to zero).
- Short put: flat at $+p$ above $K$, slope $+1$ below. Max loss $K-p$. Economically similar to agreeing to buy the stock at $K$ in exchange for being paid $p$.

### The maths
Long call P&L at expiry: $\Pi = (S_T-K)^+ - c\,e^{rT}$ (strictly, you compound the premium because you paid it at time 0; interviewers usually accept $-c$).
Breakeven for a long call: $S^* = K + c$. For a long put: $S^* = K - p$.
Before expiry: $\Pi_t = V_t - V_0$, where $V_t$ is the model value (e.g. Black-Scholes). The MtM curve is smooth and lies **above** the expiry payoff for a long option (time value), converging to the hockey stick as $t\to T$.

### Worked example with numbers
Stock 50, call $K=50$, premium 3; put $K=50$, premium 2.5.
| $S_T$ | Long call P&L | Short call P&L | Long put P&L | Short put P&L |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 40 | $-3$ | $+3$ | $+7.5$ | $-7.5$ |
| 50 | $-3$ | $+3$ | $-2.5$ | $+2.5$ |
| 53 | $0$ | $0$ | $-2.5$ | $+2.5$ |
| 60 | $+7$ | $-7$ | $-2.5$ | $+2.5$ |

Breakevens: call 53, put 47.5.

### Common pitfalls
- Drawing the payoff and calling it P&L (forgetting to shift by the premium).
- Saying a short put has unlimited loss: it is bounded by $K-p$ because a stock cannot go below zero.
- Forgetting that a trader's P&L is daily MtM: you can lose money on a long call even if it ends in the money, if you bought it at a high implied vol that then collapses.

### How to deliver it
Say the definition in one sentence, then *draw* while talking: "four hockey sticks, and each short is the long flipped around the x-axis". Always state max gain, max loss and breakeven for each - that is the language sales uses when pitching a structure to a client.
deep.opt-003:
### Context / why they ask this
It checks you understand what the premium is actually paying for. It is also the gateway to theta, vega and to "why would you never exercise an American call early" (because you would throw away time value).

### Key concepts
- **Intrinsic value**: immediate exercise value, never negative.
- **Time value (extrinsic value)**: premium minus intrinsic value. Represents optionality.
- **Moneyness**: whether the option is in-, at- or out-of-the-money (ITM/ATM/OTM).
- **Theta**: rate at which option value decreases as time passes, everything else fixed.
- **Forward intrinsic**: $\max(F-K,0)e^{-rT}$, the discounted intrinsic value against the forward $F$. Traders often prefer it because it is what the option is worth with zero vol.

### Intuition
Think of time value as the value of *waiting to decide*. An OTM option has zero intrinsic value but still costs money because the stock might move through the strike. A deep ITM call behaves almost like the stock itself: there is little extra optionality (the chance of ending OTM is small), so time value is small. A deep OTM option is also mostly "dead", so again little time value. **ATM is where the right to decide later is most valuable**, because it is a coin flip whether you end up exercising.

### The maths
$$V = \underbrace{\max(S-K,0)}_{\text{intrinsic}} + \underbrace{(V - \max(S-K,0))}_{\text{time value}}.$$
In Black-Scholes, with zero vol the call is worth $e^{-rT}\max(F-K,0)$ where $F = S e^{(r-q)T}$. The extra value above that is pure *volatility value*. ATM, a handy approximation (for $r\approx q\approx 0$) is
$$C_{ATM} \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt{T}\,S,$$
which is 100% time value, and shows it grows with $\sigma$ and with $\sqrt{T}$.

### Worked example with numbers
Stock 100, 1-year options, vol 20%, $r=q=0$ (Black-Scholes values):
- Call $K=90$: price 13.59. Intrinsic 10, time value 3.59.
- Call $K=100$: price 7.97. Intrinsic 0, time value 7.97 (maximal).
- Call $K=110$: price 4.29. Intrinsic 0, time value 4.29.
- Put $K=110$: price 14.29. Intrinsic 10, time value 4.29 (same as the 110 call - put-call parity with $r=q=0$).
Notice time value peaks at the ATM strike and is symmetric-ish around it.

### Common pitfalls
- Thinking time value is always positive: a deep ITM **European put** (or a deep ITM European call on a high-dividend stock) can trade *below* spot intrinsic, i.e. negative time value vs spot, because you must wait to receive $K$ (you lose interest). Against forward intrinsic it stays positive.
- Saying time value decays linearly: it decays roughly like $\sqrt{T}$, so faster near expiry for ATM options.

### How to deliver it
"Premium = intrinsic + time value. Intrinsic is exercise-now value; time value is the price of optionality, driven by vol and time, maximal ATM, decaying to zero at expiry." Then mention the $0.4\sigma\sqrt{T}$ rule: it shows you can put numbers on it, which traders love.
deep.opt-004:
### Context / why they ask this
Basic vocabulary, but the ATMF subtlety separates people who read a textbook from people who understand trading conventions. Sales and trading talk in "% of spot" strikes (e.g. "a 90% put"), in delta ("25-delta risk reversal"), and in ATMF.

### Key concepts
- **Spot $S_0$**: current price.
- **Forward $F_0$**: the price agreed today for delivery at $T$, $F_0 = S_0 e^{(r-q)T}$ with $r$ the interest rate and $q$ the dividend yield (for FX, $q$ is the foreign rate).
- **% moneyness**: strike as a percentage of spot, $K/S_0$. A "90% put" has $K=0.9S_0$.
- **Log-moneyness**: $\ln(K/F)$, the natural variable in Black-Scholes; often normalised by $\sigma\sqrt{T}$.
- **Delta moneyness**: characterise a strike by its option's delta. 50-delta is roughly ATM; 25-delta and 10-delta are progressively further OTM.

### Intuition
Moneyness is "how far the option is from paying off, in units of how much the stock usually moves". A 10% OTM call is very far away for a 1-week option on a low-vol stock, but almost ATM for a 5-year option on a volatile stock. That is why traders like delta or $\ln(K/F)/(\sigma\sqrt T)$ rather than raw distance: they normalise by vol and time.

### The maths
Put-call parity: $C - P = e^{-rT}(F-K)$. Hence $C=P \iff K=F$: at the ATMF strike, call and put have equal value. For a non-dividend stock with $r>0$, $F>S$, so an ATM-spot call is worth more than the ATM-spot put.
Standardised moneyness: $m = \dfrac{\ln(K/F)}{\sigma\sqrt T}$. Black-Scholes $d_2 = -m - \tfrac12\sigma\sqrt T$.

### Worked example with numbers
$S=100$, $r=5\%$, $q=0$, $T=1$, $\sigma=20\%$. Forward $F = 100e^{0.05} = 105.13$.
- ATM spot ($K=100$): call 10.45, put 5.57. Very different!
- ATMF ($K=105.13$): call = put. Using the forward form of Black-Scholes, $C = e^{-rT}F\,[N(d_1)-N(d_2)]$ with $d_{1,2}=\pm\tfrac12\sigma\sqrt T=\pm 0.1$, so $C = P = 100\times(2N(0.1)-1) = 7.97$.
This shows rates alone can create a 5-point difference between ATM-spot call and put.

### Common pitfalls
- Assuming ATM call = ATM put price without specifying spot vs forward.
- Forgetting that for puts ITM means $S<K$.
- Using %-of-spot moneyness to compare options across very different maturities.

### How to deliver it
Give the three definitions in one breath, then add the value-add: "in practice ATM usually means ATM forward, where call and put are worth the same, and in FX we quote by delta, like 25-delta." That shows market awareness.
deep.opt-005:
### Context / why they ask this
It is the entry point to a classic chain: "Which is more valuable?" then "When would you exercise early?" then "Why never for a call on a non-dividend stock?" Having the chain ready shows depth.

### Key concepts
- **Exercise style**: rule for *when* the holder can exercise.
- **Early-exercise premium**: $V_{Am} - V_{Eu} \ge 0$.
- **Optimal stopping**: pricing an American option means choosing the best exercise time; mathematically it is a free-boundary problem.
- **Exercise boundary**: the critical spot level $S^*(t)$ beyond which immediate exercise is optimal (e.g. for a put, exercise if $S<S^*(t)$).

### Intuition
More rights can never be worth less, so the American is at least the European. Whether it is *strictly* more depends on whether you would ever want to exercise early. Exercising early does two things: (1) you **lose the remaining time value / insurance** (you give up the option to wait), and (2) you **change your carry** - you pay or receive the strike earlier, and you start or stop receiving dividends.
- Call: exercising means paying $K$ now instead of later (you lose interest on $K$) and gives up the protection. The only benefit is capturing a dividend. No dividend - no reason.
- Put: exercising means receiving $K$ now (you earn interest on it). If the stock is very low, the interest on $K$ can outweigh the remaining time value, so you exercise.

### The maths
Price of an American option (risk-neutral):
$$V_{Am}(0) = \sup_{\tau \le T} \mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}\left[e^{-r\tau}\,\text{payoff}(S_\tau)\right],$$
the sup over stopping times $\tau$. No closed form in general (except the perpetual American put), so desks use **binomial trees**, finite differences (PDE with the constraint $V \ge$ payoff) or **Longstaff-Schwartz** Monte Carlo. In a tree, at each node: $V = \max(\text{exercise value}, \text{continuation value})$.

### Worked example with numbers
Stock at 1, American put strike 100, 1 year, $r=5\%$. Exercising now yields 99, which invested for a year earns about 5. Waiting, the most you can get at expiry is 100 (if the stock goes to 0), i.e. only 1 more than now. So you exercise immediately: the interest (about 5) beats the remaining upside (at most 1). The European put is worth only about $100e^{-0.05} - 1 = 94.12$, below its intrinsic value of 99. The American is worth 99.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying American options are "traded in America". Style is not location.
- Saying "American calls are always worth more than European calls". Not without dividends.
- Forgetting Bermudans: they matter a lot in rates (Bermudan swaptions, callable bonds) and in autocallables (discrete observation dates).

### How to deliver it
Define the three styles, state the ordering, then spontaneously add the early-exercise insight: "for a non-dividend call the premium is zero, for puts it is positive when rates are high and the put is deep ITM." Offer the tree method as the pricing tool.
deep.opt-006:
### Context / why they ask this
Sales desks sell hedges to corporates and investors. Explaining to a client "forward = lock in, option = insurance with upside" is a core sales skill. Interviewers also test that you know how a forward is priced (no-arbitrage cost of carry), which underpins everything in derivatives.

### Key concepts
- **Forward contract**: OTC agreement to trade at $T$ at price $F$ fixed today. **Future**: the exchange-traded, standardised, daily-margined version.
- **Cost of carry**: $F_0 = S_0e^{(r-q)T}$. Buying the stock now and holding it costs financing $r$ but earns dividends $q$; the forward price must equal that cost, otherwise there is arbitrage.
- **Linear vs non-linear**: forward value moves one-for-one with the underlying (delta 1, gamma 0). Option value moves with a delta between 0 and 1 that changes with spot (gamma $\neq 0$).
- **Convexity**: curvature of the payoff; the source of option value in volatile markets.

### Intuition
Forward: "I agree today to buy EUR at 1.10 in 6 months." If EURUSD goes to 1.20 you win, if it goes to 1.00 you lose; you are fully locked. That is why nothing is paid upfront: at the fair forward, neither side is favoured.
Option: "I have the right to buy EUR at 1.10." If it goes up, you exercise; if down, you buy in the market at the cheaper price. You got the good side without the bad side - someone must be compensated for that, hence the premium.
For a corporate: a forward is great when certainty matters (budget rate). An option is better when they want protection but believe the market might move in their favour, or when the exposure itself is uncertain (e.g. bidding on a foreign contract: if they lose the bid, an option just expires, while a forward would become a naked speculative position).

### The maths
Forward pricing by replication: borrow $S_0$, buy the stock, deliver it at $T$ for $F$. Cash flow at $T$: $F - S_0e^{rT}$ (plus dividends). No arbitrage gives $F_0 = S_0e^{(r-q)T}$.
Value at $t$ of a forward struck at $K$: $f_t = e^{-r(T-t)}(F_t-K)$.
Parity: $(S_T-K)^+ - (K-S_T)^+ = S_T-K$, so $C-P = e^{-rT}(F_0-K)$. At $K=F_0$: $C=P$, and long call + short put costs zero, just like the forward.

### Worked example with numbers
A French exporter will receive USD 10m in 6 months. EURUSD spot 1.10, EUR rate 2%, USD rate 4% (illustrative). Forward $= 1.10\times e^{(0.04-0.02)\times 0.5}\approx 1.111$ (USD per EUR; USD rates higher so the forward EURUSD is higher, meaning the USD trades at a forward discount). Two hedges:
- Sell USD forward at 1.111: locked at about EUR 9.0m, no premium.
- Buy a EUR call / USD put struck at 1.111 for, say, 1.8% of notional: protected if USD falls, but keeps the gain if USD rises. Costs about EUR 160k upfront.
Neither is "better"; it depends on the client's view and risk appetite. A popular compromise is a zero-cost **collar**.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying the forward price is the "expected future spot". It is the no-arbitrage carry price; under the real-world measure the expected spot can differ (risk premia).
- Saying a forward is "free". It costs zero at inception, but it can have large MtM value later and carries credit risk (hence collateral/CSA).

### How to deliver it
Contrast in three words each: forward = obligation, linear, zero premium; option = right, convex, premium. Then give a client example. Finish with the parity link. Crisp and client-oriented - ideal for Sales & Trading.
deep.opt-007:
### Context / why they ask this
This is probably the single most asked options question in S&T interviews. They test (1) that you can state it, (2) derive it by replication, (3) use it to spot arbitrage, and (4) draw consequences (same implied vol for call and put, synthetic positions). Traders use it daily: conversion/reversal trades, pricing synthetics, and extracting implied forwards and dividends from option prices.

### Key concepts
- **Replication**: building the same payoff from other instruments.
- **Arbitrage**: a strategy with zero initial cost, no chance of loss and a positive chance of gain (or positive cash today with no future liability).
- **Law of one price**: identical future cash flows must have identical present value.
- **Zero-coupon bond**: pays $K$ at $T$, worth $Ke^{-rT}$ today.
- **Implied forward**: the forward extracted from option prices, $F = K + e^{rT}(C-P)$.
- **Conversion / reversal**: arbitrage trades exploiting parity violations (long stock + long put + short call = conversion).

### Intuition
Draw it. Long call: hockey stick up to the right. Short put: hockey stick down to the left. Add them: a straight line of slope 1 through $K$ - that is a forward. So "call minus put" is just "the stock minus a bond paying $K$". The option-specific stuff (volatility, skew...) cancels out because whatever makes the call more valuable makes the put equally more valuable at the same strike.

### The maths
Portfolio A: one call + a zero-coupon paying $K$ at $T$. Payoff: $(S_T-K)^+ + K = \max(S_T, K)$.
Portfolio B: one put + one share (with dividends reinvested, i.e. $e^{-qT}$ shares today). Payoff: $(K-S_T)^+ + S_T = \max(S_T,K)$.
Same payoff, so same price:
$$C + Ke^{-rT} = P + S_0e^{-qT} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C-P = S_0e^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT} = e^{-rT}(F_0-K).$$
Differentiate w.r.t. spot: $\Delta_C - \Delta_P = e^{-qT}$ (about 1). Differentiate again: $\Gamma_C = \Gamma_P$. W.r.t. vol: $\mathcal V_C = \mathcal V_P$. So the implied vol of a call and a put with the same strike must be equal, otherwise parity breaks.

### Worked example with numbers
$S=100$, $K=100$, $r=5\%$, $q=0$, $T=1$. $Ke^{-rT}=95.12$. Parity says $C - P = 4.88$. Black-Scholes at 20% vol: $C=10.45$, $P=5.57$, difference $4.88$. Check.
If instead $r=q=0$ and $K=S$: $C=P$ exactly (7.97 each at 20% vol).

### Common pitfalls
- Applying it to **American** options: it becomes an inequality, $S_0 - K \le C_{Am}-P_{Am} \le S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$ (no dividends).
- Forgetting dividends: the stock leg is $S_0e^{-qT}$ (or $S_0 - PV(\text{divs})$).
- Mixing strikes or maturities: parity is for the same $K$ and $T$.
- In reality: borrow costs (hard-to-borrow stocks), funding spreads and transaction costs create small deviations. Parity then gives you the market-implied **repo/borrow cost**.

### How to deliver it
State the formula, then say "proof by replication: call plus bond equals put plus stock, both pay max(S_T, K)", sketch the two diagrams, and conclude with two consequences: same vega/gamma and same implied vol for call and put, and the fact that it is model-independent. If time permits, offer the arbitrage example.
deep.opt-008:
### Context / why they ask this
It tests whether you can go from formula to trade quickly and with correct signs, under pressure, which is what a trader does. The key is a mental checklist: compute the fair $C-P$, compare, decide which leg is rich, then hedge the rest with stock and cash.

### Key concepts
- **Rich / cheap**: overpriced / underpriced relative to fair value.
- **Conversion**: long stock + long put + short call (synthetic short forward vs actual long stock) = riskless bond paying $K$.
- **Reversal (reverse conversion)**: short stock + short put + long call = riskless borrowing.
- **Synthetic stock**: long call + short put at the same strike (plus bond) replicates the stock.
- **Locking in**: taking a position whose future value is certain.

### Intuition
Think of "call minus put" as a *synthetic forward*. In the market that synthetic forward costs 7, while a real forward (stock financed with a loan) costs 4.88. So you **sell the expensive synthetic** (short call, long put = synthetic short) and **buy the cheap real thing** (buy stock with borrowed money). All the risk nets out, and the price difference is profit.

### The maths
Fair: $C-P = S_0 - Ke^{-rT} = 100 - 100e^{-0.05} = 100 - 95.1229 = 4.8771$.
Market: $12 - 5 = 7$. Mispricing: $7 - 4.8771 = 2.1229$.
Trade at $t=0$:
| Leg | Cash flow today |
|---|---|
| Sell call | $+12$ |
| Buy put | $-5$ |
| Buy stock | $-100$ |
| Borrow PV(K) | $+95.12$ |
| **Total** | **$+2.12$** |

At $T$, position value: $S_T + (100-S_T)^+ - (S_T-100)^+ = 100$. Repay the loan: $95.12e^{0.05} = 100$. Net zero. Profit = 2.12 today (or $2.12e^{0.05}=2.23$ at $T$).
Scenario check: $S_T=130$: call assigned, you deliver the share, get 100, put expires worthless, repay 100. $S_T=70$: exercise the put, sell the share for 100, call expires, repay 100. Both zero - good.

### Worked example: the reverse case
If instead the put were 9 and call 12 ($C-P=3 < 4.88$): the call is cheap relative to the put. Do a **reversal**: buy the call, sell the put, short the stock and lend 95.12. Cash today: $-12+9+100-95.12 = +1.88$. At $T$ you buy back the stock at exactly 100 via the call or the put assignment and your deposit returns 100.

### Common pitfalls
- Getting the direction wrong: the rule is "sell whatever is expensive, buy what is cheap, then neutralise the delta with the stock and the cash with the bond".
- Forgetting to discount the strike (using 100 instead of 95.12 would make you think the fair difference is 0).
- Ignoring practicalities when asked "would this really work?": transaction costs, bid-ask, borrow cost to short a stock (for reversals), early exercise if options are American (the short put in a reversal could be assigned early), dividends not accounted for. Real parity deviations usually reflect borrow costs or dividend expectations, not free money.

### How to deliver it
Out loud: "Fair C minus P is S minus PV of K, 4.88. Market is 7, so the call is rich by 2.12. I sell the call, buy the put - that's a synthetic short - and buy the stock financed by borrowing the PV of the strike. I receive 2.12 today; at expiry the position is worth exactly 100, which repays the loan." Then do the two-scenario check. Showing the check proves you are not guessing.
deep.opt-009:
### Context / why they ask this
It checks rigorous no-arbitrage reasoning, the foundation of everything. The follow-ups (convexity in strike, why a call is worth more than $S-K$) lead to deep insights like "never exercise an American call early" and "risk-neutral density = second derivative of call price in strike".

### Key concepts
- **Dominance argument**: if payoff A $\ge$ payoff B in every state, then price A $\ge$ price B.
- **Monotonicity in strike**: $C(K_1) \ge C(K_2)$ if $K_1<K_2$.
- **Convexity in strike**: $C(K)$ is convex; equivalently, a butterfly has non-negative price.
- **Call spread bound**: $0 \le C(K_1) - C(K_2) \le e^{-rT}(K_2-K_1)$.

### Intuition
- Upper bound $C\le S$: why pay more for the right to buy the stock than for the stock itself?
- Lower bound $C \ge S - Ke^{-rT}$: the call is better than a forward (the forward forces you to buy even when $S_T<K$). A forward costs $S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$, so the call costs at least that.
- Put upper bound: the best case is the stock going to zero, you get $K$ at $T$, worth $Ke^{-rT}$ today.
- Butterfly $\ge 0$: its payoff is never negative, so its price cannot be negative. This makes call prices convex in strike.

### The maths
Dominance: $(S_T-K)^+ \ge S_T - K$ so $C \ge S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$; and $(S_T-K)^+ \ge 0$.
With dividend yield: $\max(S_0e^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT},0) \le C \le S_0e^{-qT}$.
Strike derivatives (Breeden-Litzenberger):
$$\frac{\partial C}{\partial K} = -e^{-rT}\mathbb Q(S_T>K) \in [-e^{-rT}, 0], \qquad \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial K^2} = e^{-rT} f_{\mathbb Q}(K) \ge 0,$$
where $f_{\mathbb Q}$ is the risk-neutral density. So the call curve's slope is minus a (discounted) probability and its curvature is a density - which is why convexity must hold.

### Worked example with numbers
$S_0=100$, $K=90$, $r=5\%$, $T=1$. Lower bound $100 - 90e^{-0.05} = 100 - 85.61 = 14.39$. A call trading at 13 would be an arbitrage: buy the call, short the stock, lend 85.61. Cash today: $-13+100-85.61 = +1.39$. At $T$ you have 90 from the loan; if $S_T>90$, exercise and use 90 to buy back the share; if $S_T<90$, buy the share in the market for less than 90 and keep the difference. Always $\ge 0$ at $T$ plus 1.39 today.
Note: a call worth $\ge S_0-Ke^{-rT} > S_0 - K$ shows an American call on a non-dividend stock is worth more alive than exercised.

### Common pitfalls
- Writing $C \ge S-K$ for a European and stopping there: the tighter bound uses $Ke^{-rT}$.
- Forgetting the European put *can* be below $K - S_0$ (its lower bound is $Ke^{-rT}-S_0$).
- Forgetting dividends shrink the call bounds.

### How to deliver it
Give each bound with a one-line dominance argument. Then add the insight that $C \ge S - Ke^{-rT} > S-K$ means early exercise of a non-dividend call is never optimal. Mentioning Breeden-Litzenberger shows quant depth, useful even on a trading desk.
deep.opt-010:
### Context / why they ask this
It checks that you can manipulate parity like an equation and relate client strategies to each other. Sales people constantly need to explain "this structure is actually equivalent to that".

### Key concepts
- **Synthetic**: a combination of instruments that replicates another instrument's payoff.
- **Protective put**: long stock + long put (insurance).
- **Covered call / buy-write**: long stock + short call (yield enhancement).
- **Risk reversal**: long call + short put at *different* strikes; with the same strike it is a synthetic forward.

### Intuition
Treat parity as a balance equation and move terms across: whatever you add on one side you can "manufacture" from the others. Graphically: stock payoff is a 45 degree line. Adding a put cuts off the losses below $K$ - the result is a hockey stick that looks exactly like a call (shifted up by $K$). Selling a call against stock caps the upside - result looks like a short put (shifted).

### The maths
Start: $C + Ke^{-rT} = P + S$.
- $S = C - P + Ke^{-rT}$ (synthetic stock).
- $S - Ke^{-rT} = C - P$ (synthetic forward struck at $K$).
- $P = C - S + Ke^{-rT}$ (synthetic put).
- $C = P + S - Ke^{-rT}$ (synthetic call).
- $S - C = Ke^{-rT} - P$ (covered call = cash minus a put, i.e. short put + bond).
Greeks follow: synthetic long stock has delta $\Delta_C - \Delta_P = 1$ and zero gamma/vega.

### Worked example with numbers
$S=100$, $K=100$, $r=0$, 1y, vol 20%: $C=P=7.97$.
A client holds the stock and buys a 100 put for 7.97. At expiry: if $S_T=80$, stock 80 + put 20 = 100. If $S_T=130$: 130 + 0 = 130. This equals holding 100 cash + a 100 call: $100 + (S_T-100)^+$. Same payoff, same cost (100 + 7.97).
Covered call: long stock, short 100 call: pays $\min(S_T, 100)$, identical to 100 cash minus a 100 put: $100 - (100-S_T)^+$.

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting the bond/cash leg: long call + short put is a *forward*, not the stock; you need the cash $Ke^{-rT}$ to own the share.
- Assuming synthetics are identical in practice: with American options, early exercise can break the equivalence; also dividends, borrow costs and margin treatment differ.

### How to deliver it
Write the parity equation once and derive each synthetic in one line. Then give the client translation: "a protective put is a call with cash; a covered call is a short put with cash - which is why covered call writers are really selling downside volatility." That last sentence is a great sales insight.
deep.opt-011:
### Context / why they ask this
It is the classic table question. The interviewer checks the directions but mainly the *reasons*. A strong answer links each input to a Greek and to the **forward**: most of the effects of $S$, $r$ and $q$ go through $F=Se^{(r-q)T}$.

### Key concepts
- **Greeks**: sensitivities of the price to each input: delta ($S$), vega ($\sigma$), theta ($t$), rho ($r$), and dividend sensitivity (sometimes "epsilon" or "psi").
- **Implied volatility**: the $\sigma$ which, plugged into Black-Scholes, reproduces the market price.
- **Forward**: $F=Se^{(r-q)T}$; a call is really an option on the forward.

### Intuition
- **Spot**: the call is a claim on the upside, so more spot = more value.
- **Strike**: the strike is what you pay (call) or receive (put).
- **Vol**: with a convex payoff, big moves help you on one side and cannot hurt you by more than the premium on the other. More dispersion = more expected payoff. That is why *both* call and put gain.
- **Time**: more time = more accumulated variance ($\sigma^2T$) = more optionality. But for a deep ITM European put, waiting delays receiving $K$ (costing interest), so it can lose value with more time.
- **Rates**: a call is like buying the stock later - you keep your cash invested meanwhile, so a higher rate makes it more attractive (and the forward is higher). A put is like selling later: you receive $K$ later, which is worth less when rates are high.
- **Dividends**: the option holder does not receive dividends; the stock drops by the dividend on the ex-date. Calls lose, puts gain.

### The maths
$C = e^{-rT}[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)]$, with $d_{1,2} = \frac{\ln(F/K)\pm \frac12\sigma^2T}{\sigma\sqrt T}$.
Signs of partial derivatives:
| Input up | Call | Put | Greek |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spot $S$ | + | - | Delta |
| Strike $K$ | - | + | (dual delta) |
| Vol $\sigma$ | + | + | Vega |
| Maturity $T$ | + (usually) | + (usually) | -Theta |
| Rate $r$ | + | - | Rho |
| Dividend $q$ | - | + | |

### Worked example with numbers
Base: $S=K=100$, $T=1$, $\sigma=20\%$, $r=q=0$: call = put = 7.97.
- $\sigma \to 21\%$: both gain about vega $\times 1\% \approx 0.40$.
- $r \to 5\%$: call 10.45, put 5.57 (forward rises to 105.1).
- $r = 3\%$ vs $0\%$: call 9.41 vs 7.97; put 6.46 vs 7.97.
- $T \to 1/12$ (1 month): call = put = 2.30 (roughly $7.97/\sqrt{12}$, the $\sqrt T$ scaling).

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "vol up: call up, put down". Wrong: both go up.
- Listing "expected return of the stock" as a driver: in Black-Scholes it does not appear (risk-neutral pricing).
- Forgetting the exceptions for maturity.

### How to deliver it
List the six inputs, then go through them grouped: "spot, rates and dividends act through the forward; strike is the other side of the payoff; vol and time act through total variance $\sigma^2 T$, and vol is the only unobservable, which is why options are quoted in vol." That structure sounds like a trader.
deep.opt-012:
### Context / why they ask this
A trap question: many candidates say "call up, put down" by analogy with spot. Getting it right and explaining the convexity argument shows you understand what options really are: **bets on volatility**, not just on direction.

### Key concepts
- **Volatility $\sigma$**: annualised standard deviation of log-returns.
- **Convex payoff**: the payoff curve bends upward. Formally $f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \le \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda)f(y)$.
- **Jensen's inequality**: for convex $f$, $\mathbb E[f(X)] \ge f(\mathbb E[X])$, and a mean-preserving spread increases $\mathbb E[f(X)]$.
- **Vega**: $\partial V/\partial\sigma$, usually quoted per 1 vol point (1%).
- **Long vol**: a position that gains when volatility (implied or realised) rises.

### Intuition
Two scenarios for a stock at 100, 100-strike call:
- Low vol: stock ends at 95 or 105 with equal probability. Call pays 0 or 5, expected 2.5.
- High vol: stock ends at 80 or 120. Call pays 0 or 20, expected 10.
The downside scenario got worse for the stock (80 vs 95), but the call holder does not care - they get zero either way. Only the upside counted. Same logic for the put with the downside. That asymmetry is the whole story.

### The maths
Black-Scholes vega (no dividends):
$$\mathcal V = \frac{\partial C}{\partial \sigma} = S\,\varphi(d_1)\sqrt T = K e^{-rT}\varphi(d_2)\sqrt T > 0,$$
where $\varphi$ is the standard normal density. Identical for the put (parity: $C - P$ does not depend on $\sigma$). ATM, $\varphi(d_1)\approx 0.4$, so $\mathcal V \approx 0.4 S\sqrt T$, i.e. about $0.4\sqrt T\%$ of spot per vol point. That matches the ATM approximation $C\approx 0.4\sigma\sqrt T S$, which is linear in $\sigma$: ATM options are almost linear in vol.

### Worked example with numbers
$S=K=100$, $T=1$, $r=0$: vega $= 100\times 0.397\times 1 = 39.7$ per unit of vol, i.e. **0.397 per vol point**. Vol from 20% to 25%: call and put both go from 7.97 to about 9.95 (+1.98 = 5 x 0.397). For a 1-month option vega is about 11.5 per unit, i.e. 0.115 per point: short-dated options are much less sensitive to vol (but more to gamma).

### Common pitfalls
- "Put value falls when vol rises because the stock is riskier": no, the put gains.
- Confusing implied and realised vol: vega is sensitivity to **implied** vol (the mark). Realised vol affects you through gamma P&L when you delta hedge.
- Thinking vega is highest for deep OTM options: in absolute terms it peaks near ATM; in relative terms (% of premium) OTM options are more vol-sensitive.

### How to deliver it
"Both go up. The payoff is convex: more vol means bigger favourable moves, while losses are capped at the premium. That's Jensen's inequality. The Greek is vega, identical for call and put at the same strike by parity." Then add that this is why buying any option makes you long vol, and a straddle is the purest expression of it.
deep.opt-013:
### Context / why they ask this
Tests the rho intuition and whether you can think in terms of the forward. On equity derivatives desks (especially in Paris), dividend risk is huge because structured products leave banks with large dividend exposures, so understanding the dividend effect is valued.

### Key concepts
- **Rho**: $\partial V/\partial r$. Positive for calls, negative for puts.
- **Dividend yield $q$**: continuous approximation of dividends as a % of spot per year. Discrete dividends: known cash amounts on ex-dates.
- **Ex-dividend date**: the date from which buying the stock no longer gives the right to the upcoming dividend; the stock price drops by about the dividend.
- **Cost of carry**: financing cost minus income from holding the asset, $r-q$ (plus borrow/repo effects).
- **Repo rate**: the rate at which you can lend/borrow the stock; it acts like an additional dividend yield.

### Intuition
Imagine you want exposure to a stock in one year. Option 1: buy it today, pay 100 now. Option 2: buy a call, pay a small premium, and pay $K$ only at expiry. With high rates, keeping 100 in the bank for a year is valuable, so option 2 becomes relatively more attractive: the call gains. The put is the mirror: its holder is someone who will sell the stock for $K$ later - the delay costs more when rates are high.
Dividends: the call holder "misses" the dividends that the stock owner receives, and the stock price falls by the dividend. So large expected dividends are bad for calls and good for puts.

### The maths
Forward: $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$ (or $F = (S - PV(\text{divs}))e^{rT}$ for discrete dividends).
Black-Scholes rho: $\rho_C = KTe^{-rT}N(d_2) > 0$, $\rho_P = -KTe^{-rT}N(-d_2) < 0$.
Sensitivity to $q$: $\partial C/\partial q = -STe^{-qT}N(d_1) < 0$, $\partial P/\partial q = STe^{-qT}N(-d_1) > 0$.
Note: rho is proportional to $T$, so it only matters for long-dated options (and for currency options, where both rates matter).

### Worked example with numbers
$S=K=100$, $T=1$, $\sigma=20\%$, $q=0$:
- $r=0$: call 7.97, put 7.97.
- $r=3\%$: call 9.41, put 6.46. The difference $C-P = 2.96 = 100 - 100e^{-0.03}$, just parity.
- $r=5\%$: call 10.45, put 5.57.
Rho of the call at $r=3\%$: $100\times 1\times e^{-0.03}\times N(0.05)\approx 97.0\times 0.52 = 50.4$ per unit of rate, so +0.50 per 1% rise.
Dividend example: a 3% dividend yield on top of $r=3\%$ brings the forward back to 100, so the ATM call and put become equal again (as in a 5y option at $r=q=3\%$: both 13.73 at 18% vol).

### Common pitfalls
- Explaining the rate effect only through "discounting the payoff" (which would lower both calls and puts). The dominant effect is on the forward/PV of the strike.
- Forgetting that discrete dividends need care near ex-dates, and that they create early-exercise incentives for American calls.

### How to deliver it
"Rates and dividends act through the forward. Rates up, forward up, calls up, puts down. Dividends up, forward down, calls down, puts up." Then one line of replication intuition. Mention that on long-dated equity products, dividends are a key traded risk (dividend futures and swaps).
deep.opt-014:
### Context / why they ask this
Every quant or trading interview asks this. They want you to (1) list assumptions precisely, (2) know which ones matter, and (3) understand why a "wrong" model is still the market standard. The best answers end with "BS is the wrong number in the wrong formula to get the right price" (Rebonato's famous phrase), i.e. implied vol is the fudge factor.

### Key concepts
- **Geometric Brownian motion (GBM)**: $dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t$. Relative price changes are Gaussian over short intervals; the price stays positive.
- **Lognormal**: $\ln S_T$ is normally distributed.
- **Frictionless**: no bid-ask, no fees, no margin constraints.
- **Continuous hedging**: you can rebalance the delta hedge at every instant.
- **Fat tails / leptokurtosis**: extreme moves occur much more often than a normal distribution predicts.
- **Jumps**: discontinuous price moves (overnight gaps, earnings, defaults).
- **Volatility smile/skew**: implied vol varies with strike, contradicting the constant-vol assumption.

### Intuition
The genius of BS is not the distribution; it is the **replication argument**: under these assumptions you can perfectly replicate an option by continuously trading the stock and cash, so its price is the cost of replication, not a guess of expected payoff. Each assumption is what makes perfect replication possible:
- Continuous paths + continuous trading: the hedge can always keep up.
- Constant vol: you know how much gamma P&L the hedge will cost.
- Frictionless: rebalancing costs nothing.
Break any of these and the option is no longer redundant - it carries real risk, which is why option desks exist and earn a spread.

### The maths
Under the assumptions, the value $V(S,t)$ satisfies the BS PDE
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2} + (r-q)S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - rV = 0,$$
with terminal condition $V(S,T)=\text{payoff}(S)$. The solution for a call is the BS formula. Note that the drift $\mu$ has disappeared.
Empirical failures, quantified: daily S&P 500 moves of 5+ standard deviations (like Oct 1987, -20% in a day, a ~20-sigma event under a 16%-vol normal model) should essentially never happen under GBM but do. The equity skew is the market's price for this.

### Worked example
Suppose you sell a 1-month ATM option at 20% implied vol and delta hedge once a day. Under BS your P&L would be exactly zero if realised vol is 20% and you hedged continuously. In reality: you hedge discretely (P&L noise), the stock may gap on earnings (a jump your hedge cannot follow) and realised vol may be 30% (you lose). That residual is the trader's risk.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying BS assumes "normal prices" - it is log-returns that are normal.
- Forgetting the no-arbitrage / replication logic and presenting BS as "expected payoff discounted".
- Claiming "BS is useless because vol is not constant". It is the market's quoting convention and the base for the Greeks; more advanced models (local vol, stochastic vol, jumps) are calibrated to reproduce BS implied vol surfaces.

### How to deliver it
List the assumptions in two groups: *dynamics* (GBM, constant vol and rates, no jumps) and *market* (frictionless, continuous trading, no arbitrage, shorting allowed). Then pick the three that fail most (constant vol, jumps/fat tails, continuous costless hedging), and close with "which is why traders use BS as a language: the smile is where the market corrects the model." That is the answer of someone who has thought about it.
deep.opt-015:
### Context / why they ask this
You must be able to write it cleanly and, more importantly, *read* it: which term is a probability, which is delta, why $d_1$ and $d_2$ differ by $\sigma\sqrt T$. Trading interviewers care about the interpretation; quant interviewers may ask you to derive it.

### Key concepts
- **$N(x)$**: probability that a standard normal is below $x$. $\varphi(x) = N'(x)$ the density.
- **$\sigma\sqrt T$**: total standard deviation of the log-return up to expiry ("vol times root time"). It is the natural unit of distance.
- **Discount factor** $e^{-rT}$: PV of 1 paid at $T$.
- **Forward** $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$.
- **Risk-neutral measure $\mathbb Q$**: the probability measure under which all assets grow at $r$ (minus dividends) on average; prices are discounted expectations under $\mathbb Q$.

### Intuition
A call pays $S_T - K$ when $S_T > K$. Split it into two digital-like pieces:
1. An **asset-or-nothing** claim: receive $S_T$ if $S_T>K$. Worth $Se^{-qT}N(d_1)$.
2. A **cash-or-nothing** claim: pay $K$ if $S_T>K$. Worth $Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$.
Why are the probabilities different? Because the asset-or-nothing pays *more* in the scenarios where $S_T$ is large, so it weights up-states more - measured under the "stock measure" (using the stock as numeraire), the probability of ending ITM is $N(d_1) > N(d_2)$.
$d_2$ itself is "how many standard deviations the forward is above the strike", with a small convexity correction: $d_2 = \frac{\ln(F/K)}{\sigma\sqrt T} - \frac12\sigma\sqrt T$.

### The maths
Under $\mathbb Q$: $S_T = S e^{(r-q-\frac12\sigma^2)T + \sigma\sqrt T Z}$, $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$.
$\mathbb Q(S_T > K) = \mathbb Q\left(Z > \frac{\ln(K/S) - (r-q-\frac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right) = N(d_2)$.
$\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[S_T\mathbf 1_{S_T>K}] = Se^{(r-q)T}N(d_1)$ (complete the square, or change numeraire).
So $C = e^{-rT}\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[(S_T-K)^+] = Se^{-qT}N(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$.
Put via parity: $P = C - Se^{-qT} + Ke^{-rT} = Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2) - Se^{-qT}N(-d_1)$ using $1-N(x) = N(-x)$.

### Worked example with numbers
$S=K=100$, $r=5\%$, $q=0$, $\sigma=20\%$, $T=1$.
$d_1 = \frac{0 + (0.05+0.02)}{0.2} = 0.35$, $d_2 = 0.15$.
$N(0.35) = 0.6368$, $N(0.15) = 0.5596$.
$C = 100\times 0.6368 - 95.12\times 0.5596 = 63.68 - 53.23 = 10.45$.
$P = C - S + Ke^{-rT} = 10.45 - 100 + 95.12 = 5.57$.
Delta of call 0.64, risk-neutral probability of exercise 56%.

### Common pitfalls
- Writing $d_2 = d_1 + \sigma\sqrt T$ (sign error), or forgetting the $\frac12\sigma^2$ term.
- Saying $N(d_1)$ is the probability of exercise. It is $N(d_2)$ (risk-neutral). $N(d_1)$ is delta.
- Forgetting $e^{-qT}$ on the spot term for dividend-paying underlyings.
- Saying $N(d_2)$ is the *real-world* probability: it uses the risk-neutral drift $r$, not the actual expected return.

### How to deliver it
Write it, then say: "call = PV of receiving the stock if ITM minus PV of paying the strike if ITM. $N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral probability of exercise, $N(d_1)$ is delta. $d_1$ and $d_2$ are separated by $\sigma\sqrt T$." Keep one example number ready: ATM, 20% vol, 1y, zero rates gives about 8% of spot.
deep.opt-016:
### Context / why they ask this
A favourite "do you really understand BS?" question. Traders often use delta as a probability; interviewers want to see that you know the approximation and its limits.

### Key concepts
- **Risk-neutral measure $\mathbb Q$** (money-market numeraire): prices = discounted expectations; all assets drift at $r - q$.
- **Stock measure $\mathbb Q^S$** (stock numeraire): prices divided by the stock price are martingales. Under $\mathbb Q^S$ the stock drifts at $r-q+\sigma^2$.
- **Numeraire**: the asset you use as unit of account. Changing it changes the probabilities but not the prices.
- **Digital (binary) call**: pays 1 if $S_T>K$, else 0.
- **Asset-or-nothing call**: pays $S_T$ if $S_T>K$.

### Intuition
A call = asset-or-nothing minus $K$ cash-or-nothing.
- The cash-or-nothing piece pays a fixed amount, so its value is just (discounted) probability of ITM: $e^{-rT}N(d_2)$.
- The asset-or-nothing piece pays $S_T$ - more in high states. Its value is $Se^{-qT}N(d_1)$. Think of $N(d_1)$ as "a probability of ITM where each scenario is weighted by how big the stock is in it". Since ITM scenarios are exactly the big-stock scenarios, the weighted probability is higher.
Delta: if you nudge $S$, the call changes by $N(d_1)$ times the change - the "probability" effect on the digital part and the "size" effect on the asset part combine exactly (the $\varphi(d_1)$ and $\varphi(d_2)$ terms cancel, a nice BS identity: $S\varphi(d_1) = Ke^{-rT}\varphi(d_2)$ when $q=0$).

### The maths
$\mathbb Q(S_T>K) = N(d_2)$, with $d_2 = \frac{\ln(F/K)-\frac12\sigma^2T}{\sigma\sqrt T}$.
$\mathbb Q^S(S_T>K) = N(d_1)$, with $d_1 = d_2 + \sigma\sqrt T$.
$\Delta_C = \partial C/\partial S = e^{-qT}N(d_1)$.
Gap: $N(d_1) - N(d_2) \approx \varphi(0)\sigma\sqrt T \approx 0.4\sigma\sqrt T$ near ATM. Interesting identity: the ATM (forward) call price is $e^{-rT}F[N(d_1)-N(d_2)] \approx 0.4\sigma\sqrt T\,S$ - the gap between the two probabilities *is* the ATM option price in units of the forward.

### Worked example with numbers
$S=K=100$, $r=q=0$, $\sigma=20\%$:
- $T=1$: $d_1 = 0.1$, $d_2=-0.1$. Delta $N(0.1)=0.54$, $\mathbb Q(\text{ITM}) = N(-0.1) = 0.46$. Gap 8 points.
- $T=1/12$: $d_1 = 0.029$, $N(d_1)=0.51$, $N(d_2)=0.49$. Gap 2 points - delta is a fine proxy.
- 5 years at 40% vol: $\sigma\sqrt T = 0.89$, $d_1 = 0.447$, $d_2=-0.447$: delta 0.67 vs probability 0.33 - delta badly overstates probability.
Note that the ATM-spot call probability of exercise is *below* 50% with zero rates: the lognormal median $Se^{-\frac12\sigma^2T}$ is below the mean $S$.

### Common pitfalls
- "N(d1) is the probability of exercise" - no.
- "The probability of exercise is 50% for an ATM option" - under zero rates it is $N(-\frac12\sigma\sqrt T)<50\%$.
- Treating risk-neutral probabilities as forecasts. If the stock has a positive risk premium, the real-world probability of finishing ITM is higher than $N(d_2)$.

### How to deliver it
"$N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral probability of exercise; $N(d_1)$ is delta, which is also a probability of exercise but under the stock measure, so it is a bit higher. Traders use delta as a rough probability, which works for short-dated options but breaks when $\sigma\sqrt T$ is large." Then give the 1-year ATM numbers: 54% vs 46%.
deep.opt-017:
### Context / why they ask this
The conceptual core of derivatives pricing. A typical follow-up: "Two stocks have the same vol but one has expected return 20% and the other 5%; which call is more expensive?" The answer "the same" surprises many candidates.

### Key concepts
- **Replication**: dynamic trading strategy reproducing the payoff.
- **Complete market**: every payoff can be replicated.
- **Risk-neutral measure $\mathbb Q$**: probability measure under which discounted asset prices are martingales (no expected excess return). Also called the equivalent martingale measure.
- **Real-world (physical) measure $\mathbb P$**: actual probabilities, with risk premia.
- **Fundamental theorem of asset pricing**: no arbitrage $\iff$ existence of $\mathbb Q$; completeness $\iff$ $\mathbb Q$ unique.
- **Girsanov theorem**: changing from $\mathbb P$ to $\mathbb Q$ changes the drift of the Brownian motion but not its volatility.

### Intuition
One-period coin toss: stock at 100 goes to 120 or 80. A call struck at 100 pays 20 or 0. Buy 0.5 shares and borrow 40: in the up state 60 - 40 = 20, in the down state 40 - 40 = 0. Exactly the call. Cost today: 50 - 40 = 10. Notice we **never used the probability** of up vs down. If you believe up is 90% likely, you still cannot sell this call for more than 10 - someone would buy it and short the replicating portfolio.
The probability that *does* make "discounted expectation = price" true is $p=0.5$ here (with zero rates) - that is the risk-neutral probability. It is backed out from the prices, not assumed.
Why does the drift not matter? Because the stock's price today already reflects the market's expected return and risk premium. The option is priced *relative* to the stock.

### The maths
Real world: $dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW^{\mathbb P}$. Replication (delta hedging) leads to the BS PDE where only $r$ and $\sigma$ appear. Feynman-Kac gives
$$V_0 = e^{-rT}\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[\text{payoff}(S_T)], \qquad dS = (r-q)S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW^{\mathbb Q}.$$
Girsanov: $dW^{\mathbb Q} = dW^{\mathbb P} + \frac{\mu - r}{\sigma}dt$, where $\frac{\mu-r}{\sigma}$ is the **market price of risk** (Sharpe ratio). Volatility is unchanged, which is why it is the only stochastic input that matters.

### Worked example with numbers
Binomial with rate: $S=100$, up 120, down 80, one period, gross rate $1.05$.
Risk-neutral $p = \frac{1.05\times100 - 80}{120-80} = \frac{25}{40} = 0.625$.
Call $K=100$: $\frac{0.625\times 20 + 0.375\times 0}{1.05} = 11.90$.
Replication check: $\Delta = \frac{20-0}{120-80}=0.5$; bond $= \frac{0 - 0.5\times 80}{1.05} = -38.10$; cost $= 50 - 38.10 = 11.90$. Same.
Whether the real probability of up is 30% or 90% changes nothing.

### Common pitfalls
- "Risk-neutral pricing assumes investors are risk-neutral" - no, it is a change of measure that is valid for any risk preferences because of replication.
- "Risk-neutral probabilities are market forecasts" - they mix probabilities and risk aversion (e.g. OTM equity puts are expensive because crashes happen in bad times, not only because they are likely).
- Forgetting it requires replication/completeness: with unhedgeable risks (jumps, stochastic vol) $\mathbb Q$ is not unique and the price involves a choice of risk premium (calibrated to market prices).

### How to deliver it
Start with the one-step replication example (quick, convincing), conclude "the probability never entered", then generalise: "we can price as if everything grows at $r$ and discount at $r$; the stock's drift is already in its spot price." End with the key takeaway: the only thing that matters for an option is volatility, which is why options are a vol product.
deep.opt-018:
### Context / why they ask this
Quant and technical trading interviews. With your background you should be able to do this on a whiteboard in two minutes. The payoff is the interpretation: the PDE is a statement that **theta pays for gamma**.

### Key concepts
- **Itô's lemma**: for $f(S,t)$ with $dS = a\,dt + b\,dW$: $df = (f_t + a f_S + \frac12 b^2 f_{SS})dt + b f_S\,dW$. The extra $\frac12 b^2 f_{SS}$ term comes from $(dW)^2 = dt$.
- **Self-financing portfolio**: changes in value come only from asset price changes, not from injecting cash.
- **Delta ($V_S$), gamma ($V_{SS}$), theta ($V_t$)**.
- **Feynman-Kac**: links the PDE to an expectation, $V = e^{-r(T-t)}\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[\text{payoff}]$.

### Intuition
By holding $\Delta$ shares short against the option you remove the first-order exposure to the stock's direction. What remains is the second-order term: the option's convexity earns $\frac12\Gamma (dS)^2 = \frac12\Gamma\sigma^2S^2dt$ on average from moves, and the option loses $\Theta\,dt$ from time passing. If the hedged portfolio earned more than the risk-free rate with no risk, everyone would do it. So the equation says: **time decay exactly offsets expected convexity gains (plus financing)**.

### The maths
$\Pi = V - \Delta S$ (with dividends, short $\Delta$ shares pays $q\Delta S\,dt$ in dividends).
$d\Pi = dV - \Delta\,dS - q\Delta S\,dt$
$= \left(V_t + \mu S V_S + \tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS}\right)dt + \sigma S V_S\,dW - \Delta(\mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW) - q\Delta S\,dt$.
With $\Delta = V_S$: $d\Pi = (V_t + \frac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS} - qSV_S)\,dt$.
Set $d\Pi = r\Pi\,dt = r(V - SV_S)dt$:
$$V_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS} + (r-q)SV_S - rV = 0.$$
Terminal condition $V(S,T) = (S-K)^+$. Change variables ($x=\ln S$, $\tau = T-t$) to reduce to the heat equation; solution is the BS formula.
Check with the ATM numbers ($r=q=0$, $S=100$, $\sigma=20\%$, $T=1$): $\Gamma = 0.0198$, so $\frac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma = 0.5\times0.04\times10{,}000\times0.0198 = 3.96$, and BS theta $=-3.97$ per year. They cancel.

### Worked example
Discrete version to make it tangible: you own a call with $\Gamma = 0.02$, stock 100, daily vol $1.26\%$ (20% annual / $\sqrt{252}$). Expected daily gamma gain $\frac12\times0.02\times(1.26)^2 = 0.0159$. BS theta per trading day $= 3.97/252 = 0.0158$. Balanced, as the PDE says.

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting the Itô term (writing $dV = V_t dt + V_S dS$) - then gamma disappears and so does all option value.
- Treating $\Delta$ as constant when computing $d\Pi$: it is held fixed over $dt$ (self-financing), which is legitimate to first order.
- Losing track of dividends.

### How to deliver it
Write the four lines (Itô, portfolio, choose delta, no-arbitrage) and box the PDE. Then say: "In Greek form it is $\Theta + \frac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma + rS\Delta - rV = 0$; with zero rates, theta equals minus one-half sigma squared S squared gamma - long gamma costs theta." That bridges the maths to the trading desk.

See also qnt-015 (same question, different angle).
deep.opt-019:
### Context / why they ask this
S&T interviewers love mental maths. This checks that you can put a number on an option instantly, which a trader or salesperson does all day ("how much is a 3-month ATM put on the CAC? - about 3.2-3.6% at 16-18 vol"). It also tests understanding of the $\sqrt T$ scaling.

### Key concepts
- **ATM forward**: strike = forward, where call = put.
- **$\sigma\sqrt T$**: standard deviation of the return to expiry.
- **Straddle**: long call + long put, same strike; payoff $|S_T - K|$.
- **Premium in % of spot**: how options are often quoted in equity sales ("the 1y ATM put costs 7%").

### Intuition
An ATM option pays roughly the average positive part of the move. If the return is $\sigma\sqrt T\,Z$ with $Z$ normal, then $\mathbb E[(\sigma\sqrt T Z)^+] = \sigma\sqrt T\,\mathbb E[Z^+] = \sigma\sqrt T/\sqrt{2\pi}$. So the call is about 40% of one standard-deviation move. The straddle captures both sides: 80% of one standard deviation - the mean absolute deviation.
Time enters as $\sqrt T$: four times the maturity only doubles the price. That is why short-dated options are relatively expensive per day (theta accelerates near expiry).

### The maths
Forward form with $F=K$: $C = e^{-rT}F[N(\frac12\sigma\sqrt T) - N(-\frac12\sigma\sqrt T)] = e^{-rT}F[2N(\frac12\sigma\sqrt T) - 1]$.
Taylor: $2N(x) - 1 \approx 2\varphi(0)x = \frac{2x}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ for small $x$. With $x = \frac12\sigma\sqrt T$:
$$C \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sigma\sqrt T\,F \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,F.$$
Accuracy: excellent for $\sigma\sqrt T$ up to about 0.5; above that it overestimates slightly (cubic term negative).

### Worked example with numbers
| Case | Approx | Exact BS ($r=q=0$) |
|---|---|---|
| 1y, 20% vol | 8.0 | 7.97 |
| 3m, 20% vol | 4.0 | 3.99 |
| 1m, 20% vol | $0.4\times 20\times 0.289 = 2.31$ | 2.30 |
| 1y, 40% vol | 16.0 | 15.85 |
| 5y, 18% vol, $r=q$ | $0.4\times 18\times 2.236 = 16.1$, times $e^{-rT}$ at 3% $=0.861$: 13.9 | 13.73 |

Straddle 3m 20% vol: about 8, so the stock must move about 8% either way for the buyer to break even.
Daily scaling: 1 day with $\sqrt{1/252} = 1/15.87 \approx 1/16$: an ATM 1-day option at 20% vol is worth about $0.4\times 20/16 = 0.5\%$.

### Common pitfalls
- Scaling linearly in time (a 3-month option is not a quarter of a 1-year).
- Forgetting the rates adjustment for ATM-spot options with large rates or long maturities.
- Applying 0.4 to OTM options - it is only for ATM.

### How to deliver it
Say the formula first, then the number: "0.4 times sigma root T times spot: 0.4 x 0.2 x 1 x 100 = 8; for 3 months half of that, 4." Mention the straddle = 0.8 rule and that it is the expected absolute move. Speed and structure matter more than decimals.
deep.opt-020:
### Context / why they ask this
Probably the most common technical option question for interns. It shows you understand replication, risk-neutral probabilities and delta without heavy maths. Expect variations: different numbers, a put, a rate, two steps, or "what if the real probability of going up is 90%?".

### Key concepts
- **Binomial model**: in each period the price goes up by factor $u$ or down by $d$.
- **Replicating portfolio**: $\Delta$ shares + $B$ in cash that reproduces the payoff in every state.
- **Hedge ratio / delta**: $\Delta = \frac{V_u - V_d}{S_u - S_d}$, the discrete version of $\partial V/\partial S$.
- **Risk-neutral probability**: $p = \frac{(1+r)S_0 - S_d}{S_u - S_d}$ (or with $e^{r\Delta t}$), which makes the discounted stock a martingale.
- **No-arbitrage condition**: $S_d < (1+r)S_0 < S_u$, i.e. $0<p<1$.

### Intuition
With two possible states and two instruments (stock, cash), you can match any payoff exactly: two equations, two unknowns. Once you can build the option from stock and cash, its price is forced. The risk-neutral probability is just the weights that price the stock correctly; using the same weights on the option gives the same answer as replication, because the option *is* a combination of stock and cash.
Delta = "change in option value / change in stock value" between the two states: $20/40 = 0.5$.

### The maths
General one-step:
$$\Delta = \frac{V_u - V_d}{S_u - S_d}, \quad B = \frac{V_d S_u - V_u S_d}{(S_u - S_d)(1+r)}, \quad V_0 = \Delta S_0 + B = \frac{pV_u + (1-p)V_d}{1+r}.$$
With $p = \frac{(1+r)S_0 - S_d}{S_u - S_d}$.
If $(1+r)S_0 \ge S_u$ (the bond beats the stock in every state), there is an arbitrage: short the stock, invest in cash.

### Worked example with numbers
Base case ($r=0$): call $K=100$ = 10, $\Delta = 0.5$, borrow 40.
Put $K=100$: payoffs 0 (up) and 20 (down). $\Delta = \frac{0-20}{40} = -0.5$, $B = 20 + 0.5\times 80 = 60$. Cost: $-50 + 60 = 10$. Parity check: $C - P = 0 = S - K$. OK.
With $r=5\%$: $p = (105-80)/40 = 0.625$; call $= 0.625\times 20/1.05 = 11.90$; put $= 0.375\times 20/1.05 = 7.14$. Parity: $11.90 - 7.14 = 4.76 = 100 - 100/1.05$. OK.
If someone offers the call at 12 (with $r=0$), sell it, buy 0.5 shares and borrow 40: you pocket 2 today and are perfectly hedged.

### Common pitfalls
- Using the "real" probability (e.g. 60% up) to compute an expected payoff: that gives a wrong price.
- Forgetting to discount with non-zero rates.
- Mixing up $\Delta$ sign for the put.

### How to deliver it
Do replication first (it is the *reason*), then risk-neutral (the *shortcut*), and state explicitly that the real-world probability is irrelevant. Finish by noting that iterating this over many small steps converges to Black-Scholes (Cox-Ross-Rubinstein). Doing both methods in under two minutes is exactly what they want.
deep.opt-021:
### Context / why they ask this
Trees are the standard tool for American options and the most intuitive numerical method. Showing the max(exercise, continuation) step proves you understand optimal early exercise. This often follows the one-step question.

### Key concepts
- **Recombining tree**: up-then-down reaches the same node as down-then-up (because $ud$ = constant), so $n$ steps give $n+1$ final nodes rather than $2^n$.
- **Backward induction**: price at maturity first, then step back.
- **Continuation value**: value of keeping the option alive one more step.
- **Exercise boundary**: the set of nodes where exercising is optimal.
- **CRR parametrisation**: $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, $d = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$ matches the variance of GBM; converges to BS as $\Delta t\to0$.

### Intuition
At each node, the holder of an American put asks: "Do I take $K - S$ now, or keep the option?" Exercising early is attractive when the put is deep ITM: the remaining optionality (chance of going even lower) is small, while receiving $K$ now instead of later earns interest. The tree makes this trade-off explicit at every node.

### The maths
Step size $\Delta t = T/n$. Node $(i,j)$: $S_{i,j} = S_0u^jd^{i-j}$.
Terminal: $V_{n,j} = (K - S_{n,j})^+$.
Rollback: $V_{i,j} = \max\left((K-S_{i,j})^+, \; e^{-r\Delta t}[pV_{i+1,j+1} + (1-p)V_{i+1,j}]\right)$.
Delta at the root: $\Delta \approx \frac{V_{1,1} - V_{1,0}}{S_{1,1} - S_{1,0}}$. Gamma from the second step.

### Worked example with numbers
$S_0=100$, $u=1.1$, $d=0.9$, gross interest 1.02 per step, $K=100$ put, 2 steps.
$p = \frac{1.02 - 0.9}{1.1 - 0.9} = 0.6$.
Terminal stock: 121, 99, 81. Put payoffs: 0, 1, 19.
Step 1:
- Up node (110): continuation $= \frac{0.6\times0 + 0.4\times1}{1.02} = 0.392$; exercise $= 0$. Value 0.392.
- Down node (90): continuation $= \frac{0.6\times1 + 0.4\times19}{1.02} = \frac{8.2}{1.02} = 8.04$; exercise $= 10$. **Exercise**: value 10.
Root:
- European: $\frac{0.6\times0.392 + 0.4\times8.04}{1.02} = \frac{0.235 + 3.216}{1.02} = 3.38$.
- American: $\frac{0.6\times0.392 + 0.4\times10}{1.02} = \frac{4.235}{1.02} = 4.15$; exercise at root $=0$. Value **4.15**.
The call (European = American, no dividends): payoffs 21, 0, 0. Up node: $0.6\times21/1.02 = 12.35$ (vs exercise 10 - never exercise). Root: $0.6\times12.35/1.02 = 7.27$.

### Common pitfalls
- Only checking early exercise at maturity, or at the root.
- Using the real-world probability instead of $p$.
- Non-recombining trees (exponential blow-up) when the parametrisation is inconsistent.
- Discrete dividends make trees non-recombining if modelled as cash amounts; common fix: model the stock minus PV of dividends.

### How to deliver it
Describe the algorithm in three sentences (build, payoffs, roll back with max), then run the two-step example, highlighting the node where exercise beats continuation. Mention convergence to BS and that the same backward induction handles Bermudans (check exercise only on allowed dates).
deep.opt-022:
### Context / why they ask this
Shows you know the "forward-based" view of options, which is how traders actually think in rates, commodities and FX. On a rates desk, "Black vol" (lognormal) vs "normal vol" (Bachelier) is daily vocabulary.

### Key concepts
- **Futures / forward price $F$**: the price agreed today for delivery at a future date. A futures contract is exchange-traded and marked-to-market daily.
- **Caplet / floorlet**: a call / put on a forward interest rate (e.g. 3-month Euribor) over one period. A **cap** is a strip of caplets; a borrower buys a cap to limit floating-rate costs.
- **Swaption**: an option to enter a swap at a fixed rate $K$ (payer swaption = right to pay fixed = call on the swap rate).
- **Convenience yield**: implicit benefit of holding a physical commodity; embedded in commodity forwards.
- **Annuity / PVBP**: for swaptions, the discounting factor that multiplies the Black formula instead of $e^{-rT}$.

### Intuition
Any European option on $S_T$ is really an option on $F_{0,T}$, since at expiry $F_{T,T} = S_T$. So instead of modelling spot plus all the carry (rates, dividends, storage), take the forward as the underlying directly. The forward has zero drift in the appropriate (forward) measure, so the formula is simpler: no $r - q$ in $d_1$.
For interest rates, the rate itself is the "asset": a caplet pays $N\tau(L_T - K)^+$ at the end of the period, and Black treats the forward Libor/Euribor $L$ as lognormal.

### The maths
Under the $T$-forward measure, $dF = \sigma F\,dW$ (martingale). Then
$$C = P(0,T)\,[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)], \quad d_1 = \frac{\ln(F/K) + \frac12\sigma^2T}{\sigma\sqrt T}, \; d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt T,$$
where $P(0,T)$ is the discount factor to the payment date.
Consistency with BS: plug $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$ and you recover BS exactly.
Swaption (payer): $V = A(0)\,[S_0 N(d_1) - K N(d_2)]$ with $A(0) = \sum_i \tau_i P(0,t_i)$ the annuity and $S_0$ the forward swap rate.
Bachelier (normal) variant, used since rates went negative: $C = P(0,T)[(F-K)N(d) + \sigma_N\sqrt T\,\varphi(d)]$, $d = \frac{F-K}{\sigma_N\sqrt T}$.

### Worked example with numbers
Brent futures at 80, 6-month call struck at 85, Black vol 30%, $r=4\%$.
$\sigma\sqrt T = 0.3\times0.707 = 0.212$. $\ln(80/85) = -0.0606$.
$d_1 = (-0.0606 + 0.0225)/0.212 = -0.180$; $d_2 = -0.392$.
$N(d_1) = 0.429$, $N(d_2) = 0.348$.
$C = e^{-0.02}[80\times0.429 - 85\times0.348] = 0.980\times[34.3 - 29.6] = 0.980\times4.74 \approx 4.65$ per barrel.
Sanity check with the ATM rule: ATM would be $0.4\times0.3\times0.707\times80 \approx 6.8$; 85 is OTM so 4.6 is sensible.

### Common pitfalls
- Adding a carry term inside $d_1$ when the underlying is already a forward.
- Discounting to the wrong date (use the payment date of the option payoff).
- For rates: lognormal Black cannot handle negative rates - hence the shift to normal (Bachelier) vols or shifted-lognormal models in EUR rates after 2014.

### How to deliver it
"Black-76 is Black-Scholes written on the forward: the forward has no drift, so the formula is discounted $FN(d_1) - KN(d_2)$. It is the standard for options on futures, caps/floors and swaptions." Then mention the normal-vol convention for rates as a sign of market awareness.
deep.opt-023:
### Context / why they ask this
FX options are one of the most liquid option markets and a big client business (corporate hedging). French banks have large FX sales teams. They test that you can adapt BS and that you know the quoting conventions.

### Key concepts
- **Currency pair notation**: EURUSD = 1.10 means 1 EUR costs 1.10 USD. EUR is the **base / foreign** currency, USD the **quote / domestic** currency.
- **Covered interest parity**: $F = S e^{(r_d - r_f)T}$. The currency with the higher rate trades at a forward discount.
- **Pips**: smallest quote increment, e.g. 0.0001 in EURUSD.
- **Risk reversal (RR)**: $\sigma_{25\Delta\,call} - \sigma_{25\Delta\,put}$; measures skew.
- **Butterfly (BF)**: $\frac12(\sigma_{25\Delta C} + \sigma_{25\Delta P}) - \sigma_{ATM}$; measures smile curvature.
- **ATM DNS**: delta-neutral straddle strike, the standard ATM definition in FX.

### Intuition
To replicate a EUR call you hold EUR, which earn the EUR rate - just like holding a stock earns dividends. So $r_f$ enters exactly where $q$ was. The symmetry is natural: the right to buy 1m EUR at 1.10 is the same as the right to sell 1.1m USD at 1/1.10 EUR per USD. A corporate importer (needs USD) and an exporter (receives USD) are on opposite sides of the same product.
Quoting by delta instead of strike makes quotes comparable as spot moves: "25-delta" always means "moderately OTM" whatever the spot level.

### The maths
$$C = e^{-r_dT}[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)], \quad F = Se^{(r_d - r_f)T}.$$
Put-call parity: $C - P = Se^{-r_fT} - Ke^{-r_dT}$.
Recovering smile points from the quotes (simplified): $\sigma_{25C} = \sigma_{ATM} + BF + \frac12 RR$, $\sigma_{25P} = \sigma_{ATM} + BF - \frac12 RR$.

### Worked example with numbers
EURUSD spot 1.10, $r_{USD} = 4\%$, $r_{EUR}=2\%$ (illustrative levels), 6 months. Forward $= 1.10\,e^{0.01} = 1.1111$.
Market: ATM 7.0%, 25d RR $-0.5\%$, 25d BF $0.25\%$.
Then $\sigma_{25C} = 7.0 + 0.25 - 0.25 = 7.0\%$ and $\sigma_{25P} = 7.0 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 7.5\%$: EUR puts are more expensive than EUR calls - the market pays more for protection against a EUR fall.
ATM 6m option price $\approx 0.4\times0.07\times\sqrt{0.5}\approx 1.98\%$ of notional, so about EUR 198k on EUR 10m.

### Common pitfalls
- Inverting domestic and foreign rates.
- Forgetting that "call" is ambiguous in FX: always say "EUR call / USD put".
- Ignoring premium currency: if the premium is paid in the foreign currency, the delta hedge must include it (premium-adjusted delta), common in USDJPY and EM pairs.

### How to deliver it
"Garman-Kohlhagen: Black-Scholes with the foreign rate as dividend yield. Every FX option is a call on one currency and a put on the other. Vols are quoted in delta terms: ATM, 25-delta risk reversal for skew, butterfly for curvature." Add a client use: a French exporter buying EUR calls/USD puts to protect against USD weakness.
deep.opt-024:
### Context / why they ask this
Equity derivatives desks trade index options all day: flow (clients hedging portfolios), exotic hedging (structured products on indices) and vol trading. Knowing the correlation and skew features shows real market understanding.

### Key concepts
- **Cash settlement**: payoff paid in cash based on the index settlement level.
- **Contract multiplier**: e.g. Euro Stoxx 50 options: EUR 10 per index point; SPX: USD 100 per point.
- **Index dividend yield**: aggregated dividends of constituents; traded via dividend futures (e.g. Euro Stoxx 50 dividend futures).
- **Implied correlation**: the average pairwise correlation implied by index vol and component vols.
- **Dispersion trade**: sell index vol, buy single-stock vol (or vice versa) to trade correlation.
- **Skew**: implied vol of OTM puts higher than ATM.

### Intuition
An index is a basket. Its variance $\sigma_I^2 = \sum_i\sum_j w_iw_j\rho_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j$. Unless all correlations are 1, the index is less volatile than its components - diversification. In a crisis, correlations spike ("everything goes down together"), so index vol rises more than proportionally and OTM index puts pay off massively. Knowing this, index puts are the ultimate portfolio insurance - demand pushes up their implied vol: steep skew.
Selling index vol and buying single-stock vol = being long **dispersion** (short correlation): you win if stocks move a lot individually but offset each other.

### The maths
Index variance: $\sigma_I^2 = \sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2 + \sum_{i\ne j}w_iw_j\rho_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j$.
Implied (average) correlation, assuming a single $\rho$:
$$\rho_{impl} = \frac{\sigma_I^2 - \sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i\ne j} w_iw_j\sigma_i\sigma_j}.$$
Rough rule: $\rho \approx \sigma_I^2 / (\sum_i w_i\sigma_i)^2$ for many constituents.
Forward: $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$ where $q$ is the index dividend yield (or $S - PV(\text{divs})$ with discrete dividends).

### Worked example with numbers
Suppose the average single-stock implied vol in the Euro Stoxx 50 is 25% and index vol is 16%. Rough implied correlation $\approx (0.16/0.25)^2 = 0.41$. If a crash makes correlation go to 0.8, index vol with the same stock vols would be about $0.25\times\sqrt{0.8} = 22\%$ even before stock vols rise.
Contract: 1 Euro Stoxx 50 put, strike 4,500, index at 4,800 (illustrative), 3 months, 18% vol: ATM would cost about $0.4\times0.18\times0.5\times4800 = 173$ points; the 6% OTM put perhaps 70-80 points, i.e. EUR 700-800 per contract.

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting dividends in the forward (for long-dated index options they are a major driver).
- Assuming index vol = average stock vol.
- Assuming American exercise for SPX/Euro Stoxx options (they are European).

### How to deliver it
Structure: "contract features (European, cash-settled), pricing (forward with dividends), vol features (lower vol due to correlation, steeper skew due to crash correlation and hedging demand), uses (portfolio hedging, structured products, VIX)." Then drop the dispersion concept as a bonus.
deep.opt-025:
### Context / why they ask this
It checks whether you understand the market's language. On a flow vol desk everything is in vol: RFQs, quotes, P&L explanations ("we lost 2 vols on the front end"). Salespeople translate vol into price for clients.

### Key concepts
- **Implied volatility**: the $\sigma$ that makes the model price match the market price; solved numerically (Newton's method using vega).
- **Vol point**: 1% of volatility (e.g. from 20% to 21%).
- **Bid/offer in vol**: "23.5/24.5" means the market maker buys at 23.5 vol and sells at 24.5 vol.
- **Premium**: the cash price, in currency or in % of notional.
- **Delta exchange / "delta-neutral quote"**: vol quotes are usually for a delta-hedged option, with the hedge stock traded at a reference spot at the same time, so the quote is not sensitive to spot moves.

### Intuition
Think of it like quoting bonds in yield rather than price. A bond price depends on coupon and maturity; yield makes bonds comparable. Implied vol is the "yield" of an option. And since BS is a monotonic mapping (vega > 0), each price corresponds to exactly one vol, so nothing is lost.
Stability: if the stock jumps 2%, the call price might move 10% but the implied vol may not move at all, so the quote is still valid. Combined with a delta exchange (the client also trades the delta hedge at an agreed spot reference), the trade is then about volatility only.

### The maths
Implied vol $\sigma_{impl}$ solves $C_{BS}(S,K,T,r,q,\sigma_{impl}) = C_{mkt}$. Because $\partial C/\partial \sigma = \mathcal V > 0$, the solution is unique. Newton iteration: $\sigma_{n+1} = \sigma_n - \frac{C_{BS}(\sigma_n) - C_{mkt}}{\mathcal V(\sigma_n)}$.
Price change from a vol change: $\Delta C \approx \mathcal V\,\Delta\sigma$. ATM: $\mathcal V\approx0.4S\sqrt T$ per unit vol.

### Worked example with numbers
Two options on a stock at 100: a 1-month ATM call at 2.30 and a 1-year ATM call at 7.97. Which is more expensive? Both correspond to 20% implied vol - equally "priced". Now if the 1-month were 2.88, its implied vol would be about 25%: now the short-dated one is relatively expensive (vega 0.115 per point: $(2.88-2.30)/0.115 \approx 5$ vol points).
Sales example: a client wants a 1y 100% call on 10m notional; the desk quotes 20.5 vol offer; at vega about 0.40% per vol point, 20.5 vol corresponds to about $7.97\% + 0.5\times0.40\% = 8.17\%$ premium, i.e. 817k EUR.

### Common pitfalls
- Thinking implied vol is a forecast only: it also embeds risk premia and supply/demand.
- Forgetting that the price-vol mapping depends on the model conventions (dividends, rates, day counts), which must be agreed.

### How to deliver it
Three reasons: comparability (normalises strike/maturity/spot), stability (quotes don't go stale as spot moves, especially with a delta exchange), and it isolates the only real unknown. Mention the bond-yield analogy. Short and confident.
deep.opt-026:
### Context / why they ask this
Quant and structuring roles, sometimes trading. With an applied-maths engineering degree you are expected to know the trade-offs. Keep it practical: which method for which product.

### Key concepts
- **Curse of dimensionality**: grid methods need $M^d$ points for $d$ underlyings; infeasible above about 3.
- **Monte Carlo error**: standard error $\sigma_{payoff}/\sqrt N$; to halve the error, quadruple the paths.
- **Variance reduction**: antithetic variates, control variates (e.g. use the vanilla with known price), importance sampling, quasi-random (Sobol) sequences.
- **Longstaff-Schwartz**: estimate the continuation value by regressing discounted future cash flows on basis functions of the current state; used for American/Bermudan features in MC.
- **Bump-and-revalue**: compute Greeks by re-pricing with shifted inputs; with MC use the same random numbers (common random numbers) to reduce noise.

### Intuition
- Tree/PDE go **backward** in time from the payoff: perfect for "what is it worth at each state if I behave optimally from here", i.e. early exercise.
- MC goes **forward**: simulate paths, compute payoff along each path, average. Perfect for "the payoff depends on the whole path of several assets", terrible for "what should I do at this node".
- Discontinuous payoffs (digitals, barriers) are hard for both: grids need nodes aligned on the barrier; MC Greeks become very noisy (use smoothing or pathwise/likelihood-ratio methods).

### The maths
MC estimator: $\hat V = e^{-rT}\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N h(S^{(k)})$, with $S^{(k)}$ simulated under $\mathbb Q$, e.g. $S_{t+\Delta t} = S_te^{(r-q-\frac12\sigma^2)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}Z}$. 95% CI: $\hat V \pm 1.96\,\hat s/\sqrt N$.
Crank-Nicolson for the BS PDE: second-order in time and space, unconditionally stable (but may oscillate with non-smooth payoffs - use a few implicit steps first, "Rannacher smoothing").
Correlated assets in MC: Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix, $Z = LW$ with $LL^\top = \Sigma$.

### Worked example
A 5-year autocallable on the worst of Euro Stoxx 50, S&P 500 and Nikkei, with annual autocall observations and a daily-monitored 60% down-and-in barrier: three correlated underlyings, path-dependent -> Monte Carlo (e.g. 100k-1m paths, local-stochastic vol). Pricing error with $N=100{,}000$ and payoff standard deviation 30% of notional: $0.30/\sqrt{100{,}000} \approx 0.095\%$ of notional - acceptable for pricing, too noisy for gamma, hence variance reduction and careful Greek methods.
An American put on a single stock -> tree or PDE, sub-second.

### Common pitfalls
- Using MC for a simple American put (wasteful) or a PDE for a 5-asset basket (impossible).
- Not using common random numbers when bumping for Greeks.
- Forgetting discretisation bias for continuously monitored barriers in MC (correct with Brownian bridge or the Broadie-Glasserman-Kou shift).

### How to deliver it
