### Context / why they ask this
Pitching a steepener is easy; executing it is what a trader is paid for. This question tests three things: that you size curve trades in **DV01**, not notional; that you know how a **bond future's** risk is measured; and that you know what is left after the hedge. It is very current: on 30 September 2026 the 2-year was about 4.88-4.90% and the 10-year about 5.29%, so 2s10s was about +41bp (FRED T10Y2Y), after +32bp on 28 September. The long end keeps rising on term premium while the 2-year is held down by fading October hike odds: a textbook **bear steepener** (all yields up, long ones more).

### Key concepts
- **2s10s**: 10-year yield minus 2-year yield. **Steepener** = position that gains if it widens.
- **DV01**: P&L for a 1bp fall in yield. **DV01-neutral** = both legs have the same DV01, so only the spread matters.
- **Treasury futures (CBOT)**: TU (2-year, USD 200k face), FV (5-year), TY (10-year note, USD 100k), US (bond), UB (ultra bond). The seller delivers any eligible bond; the cheapest one is the **cheapest-to-deliver (CTD)**.
- **Conversion factor (CF)**: the price of each deliverable bond at a 6% yield, divided by 100; it scales the futures price for each bond.
- **Futures DV01**: $\text{DV01}_{fut} \approx \text{DV01}_{CTD}/\text{CF}$, per contract.

### Intuition
A future behaves like a forward on its CTD. Because yields are below 6%, the CTD tends to be the shortest-duration deliverable bond, and the CF is below 1, so the futures DV01 is a bit **larger** than the CTD's. A 2-year contract has a small DV01 per unit of notional but twice the notional, so you need about 1.5 TU per TY.

### The maths (python-checked, illustrative CTDs)
Using a 4.00% CTD of 1.9 years at 4.85% for TU and a 4.25% CTD of 6.6 years at 5.10% for TY (semiannual coupons):
| | CF | CTD price | CTD DV01 per contract | Futures DV01 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TU (200k) | 0.963 | 98.40 | 37.3 | **about 38.7** |
| TY (100k) | 0.907 | 95.35 | 53.2 | **about 58.7** |

Number of contracts for 100k DV01 per leg:
$$N_{TU} = \frac{100{,}000}{38.7} \approx 2{,}584, \qquad N_{TY} = \frac{100{,}000}{58.7} \approx 1{,}704$$
P&L: $\Delta \text{P\&L} \approx 100{,}000 \times \Delta(\text{2s10s in bp})$. A move from +41 to +51bp gives about **USD +1.0m**; to +31bp, about **USD -1.0m**.
**Beta-weighting**: when the Fed drives the move, the 2-year can move more than the 10-year. Some desks weight the 2-year leg by a regression beta (for example 0.8 of the 10y DV01) so the trade is neutral to the typical move, not to a parallel one. Say which one you do.

### Worked example: a bear steepening day
Yields rise 6bp in 2-year and 14bp in 10-year (2s10s +8bp). TU leg (long): $-6 \times 100\text{k} = -0.6$m. TY leg (short): $+14 \times 100\text{k} = +1.4$m. Net **+0.8m**, exactly $8 \times 100$k.

### What can go wrong
- **CTD switch**: if yields move a lot, another bond becomes cheapest; the future's DV01 jumps and the hedge ratio drifts. Recompute daily.
- **Futures basis**: each future can richen or cheapen versus cash, for example when hedge funds unwind the Treasury basis trade.
- **Roll**: December contracts must be rolled to March in late November; the calendar spread can move against you.
- **Carry**: unlike cash, futures embed carry in the price, but a curve steepener built in cash would typically have slightly negative carry and roll on a positively sloped curve; that cost shows up in the futures prices too.
- **Margin**: variation margin is paid daily, which a big adverse move turns into a funding need.

### What I'd say on the desk
"I'd do the 2s10s steepener in futures: long about 2,580 TU, short about 1,700 TY, 100k DV01 per leg, checked against the screen DV01s. Entry +41, target +60, stop +30, so roughly 1.9m upside for 1.1m risk. Catalysts: payrolls on 2 October, the 10- and 30-year auctions, the 28 October FOMC. The risk is a flight to quality that bull flattens the curve, or a hawkish Fed surprise that lifts the 2-year."

### How to deliver it
Direction (buy short, sell long), sizing formula, numbers, then the three residual risks (CTD, basis, roll). Link to the cash version (rfc-021), the pitch (mkt-610) and the conditional version with options (rfc-741).
deep.rfc-741:
### Context / why they ask this
Structurers and options traders love this question because it shows that you think in **scenarios**, not just direction. In September 2026 the US curve bear steepens (10-year about 5.29%, 2s10s about +41bp on 30 September), but a candidate who simply says "steepener" is exposed to the classic trap: in a big risk-off rally the curve can also steepen (bull steepener), and in a hawkish Fed surprise it flattens. A conditional trade lets you choose **which** steepening you own.

### Key concepts
- **Swaption**: an option to enter a swap at a fixed strike. A **payer swaption** gives the right to **pay** fixed: it gains when rates rise. A **receiver** gains when rates fall.
- **1y10y**: expiry in 1 year, on a 10-year swap starting then. The **forward swap rate** is the strike of an at-the-money-forward (ATMF) option.
- **Normal (bp) volatility** $\sigma_N$: standard deviation of the rate change in basis points per year (Bachelier model), the standard quote in rates.
- **Annuity / DV01**: the value of 1bp running over the life of the underlying swap; option premiums are often quoted in "bp running" times this annuity.
- **Conditional steepener**: long a payer on the long tenor, short a payer on the short tenor (bear version), or long a receiver on the short tenor, short a receiver on the long tenor (bull version).

### Intuition
At expiry, a payer is worth $\max(\Delta F, 0)$ times its DV01, where $\Delta F$ is the move of its forward rate. Long a 10y payer and short a 2y payer, with the same DV01:
- rates **down**: both are out of the money, payoff 0, I keep the net premium;
- rates **up**: both are in the money, payoff $\Delta F_{10} - \Delta F_{2}$, the change of the forward slope: a steepener.
So the curve exposure is "switched on" only in a sell-off.

### The maths
ATMF premium under Bachelier, in bp of running DV01:
$$\text{Prem} = \sigma_N \sqrt{T}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.399\,\sigma_N\sqrt{T}$$
With illustrative $\sigma_N$ of 110bp for 1y10y and 120bp for 1y2y (I have not verified today's levels; check the screen):
$$0.399 \times 110 \approx 43.9\text{bp}, \qquad 0.399 \times 120 \approx 47.9\text{bp}$$
Net: I **receive** about 4bp of DV01, i.e. **USD 0.4m on 100k DV01**.

### Worked example at expiry (python-checked, 100k DV01 per leg, moves of forward rates)
| Scenario | 2y fwd | 10y fwd | Payoff incl. premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bear steepener | +40bp | +60bp | +24bp, **+2.4m** |
| Big term-premium sell-off | +20bp | +50bp | +34bp, **+3.4m** |
| Rally | -50bp | -30bp | +4bp, **+0.4m** |
| Unchanged | 0 | 0 | +0.4m |
| **Bear flattener** (hawkish Fed) | +60bp | +40bp | -16bp, **-1.6m** |

Compare with a plain cash steepener: in the rally case a bull flattener would lose, in a bull steepener it would win; the conditional version is flat in both.

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting that the short 2y payer is an **open-ended** short option: a Fed shock can cost a lot.
- Comparing premiums in notional instead of DV01: a 1y2y payer needs about four times the notional of a 1y10y payer for the same DV01.
- Ignoring that the deltas at inception are about 0.5 each, so before expiry the position is roughly half a steepener plus a vega position (long 10y vol, short 2y vol).
- Saying "free trade": zero premium means you sold optionality somewhere, here front-end vol.

### What I'd say on the desk
"Curve is +41 and bear steepening on term premium. I don't want to own a steepener in a rally, so I'd do it conditionally: long 1y10y payers, short 1y2y payers ATMF, DV01-matched at 100k, roughly zero cost, small premium received with front-end vol richer. Payoff about +2-3m in a supply-driven sell-off, flat in a rally. My risk is a hawkish Fed: if October is priced above 60% after payrolls or CPI, I buy back the 2y payer."

### How to deliver it
State the view as a scenario, build the two legs, explain the payoff in three scenarios, and name the short-option risk. Link to the futures steepener (rfc-740) and to options basics (put-call parity, Bachelier).
deep.rfc-742:
### Context / why they ask this
Negative swap spreads look like an arbitrage: a risk-free government bond yields more than a swap on an overnight rate. The question tests whether you know **how the trade is built**, **what it really carries**, and **why the arbitrage persists**. It is current: at the end of September 2026 the 10-year SOFR swap was about 4.91% and the 10-year Treasury about 5.26-5.29%, so a 10-year spread of about **-35 to -41bp** (fd-037 uses -38), with the 2-year near -20bp and the 30-year near -62bp. (mkt-613 covers the opposite trade, the swap spread tightener.)

### Key concepts
- **Swap spread** (US convention): swap rate minus Treasury yield of the same maturity. Negative = Treasuries cheap versus swaps.
- **Long swap spread**: buy Treasury + pay fixed. Gains if the spread widens back up (towards zero or positive). **Short swap spread** (tightener): the opposite.
- **Repo**: the Treasury is financed overnight against collateral; the rate is close to SOFR (SOFR is itself a Treasury repo rate) but specific issues can trade above or below.
- **SLR / eSLR**: US leverage ratio. Capital must cover a percentage of total exposure, **whatever the risk** of the asset; a Treasury counts like a loan. The 2025 final rule (effective 1 April 2026) set the GSIB holding-company buffer at half of the method 1 surcharge, on top of the 3% minimum.

### Intuition
The trade swaps "Treasury minus repo" for "fixed minus SOFR". If repo were exactly SOFR, the carry would be exactly minus the spread. But repo is often a few bp above SOFR, and quarter-ends make it spike, so the carry is **a bit less than the spread**. More importantly, a swap uses almost no balance sheet while a bond position uses all of it. Negative spreads are the price of balance sheet: heavy Treasury supply has to be held by somebody, and dealers charge for it.

### The maths (python-checked, repo and capital ratio illustrative)
Carry per year:
$$\text{carry} = (y_{UST} - r_{repo}) - (S_{swap} - r_{SOFR}) = (5.29 - 3.93) - (4.91 - 3.88) = 1.36 - 1.03 = 0.33\%$$
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Spread | -38bp |
| Carry | +33bp/yr, USD 330k per USD 100m |
| DV01 (10y par bond) | about USD 76.9k per USD 100m |
| Carry in spread bp | 4.3bp/yr, about **1.1bp per quarter** |
| Capital at 5% / 4% / 3.5% | USD 5m / 4m / 3.5m |
| Return on capital | **6.6% / 8.3% / 9.4%** |

At a 12% hurdle and 4% capital, required carry is USD 480k, which means a spread near **-53bp** (48bp plus 5bp of repo cost). A 3-month spread move of 8bp (illustrative vol) is worth about USD 615k, almost two years of carry.

### Worked example
USD 100m Treasury against a USD 100m pay-fixed swap, DV01-matched. Three months later the spread is unchanged: P&L about **USD +82k** of carry. If heavy coupon auctions push the spread from -38 to -45bp, the loss is about $7 \times 76.9\text{k} \approx$ USD 540k, more than six quarters of carry. If regulators exempt Treasuries from the SLR and the spread snaps to -28bp, the gain is about USD 770k.

### What can go wrong
- **Further cheapening**: deficits and coupon supply keep Treasuries cheap; the spread trended more negative for years.
- **Repo spikes**: at quarter-ends and year-end repo can trade well above SOFR; 30 September is one of them, and the carry turns negative on those days.
- **Basis-trade unwind**: hedge funds long cash / short futures may be forced to sell Treasuries, hitting spreads.
- **Specialness**: an on-the-run bond that trades special in repo helps the carry; off-the-runs do not.
- **Capital**: if your desk's leverage budget is cut, you are forced out at the worst time.

### What I'd say on the desk
"The 10-year spread at -38 earns about 33bp of carry, but that is only a bp a quarter against an 8bp quarterly range, and it eats leverage capital at about 8% return. I'd do it small, ahead of a catalyst: a Treasury carve-out from the SLR, buybacks, or a softer refunding. Stop at -48, target -28."

### How to deliver it
Build the trade (buy, repo, pay fixed), write the carry formula, show it is smaller than the spread and tiny in spread bp, then explain balance sheet and the eSLR. End with the catalysts. Link to fd-037 (levels), mkt-613 (tightener) and rfc-740 (curve trades in futures).
deep.rfc-743:
### Context / why they ask this
For two decades the Bund was the euro area's collateral of choice and traded **rich**: its yield was tens of bp below swaps, and in 2022 collateral scarcity pushed short-dated Schatz spreads towards 100bp. Since 2025 this has largely reversed; the 10-year spread first dipped below zero in 2025. The question tests whether you can explain a **relative-value level** with flows (supply, central bank, pensions) rather than just quote it, and whether you know which **floating index** you compare against. Data at the end of September 2026: Bund 10-year 3.63% on 29 September (a 17-year high of about 3.65% earlier that week, 3.57% on 30 September), EUR 10-year swap 3.687% on 29 September, OAT-Bund 10-year 111-117bp.

### Key concepts
- **Bund swap spread** (EUR convention): swap rate minus Bund yield. Positive = Bund rich (yields less than swaps). Near zero or negative = Bund cheap.
- **Euribor vs €STR swaps**: the standard EUR swap is against 6-month Euribor, which includes bank credit risk. An €STR OIS rate is lower; the gap (about 28bp at 10 years here, low confidence) is the **Euribor-€STR basis**.
- **Asset swap (ASW)**: buy the bond, pay fixed on a swap of the same maturity. You keep the bond's spread to the swap curve plus the floating leg you receive.
- **Dutch pension reform (Wtp)**: funds move from guaranteed to defined-contribution-like contracts and need **less long-dated hedging**: about EUR 550-600bn switched on 1 January 2026, with ABP (EUR 530bn) and more than EUR 900bn in total on 1 January 2027.

### Intuition
A swap spread is the price of a government bond versus a bank-credit derivative. When a sovereign issues much more, and the central bank stops buying, investors need a bigger concession to hold it: the Bund cheapens versus swaps. At the same time, Dutch funds **receiving fixed** in maturities below 25 years push those swap rates down, which compresses the spread from the other side. Against €STR, which carries no bank risk, the Bund now yields more than an overnight swap: the market is charging for duration supply, not for German credit.

### The maths (python-checked, repo and Euribor fixing illustrative)
Spreads on 29 September:
$$SS_{10y} = 3.687 - 3.63 = +5.7\text{bp}, \qquad \text{Bund} - \text{OIS} = 3.63 - 3.41 = +22\text{bp}$$
Asset swap carry per year (buy Bund, repo at 2.40%, pay 3.687%, receive 6-month Euribor 2.85%):
$$(3.63 - 2.40) - (3.687 - 2.85) = 1.23 - 0.837 = 0.393\% \approx 39\text{bp}$$
| Piece | bp/yr |
|---|---|
| Bund minus swap (ASW spread) | -5.7 |
| Euribor minus repo | +45 |
| Total carry | **+39.3** |

On EUR 100m: EUR 393k a year, about EUR 98k a quarter. DV01 of the 10-year Bund about **EUR 82.6k**, so carry is about **1.2bp of spread per quarter**. Spread widening from +5.7 to +15bp makes about EUR 770k; a move to -2bp loses about EUR 640k.

### Worked example: where the risk really is
Most of the carry is the **Euribor-repo gap**, not the Bund. If 6-month Euribor fixes 6bp lower relative to Bund repo for a year, carry falls by EUR 60k. If Bund repo goes special at year-end (strong collateral demand), carry improves. So an ASW is a spread trade **plus** a money-market basis position; the desk must say which one it wants.

### What can go wrong
- **More supply**: the 2027 German budget and defence plans can add issuance; the Finanzagentur's Q4 calendar matters.
- **ABP and the 1 January 2027 wave**: receiving below 25 years and unwinding long receivers can push 10-year swaps down further, i.e. the spread lower.
- **OAT contagion**: with OAT-Bund near 111-121bp and rating reviews (rfc-754), safe-haven flows **into** Bunds would richen them (good for this trade), but a broad euro government sell-off would cheapen all of them.
- **ECB**: faster balance-sheet reduction or a change in collateral rules shifts the scarcity premium.

### What I'd say on the desk
"Bund swap spreads at +6 and Bunds 22bp over €STR OIS already price a lot of German supply. Into year-end, collateral demand usually richens Bunds, and the ABP transition can be lumpier than feared. I'd buy 10-year Bund asset swaps small: entry +6, stop -2, target +15, about 0.8m up for 0.6m risk on EUR 100m, carrying about a bp a quarter."

### How to deliver it
Define the spread and its sign, give the level against both Euribor and €STR, explain the three flows, then the asset swap carry decomposition and the year-end catalyst. Link to the USD version (rfc-742), the OAT-Bund widener (mkt-612), the €STR curve (rfc-744) and the USD tightener (mkt-613).

### Context / why they ask this
"Carry and roll" is the first screen every rates desk runs: what do I earn if the curve does not move? Interviewers want to see that you can compute it **in bp of rate**, that you separate carry from roll-down, that you **normalise by volatility**, and that you understand that carry is **the market's forecast you are betting against**. It is very current: after a first hike in June (to 2.25%) and the move to a 2.50% deposit rate on 10 September 2026, euro inflation is rising on the energy shock (September flash consensus 3.6% from 3.2%, due on 2 October), and the front of the €STR curve is steep.

### Key concepts
- **Carry**: for a swap, the fixed rate received minus the floating rate paid over the horizon.
- **Roll-down**: after 3 months a 2-year swap is a 1.75-year swap; on an unchanged curve it is revalued at the 1.75-year rate.
- **Annuity / DV01**: $A_n$ is the PV of 1 per year paid on the fixed leg; it converts a running rate difference into bp of the swap rate.
- **Carry-to-vol**: total carry + roll over the horizon divided by the standard deviation of the rate over the same horizon ($\sigma\sqrt{0.25}$ with normal vol $\sigma$ in bp/yr). It is a Sharpe ratio for one quarter.

### Intuition
On a steep curve, a receiver gets a high fixed rate and pays a low overnight rate (carry), and as time passes the swap slides down to lower, shorter rates (roll-down). Both are largest where the curve is **steepest**: here between 3 months and 2 years, because hikes are priced. The long end (10s30s nearly flat) carries almost nothing.

### The maths (python-checked; 5y point illustrative, vols illustrative)
$$\text{carry}_n = \frac{(S_n - r_{3m}) \times 0.25}{A_n}, \quad \text{roll}_n = S_n - S_{n-0.25}, \quad \text{ratio} = \frac{\text{carry} + \text{roll}}{\sigma_n \sqrt{0.25}}$$
Receivers, 3-month horizon, $r_{3m} = 2.52\%$, curve linearly interpolated:
| Tenor | $S_n$ | Carry (bp) | Roll (bp) | Total | 3m vol (bp) | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1y | 2.98 | 11.8 | 15.3 | **27.2** | 35 | **0.78** |
| 2y | 3.16 | 8.4 | 4.5 | **12.9** | 42.5 | **0.30** |
| 5y | 3.30 | 4.3 | 1.2 | 5.5 | 45 | 0.12 |
| 10y | 3.41 | 2.7 | 0.6 | 3.2 | 42.5 | 0.08 |
| 30y | 3.42 | 1.2 | 0.0 | 1.2 | 40 | 0.03 |

Annualised (multiply by $\sqrt{4} = 2$), the 1-year receiver is a Sharpe of about **1.6**, the 2-year about 0.6. The 1-year roll is large because the 9-month point (2.83% interpolated) is far below 2.98%: be careful, linear interpolation between 3 months and 1 year overstates it if the hikes are bunched.

### Worked example
Receive EUR 100m 2-year €STR at 3.16%. Over 3 months: accrual $(3.16\% - 2.52\%) \times 0.25 \times 100\text{m}$ = EUR 160k; roll-down 4.5bp times the 1.75-year DV01 (about EUR 16.8k) = EUR 76k. Total about **EUR 236k**, i.e. the 1.75-year rate can rise by about 14bp before I lose money. One extra 25bp hike that is not priced would wipe that out and more.

### What can go wrong
- **The forwards realise**: carry is the gap between today's curve and the path if the curve is unchanged. If the ECB hikes as priced, the 1.75-year rate does not stay put; the "roll" disappears.
- **Event risk**: HICP on 2 October and the ECB on 29 October (rfc-746) are jumps, not diffusion; vol-scaling with a smooth $\sigma$ understates them.
- **Wrong benchmark**: carry versus €STR or versus 6-month Euribor gives different numbers (the Euribor-€STR basis, rfc-743).
- **Data**: these OIS quotes are medium-to-low confidence; recompute on the desk's curve.
- **Payers**: a payer in the 1-2 year area has **negative** carry of the same size; it is the price of protection against more hikes.

### What I'd say on the desk
"On an unchanged curve the best carry is receiving 1-year to 2-year €STR: about 27bp and 13bp a quarter, 0.8 and 0.3 of a quarterly standard deviation. Beyond 5 years carry is nearly zero. But the front-end carry is the hike premium: I'd receive 2-year only if I think the energy shock fades before the ECB delivers four more hikes, with a stop if the September HICP prints well above 3.6%."

### How to deliver it
Formula, table, ratio, then the punchline: carry is a view against the forwards. Link to the FOMC/ECB pricing cards (rfc-746, rfc-747), the 1y1y divergence trade (rfc-745) and the Bund asset swap (rfc-743).

### Context / why they ask this
"Divergence" is the most quoted macro theme in rates and FX, and the interviewer wants to see you turn it into **numbers and a trade**. Spot rate gaps are backward-looking; the **forward gap** is what you can trade. At the end of September 2026 the Fed funds target is 3.75-4.00% with October hike odds of about 35% (CNBC; another FedWatch reading after PCE showed 47%), and December pricing of about +32bp cumulative (10% unchanged, 51.8% +25bp, 38.2% +50bp). The ECB took its deposit rate to 2.50% on 10 September and markets expect about four more hikes over the next year as the energy shock lifts inflation.

### Key concepts
- **1y1y forward**: the 1-year rate that starts in one year, implied by the 1-year and 2-year rates (annual compounding here).
- **Forward spread**: $F^{SOFR}_{1y1y} - F^{\text{€STR}}_{1y1y}$. A trade on it is a **cross-market spread**, insensitive to a global move in rates if DV01s are matched.
- **DV01 matching across currencies**: match the USD value of 1bp in each leg, converting EUR DV01 at spot FX.
- **Covered interest parity (CIP)**: $F_{FX} = S_{FX} \times (1 + r_{EUR}) / (1 + r_{USD})$, before the cross-currency basis (rfc-751).

### Intuition
The 1-year rate mostly reflects the next three or four meetings. The 1y1y tells you where each central bank ends up **after** that. Today both curves slope up, but the SOFR curve slopes more: the market thinks US hikes run longer. Fading that is a bet that inflation pressure is relatively worse in Europe (energy importer) or that the US slows first. Being DV01-neutral means you do not care if both banks hike more; you only care **who hikes more**.

### The maths (python-checked; SOFR 1-year illustrative)
$$F_{1y1y} = \frac{(1+S_2)^2}{1+S_1} - 1, \quad F^{SOFR} = \frac{1.0469^2}{1.0440} - 1 = 4.98\%, \quad F^{\text{€STR}} = \frac{1.0316^2}{1.0298} - 1 = 3.34\%$$
| Gap | bp |
|---|---|
| Spot (SOFR 3.88 - €STR 2.44) | 144 |
| 1-year swaps (4.40 - 2.98) | 142 |
| 1y1y forwards | **164** |
| Year-two increase: SOFR / €STR | +58 / +36 |

DV01 of a 1y1y swap per 1m notional: $10^6 \times 10^{-4} / ((1+S_1)(1+F))$, about USD 91.2 (SOFR) and EUR 94.0 (€STR). For USD 100k per bp: SOFR notional about **USD 1,096m**; €STR leg EUR 88.5k per bp, notional about **EUR 942m**. P&L: about USD 100k per bp of the gap: 164 to 134 is **+3.0m**, 164 to 184 is **-2.0m**.
FX check (CIP, no basis): $1.13 \times 1.0298 / 1.0440 = 1.1146$, about -154 pips.

### Worked example: a European inflation surprise
On 2 October HICP prints 3.9% versus 3.6% consensus. €STR 1y1y rises 12bp; SOFR 1y1y rises 4bp in sympathy. The gap narrows 8bp: **+USD 0.8m**. A US payrolls beat the same day moving SOFR 1y1y up 10bp would cost USD 1.0m: the trade is a bet on **relative** surprises, so list the catalysts in both regions: HICP (2 October), payrolls, FOMC (28 October, rfc-747) and ECB (29 October, rfc-746).

### What can go wrong
- **US term premium**: the US curve can keep steepening on supply (10-year about 5.29%), pushing SOFR forwards up regardless of the Fed.
- **ECB credibility**: if the ECB looks through the energy shock (supply shock), €STR forwards fall and the gap widens.
- **Correlation**: in a global risk-off, USD rates often rally more (higher beta), which helps; in a global sell-off they sell off more, which hurts. Check the beta and consider beta-weighting.
- **FX translation**: the EUR leg's P&L is in EUR; hedge it or accept EURUSD exposure on the P&L.
- **Data quality**: the SOFR 1-year point is illustrative and the €STR quotes are low confidence; rebuild on the desk curve.

### What I'd say on the desk
"The forward gap is 164bp versus 144 spot: the market prices the Fed outrunning the ECB into 2027. With an energy shock that hits Europe harder, I'd fade it: receive SOFR 1y1y, pay €STR 1y1y, 100k a bp, about USD 1.1bn against EUR 0.94bn. Target 135, stop 180. It also fits a modestly bullish EURUSD view, since a narrower gap supports the euro."

### How to deliver it
Formula, the three gaps (spot, 1y, 1y1y), the conclusion (more divergence priced), then the DV01-neutral trade, its catalysts and the FX link. Link to rfc-744 (€STR carry), rfc-747 (fed funds futures), rfc-749 (hedging costs) and mkt-615 (EURUSD).

### Context / why they ask this
Every central bank meeting is a binary-looking event that rates desks trade through **meeting-dated swaps**. The interviewer checks that you know the mechanics (effective dates, the €STR-deposit spread), can turn a rate into a **probability**, and can build **scenarios** around a data release. It is live: the ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.50% on 10 September 2026 (its second hike of 2026, after June), September inflation is jumping on the energy-price shock (France HICP 3.4% from 2.6%, Italy 4.1% from 3.2%, both above forecast; euro area flash consensus 3.6% from 3.2%, released on Friday 2 October), and the next decision is on 29 October. Published odds for October diverge: about 60% on 24 September, one OIS tracker at about +18.7bp (75%), another at 61% no change.

### Key concepts
- **€STR**: the euro overnight unsecured rate; it trades a few bp below the deposit facility rate (about -6bp here) because of excess liquidity.
- **Meeting-dated OIS (MPC swaps)**: €STR swaps whose start and end match the ECB's effective dates. The rate is the expected average €STR over that window.
- **Effective date**: an ECB decision applies from the start of the next maintenance period, the **Wednesday after** the meeting (here 4 November).
- **Implied move**: $\Delta = F_{dated} - \text{€STR}_{today}$, assuming the €STR-deposit spread is stable. Probability of a 25bp move $p = \Delta / 25$ (if only 0 or 25 are possible).

### Intuition
A dated swap is a clean bet on one meeting: nothing else happens inside its window. If the market is sure of no change, the dated rate equals today's €STR; if it is sure of a hike, it is 25bp higher. Anything in between is a probability. The 3-month OIS mixes the days before and after the meeting, so it dilutes the signal; the dated swap does not.

### The maths (python-checked; dated rate, window and scenario weights illustrative)
$$p = \frac{F_{dated} - \text{€STR}}{25\text{bp}} = \frac{2.58 - 2.44}{0.25} = 0.56$$
Consistency with the 3-month OIS (1 October to 31 December, 91 days, 34 days before 4 November): $(2.44 \times 34 + 2.58 \times 57)/91 = 2.53\%$, close to the 2.52% quote (ignoring the December meeting).
| HICP flash (2 Oct) | Hike odds after | Dated OIS move | P&L paying EUR 1bn |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.9% or more (upside) | 85% | **+7.25bp** | **EUR +99k** |
| 3.6% (in line) | 56% | 0 | 0 |
| 3.3% (downside) | 35% | **-5.25bp** | **EUR -71k** |

DV01 of EUR 1bn over a 49-day window: $10^9 \times 49/360 \times 10^{-4} \approx$ EUR 13.6k. Expected move with weights 30/50/20: $0.3 \times 7.25 - 0.2 \times 5.25 = +1.1$bp, about **EUR +15k**: positive, but small versus the downside.

### Worked example: reading a 50bp tail
If some investors price a 50bp move, $p_{25} + 2p_{50} = 0.56$: 56% of one hike, or 36% of 25bp plus 10% of 50bp, give the same dated rate. The swap cannot tell them apart; **options** (on 3-month Euribor futures) or the skew can. That matters for sizing: a 50bp surprise would move the dated swap about +36bp from here (to 2.94%), a loss of about EUR 490k for a receiver of EUR 1bn.

### What can go wrong
- **Spread drift**: if excess liquidity falls (balance-sheet run-off, TLTRO maturities), €STR can drift closer to the deposit rate and fake a "hike".
- **Bad window**: the December meeting date and the year-end turn affect the last days of the window; check the exact dates on the ECB calendar.
- **Data noise**: the flash is headline-driven by energy; the ECB may look through it if core is stable, so map core too.
- **Liquidity**: dated swaps are liquid in the next two or three meetings only; beyond, use forwards or futures.
- **Cross-market**: a hawkish Fed on 28 October (rfc-747) can move euro pricing the day before the ECB.

### What I'd say on the desk
"The October ECB is priced at about 56% of a hike, 14bp in the dated OIS, with screens quoting anything from 40% to 75%. The risk into the flash is skewed up because the country data beat, but much of that is already in the price. I'd pay the October dated swap small, EUR 1bn, about EUR 14k a bp, and buy Euribor-futures puts for a 50bp tail rather than size up the swap."

### How to deliver it
Effective date, formula, probability, cross-check with the 3-month OIS, then the scenario table with P&L and expected value. Close on what the swap cannot tell you (the 50bp tail). Link to rfc-747 (fed funds futures), rfc-744 (front-end carry) and rfc-745 (Fed-ECB divergence).
deep.rfc-747:
### Context / why they ask this
"What is the market pricing for the next meeting?" is the most common rates question on a desk, and a natural follow-up to any view on the Fed. The interviewer checks that you know where the number comes from (futures, not opinion), that you can redo the arithmetic, and that you separate the market's price from your own forecast. With the FOMC on **27-28 October 2026** and a hike priced at about 35% at the 30 September close (CME FedWatch, reported by CNBC and 247wallst; another FedWatch snapshot the same evening showed about 47%, so check the live number on the day), it is the perfect live example.

### Key concepts
- **EFFR (effective fed funds rate)**: the volume-weighted median rate on overnight unsecured loans between banks, published daily by the New York Fed. It trades inside the target range, today about **3.88%** within 3.75-4.00%, a little below interest on reserves (IORB, 3.90%).
- **30-day fed funds future (CME, code ZQ)**: settles on **100 minus the average EFFR** over the calendar month. Notional USD 5 million; one basis point is worth $5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.0001 \times 30/360 \approx$ **USD 41.67** per contract.
- **Meeting-dated pricing**: a decision announced on day $d$ takes effect the next day, so a month's contract only partly reflects a meeting held inside it.
- **Risk-neutral probability**: the probability that makes the futures price fair if nobody demanded a risk premium. It is a price, not the market's honest forecast.
- **FedWatch**: CME's free tool that does exactly this calculation from the futures.

### Intuition
The futures market is a bet on the **average** overnight rate of a month. If the market thinks there is a chance $p$ of a 25bp hike, the expected average rate after the decision is $3.88 + 0.25p$. So you invert the price to get $p$. The only trap is the calendar: a meeting late in the month barely moves that month's average.

### The maths
For a month with $N$ days, a decision effective on day $k$ and a hike of size $h$ with probability $p$:
$$\bar r = r_0 + p\,h\,\frac{N-k+1}{N}, \qquad \text{price} = 100 - \bar r$$
- **October** (31 days, decision effective 29 October, 3 days left): $\bar r = 3.88 + p \times 0.25 \times 3/31$. Even with $p=1$ it only adds **2.4bp** (price 96.096 instead of 96.12). Noise in the EFFR (month-end, quarter-end) is of the same size, so you cannot read $p$ from it.
- **November** (no FOMC in November, next meeting 8-9 December): the whole month sits after the October decision, so
$$p = \frac{(100 - P_{Nov}) - r_0}{0.25}$$
With $P_{Nov} = 96.0325$: $p = (3.9675 - 3.88)/0.25 = 0.35$.
- **December** (decision effective 10 December, 22 of 31 days after it): $\bar r_{Dec} = r_0 + 0.25\,p_{Oct} + 0.25\,p_{Dec}\times 22/31$. With $p_{Oct}=0.35$ and a further December hike priced at, say, 60% (illustrative), $\bar r = 4.074$%, price about 95.93. You strip the October part first, then read December: that is "bootstrapping" the meeting path.

### Worked example with numbers (python-checked)
| Probability of an October hike | October contract | November contract |
|---|---|---|
| 35% | 96.1115 | 96.0325 |
| 50% | 96.1079 | 95.9950 |
| 70% | 96.1031 | 95.9450 |
| 100% | 96.0958 | 95.8700 |

Going from 70% (mid-September) to 35% (30 September) moved November by about 8.75bp, i.e. **about USD 365 per contract**. A fund that was short 2,000 November contracts lost about USD 0.73m on the repricing.

### Common pitfalls
- Reading the October contract for an October-end meeting: the effect is diluted by 3/31.
- Assuming where the EFFR sits in the range: it prints about 13bp above the bottom (3.88%, just above the 3.875% midpoint and 2bp below IORB) and can drift at month- and quarter-ends; use the actual EFFR print, not the bottom of the range or the midpoint.
- Calling 35% "the market thinks it is unlikely": it is a price that includes risk premium, and in this cycle it swung from 70% to 35% in a week, so it is not stable.
- Mixing up fed funds futures and **SOFR futures**: SOFR futures (3-month contracts) are better for the path further out; SOFR also jumps at quarter-ends.

### What I'd say on the desk
"Fed funds at 3.75-4.00, EFFR 3.88. November ZQ at about 96.03, so roughly 9bp, a 35% chance of 25 in October, down from about 70% before Williams and the soft core PCE. December is still priced for a hike. My base case is a **hawkish hold** in October: the Fed has just hiked and Williams has signalled patience. The asymmetry is in the payrolls tomorrow: a print well above the 90k consensus, with unemployment at or below 4.1%, puts October back toward a coin flip and the 2-year leads the sell-off. I would not fight December."

### How to deliver it
Say the instrument, the formula, the contract choice (November, not October) and the number in 30 seconds, then give your own view separately and name the catalyst (payrolls 2 October, CPI mid-October, PCE 29 October after the meeting). Link to the market-implied path card (rfc-029) and to how you would trade a different view (rfc-748).
deep.rfc-748:
### Context / why they ask this
Every candidate has a Fed view; few can turn it into a trade with a number attached. This question tests whether you understand that **you trade the difference between your probability and the market's**, that a binary event has an asymmetric payoff that depends on the price, and that sizing comes from risk, not conviction. It is very current: on 30 September 2026 the target range is 3.75-4.00%, the next FOMC is on 28 October, and the October hike probability was quoted at about 35% (CNBC) while another FedWatch reading the same day showed 47.1%. That discrepancy itself is part of a good answer.

### Key concepts
- **Fed funds future (ZQ)**: settles on 100 minus the average EFFR of the month; USD 5m notional, so **USD 41.67 per bp**.
- **Implied probability**: (implied rate - current rate) / 25bp (rfc-747).
- **Expected value (EV)**: (your probability - market probability) x 25bp, per contract.
- **Asymmetry**: at a 35% price, being right pays 65% of 25bp, being wrong costs 35% of 25bp.
- **SOFR futures options (SR3)**: options on 3-month SOFR futures, much more liquid than options on fed funds futures; USD 25 per bp.

### Intuition
The futures price is already the market's expected outcome. If you agree with 35%, the trade has zero EV whatever your conviction. A cheap price for an event (35%) gives a big payoff if it happens, which is why buyers of "hike" at 35% get almost 2:1 odds. When the price moves to 47%, the same view earns half as much and the odds become close to even.

### The maths (python-checked, EFFR 3.88%, November contract)
| | Market 35% | Market 47% |
|---|---|---|
| November price | 96.0325 | 96.0025 |
| Short pays if hike (bp) | +16.25 | +13.25 |
| Short loses if hold (bp) | -8.75 | -11.75 |
| EV at a 60% view (bp) | +6.25 | +3.25 |
| EV per contract (USD) | 260 | 135 |
| Contracts for USD 500k loss on hold | 1,371 | 1,021 |
| P&L if hike (USD) | +928k | +564k |
| Edge / standard deviation | 0.51 | 0.27 |

The EV formula is simply $\text{EV} = (q - p) \times 25\text{bp}$, with $q$ your probability and $p$ the market's. The standard deviation of a binary outcome is $25\sqrt{q(1-q)} \approx 12.2$bp at $q = 60\%$, so even a strong view has a modest edge per unit of risk. The Kelly fraction $f = (q b - (1-q))/b$ with odds $b = (1-p)/p$ gives 38% at a 35% price and 24% at 47%; desks use a fraction of it, but the ratio tells you how much the 47% reading should shrink the trade.

### Worked example: options for timing risk (illustrative premium)
If you are sure the Fed hikes by December but not sure it is October, the November future can lose while you are "right". Buy a December SR3 put spread, top strike at the money and the lower one 12.5bp below, for an **illustrative 3bp** (USD 75 per spread). Maximum payoff is 9.5bp net, USD 237.5, about **3.2 times the premium**, and the loss is capped at USD 75. It pays in full if the December contract prices about half a hike more than today, whichever meeting delivers it.

### What can go wrong
- **Stale price**: 35% versus 47% changes the EV by half. Check the screen, not the headline.
- **Data before the meeting**: payrolls on 2 October, CPI, Fed speakers. The price can go against you before the decision, so you need a stop, not only a scenario.
- **A 50bp move or a hold with hawkish guidance**: the November future only captures October; a hawkish hold reprices December, not November.
- **EFFR drift**: the effective rate can move inside the range (quarter-end, reserves), which changes the settlement by a few bp.
- **Correlation with the book**: if the desk is already short front-end, your trade adds to the same risk.

### What I'd say on the desk
"The market is at 35% on October, though I've also seen 47% on FedWatch so I'll check the live number. I'm at 60%. I'd sell November fed funds, about 1,370 contracts, to lose 500k on a hold and make about 930k on a hike; EV about 360k. If the price is really 47%, I cut to about 1,000. For timing risk I'd add a December SOFR put spread at about 3bp, roughly 3 to 1. Stop if payrolls on 2 October are weak."

### How to deliver it
Market probability, your probability, EV per contract, size from max loss, then the asymmetry and the option alternative. Link to the futures maths (rfc-747) and the curve expression (rfc-740).
deep.rfc-749:
### Context / why they ask this
"Treasuries at 5.3%!" is the headline every European client reads. The sales or strategist answer must be: **in euros, hedged, it is much less**. It is a classic question because it combines covered interest parity, the cross-currency basis, the difference between carry and locked return, and a client constraint (the hedge ratio). On 30 September 2026 the 10-year Treasury was about 5.29%, SOFR about 3.88%, €STR about 2.44%, EURUSD about 1.13: a big rate gap, so hedging is expensive. Older numbers on the same idea are in trp-070 (Japanese investor); the mirror trade is rfc-750.

### Key concepts
- **FX forward**: $F = S \times \frac{1 + r_{USD} T}{1 + r_{EUR} T}$ with EURUSD quoted in USD per EUR. When USD rates are higher, the EUR is at a **forward premium**: you sell USD forward at a worse rate than spot.
- **Hedging cost**: about $r_{USD} - r_{EUR} - \text{basis}$, where a negative basis (EURUSD typically) makes it more expensive to get dollars (rfc-067, rfc-751).
- **Hedged yield**: bond yield minus annualised hedging cost.
- **Hedge ratio**: share of the market value hedged; 100% removes FX risk, less adds carry and FX risk.

### Intuition
Hedging a dollar bond means you are, in effect, borrowing dollars short term and lending euros short term. You pay the short dollar rate and receive the short euro rate. So a hedged Treasury is really **10-year US yield minus the 3-month US-EUR rate gap**: it is a bet on the US curve's steepness, not on US yields being high.

### The maths (python-checked; 3m USD OIS, basis and Bund level illustrative)
Inputs: spot 1.13, 3-month USD 3.95%, 3-month EUR 2.52%, basis -15bp.
- Implied USD rate in the FX swap: 3.95 + 0.15 = 4.10%.
- 3-month forward: $1.13 \times \frac{1 + 0.041/4}{1 + 0.0252/4} = 1.13444$, i.e. **+44.4 pips**, about 1.57% annualised.
- Hedging cost about **1.58%** a year.
| Asset | Yield (%) | Hedged into EUR (%) |
|---|---|---|
| UST 10y | 5.29 | **3.71** |
| Bund 10y (illustrative) | 3.60 | 3.60 |
| OAT 10y (Bund + about 115bp) | 4.75 | 4.75 |

Hedged UST minus Bund: **+0.11%**; minus OAT: **-1.04%**.
- On USD 100m (about EUR 88.5m): about **USD 1.58m a year**, **USD 395k per quarterly roll**.
- **Locked alternative**: a 10-year SOFR/€STR cross-currency swap turns the UST into a EUR fixed yield of about $5.29 - 4.91 + 3.41 - 0.10 = 3.69\%$ (10y SOFR swap 4.91, 10y €STR swap 3.41, illustrative 10y basis -10bp). Same level as the rolling hedge, but without Fed risk.

### Worked example: hedge ratio choice
| Hedge ratio | Carry in EUR (approx.) | Hedge cost on USD 100m | FX risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100% | 3.71% | USD 1.58m | none |
| 50% | about 4.50% | USD 0.79m | half the position |

A 5% fall of the dollar costs about EUR 4.4m on a fully unhedged USD 100m, more than two years of the pickup. The breakeven is the forward: about 1.148 in a year. If EURUSD ends below that, unhedged beats hedged.

### What can go wrong
- **Fed hike**: the rolling cost rises about 25bp; the hedged yield falls toward 3.46%.
- **Basis widening at quarter- and year-end**: rolls crossing 31 December cost more (rfc-751).
- **Hedge drift**: if the bond falls 5%, a hedge on the original value is now 105% of the asset. Rebalance.
- **Cash settlement of forwards**: a stronger dollar means paying cash on the hedge at each roll while the bond gain is unrealised, a liquidity need.
- **Duration risk stays**: hedging FX does nothing for a sell-off in US yields.

### What I'd say on the desk
"In euros, hedged, the 10-year Treasury yields about 3.7%, roughly Bund plus 10 and about 100bp below OATs. The hedge costs about 1.6% a year because US short rates are about 1.4% above euro rates and the basis adds about 15bp. So the reason to buy is diversification and a view that the US curve flattens or US yields fall, not carry. If you want pickup, a 50% hedge gives about 4.5% but with real FX risk; or lock about 3.7% with a cross-currency swap if you fear a Fed hike."

### How to deliver it
Headline yield, hedging cost formula with numbers, hedged yield against the local alternatives, then the two traps (carry is not locked, hedge ratio). Link to rfc-750 for the mirror and rfc-751 for the basis.

### Context / why they ask this
The mirror of rfc-749 is a classic sales pitch: when US short rates are well above euro short rates, **a US investor gets paid to hedge euros**. The question tests whether you know the sign of the hedge, can compute the hedged yield, and understand that the pickup is compensation for a risk (here French spread), not a free lunch. On 30 September 2026: UST 10y about 5.29%, SOFR about 3.88%, €STR about 2.44%, OAT-Bund 10y about 111-121bp, CDS France 5y about 65bp (USD), Moody's Aa3 negative with a review on 23 October.

### Key concepts
- **Hedging a EUR asset into USD**: buy EUR spot, sell EUR forward. Because EUR is at a forward premium (higher USD rates), you sell it forward at a better rate than spot: the forward points are a **gain**.
- **Hedge pickup**: about $r_{USD} - r_{EUR} - \text{basis}$; with a negative basis the US investor, who supplies dollars, earns it.
- **Hedged yield**: local yield plus hedge pickup.
- **Spread risk**: the risk that OATs underperform; the hedge removes FX, not this.

### Intuition
The investor is, in effect, a dollar lender in the FX swap market: they give dollars today and get them back in 3 months, holding euros in between. Dollar lending pays the dollar rate plus the basis; the euros cost the euro rate. That gap is about 1.6% today. The Bund then looks like a Treasury in dollars; the extra yield on OATs is the French risk premium, now worth about 1% in dollars.

### The maths (python-checked; 3m USD OIS, basis and Bund level illustrative)
Hedge pickup: 3.95 - 2.52 + 0.15 = **1.58%** a year (same inputs as rfc-749).
| Asset | Local yield (%) | Hedged into USD (%) | vs UST 10y (bp) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bund 10y (illustrative) | 3.60 | 5.18 | -11 |
| OAT 10y (Bund + about 115bp) | 4.75 | **6.33** | **+104** |
| UST 10y | 5.29 | 5.29 | 0 |

Rough comparisons: US IG at Treasury plus 84bp is about 6.13%, so hedged OATs are about 20bp above. Taking off the 65bp CDS as a crude credit charge leaves about 5.68%, still about 39bp above Treasuries: part of the pickup is the euro curve and the basis, not only French credit.
**Breakeven**: on USD 100m with a duration of about 8, the DV01 is USD 80k per bp. Carry pickup is USD 1.04m a year, i.e. 26bp a quarter. The quarterly breakeven is
$$\frac{26}{8} \approx 3.25\text{bp of OAT underperformance versus Treasuries}$$
and about 13bp over a year.

### Worked example: a bad October
Moody's downgrades France on 23 October and OATs widen 10bp versus Bunds while Bunds track Treasuries. Loss on USD 100m: $10 \times 80\text{k} = 800\text{k}$, about **9 months of the carry** pickup. If instead the Fed hikes in October, the hedge pickup rises about 25bp on the next roll: the investor gains carry, since they are lending dollars.

### Flows: why this matters for the market
- **US real money and insurers** buying hedged European bonds lend dollars through FX swaps, which pushes the EURUSD basis toward zero.
- **Reverse Yankee issuance**: US companies issue in euros and swap back to dollars when the basis and euro spreads make it cheaper (cf-922). They also receive dollars, which works against the basis.
- **On the other side**, European and Japanese investors buying Treasuries need dollars and push the basis more negative (rfc-749, rfc-751). The basis is the price that clears both flows.
- When the rate gap is this wide, hedged euro assets look good to US buyers, which supports OAT demand even through French political noise.

### What can go wrong
- **French spread**: rating actions, the PLF vote on 17 November, political news. This is the main risk.
- **EUR duration**: a hawkish ECB on 29 October or a global sell-off hits the bond.
- **Rate gap closes**: Fed cuts or ECB hikes reduce the pickup on future rolls.
- **Basis moves**: a less negative basis cuts the pickup; year-end rolls can be distorted.
- **Liquidity and cash settlement**: a weaker dollar at roll means paying cash on the FX forwards.

### What I'd say on the desk
"For a US client, hedged OATs yield about 6.3% in dollars, Treasuries plus about 100, and about 20bp over US IG. The hedge pays about 1.6% because they are lending dollars when US short rates are 1.4% above euro rates, plus the basis. The catch is French spread: with a duration of 8, OATs only need to underperform by about 3bp a quarter to lose the carry. I'd size it on spread DV01 and have them watch Moody's on 23 October."

### How to deliver it
Sign of the hedge (it pays), the hedged yields table, then what risk is being paid (French spread), the breakeven, and the flow story. Link to rfc-749 (mirror), mkt-612 (OAT-Bund trade) and rfc-751 (basis).

### Context / why they ask this
The generic definition of the basis is in rfc-067. This question is about **today's prices**: why hedging and funding quotes do not match covered interest parity, and why anything crossing 31 December looks terrible. It comes up every October, when 3-month trades start to span year-end. Context on 30 September 2026: SOFR about 3.88%, €STR about 2.44%, EURUSD about 1.13, quarter-end just passed. Basis levels are not public in free sources, so all numbers below are **illustrative**.

### Key concepts
- **Cross-currency basis**: spread $b$ such that the FX-implied USD rate equals $r_{USD} - b$ (with $b < 0$, dollars cost more). Equivalent: EUR leg pays €STR + $b$ against SOFR flat in a cross-currency swap.
- **The turn**: the period over a reporting date (quarter-end, year-end) when banks shrink balance sheets. Quotes covering it embed a premium.
- **Ex-turn basis**: basis on a period not covering the turn.
- **Ceiling**: the Fed's swap lines with the ECB lend dollars at USD OIS plus 25bp, which limits how negative the very short basis can get for banks with access.

### Intuition
An FX swap is a secured loan of dollars against euros. If dollars were freely available, its implied rate would equal USD OIS (covered parity). Since 2008 it doesn't, because arbitrage needs balance sheet, and balance sheet is costly, especially when it is measured. At year-end the cost peaks for a few days, so a short trade covering those days shows a huge annualised basis even though the actual cost is small.

### The maths (python-checked, illustrative basis)
Model: ex-turn basis $b_0 = -6$bp, plus a turn premium $X = 200$bp annualised over the $n = 4$ nights of 31 December to 4 January. A swap of $D$ days covering the turn shows
$$b(D) \approx b_0 - X \frac{n}{D}$$
| Swap | Days | Quoted basis (bp) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 month, 15 Dec - 15 Jan | 31 | **-31.8** |
| 3 months, 5 Oct - 5 Jan | 92 | **-14.7** (turn: 8.7bp) |
| 1 year | 365 | -8.2 |

Turn cost on USD 1bn: $1\text{bn} \times 2\% \times 4/360 \approx$ **USD 222k**. The same 3-month basis on USD 1bn costs about USD 376k over the quarter: more than half of it comes from 4 days.

### Where the basis enters prices today
- **Hedging Treasuries for a European**: hedge cost about 3.95 - 2.52 + 0.15 = 1.58% (rfc-749). The basis is about a tenth, but it is the part that jumps at year-end.
- **US investor in OATs**: earns 1.58%, including the basis (rfc-750).
- **Non-US bank funding**: the FX-implied USD rate is about 4.10% versus 3.95% OIS. Banks that can, use unsecured or repo funding instead.
- **Issuers**: a US company issuing EUR 500m 5-year and swapping back with an illustrative 5-year basis of -10bp saves about EUR 2.25m in present value (annuity 4.50). This is one driver of reverse Yankee issuance (cf-922).
- **USDJPY**: usually more negative than EURUSD because Japanese investors are large dollar buyers; it shapes their hedged Treasury yields (trp-070).

### Worked example: a client rolling a hedge into year-end
An insurer has a USD 1bn hedge maturing 15 December. Option A: roll 1 month to 15 January at -31.8bp, paying the full turn. Option B: roll 2 months to 15 February, spreading the 4 nights over about 62 days: $-6 - 200 \times 4/62 \approx -18.9$bp. The cost in dollars of the turn is the same (about USD 222k); what changes is how it looks annualised and how much rollover risk sits in mid-January. Option C: roll in October, before banks fully price the turn, if the desk expects it to widen.

### What can go wrong
- **Turn widens late**: if balance sheets are tight (large Treasury issuance, money-market stress), the premium can jump in December.
- **Confusing the turn with stress**: a -32bp 1-month crossing year-end is not a funding crisis; compare with the forward ex-turn.
- **Quarter-ends**: smaller turns also appear at 31 March, 30 June, 30 September.
- **Liquidity of quotes**: the basis is quoted by dealers and varies a lot by name and size.

### What I'd say on the desk
"The 3-month at about -15 includes about 9bp of turn, so ex-turn the basis is only about -6; the 1-month over year-end at -32 is just the 4 nights from 31 December to 4 January priced at about 2% annualised, roughly 222k per billion. For clients I'd show the turn cost in dollars, suggest rolling past mid-January or early in Q4, and keep any 'dollar shortage' view for the ex-turn forwards."

### How to deliver it
Definition in one line, the three places it enters prices, then the turn formula with the 4 nights. Link to rfc-067 (theory), rfc-749/750 (hedging), cf-922 (issuers).
deep.rfc-752:
### Context / why they ask this
French sovereign risk is the main European credit story of autumn 2026: Scope cut France to A+ on 18 September, DBRS put its AA on a negative trend the same day, Moody's is Aa3 negative with a review on 23 October, and the 2027 budget (target deficit 5%) is voted on 17 November. CDS France 5y rose from about 39bp (16 September) to about 65bp (29 September, investing.com, USD contract), above Italy at about 50bp. The interviewer wants three things: the default-probability maths, the reason for USD quotation (quanto), and a sensible reading of the level.

### Key concepts
- **CDS**: protection buyer pays a running spread; on a **credit event** (failure to pay, repudiation/moratorium, restructuring for sovereigns) the seller pays par minus recovery.
- **Credit triangle**: $s \approx \lambda (1 - R)$, with $\lambda$ the default intensity and $R$ recovery.
- **Risk-neutral probability**: the probability implied by prices, including risk premia; not a forecast.
- **Standard contracts**: fixed coupon plus upfront payment, quarterly dates.
- **Quanto CDS**: the same reference entity in another currency; the price difference reflects the expected FX move at default.

### Intuition
CDS spread is an insurance premium. If you lose 60% of the notional on default and pay 0.65% a year, the market implies about a 1.1% annual chance of default. Insurance against France is most valuable in a world where France defaults, and in that world the euro is probably weaker, so a dollar payout is worth more: dollar protection costs more than euro protection.

### The maths (python-checked; recovery and FX jump illustrative)
Intensity at 40% recovery: $\lambda = 0.0065 / 0.6 = 1.083\%$ a year.
Cumulative probability: $P(T) = 1 - e^{-\lambda T}$.
| Recovery | 1y PD | 5y PD |
|---|---|---|
| 25% | 0.86% | 4.24% |
| 40% | 1.08% | **5.27%** |
| 60% | 1.61% | 7.80% |

Risky annuity (RPV01) with quarterly premiums, USD discounting at 3.9%: about **4.40**. CS01 on USD 10m: $10\text{m} \times 0.0001 \times 4.40 \approx$ **USD 4.4k per bp**.
Upfront on a standard contract: $(s - c) \times \text{RPV01}$. Developed-market sovereign CDS such as France trade with the standard 100bp coupon, so at 65bp the protection buyer **receives** about 1.54% upfront (USD 154k on 10m). With a 25bp coupon (also a standard coupon, used for very tight names), the buyer would instead pay about 1.76% (USD 176k).
Quanto: $s_{EUR} \approx s_{USD}(1 - d)$, where $d$ is the euro's fall on default. With $d$ = 20% to 30%, $s_{EUR} \approx$ 52 to 45.5bp.

### Worked example: reading 65bp before 23 October
- **Versus Italy (about 50bp)**: France now prices more risk than Italy, even though its rating is still higher. This is a market view on fiscal politics, not on near-term default.
- **Versus OAT-Bund 111-121bp**: the bond spread is not only credit. It includes the Bund's own richness, OAT supply and liquidity, and it is in euros. In euro-CDS terms (about 50bp), credit explains less than half of the OAT-Bund spread; the rest is technicals.
- **Moody's review**: a downgrade to A1 is not a credit event, so the CDS does not pay. It matters through mandates, index and collateral effects on bonds, and through hedging demand that lifts CDS further.

### What can go wrong
- **Hedging-driven moves**: banks and bond holders buy protection as a proxy hedge; spreads can overshoot fundamentals and then reverse fast.
- **Recovery uncertainty**: the 5% depends strongly on 40%; sovereign recoveries vary widely.
- **Quote quality**: free sites and press disagree (65 versus about 52bp). Single-name sovereign CDS liquidity is thinner than bonds; use dealer runs.
- **Quanto assumptions**: the FX jump at default is unobservable; treat EUR-equivalent levels as approximate.
- **Counterparty and wrong-way risk**: buying protection on France from a French bank is a poor hedge.

### What I'd say on the desk
"France 5-year CDS at about 65 in dollars implies about a 1.1% annual default intensity and about a 5% five-year risk-neutral probability at 40% recovery. In euro terms it is closer to 45-52, so pure credit explains less than half of the OAT-Bund spread. A Moody's downgrade on 23 October isn't a credit event; the CDS move would come from hedging demand. For clients long OATs it is a liquid political-risk hedge: about 4.4k of CS01 per 10m."

### How to deliver it
Credit triangle and the number, the risk-neutral caveat, why USD (quanto), then the comparison with Italy and OAT-Bund and the rating-event point. Link to rfc-753 (CDS-bond basis), mkt-612 (OAT-Bund trade) and rfc-060 (basis theory).

### Context / why they ask this
The generic theory of the CDS-bond basis is in rfc-060. Applied to France in autumn 2026, it becomes a test of rigour: the CDS everyone quotes is in **dollars**, the bond is in **euros**, and "the spread" can be measured against Euribor swaps, €STR OIS or Bunds. A candidate who says "65bp CDS vs 117bp OAT-Bund, so the basis is -52" fails. Context: CDS France 5y about 65bp (29 September, USD); OAT-Bund 10y 111-121bp; Moody's Aa3 negative, review on 23 October; Scope A+ since 18 September. The 5-year OAT and swap levels below are of medium-to-low confidence and used as illustrations.

### Key concepts
- **CDS-bond basis**: $\text{basis} = s_{CDS} - s_{bond}$, with $s_{bond}$ usually the par asset-swap spread or the Z-spread over the swap curve.
- **Negative basis**: bond cheap versus CDS; trade = buy bond (asset-swapped) + buy protection.
- **Positive basis**: CDS expensive versus bond; trade = sell protection + short the bond (via repo), harder to do.
- **Quanto**: USD CDS on a euro sovereign trades above EUR CDS (rfc-752).
- **Cheapest-to-deliver option**: the protection buyer delivers the cheapest bond after an event, which makes CDS slightly more valuable.

### Intuition
If a bond and a CDS carry the same default risk, buying both should be riskless and earn the basis. In practice the two legs differ: currency, funding (the bond needs repo or balance sheet; the CDS doesn't), delivery options, and who is buying each. In a stress like France's, hedgers buy CDS first because it is fast and unfunded, so CDS leads and the basis rises; then forced or rating-driven bond selling can push it back down.

### The maths (python-checked; OAT 5y, swap and FX jump illustrative)
Bond spreads (approximate, yield minus swap rate):
- vs 6-month Euribor 5y swap (3.60%): $4.18 - 3.60 =$ **58bp**
- vs €STR OIS 5y (interpolated $3.16 + (3.41 - 3.16) \times 3/8 \approx 3.25\%$): **93bp**
CDS: USD 65bp; euro-equivalent $65 \times (1 - 0.25) \approx 48.75$bp.
| Basis (bp) | vs Euribor ASW | vs €STR OIS |
|---|---|---|
| USD CDS 65 | **+7** | -28 |
| EUR-equivalent CDS 49 | **-9** | -44 |

The range, from +7 to -44, is the point: the benchmark and the currency matter more than the market move. Desks usually quote OAT basis against the swap ASW, which mixes in about 35bp of Euribor-€STR spread here.

### Worked example: a negative basis package on EUR 50m
Buy EUR 50m of the 5-year OAT on asset swap (receive Euribor + 58bp) and buy 5-year protection (49bp in euro terms). Locked spread about **9bp**, i.e. **EUR 45k a year**, before funding: if the bond is financed in repo at Euribor flat, that is the carry. The CDS leg adds CS01 of about EUR 22k per bp (RPV01 about 4.4), so a 2bp move in the basis is a year of carry. Balance sheet: with an illustrative 5% capital charge and a 12% hurdle, the package must earn $50\text{m} \times 5\% \times 12\% = 300\text{k}$ a year, i.e. **60bp**. The basis would need to be far more negative to be worth it, which is why it can persist. If you hedge with the USD contract instead, you pay 65bp but hold a long quanto position: on default you receive dollars, worth more in euros if the euro falls.

### What drives the French basis now
- **Hedging demand** (banks, OAT holders, macro funds): pushes CDS up; basis up. CDS rose from about 39 to 65bp between 16 and 29 September; compare with the ASW move over the same days to see who led.
- **Rating-driven selling**: some mandates and indices react to downgrades; bonds cheapen, basis down.
- **Supply**: heavy OAT issuance and the 2027 budget (vote 17 November) cheapen bonds.
- **Repo**: if some OATs trade special, they are richer, basis up for those lines.
- **Delivery option**: long low-coupon OATs below par make the CTD option more valuable.

### What can go wrong
- **Mismatched comparison**: USD CDS against a euro spread, or CDS against OAT-Bund (which includes Bund's own premium and is not a credit spread).
- **Basis can go further**: in stress, negative bases widen before they close; mark-to-market can force exits.
- **Funding**: repo rates can rise at quarter- and year-end.
- **Liquidity**: sovereign single-name CDS is thinner than OATs; quotes diverge (65 versus about 52bp in press).
- **Event mismatch**: a restructuring might affect bonds differently from CDS delivery.

### What I'd say on the desk
"Like-for-like, in euro CDS terms and against Euribor swaps, the OAT basis is about -10: the bond is a bit cheap to CDS. In dollar CDS it is about +7, and against €STR it is about -44, so I always state the convention. The trade earns about 45k a year on 50m and needs about 300k of balance sheet return, so it doesn't pay. I'd watch it as a signal: CDS rising faster than ASW means hedgers are leading; bonds catching up after Moody's would be the next step."

### How to deliver it
Definition, the three measures and why they differ, then drivers and the balance sheet economics. Link to rfc-060 (theory), rfc-752 (CDS and quanto) and mkt-612 (OAT-Bund).
deep.rfc-754:
### Context / why they ask this
Rating headlines are frequent for France in 2026, and clients always ask the same thing: "Will there be forced selling?" The interviewer wants you to separate the **mechanical** channels (central bank collateral, index rules, mandates, capital) from the **signal** channel (new information about fiscal risk). As of end September 2026: Moody's **Aa3, negative outlook**, review on **23 October**; S&P and Fitch **A+** (both cut in 2025); **Scope** cut France to A+ on 18 September 2026; **DBRS** kept **AA** but moved the trend to negative the same day. OAT-Bund 10y was about 111bp on 29 September and about 117bp on 30 September; France 5y CDS about 65bp (29 September), above Italy at about 50bp. The 2027 budget (PLF) targets a 5% deficit, with a vote expected on 17 November.

### Key concepts
- **Notch**: one step on the rating scale (Aa3 -> A1 at Moody's is like AA- -> A+ at S&P).
- **ECAF and the first-best rule**: the Eurosystem accepts ratings from S&P, Moody's, Fitch, DBRS Morningstar and Scope. For **public sector** assets it uses the **best** available rating. (In 2025 the ECB decided to move to the second-best rating for **private** sector assets only.)
- **Credit quality steps (CQS)**: CQS1 = AAA to AA-, CQS2 = A+ to A-, CQS3 = BBB+ to BBB-, the minimum for eligibility. Haircuts for central government debt are the same for CQS1 and CQS2.
- **Index rating**: Bloomberg indices take the middle of Moody's, S&P and Fitch (the lower if only two, the single one if only one).
- **Mandate rules**: an investment guideline such as "minimum AA-", which can be applied to the lowest, the middle or the best rating.

### Intuition
A downgrade only forces selling if it crosses a **threshold** someone has written into a rule. For France, the big thresholds are far away: ECB eligibility needs BBB- (CQS3), and the index rating is already A+. The one-notch cut changes the **label**, not the plumbing. What can still move prices is the **information**: an agency saying the fiscal path is worse than thought.

### The maths (python-checked, illustrative OAT)
Index rating, middle of three:
| | Moody's | S&P | Fitch | Middle (index) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Today | Aa3 (= AA-) | A+ | A+ | **A+** |
| After a cut | A1 (= A+) | A+ | A+ | **A+** |

ECB first-best: best of {Aa3/A1, A+, A+, AA (DBRS), A+ (Scope)} = **AA**, CQS1. Even if DBRS also cut, A+ = CQS2, same haircut for central government bonds.
Price impact, illustrative 10y OAT with a 3.5% annual coupon at a 4.85% yield: price about 89.50, modified duration about 8.1, DV01 about **EUR 72.7k per EUR 100m**:
$$\Delta P \approx -\text{DV01} \times \Delta s \Rightarrow 5\text{bp} \to -0.36\text{m}, \quad 10\text{bp} \to -0.73\text{m}, \quad 15\text{bp} \to -1.09\text{m}$$
CDS reading: with 40% recovery, 65bp implies a risk-neutral default intensity of about $0.0065/0.6 \approx 1.08\%$ per year (rfc-752 covers the CDS in detail).

### Who could actually sell
- **"AA by every agency" or "lowest rating" mandates**: they mostly crossed their line in 2025, when Fitch and S&P went to A+. A Moody's cut adds little.
- **Some reserve managers and conservative funds** using the middle rating are already looking at A+.
- **Banks**: under EU rules euro area sovereign bonds in euro keep a 0% risk weight, so no capital trigger. **Insurers** (Solvency II): no spread-risk charge on EEA sovereign debt in domestic currency.
- **Repo**: private repo haircuts (CCPs such as LCH) can depend on spreads and ratings; check the CCP's own rules, but a single notch rarely moves them.

### What can go wrong
- **Two agencies on the same week**: if Moody's cuts **and** the outlook stays negative, the market starts to price **A** (two notches) and some single-A thresholds come into view.
- **DBRS**: it is the one agency keeping France in CQS1 at the ECB. A DBRS cut would not change haircuts today, but the headline "France loses its last AA" could matter for sentiment.
- **Budget politics**: a failed vote or a government fall around 17 November is a bigger driver than the notch itself.
- **Liquidity**: OAT-Bund can gap at the Monday open after a Friday evening release.

### What I'd say on the desk
"Moody's at A1 does not change ECB eligibility, haircuts or the Bloomberg index rating, which is already A+. The forced sellers acted in 2025. I'd expect a few basis points of widening at the open, maybe 3-5bp, then the market goes back to the budget. I'd fade OAT-Bund above 120bp with a stop at 130, and keep the CDS (65bp) as the cleaner hedge if the budget fails."

### How to deliver it
Four channels in order (ECB, index, mandates, capital), say "threshold" for each, then the price estimate in DV01 terms. Link to the OAT-Bund widener (mkt-612) and the CDS card (rfc-752).

See also mkt-775 (same question, different angle).

### Context / why they ask this
Credit strategists love to quote IG spreads near their tights. A good desk answer asks: **tight against what?** In September 2026 the benchmark itself is distorted. On 29 September the FRED/ICE BofA US IG OAS was **84bp** (US HY 308bp). At the same time the 10y SOFR swap was about **4.91%** against a 10y Treasury around **5.26-5.29%**: the 10y swap spread is about **-35 to -41bp** (2y about -21bp, 30y about -62bp). The question tests whether you can move between spread measures and say who earns which.

### Key concepts
- **OAS (option-adjusted spread)**: spread of the bond over the Treasury curve, after removing embedded options. ICE indices use Treasuries.
- **Swap spread**: swap rate minus Treasury yield of the same tenor. Negative = Treasuries yield more than swaps.
- **Asset swap spread (ASW)**: the bond's fixed coupon is swapped into floating; the investor earns SOFR + ASW. Roughly, ASW ≈ spread to swaps.
- **Z-spread / I-spread**: spreads over the swap curve (zero or interpolated); close relatives of ASW.
- **Identity**: $s_{swap} = s_{UST} - SS$, with $SS$ the swap spread.

### Intuition
Picture three yields on one line: swap (lowest, 4.91%), Treasury (5.29%), corporate bond (Treasury + 84bp, about 6.13%). The corporate is 84bp above Treasuries but **122bp above swaps**. If Treasuries were back to "normal" (swap spread around zero), the same corporate yield would show an OAS of about 120bp, which nobody would call tight. Treasuries are cheap because of supply and dealer balance sheet costs, not because the government got riskier than banks.

### The maths (python-checked)
Swap spreads from the levels above: 2y $4.69 - 4.90 = -21$bp, 10y $4.91 - 5.29 = -38$bp. Linear interpolation at the 7y index duration:
$$SS_{7y} \approx -21 + \frac{7-2}{10-2}(-38+21) \approx -31.6\text{bp}$$
| Measure | 10y point | Index (about 7y duration) |
|---|---|---|
| OAS vs Treasuries | 84bp | 84bp |
| Swap spread | -38bp | -31.6bp |
| Spread vs SOFR swaps | **122bp** | **about 116bp** |

Breakeven widening over one year (spread carry / duration): $84/7 \approx 12$bp on the Treasury measure, $116/7 \approx 16.5$bp on the swap measure. (Simplified: ignores roll-down and treats the 7y duration as constant.)

### Who earns what
- **Swapped buyers** (bank treasuries buying bonds for their liquidity or loan books, Japanese and European investors who swap and hedge, insurers matching floating liabilities): they earn **SOFR + about 116bp**. For them, credit is fair.
- **Unhedged total-return buyers** (US mutual funds, pension funds against a Treasury benchmark): they compare with Treasuries, and 84bp is near the tights.
- **Relative value**: if swap spreads normalise (Treasuries richen, swap spread goes from -38 to -20bp), the Treasury OAS **widens** by about 18bp with no change in credit risk. That is a hidden risk for anyone hedging corporates with Treasury futures.

### What can go wrong
- **Hedge choice**: a desk that hedges corporate inventory with Treasury futures is long the swap spread by construction; a desk hedging with swaps is not. The P&L of the same bond looks different.
- **Swap spread moves**: a regulatory change (SLR relief) or a slowdown in Treasury supply can richen Treasuries quickly; see mkt-613 for the swap spread tightener and fd-037 for the levels.
- **Index composition**: the IG index has a lot of BBB and long-dated paper; at 30y the swap spread is about -62bp, so the long-end gap is even bigger.
- **Credit risk is still credit risk**: the swap measure does not make defaults or downgrades less likely; it only says what you are paid.

### What I'd say on the desk
"IG is 84 over Treasuries, but Treasuries are 32-38bp cheap to swaps, so the index is about SOFR + 116 on an asset-swap basis and the 10y point is about +122. For a swapped buyer that is fair value, and the breakeven is about 16bp of widening a year. I would not short IG just because the OAS is at the tights; I'd short it only with a credit view, and I'd hedge the rates leg with swaps, not futures."

### How to deliver it
State the identity first, then the three yields on a line, then who earns which spread. Link to mkt-618 (credit spreads), mkt-613 (swap spread trade) and fd-037 (levels).

### Context / why they ask this
AT1 (Additional Tier 1) is the riskiest layer of bank capital that is still a bond, and its call decisions are a classic interview topic since **Santander** skipped a call in 2019 and **Credit Suisse**'s AT1s (about CHF 16bn) were written down in 2023. In 2026 the angle is rates: with the US 2y near 4.9% and the 10y near 5.3%, the 5y Treasury that drives the **reset** is high, which changes the call economics bond by bond. All bond terms and the new-issue yield below are **illustrative**: the logic, not the exact numbers, is what the interviewer wants.

### Key concepts
- **AT1**: perpetual, coupons can be cancelled at the issuer's discretion, converts to equity or is written down if the CET1 ratio falls below a trigger (often 5.125% or 7%).
- **First call date**: usually 5 to 10 years after issue; then often every 5 years (or every coupon date).
- **Reset**: if not called, coupon = 5y Treasury (USD) or 5y mid-swap (EUR) + the **original** reset spread, fixed for the next 5 years.
- **Regulatory approval**: in the EU, calling needs supervisory permission (CRR Articles 77-78): replace with capital of equal or better quality, or show capital well above requirements.
- **Yield to call / yield to extension**: the yield assuming a call at the first date, or assuming the bond runs to the next call at the reset coupon.

### Intuition
The bank owns the call option; the investor is short it. The bank calls when the bond is **expensive** to keep (reset coupon above its new-issue cost) and leaves it outstanding when it is **cheap**. So the investor always gets the worse outcome: the price is roughly the minimum of the "to call" and "to extension" prices. A high 5y rate pushes reset coupons up, so it **reduces** extension risk, the opposite of what many people guess.

### The maths (python-checked, illustrative)
5y Treasury taken at **5.06%**, new-issue AT1 yield **7.25%**, first call in 1 year at par, next call in year 6 at par, annual coupons, all discounted at 7.25%:
| Bond | Coupon to call | Reset spread | Reset coupon | Price to call | Price to extension | Bank's saving if it acts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 4.000% | 2.75% | 7.81% | **96.97** | 99.10 | calls: 56bp/yr |
| B | 3.625% | 2.25% | 7.31% | **96.62** | 96.85 | calls: 6bp/yr (marginal) |
| C | 3.250% | 1.75% | 6.81% | 96.27 | **94.60** | extends: 44bp/yr |

$$c_{reset} = y_{5y} + s_{reset}, \qquad \text{call if } c_{reset} > y_{new\ AT1}$$
For bond A, $P_{call} = 104.00/1.0725 = 96.97$. For bond C, the extension price is 1.67 points below the call price, and if the market assumed it would **never** be called (a perpetual at 6.81%), the price would be about **90.61**. Saving per USD 1bn: bond A about USD 5.6m a year by calling; bond C about USD 4.4m a year by extending.

### What else drives the decision
- **Regulator**: even an economic call can be blocked if capital is tight; a bank under stress may prefer to keep the capital.
- **Reputation**: European banks have mostly called on the first date to keep access to the market; a skipped call can cost more on the next issue than the coupon it saves. Bond B (6bp of saving) will usually be called for that reason.
- **Currency and tax**: the bank compares across currencies (EUR AT1 versus USD AT1, after the cross-currency swap) and tax deductibility of coupons.
- **Spreads**: if AT1 spreads widen (a bank failure, a risk-off), the new-issue yield jumps and bond A can flip to extension.

### What can go wrong
- **Spread shock**: a 100bp widening in new-issue AT1 yields (to 8.25%) would make even bond A (7.81%) an extension candidate.
- **Rate rally**: a fall in the 5y Treasury lowers every reset coupon and raises extension risk across the market.
- **Coupon cancellation and write-down**: the call question sits on top of the real risk, which is loss absorption (Credit Suisse 2023).
- **Liquidity**: AT1s gap on headlines; bid-offer can widen to more than a point.

### What I'd say on the desk
"With 5y Treasuries above 5%, the high-reset AT1s (spreads near 3%) are calls and I'd price them to call; the low-reset 2020-21 paper, with spreads under 2%, resets below new-issue levels, so I price it to extension and want at least 1.5-2 points of discount for that. The trade I like is long the high-reset bonds that the market prices with some extension doubt."

### How to deliver it
Define the reset, give the call rule in one line, then show one call case and one extension case with prices. Mention the regulator and reputation before the interviewer does. For the rates side of the 5y Treasury, see rfc-740; for options logic, rfc-741.

### Context / why they ask this
Japanese life insurers and pension funds are among the largest foreign holders of Treasuries and euro government bonds, and they are **hedged** investors: the FX forward cost decides what they buy. With the BoJ now at **1.25%** and the Fed at **3.75-4.00%** (SOFR about 3.88% on 29 September 2026), hedging dollars is expensive. The question tests whether you can compute a hedged yield, compare it with the domestic alternative, and explain what "repatriation" means for markets. trp-070 covers the same logic with older numbers and mkt-770 the Treasury-versus-JGB choice in 2026; here the point is the comparison with hedged euro paper. The 10y JGB is about 3.07% (30 September 2026); JPY rates, the basis and the OAT yield below are **illustrative**.

### Key concepts
- **FX hedge with forwards**: the investor sells USD forward 3 months, rolls each quarter. By covered interest parity, the forward points pay or cost the rate gap.
- **Hedge cost**: $\approx r_{USD,3m} - r_{JPY,3m} - b$, with $b$ the 3m cross-currency basis (negative $b$ makes hedging dollars more expensive for a yen investor).
- **Hedged yield**: foreign bond yield minus annual hedge cost. It mixes a 10y yield with a 3m funding cost: a **curve trade**, not a pure bond.
- **Hedge ratio**: share of the FX exposure that is hedged; insurers move it between about 0% and 100% depending on the view and on regulation.
- **Repatriation**: selling foreign assets and buying domestic ones; it means buying yen.

### Intuition
Hedging removes the currency risk but gives back the **short-rate difference**. When US short rates are far above Japanese ones, a 5.3% Treasury becomes a 2.5% yen asset. The investor is really earning **the US term premium** (10y minus 3m) plus the basis, not the US yield. When the US curve is flat or the Fed hikes, that premium shrinks.

### The maths (python-checked, illustrative)
| | USD Treasury 10y | EUR OAT 10y | JGB 10y |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yield | 5.29% | 4.85% (illustrative) | 3.07% |
| Foreign 3m rate | SOFR 3.88% | €STR 2.44% | - |
| Yen 3m rate | 1.25% | 1.25% | - |
| Basis cost | 0.15% | 0.10% | - |
| Hedge cost | **2.78%** | **1.29%** | 0 |
| Hedged yield in yen | **2.51%** | **3.56%** | 3.07% |

$$y_{hedged} = y_{10y} - (r_{USD} - r_{JPY} - b) = 5.29 - (3.88 - 1.25 + 0.15) = 2.51\%$$
After a 25bp Fed hike, with nothing else moving: $2.51 - 0.25 = 2.26\%$, about **81bp** below JGBs (56bp below before the hike). A 50% hedge ratio gives $5.29 - 0.5 \times 2.78 = 3.90\%$, but half the position is exposed to USDJPY. The unhedged 5.29% beats the JGB by 2.22% a year: that is how much yen appreciation per year it can absorb before losing.

### What drives repatriation
- **The domestic yield**: each BoJ hike and each rise in JGB yields makes home assets more attractive, and also lowers the hedge cost a little (the yen 3m rate rises).
- **The Fed**: a hike raises the hedge cost one for one; cuts do the opposite.
- **Accounting and regulation**: Japanese insurers face economic solvency rules (ESR) from fiscal year 2025, which reward long-dated yen assets that match their liabilities; this pushes towards 20y-30y JGBs.
- **Market effect**: repatriation means buying yen and selling foreign bonds, often at the long end; it is one reason why big moves in JGB yields can spill into Treasuries and Bunds.

### What can go wrong
