### Context / why they ask this
On a desk you meet two very different data workloads. The booking system must record each trade exactly once, safely, while hundreds of users write at the same time. Research and risk want to scan years of ticks or positions. The interviewer checks that you understand why one database is not good at both, and that your PostgreSQL experience does not make you think it is the answer to everything.

### Key concepts
- **OLTP (online transaction processing)**: short transactions on few rows (insert a trade, update a position); needs ACID guarantees and row-level locking (see cv-254).
- **OLAP (online analytical processing)**: long read-only queries that aggregate many rows (P&L by desk over a year, average spread by hour).
- **Row store**: each row's columns are stored together on disk (PostgreSQL, MySQL). Fast to fetch or update one whole row.
- **Column store**: each column is stored on its own (kdb+, ClickHouse, Parquet files, Snowflake, BigQuery). Fast to scan a few columns over many rows.
- **Compression**: a column of similar values (sorted timestamps, repeated symbols) compresses well, for example by run-length or delta encoding.
- **Vectorised execution**: the engine processes a block of values from one column at a time, which suits CPU caches and SIMD instructions (see cv-249).
- **Time-series database**: optimised for data indexed by time: append-heavy, range queries, time bucketing.
- **kdb+ / q**: a column-oriented database from KX, widely used for tick data in banks and funds; q is its compact array language.
- **As-of join**: for each row of one table, take the latest row of another table at or before that time (each trade gets the quote that was live when it happened).

### Intuition
Think of a spreadsheet of ticks. To change one trade, you want its whole row in one place: row store. To average one column over 100 million rows, you want that column in one place and the other 49 columns out of the way: column store. Disk and memory bandwidth are the bottleneck in analytics, so "read less" is the whole game.

### The maths
Bytes scanned for a query that touches $k$ of $m$ columns, $n$ rows of $b$ bytes each:
$$\text{row store} \approx n \, m \, b, \qquad \text{column store} \approx n \, k \, b$$
The ratio is $m / k$ before compression. With a compression factor $r$, the column store reads about $n k b / r$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
100 million ticks, 50 columns, 8 bytes each (illustrative):
| Query | Row store reads | Column store reads | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average of 1 column | 40 GB | 0.8 GB | 50 |
| 2 columns (symbol and spread) | 40 GB | 1.6 GB | 25 |
| 1 column, compressed 4 to 1 | 40 GB | 0.2 GB | 200 |

The opposite case: fetching one full trade by id. The row store reads one page; the column store must touch 50 separate column files. That is why the booking system stays on a row store.

A typical q query for a one-minute average spread looks like:
```q
select avg ask-bid by sym, 1 xbar time.minute from quote where date=2026.09.30
```
And `` aj[`sym`time; trade; quote] `` attaches the prevailing quote to each trade.

### Common pitfalls
- "Postgres is slow, so it is bad": it is slow at full scans of wide tables, which is not its job. Extensions such as TimescaleDB, or a good index on (symbol, time), help, but a column store is still better for heavy analytics.
- Running large analytical queries on the production OLTP database, slowing down the booking system for everyone.
- Joining trades and quotes on exact timestamps: they almost never match; you need an as-of join, and it must not look into the future (see cv-252 on point-in-time data).
- Forgetting that column stores are poor at frequent updates and deletes of single rows.
- Assuming kdb+ is just "a fast SQL database": its language and data model are different, and it is a licensed product.

### How to deliver it
Give the two definitions in one line each, then the 40 GB versus 0.8 GB example, then the desk split: OLTP for booking, column store for history and research. Be honest about your level: you have used PostgreSQL; you know what kdb+ is for and why, and you would expect to learn q on the job.
deep.cv-350:
### Context / why they ask this
Banks' core pricing and risk libraries are often written in C++, while quants and traders work in Python on top of them. The interviewer checks that you understand *why* the split exists, not just "C++ is fast", and that your CV line matches your real level. cv-039 covers how to describe your level in each language; cv-249 goes deeper into memory layout and caches; qnt-457 covers pointers and memory. This card is about the language model itself.

### Key concepts
- **Compiler**: a program that translates source code into machine code once, ahead of time (for example clang or g++). Optimisation flags such as `-O2` let it rewrite code to run faster.
- **Interpreter**: a program that reads and executes code while it runs. CPython first compiles to **bytecode**, then a loop in C executes each bytecode instruction.
- **Static typing**: types are fixed and checked at compile time (`double x;`). Errors such as adding a string to a number are caught before running.
- **Dynamic typing**: types belong to values, checked at run time (`x = 1.5`, then `x = "a"` is legal).
- **Boxing**: in Python every number is an object with a header and a reference count; a list of floats is an array of pointers to such objects.
- **JIT (just-in-time) compilation**: compiling hot code while the program runs (Numba, PyPy), a middle way.
- **Bindings**: wrappers (pybind11, Cython) that let Python call a C++ library.

### Intuition
In C++, `s += v[i]` on doubles becomes a load, an add and a loop counter. In Python, the same line means: fetch the object `v[i]`, look up its type, find the `__add__` for float plus float, allocate a new float object for the result, update reference counts, and move to the next bytecode. Same mathematics, tens of times more work per element. NumPy wins back the speed because the loop over the array runs in compiled code, once per call, not once per element in Python.

### The maths
If the per-element cost is $c$ and the fixed overhead per call is $h$, the time for $n$ elements is $T(n) = h + c\,n$. Pure Python has a large $c$; NumPy has a small $c$ but a call overhead $h$, so it only wins on arrays, not on one scalar at a time. That is why vectorising (one call on a whole array) matters more than micro-optimising a Python loop.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Sum of $x_i \times 1.0000001$ over 10 million doubles, measured on one laptop (Apple clang, CPython, NumPy; your numbers will differ, the ratios are the point):
| Version | Time | Per element |
|---|---|---|
| C++ with `-O2` | 15.7 ms | 1.57 ns |
| C++ with `-O0` (no optimisation) | 56.6 ms | 5.66 ns |
| Pure Python `for` loop | 1.15 s | 115 ns |
| NumPy `(a * 1.0000001).sum()` | 7.1 ms | 0.71 ns |

So pure Python is about 73 times slower than optimised C++, and optimisation alone is worth a factor of about 3.6. NumPy even beats this simple C++ loop by about 2.2, because it uses SIMD instructions and pairwise summation, while the compiler may not reorder floating-point additions in the C++ loop (that would change the rounding). Lesson: "C++ is fast" assumes you write it well and compile it with optimisation.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "Python is slow" without nuance: well-vectorised NumPy or pandas code is close to C speed.
- Forgetting compile-time safety as an advantage of C++: many bugs are caught before running, but others (memory errors, undefined behaviour, see cv-351) are not.
- Overclaiming C++: templates, move semantics, multi-threading and large builds are a real learning curve. Say what you have actually written.
- Benchmarking a debug build (`-O0`) and concluding C++ is barely faster.
- Ignoring development time: a model prototyped in Python in one day may never need C++ if it runs once a night.

### How to deliver it
One sentence each on compiled versus interpreted and static versus dynamic typing, then the 10-million sum with its numbers, then the desk split (C++ libraries, Python research and glue). End with an honest, specific statement of your C++ level; interviewers value it more than a vague "advanced".

### Context / why they ask this
Excel is still the common language on desks and in corporate finance. The NPV off-by-one is the most frequent spreadsheet error in valuation, and interviewers love it because it looks right: the formula has no error and the number is plausible. Knowing the trap shows you check what a built-in function actually computes. cv-256 covers building a pricer in Excel; this card is about the cash-flow functions.

### Key concepts
- **Present value**: a cash flow $C$ received in $t$ years is worth $C / (1+r)^t$ today at rate $r$.
- **NPV (net present value)**: the sum of present values of all flows, including the initial cost (negative).
- **Excel `NPV(rate, values)`**: computes $\sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i / (1+r)^i$. The first value is discounted one period.
- **IRR (internal rate of return)**: the rate $r^*$ such that NPV is zero. Excel's `IRR(values)` assumes the first value is at time 0 and the others one period apart.
- **XNPV / XIRR**: versions with dates; the exponent is (date minus first date) in days divided by 365.
- **Periodic vs annual rate**: a monthly rate $i$ is $(1+i)^{12} - 1$ effective per year; $12 i$ is the nominal annual rate.

### Intuition
`NPV` was designed for "a stream of flows starting next period". If your first flow is today, it is not part of that stream, so add it outside. IRR is a root of a polynomial: one sign change in the flows guarantees exactly one positive root (by Descartes' rule of signs), more sign changes can give several roots or none. XIRR rewards speed: the same euros arriving earlier mean a much higher annual rate.

### The maths
$$\text{NPV} = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{C_t}{(1+r)^t}, \qquad \texttt{NPV}(r, C_0..C_n) = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{C_t}{(1+r)^{t+1}} = \frac{\text{NPV}}{1+r}$$
For XIRR, with $d_i$ the dates:
$$\sum_i \frac{C_i}{(1+r)^{(d_i - d_0)/365}} = 0$$
Multiple IRRs: $-100 + 230x - 132x^2 = 0$ with $x = 1/(1+r)$ has roots $x = 1/1.1$ and $x = 1/1.2$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Flows -1,000, 300, 400, 500, 200 at 10%:
| Formula | Result | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| True NPV | 115.57 | time-0 flow not discounted |
| `=NPV(10%,B1:B5)` | 105.06 | = 115.57 / 1.1, wrong |
| `=B1+NPV(10%,B2:B5)` | 115.57 | correct |
| `=IRR(B1:B5)` | 15.32% | yearly flows |
| `=XIRR(B1:B5,A1:A5)` | 36.51% | dates 2026-01-01, 2026-03-01, 2026-12-31, 2027-06-30, 2028-01-01 |
| `=XNPV(10%,B1:B5,A1:A5)` | 258.11 | XNPV does not shift the first flow |

Multiple IRRs: -100, 230, -132 gives NPV zero at both 10% and 20%; Excel returns whichever root is closest to its starting guess, so the answer depends on the guess.
Monthly: -1,000 then twelve payments of 90: `IRR` returns 1.2043% per month; times 12 gives 14.45% nominal; $(1.012043)^{12} - 1$ gives 15.45% effective.

### Common pitfalls
- Using `NPV` on a range that starts with today's flow (the classic).
- Mixing periodic rate and annual rate: a monthly IRR quoted as if it were annual, or a yearly rate fed to `NPV` on monthly flows.
- Trusting IRR when flows change sign several times (projects with a large final clean-up cost, or a loan from the borrower's side with fees): compute NPV at the cost of capital instead.
- Ranking projects by IRR: a small project with a high IRR can create less value than a large one with a lower IRR. NPV is the decision rule.
- Empty cells or text in the range: `NPV` ignores them silently, so a missing year just disappears instead of counting as zero.
- XIRR returns an error if no sign change exists or the guess is far off; give it a guess.

### How to deliver it
Say "no, NPV discounts the first flow", give 105.06 versus 115.57 and the fix, then list the IRR traps in one breath: multiple roots, regular periods only (use XIRR), and periodic versus annual rate. If you have time, add that NPV, not IRR, is what you decide on.
deep.cv-353:
### Context / why they ask this
Sales, structuring and research produce slides every day: pitch books, trade ideas, market updates. A treasurer or portfolio manager gives each slide a few seconds. The interviewer checks that you can turn analysis into a message a client will act on, which is a real skill behind the "PowerPoint" line on a CV. It is not about animations or colours.

### Key concepts
- **Action title (headline)**: a sentence at the top of the slide that states the conclusion, ideally in two lines or fewer. The body proves it.
- **Topic title**: a label such as "Market overview". It tells the reader what the slide is about, not what to think. Avoid it.
- **Minto pyramid (Pyramid Principle)**: Barbara Minto's method from McKinsey: start with the governing idea, then group supporting arguments below it; each level summarises the level beneath.
- **SCQA**: Situation, Complication, Question, Answer; a way to write the introduction so the reader arrives at the question your answer solves.
- **MECE**: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive; the supporting points should not overlap and should together cover the case.
- **Horizontal logic**: reading the titles of all slides in a row tells the story. **Vertical logic**: on each slide, everything under the title supports it.
- **Ghost deck**: a draft with only the titles and sketches of the charts, written before any analysis is finished, to agree on the storyline.
- **Appendix**: where detail, methodology and backup tables go.

### Intuition
Readers are busy and read top-down. If the conclusion is at the bottom, many never get there. Putting the answer first feels unnatural to scientists, who are trained to go from data to conclusion, but a client wants the conclusion and then the reasons to trust it.

### The maths
There is little maths in a slide, but the numbers on it must be exact and consistent. For an importer paying USD $N$ per quarter at rate $S$ (USD per EUR), the cost in euros is $N / S$. A fall in $S$ raises the cost:
$$\Delta = \frac{N}{S_1} - \frac{N}{S_0}$$

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Illustrative client: pays USD 20m per quarter, spot EUR/USD 1.10.
| EUR/USD | Cost in EUR per quarter | Change vs today |
|---|---|---|
| 1.10 (today) | 18.18m | 0 |
| 1.045 (5% lower) | 19.14m | +0.96m |

Over four quarters, the extra cost would be about EUR 3.83m. The slide:
- **Title**: "A 5% fall in EUR/USD would cost you about EUR 0.96m a quarter; a forward locks in today's rate."
- **Body**: one small table or bar chart of the cost at three or four rates, a line showing the hedged cost, and two bullets: what a forward does, and what you give up (the gain if EUR/USD rises).
- **Footer**: source of the rates, date, "indicative, not an offer" (the forward price would include the interest rate differential, not just spot).
Pyramid behind it: answer (hedge 50% to 75% of the next four quarters) supported by three reasons: the budget is fixed in euros, the exposure is large relative to margin, and the cost of hedging is known today.

### Common pitfalls
- Topic titles ("Overview", "Analysis") that force the reader to guess the point.
- Two messages on one slide: the reader keeps neither.
- Charts without units, dates or sources; inconsistent numbers between the title and the table.
- Showing the method before the answer, in the order you did the work.
- Text walls: if you would read it aloud, it belongs in the speaker notes or the appendix.
- Overselling: a client slide on a hedge must show the downside (lost upside if the rate moves your way). Compliance will check it.

### How to deliver it
Say the title out loud first, then explain the pyramid and SCQA in one sentence each, then describe what is in the body and what goes to the appendix. End with the titles-only test. If they push, add that you write the ghost deck first and fill the analysis after.
deep.cv-354:
### Context / why they ask this
Every backtest is a hypothesis test, whether you write it down or not. The interviewer checks that you know the two ways to be wrong, that a "significant" result can still be a false positive, and that an honest test can simply lack the data to detect a real effect. It connects directly to the z-test and testing protocol on your CV. Related cards: qnt-505 (testing a proportion, sample size), qnt-036 to qnt-038 (statistics), and the project deck for the details of your own test.

### Key concepts
- **Null hypothesis $H_0$**: the boring default, for example "the strategy's mean return is zero".
- **Alternative $H_1$**: what you hope to show, for example "the mean is positive".
- **Significance level $\alpha$**: the probability of a type I error you accept, often 5%.
- **Type I error**: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true (false positive).
- **Type II error**: not rejecting $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true (false negative), probability $\beta$.
- **Power**: $1 - \beta$, the probability of detecting a real effect. It grows with the effect size and the sample size.
- **p-value**: the probability, if $H_0$ is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
- **z-test**: uses the normal distribution; valid when the standard deviation is known or $n$ is large.
- **t-test**: uses Student's t distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom when the standard deviation is estimated from the sample.
- **Multiple testing**: running many tests raises the chance that at least one is a false positive.

### Intuition
The test sets a bar. A high bar (small $\alpha$) means few false positives but more missed real effects; a low bar the opposite. The only way to reduce both errors at once is more data or a bigger effect. Markets are noisy: a Sharpe of 1 is a very good strategy, yet in one year of data it is indistinguishable from luck most of the time.

### The maths
With daily returns, the annualised Sharpe estimate over $T$ years has a standard error of roughly $1/\sqrt{T}$ (normal returns, small Sharpe), so the test statistic is about $\text{SR}\sqrt{T}$. For a one-sided test at level $\alpha$:
$$\text{power} = 1 - \Phi\left(z_{1-\alpha} - \text{SR}\sqrt{T}\right), \qquad T_{80\%} = \left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha} + z_{0.8}}{\text{SR}}\right)^2$$
With $z_{0.95} = 1.645$ and $z_{0.8} = 0.842$. For a sample mean: $t = \bar{x} / (s / \sqrt{n})$, compared with a t distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.
Multiple tests: $P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m$ for $m$ independent tests.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Power to detect a true Sharpe of 1, one-sided 5%:
| Years of data | Power |
|---|---|
| 1 | 26.0% |
| 2 | 40.9% |
| 4 | 63.9% |
| 10 | 93.5% |

80% power needs about 6.18 years.
Small sample: $n = 10$, $\bar{x} = 0.8$, $s = 1.2$, so the statistic is 2.108.
| Test | Critical value (two-sided 5%) | p-value | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| z (wrong here) | 1.96 | 0.035 | reject |
| t with 9 df | 2.262 | 0.064 | do not reject |

With 30 observations the t critical value is 2.045, already close to 1.96: the difference matters for small samples.
20 independent strategies tested at 5%: $1 - 0.95^{20} = 64.2\%$ chance of at least one false positive; the Bonferroni fix tests each at $0.05 / 20 = 0.0025$.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "p = 0.04 means a 96% chance the strategy works": the p-value is computed assuming $H_0$ is true; it is not the probability that $H_0$ is false.
- Treating "not significant" as "no effect": with low power, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- Using a z-test on 10 points with an estimated standard deviation.
- Ignoring dependence: overlapping or clustered signals are not independent, which inflates the z (this is why a cluster bootstrap exists).
- Testing many variants and reporting only the best (multiple testing, data snooping).
- Choosing the test after seeing the data, instead of fixing it in advance.

### How to deliver it
Define the two errors with the strategy example, give the power table and the 6.18-year figure to show you know how noisy markets are, then the z versus t rule with the 10-observation example where the verdict flips. Finish with multiple testing in one sentence.
deep.cv-355:
### Context / why they ask this
Every trading desk is limited by VaR or ES, and every risk interview contains a version of this question. The trap is not the definition, it is the hand calculation and the subtle point that ES 97.5% and VaR 99% are almost equal under a normal law. Here we focus on computation; the limits of VaR and the sub-additivity example are in mkt-068 and trp-039, and extreme value theory at 99.9% in cv-259.

### Key concepts
- **P&L**: profit and loss; a loss $L$ is minus the P&L.
- **VaR at level $\alpha$**: the $\alpha$ quantile of the loss distribution. "1-day 99% VaR of 23k" means a daily loss above 23k happens on about 1 day in 100.
- **Expected shortfall (ES), also CVaR**: the expected loss given that the loss is beyond the $\alpha$ quantile.
- **Parametric (variance-covariance) method**: assume a distribution, usually normal, and use its formula.
- **Historical simulation**: take the last $N$ days of real market moves, revalue today's portfolio under each one, and read the quantile from the sorted results.
- **Fat tails**: extreme moves more frequent than the normal law predicts; measured by kurtosis.
- **FRTB**: the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book, the Basel market risk framework that replaced 99% VaR by 97.5% ES for internal models.
- **Square-root-of-time rule**: scale a 1-day risk to $h$ days by $\sqrt{h}$.

### Intuition
VaR is the height of the wall at the edge of the cliff; ES is the average depth of the drop beyond it. Two portfolios can have the same wall but very different drops. Under a normal law the drop beyond 97.5% averages almost exactly the 99% quantile, so the regulator kept roughly the same level of capital for "normal" portfolios while making fat-tailed ones pay more.

### The maths
For a normal loss with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sigma$:
$$\text{VaR}_\alpha = \sigma z_\alpha, \qquad \text{ES}_\alpha = \sigma \frac{\varphi(z_\alpha)}{1-\alpha}$$
where $\varphi$ is the standard normal density. Numerically $z_{0.99} = 2.326$, $\varphi(z_{0.975})/0.025 = 2.338$, and $\text{ES}_{0.99} = 2.665$.
For a Student t with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, scaled to unit variance by $\sqrt{(\nu-2)/\nu}$, with $\nu = 4$: $\text{VaR}_{0.99} = 2.649$ and $\text{ES}_{0.975} = 2.824$.
Scaling: $\text{VaR}_{10d} = \sqrt{10}\, \text{VaR}_{1d}$, so $2.326 \sqrt{10} = 7.357$ and $2.338 \sqrt{10} = 7.393$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
**Parametric**: position 1 million euros, daily volatility 1%, so $\sigma$ = 10,000 euros. VaR 99% = 23,263 euros; ES 97.5% = 23,378 euros.
**Historical**: 250 days, the 7 worst losses in thousands of euros are 9.1, 7.4, 6.0, 5.2, 4.8, 4.5, 4.1.
| Measure | Rule | Result |
|---|---|---|
| VaR 99% | 2.5 losses in the tail, take the 3rd worst | 6.0 |
| VaR 99% (interpolated) | halfway between 2nd and 3rd | 6.7 |
| ES 97.5% | tail of 6.25 losses: (9.1+7.4+6.0+5.2+4.8+4.5 + 0.25 x 4.1) / 6.25 | 6.084 |

Different conventions give different VaR numbers from the same data; a bank fixes one and documents it.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "VaR is the maximum loss": it is a threshold, losses can be much larger.
- Comparing ES 97.5% with ES 99% instead of VaR 99%.
- Applying $\sqrt{10}$ to returns that are autocorrelated or have volatility clustering.
- Forgetting that historical VaR only knows the past window: a calm year gives a low VaR before a crisis.
- Mixing up loss sign conventions (losses positive versus P&L negative).

### How to deliver it
Define both measures in one sentence, then give the normal numbers 2.326 and 2.338 and say why they are close, then the fat-tail numbers 2.649 and 2.824. Do the historical tail count out loud (1% of 250 = 2.5). Finish with the reasons for the switch: tail size and sub-additivity.
deep.cv-356:
### Context / why they ask this
Student loans are a standard product of French retail banks: the student borrows during studies and repays after graduation. Because Pierre's CV mentions supporting a student loans team, an interviewer can test whether he understands the product's mechanics with simple time-value-of-money maths. The analysis side (PD, LGD, EAD, State guarantee) is in cv-319; this card is about the cash flows.

### Key concepts
- **Principal**: the amount borrowed, here 20,000 euros.
- **Nominal annual rate**: 4% a year; the monthly rate is $r = 0.04/12$.
- **Deferral (différé)**: a period at the start where the borrower does not repay the principal.
- **Total deferral**: no payment at all; interest is capitalised.
- **Partial deferral**: the borrower pays only the interest; the principal stays the same.
- **Capitalised interest**: unpaid interest added to the principal, so it earns interest itself.
- **Annuity (amortising loan)**: constant monthly payments that cover interest and repay part of the principal each month.
- **APR / TAEG**: the annual cost including fees and insurance, used for legal comparisons and the usury cap (see cv-359).
- **EAD**: exposure at default, how much the bank can lose if the borrower stops paying.

### Intuition
During a total deferral the debt snowballs: each month's interest is added and next month's interest is computed on a bigger amount. A partial deferral stops the snowball by paying the interest as it comes. The longer the money stays borrowed, the more it costs, so the earliest repayment is always the cheapest for the student, and the most comfortable is the most expensive.

### The maths
Principal after a total deferral of $d$ months:
$$K = P (1+r)^{d}$$
Constant payment that repays $K$ in $n$ months:
$$M = K \frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-n}}$$
Total interest cost = sum of all payments minus $P$. The annuity formula comes from setting the present value of $n$ payments equal to the principal: $K = M \sum_{k=1}^{n} (1+r)^{-k}$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
$P$ = 20,000 euros, 4% a year, $r = 0.04/12$, 24 months of deferral then 60 months of repayment.
| Option | During 24 months | Payment over 60 months | Total interest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total deferral | 0, debt grows to 21,662.86 | 398.95 | 3,937.27 |
| Partial deferral | 66.67 a month (1,600 in total) | 368.33 | 3,699.83 |
| No deferral, 60 months | starts at once | 368.33 | 2,099.83 |
| No deferral, 84 months | starts at once | 273.38 | 2,963.59 |

The capitalised interest is 1,662.86 euros, more than the 1,600 euros of interest paid in a partial deferral, because of monthly compounding. With annual compounding you would get 21,632 euros, a classic small error.

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting that interest runs during a total deferral: the payment is not 20,000 over 60 months.
- Using the annual rate in the monthly formula, or dividing the effective annual rate by 12 without saying so.
- Comparing total interest only: the 84-month loan has a lower payment but costs more than the 60-month one.
- Forgetting insurance and fees, which are part of the TAEG.
- For the bank, ignoring that EAD rises during the deferral, from 20,000 to 21,662.86 euros.

### How to deliver it
State the two formulas, compute the capitalised principal, then the payment. Give the comparison table in words: the deferral is comfort paid for with about 1,800 euros of extra interest versus no deferral. Close with the bank's view: exposure grows and repayment starts only when the graduate has an income, which is why these loans are often guaranteed (see cv-319).
deep.cv-357:
### Context / why they ask this
Pricing is where credit risk becomes money. The interviewer checks that you know a loan is not profitable just because its rate is above the funding cost: expected losses and the capital the regulator requires must be paid for too. The same building blocks price a corporate loan (see cf-056 for the corporate RAROC); here they are applied to a student loan, with the guarantee angle from cv-319.

### Key concepts
- **Funding cost**: the rate the bank pays on the money it lends (deposits, bonds, internal transfer price from treasury).
- **PD**: probability of default over one year.
- **LGD**: loss given default, the share of the exposure lost after recoveries.
- **EL (expected loss)**: $PD \times LGD \times EAD$; an average cost, priced into the margin like a cost of goods.
- **RWA (risk-weighted assets)**: the exposure times a regulatory risk weight; retail loans get 75% under the standardised approach (see cv-362).
- **Capital ratio**: equity the bank holds per euro of RWA; we use 12% of CET1 as an illustrative target including buffers.
- **Cost of equity / hurdle rate**: the return shareholders require, here 10%.
- **RAROC**: risk-adjusted return on capital, (revenues - costs - EL) / capital; the loan creates value if RAROC exceeds the hurdle.
- **Guarantee**: a third party, here the State through Bpifrance, covers part of the loss.

### Intuition
Think of three bills the borrower's rate must pay: the supplier of money (funding), the average breakages (expected loss) and the shareholders who absorb the unexpected losses (capital). Expected loss is paid every year like insurance; capital is the cushion for bad years, and that cushion is expensive because equity holders want a high return. A guarantee shrinks both the breakages and the cushion.

### The maths
With $f$ the funding rate, $c$ the operating cost, $k$ the capital per euro of loan and $r_E$ the cost of equity:
$$y_{min} = f + PD \cdot LGD + c + (r_E - f)\, k$$
The term $(r_E - f)k$ appears because the capital also funds part of the loan, so it saves funding cost. RAROC at a rate $y$:
$$\text{RAROC} = \frac{y - f(1-k) - PD \cdot LGD - c}{k}$$
Setting RAROC equal to $r_E$ gives back $y_{min}$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Loan 20,000 euros, $f$ = 3%, PD = 1.5%, LGD = 45%, $c$ = 0.5%, risk weight 75%, capital ratio 12%, $r_E$ = 10%.
| Block | Calculation | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| Funding | 3% | 3.000% |
| Expected loss | 1.5% x 45% | 0.675% (135 euros) |
| Operating cost | 0.5% | 0.500% |
| Capital charge | (10% - 3%) x 9% | 0.630% |
| Minimum rate | sum | 4.805% |

Capital = 9% of 20,000 = 1,800 euros. RAROC: 1.06% at a 4% rate, 10% at 4.805%, 12.17% at 5%.
With a 70% State guarantee, illustrative and assuming the guaranteed part is eligible for a 0% weight: EL = 0.2025%, capital = 2.7%, capital charge = 0.189%, minimum rate about 3.89%.

### Common pitfalls
- Comparing the loan rate with the funding cost only: margin 1% looks fine but RAROC is about 1%.
- Treating expected loss as a risk to hold capital against: capital covers unexpected loss, EL is a cost.
- Forgetting that capital replaces some funding, which double-counts cost.
- Ignoring relationship value: banks accept a low RAROC on student loans because the client may stay for decades (see cv-360).
- Forgetting the legal cap: the rate including fees must stay under the usury rate (see cv-359).

### How to deliver it
Build the rate block by block out loud, with one number each, then give the total 4.805%. Then RAROC at 4%, and the conclusion: a 4% student loan without a guarantee destroys value on a stand-alone basis, so the guarantee and the lifetime value of the client are what make the product work. Say the numbers are illustrative.
deep.cv-358:
### Context / why they ask this
IFRS 9 replaced IAS 39 in 2018 after the crisis showed that provisioning only incurred losses was "too little, too late". Every bank's results depend on it, and student loans are a good test case because of the deferral: the borrower pays nothing for years, so "days past due", the usual warning signal, is silent. This card is the retail version of cf-717 (IFRS 9 for corporates); PD, LGD and EAD are explained in cv-319.

### Key concepts
- **ECL (expected credit loss)**: probability-weighted, discounted credit loss; roughly PD x LGD x EAD summed over time.
- **12-month ECL**: losses from defaults that may happen in the next 12 months.
- **Lifetime ECL**: losses from defaults over the whole remaining life.
- **Stage 1 / 2 / 3**: performing, significantly deteriorated, credit-impaired.
- **SICR (significant increase in credit risk)**: the test that moves a loan to stage 2; it compares the risk now with the risk at origination. 30 days past due is a backstop (rebuttable presumption), not the main criterion.
- **Default**: usually 90 days past due or unlikely to pay.
- **EIR (effective interest rate)**: the loan's own rate, used to discount expected losses.
- **Forward-looking information**: ECL must include macroeconomic scenarios (for example graduate unemployment), weighted by probability.
- **Cliff effect**: the jump in provision when a loan moves from 12-month to lifetime ECL.

### Intuition
Stage 1 says: this borrower is fine, I set aside for the next year's bad luck. Stage 2 says: things got worse, I now set aside for everything that can go wrong until the loan ends. For a long loan with a deferral, "until the end" means many years, so the provision can multiply by four or five overnight. Stage 3 says: the loss has mostly happened, I now estimate how much I will not recover.

### The maths
With annual PD $p$, constant LGD and EAD, and discount rate $r$:
$$\text{ECL}_{12m} = p \cdot LGD \cdot EAD$$
$$\text{ECL}_{life} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} (1-p)^{t-1} p \cdot \frac{LGD \cdot EAD}{(1+r)^t}$$
The weight $(1-p)^{t-1}p$ is the probability of defaulting exactly in year $t$. Cumulative lifetime PD is $1-(1-p)^T$: with $p = 4\%$ and $T = 6$, it is 21.72%.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
1,000 loans of 20,000 euros (20 million euros), LGD 45%, EIR 4%, EAD kept constant for simplicity.
| Stage | Loans | Rule | ECL per loan | ECL total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 920 | 12-month PD 1% | 90 | 82,800 |
| 2 | 60 | 4% a year, 6 years left, discounted | 1,716.19 | 102,971 |
| 3 | 20 | defaulted, LGD 45% | 9,000 | 180,000 |
| Total | 1,000 | | | 365,771 (1.83%) |

For the 60 stage 2 loans a 12-month ECL would have been 360 euros each, 21,600 in total: the move to stage 2 multiplies the provision by almost five.
Deferral effect: with a 24-month total deferral at 4%, EAD grows to 21,662.86 euros (see cv-356), so even a stage 1 provision rises to about 97.48 euros per loan.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying stage 2 means "past due": SICR is about change in risk since origination, and days past due are only a backstop.
- Relying on days past due during a deferral: no payment is due, so the bank needs other signals (exam results, graduation, employment, bureau data).
- Forgetting the discounting and the macro scenarios.
- Confusing IFRS 9 provisions (accounting) with regulatory capital (Basel): provisions cover expected loss, capital covers unexpected loss.
- Ignoring the guarantee: a State guarantee reduces LGD on the covered part (see cv-319).

### How to deliver it
Explain the three stages in one line each, insist that SICR compares with origination, then give the portfolio table and the cliff effect number (360 versus 1,716 euros per loan). Finish with the student-loan twist: during the deferral, days past due tell you nothing, so you need forward-looking signals.
deep.cv-359:
### Context / why they ask this
On the CV line "student loans team, 500k+ euros of loan applications analysed", an interviewer can check that you know the rules every French loan officer applies without thinking. Two of them are classic traps: the usury rate (a price ceiling, for every loan) and the HCSF rule (an affordability cap, for mortgages only). Mixing them up, or saying the 35% rule applies to a student loan, is a quick red flag. Figures below are as of October 2026 and change every quarter.

### Key concepts
- **TAEG (taux annuel effectif global)**: the all-in annual cost of a loan, interest plus mandatory fees and insurance. It is what is compared with the usury rate.
- **Usury rate**: the legal maximum TAEG, by category (consumer loans by amount, mortgages by length and type). Lending above it is a criminal offence and the excess interest is refunded.
- **How it is set**: average effective rate observed by the Banque de France in the previous quarter, increased by one third, published in the Journal officiel before each quarter.
- **HCSF (Haut Conseil de stabilité financière)**: the French macroprudential authority. Its decision D-HCSF-2021-7 made the mortgage criteria legally binding on banks from 1 January 2022.
- **Debt-to-income ratio (taux d'effort)**: total monthly loan payments, insurance included, divided by net monthly income.
- **Flexibility margin**: 20% of each bank's quarterly mortgage production may exceed the criteria, mostly reserved for primary residences and first-time buyers.

### Intuition
The usury rate protects the borrower against an excessive price; the HCSF rule protects the financial system against households borrowing too much for housing. One is about the rate, the other about the amount and length. A student loan is a consumer loan: it faces the first but not the second, until the day it becomes a monthly payment inside a mortgage application.

### The maths
Usury rate: $u = \tfrac{4}{3} \times \bar{t}$, where $\bar{t}$ is the average effective rate of the previous quarter. For consumer loans above 6,000 euros, an average of 6.42% gives 6.42 x 4/3 = 8.56%.
Borrowing capacity with payment $m$, monthly rate $i$ and $n$ months: $K = m \cdot \frac{1-(1+i)^{-n}}{i}$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Usury grid applicable from 1 October 2026 (Banque de France):
| Category | Ceiling (TAEG) |
|---|---|
| Consumer loan up to 3,000 euros | 23.60% |
| Consumer loan 3,000 to 6,000 euros | 15.76% |
| Consumer loan above 6,000 euros | 8.56% |
| Fixed mortgage under 10 years | 4.09% |
| Fixed mortgage 10 to 20 years | 4.68% |
| Fixed mortgage 20 years or more | 5.40% |

A student loan of 20,000 euros at 4% plus fees is well below 8.56%, so usury is not a constraint today; it was one for mortgages in 2022-2023, when market rates rose faster than the backward-looking ceiling.
HCSF effect on a later mortgage: net income 2,800 euros a month, cap 35% x 2,800 = 980 euros. Student loan payment 368.33 euros (20,000 euros with partial deferral, see cv-356), so 611.67 euros remain. At 3.5% over 25 years ($n = 300$): capacity 122,182 euros, versus 195,756 euros without the student loan, a loss of about 37%.

### Common pitfalls
- Applying the 35% cap to a student loan or a car loan on its own: it is a mortgage rule.
- Forgetting that insurance is inside both the TAEG and the 35% ratio.
- Comparing the nominal rate with the usury rate instead of the TAEG.
- Quoting the grid as fixed: it changes every quarter, so always say "as of".
- Thinking usury is only a consumer-credit issue: it blocked mortgages when rates rose quickly.

### How to deliver it
Separate the two rules in one sentence (price ceiling for all loans, affordability cap for mortgages only), give the current consumer ceiling with its date, then show the interaction with the 980 versus 611.67 euro example. It shows you understand the client's whole credit life, which is why banks like student loans.
deep.cv-360:
### Context / why they ask this
"2 partnerships signed with schools and the entrepreneurial ecosystem" is a sales line; an interviewer on a desk wants to see if you understand the economics behind it. The answer is the same logic as any subscription business (see cf-513 for LTV/CAC in SaaS): pay to acquire a client early, when they are cheap to win and loyal, and earn the margin later. The student loan is the hook because the first lender often keeps the main account.

### Key concepts
- **Margin per year**: net revenue from the client minus the cost of serving them (not the revenue alone).
- **Retention rate**: probability that a client present this year is still a client next year. The probability of still being a client after $t-1$ years is the retention rate to the power $t-1$.
- **Discount rate**: the bank's cost of capital; money earned in 20 years is worth much less than money earned today.
- **CLV (customer lifetime value)**: discounted, retention-weighted sum of future margins.
- **CAC (customer acquisition cost)**: total cost of the partnership divided by the clients it brings.
- **Entry product**: a product sold at low margin to start a relationship (student loan, free account).

### Intuition
A student is a client with little money today but a high chance of earning a salary soon, and people rarely change their main bank. The bank accepts low or even negative margins for five years in exchange for decades of salary-account, card, insurance and mortgage margin. The partnership with a school is a cheap way to meet hundreds of these future clients at once.

### The maths
With margin $m_t$, retention $\rho$, discount rate $d$ and horizon $T$, margins received at the start of each year:
$$\text{CLV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} m_t \, \frac{\rho^{t-1}}{(1+d)^{t-1}}$$
The partnership is worth signing if $N \cdot c \cdot \text{CLV} > K$, with $K$ its cost, $N$ students and conversion rate $c$, which is the same as $\text{CLV} > \text{CAC}$.

### Worked example (verified numerically, illustrative assumptions)
$m_t = 40$ for $t \le 5$, $m_t = 300$ after, $d = 8\%$, $T = 40$.
| Retention | CLV (euros) |
|---|---|
| 85% | 556 |
| 90% | 866 |
| 92% | 1,054 |
| 95% | 1,455 |

At 92%: 148.89 euros from the student years, 905.01 from after graduation.
Partnership: 500 students x 20% = 100 clients, cost 30,000 euros, CAC = 300 euros, net value 100 x 1,053.9 - 30,000 = 75,390 euros. Break-even retention (CLV = CAC = 300): about 76.7%.

### Common pitfalls
- Using revenue instead of margin: the CLV becomes far too large.
- Forgetting to discount: 300 euros a year for 35 years is not 10,500 euros today.
- Ignoring credit risk: the student loan has an expected loss (see cv-358), which must be subtracted in the early years.
- Treating retention as a detail: going from 90% to 95% adds about 68% to the CLV.
- Presenting these numbers as the bank's own: they are assumptions to show the method.

### How to deliver it
Start with the sentence "the bank buys the client of the next 40 years", write the CLV formula, give the retention table, then the partnership calculation with the CAC. Close with the lesson: retention and the conversion rate are what the partnership must deliver, which is exactly what the follow-up work after signing (events, onboarding, keeping the school relationship alive) is for.
deep.cv-361:
### Context / why they ask this
"I analysed student loan applications" invites the question: with what tool? Retail credit decisions in banks are largely driven by scorecards, and a risk interviewer checks that you know how one works, how it is read and how it is judged. It also tests your statistics: logistic regression, odds, ROC curve. Do not claim you built a scorecard at BNP; answer the technical question. The loss side (PD × LGD × EAD, State guarantee) is in cv-319.

### Key concepts
- **Good / bad**: the target. "Bad" is typically 90+ days past due within a fixed window (often 12 months) after the loan starts.
- **Odds**: $P(\text{good})/P(\text{bad})$. Odds of 50 to 1 means a PD of $1/51 \approx 1.96\%$.
- **PD** (probability of default): $1/(1+\text{odds})$ here.
- **Binning and WoE**: each variable (age, income, school, banking history) is cut into bins; each bin gets a *weight of evidence* $\ln(\%\text{goods}/\%\text{bads})$. This makes the relation monotone and robust to outliers.
- **PDO** (points to double the odds): how many points you add when the odds double.
- **AUC / Gini**: rank-ordering power of the score. **KS** is another common measure (max gap between the cumulative score distributions of goods and bads).
- **Reject inference**: guessing how rejected applicants would have behaved.

### Intuition
The bank wants a number a credit officer can read without statistics: "+35 points for a stable income bin, −20 for no banking history". The logistic model gives additive log-odds, so after scaling each characteristic contributes additive points. The score ranks people; the cut-off (accept above 560, say) is a business choice that trades volume against losses.

### The maths
Logistic model: $P(\text{good}\mid x) = 1/(1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta^\top x)})$, fitted by maximum likelihood.
Scaling: choose a target score $S_0$ at odds $o_0$ and a PDO. Then
$$\text{Factor} = \frac{\text{PDO}}{\ln 2},\qquad \text{Offset} = S_0 - \text{Factor}\cdot\ln o_0.$$
AUC equals the Mann-Whitney statistic: over all (good, bad) pairs, count 1 when the good scores higher, 0.5 for a tie, and divide by the number of pairs. Gini (accuracy ratio) is $2\,\text{AUC} - 1$, so 0 is random and 1 is perfect.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Convention: 600 points at odds 50 to 1, PDO = 20. Factor = 20 / 0.6931 = 28.85, Offset = 600 − 28.85 × ln 50 = 487.12.

| Odds (good:bad) | PD | Score |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 9.09% | 553.6 |
| 20 | 4.76% | 573.6 |
| 50 | 1.96% | 600.0 |
| 100 | 0.99% | 620.0 |

Going from 600 to 620 doubles the odds, as designed. A score of 540 gives odds of only 6.25 to 1, a PD of about 13.8%.

AUC by hand: goods score 720, 690, 650, 610; bads score 640 and 580. Of the 8 pairs, the good wins in 7 (only 610 vs 640 is lost). AUC = 7/8 = 0.875 and Gini = 0.75. On real retail portfolios, Gini values around 0.4 to 0.7 are common; a validation team would worry about a sharp drop over time.

### Reject inference
Outcomes exist only for accepted applicants. If you train on them alone, the model learns on a population with the riskiest profiles removed, and it can underestimate risk where you most need it. Common fixes: *augmentation / reweighting* (give accepted applicants who look like rejects more weight), *parcelling* (assign rejected applicants a good or bad label at random with a PD from the current model, often inflated), or buying bureau data on what rejects did elsewhere. None is perfect, which is why banks sometimes accept a small random sample below the cut-off to learn.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "Gini = AUC". Gini = 2 AUC − 1.
- Confusing discrimination (ranking) with calibration (are the PDs right in level?). A model can rank well and still predict PDs that are too low; calibration is checked separately, by score band.
- Forgetting the sign convention: here a higher score means a lower risk.
- Ignoring drift: a scorecard built before a crisis can rank badly afterwards (see cv-367 on PSI).

### How to deliver it
Model, then scaling with one number (620 = odds 100 to 1), then AUC with the Gini identity, then the selection-bias trap. Close with the link: "the score feeds the PD, and the PD feeds both the expected loss (cv-319) and the capital (cv-362)."
deep.cv-362:
### Context / why they ask this
"I analysed student loan applications" leads naturally to: what does one loan cost the bank in capital? Capital is the scarce resource of a bank, and every desk, including Global Markets, is judged on return on capital. The interviewer checks that you know the chain exposure → risk weight → RWA → capital ratio, and that a guarantee changes it. Answer the technical question; do not claim you computed capital at BNP. The loss side (PD × LGD × EAD, the 70% State guarantee) is in cv-319, the scorecard that produces the PD in cv-361.

### Key concepts
- **EAD** (exposure at default): what the bank is owed if the borrower defaults, here 20,000 EUR.
- **Risk weight (RW)**: a percentage set by the rules (standardised approach) or by a formula fed with the bank's own estimates (IRB, internal ratings-based).
- **RWA** (risk-weighted assets): $\text{EAD}\times\text{RW}$, summed over all exposures, plus market and operational risk charges.
- **Capital ratios**: CET1 (common equity) at least 4.5% of RWA, Tier 1 at least 6%, total capital at least 8%. On top: the 2.5% conservation buffer, the countercyclical buffer, systemic buffers for large banks and a bank-specific Pillar 2 add-on.
- **CRR3**: Regulation (EU) 2024/1623, the EU version of the final Basel III package. Retail exposures: 75%; "transactors" (revolving lines like credit cards repaid in full each month): 45%.
- **Credit risk mitigation**: an eligible guarantee lets the bank replace the borrower's weight with the guarantor's weight on the covered part (substitution).
- **Output floor**: an IRB bank's RWA cannot fall below a share of the standardised RWA, phased in from 50% in 2025 to 72.5% in 2030.

### Intuition
Provisions are the losses you expect; capital is the cushion for losses worse than expected. A risk weight is a shortcut for "how much worse than expected can this get". A diversified pool of small retail loans is less volatile than a single corporate loan, hence 75% instead of 100%. A sovereign guarantee in the State's own currency moves the covered risk onto a borrower assumed to be very safe, hence 0%.

### The maths
Standardised: $K = 8\%\times\text{EAD}\times\text{RW}$.
IRB, other retail (no maturity adjustment):
$$R = 0.03\,\frac{1-e^{-35\,PD}}{1-e^{-35}} + 0.16\left(1-\frac{1-e^{-35\,PD}}{1-e^{-35}}\right)$$
$$K = LGD\cdot N\!\left(\frac{G(PD)+\sqrt{R}\,G(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-R}}\right) - PD\cdot LGD,\qquad \text{RWA} = 12.5\,K\cdot\text{EAD}$$
$N$ is the normal cdf, $G$ its inverse. It is a one-factor (Vasicek) model: the 99.9% quantile of the loss rate, minus the expected loss. The factor 12.5 is just 1/8%.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Loan of 20,000 EUR, capital at 8% and at 10.5% (8% plus the conservation buffer):

| Approach | Effective RW | RWA (EUR) | Capital 8% | Capital 10.5% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standardised, no guarantee | 75% | 15,000 | 1,200 | 1,575 |
| Standardised, 70% guaranteed (illustrative) | 22.5% | 4,500 | 360 | 472.5 |
| IRB, PD 1%, LGD 45% | 45.8% | 9,155 | 732 | 961 |
| IRB, PD 2%, LGD 45% | 58.0% | 11,597 | 928 | 1,218 |
| IRB, PD 5%, LGD 45% | 66.4% | 13,283 | 1,063 | 1,395 |

Guaranteed case: 30% × 20,000 = 6,000 EUR at 75% = 4,500; the 14,000 EUR covered part at 0% adds nothing. The 0% weight assumes the guarantee is eligible (direct, irrevocable, unconditional enough under the CRR rules); the State guarantee here covers principal, not interest, which a real computation would split out.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "the bank holds 8% of the loan". It is 8% of RWA, so 6% of the loan at a 75% weight.
- Mixing provisions (expected loss) and capital (unexpected loss).
- Forgetting the buffers: the real CET1 requirement of a large bank is well above 4.5%.
- Assuming IRB always gives lower capital: at high PD the IRB weight can come close to, or exceed, the standardised one, and the output floor limits the gain.
- Giving the 0% weight to a guarantee without checking eligibility.

### How to deliver it
Give the chain in one line (EAD × RW = RWA, capital 8% of RWA), then the number: 15,000 RWA and 1,200 EUR. Then the guarantee: 4,500 RWA, "if eligible". Close with IRB in one sentence and the link to markets: desks are also charged capital, so a trade's profit is always read against the capital it uses.
deep.cv-363:
### Context / why they ask this
The CV line "mapped the operational and financial risks of AI architectures" (an academic project with Wavestone, report co-written) invites a check: do you know what operational risk means in a bank, beyond the everyday word "risk"? A risk interviewer wants the official definition, the taxonomy and a quantification method. Answer the technical question; for what the project itself covered, stay generic (see cv-033 and cv-114). The regulatory side of AI is in cv-364, model risk in cv-367, cyber losses in cv-368.

### Key concepts
- **Operational risk** (Basel): loss from failed processes, people, systems or external events. Includes legal risk (fines, lawsuits). Excludes strategic risk (a bad business choice) and reputational risk.
- **The 7 event types** (Basel level 1): internal fraud; external fraud; employment practices and workplace safety; clients, products and business practices; damage to physical assets; business disruption and system failures; execution, delivery and process management.
- **Frequency / severity**: how often events happen, and how much each one costs.
- **Expected loss (EL)**: the mean of the annual loss, normally priced in or provisioned.
- **Tail quantile**: the loss exceeded only once in, say, 1,000 years (99.9%).
- **Standardised approach (SMA)**: under the final Basel III rules, applied in the EU through CRR3 since 2025, op risk capital is based on a Business Indicator (a size measure built from income), not on internal models. Internal models such as the loss distribution approach remain used for internal risk assessment and scenarios.

### Intuition
Operational losses are a mix of many small events (processing errors) and rare, huge ones (a rogue trader, a major outage, a large fine). So the distribution is skewed with a heavy right tail: the mean says little, a few events dominate. For AI systems this matches the intuition: most hallucinations cost little, one wrong answer in a regulated context can cost a lot.

A simple AI risk map:

| AI risk | Basel event type |
|---|---|
| Hallucinated advice to a client | Clients, products and business practices |
| Prompt injection, data leak | External fraud (and legal risk via GDPR) |
| Cloud or model provider outage | Business disruption and system failures |
| Wrong automated processing step | Execution, delivery and process management |
| Employee pasting client data into a public tool | Internal process failure, often execution or clients-and-practices |

### The maths
Annual loss $S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i$ with $N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ and $X_i$ i.i.d. lognormal: $\ln X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.
Median of $X$ is $e^{\mu}$, mean is $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$. Then
$$E[S] = \lambda\, e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}.$$
The quantile of $S$ has no closed form: compute it by Monte Carlo or with a fast Fourier transform on a discretised severity.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
$\lambda = 4$ events a year, median loss 50,000 EUR, $\sigma = 1.5$.
- Mean loss per event: 50,000 × e^1.125 ≈ 154,000 EUR (three times the median, because of the skew).
- Expected annual loss: 4 × 154,000 ≈ 616,000 EUR.
- 99% quantile of the annual loss: about 4.05 million EUR.
- 99.9% quantile: about 9.98 million EUR (FFT; a 2 million path Monte Carlo gives about 10.0 million).
- Probability of at least one event in a year: 1 − e^(−4) ≈ 98.2%.

So the one-in-a-thousand year is about 16 times the average year. A budget built on the 616,000 EUR average would be blown by a single bad event. Also note the sensitivity: $\sigma$ enters squared in the exponent, so a small error on $\sigma$ moves the tail a lot.

### Common pitfalls
- Calling reputational or strategic risk "operational". They are excluded from the Basel definition, even if an op loss often causes reputational damage.
- Reporting only the expected loss for heavy-tailed risks.
- Fitting the severity on internal data only: a firm rarely has enough large losses, so it adds external loss data and expert scenarios.
- Saying banks hold op risk capital from internal models: in the EU the standardised approach replaced them for capital since 2025.
- Treating AI risk as purely technical: most AI losses show up as client harm, legal cost or process failure.

### How to deliver it
Definition with the two exclusions, the 7 boxes (no need to recite them perfectly, but know four or five), one AI example per box, then the model in one sentence and the two numbers: 616,000 average, about 10 million at 99.9%. End with: "the tail, not the mean, sets the controls and the insurance."
deep.cv-364:
### Context / why they ask this
"Compliance" is one of the three risk axes on the Wavestone line (an academic project, report co-written). A bank interviewer will test whether you know the one regulation that matters most for AI in Europe, and whether you know its timeline, which moved in 2026. Answer with the rules; keep the link to the project generic (see cv-033). Related: operational risk in cv-363, model risk in cv-367, the scoring model itself in cv-361.

### Key concepts
- **Provider**: whoever develops the AI system and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name. **Deployer**: whoever uses it professionally (the bank using a vendor's scoring tool).
- **Prohibited practices** (Article 5): for example social scoring and manipulative techniques. Banned since 2 February 2025.
- **High-risk**: either AI that is a safety component of a product under the EU product laws listed in Annex I, or a use listed in Annex III (employment, education, essential services such as credit, and others).
- **Annex III, 5(b)**: AI used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, except fraud detection. Corporate credit scoring is not in that point.
- **Article 50**: transparency duties (tell people they interact with an AI, mark synthetic content).
- **General-purpose AI (GPAI)**: duties on the providers of large models (documentation, copyright policy), applicable since 2 August 2025.
- **FRIA** (Article 27): fundamental rights impact assessment, required from deployers of credit scoring systems.
- **Digital omnibus**: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026, which delays the high-risk deadlines.

### Intuition
The Act regulates uses, not technologies. The same model can be minimal risk when it summarises internal notes and high-risk when it decides who gets a loan. The test is: does the output materially affect a person's access to something essential? If yes, the burden of proof (documentation, testing, oversight) is on the firm.

### The maths
Fine caps (Article 99), for a firm with worldwide annual turnover $T$:
$$\text{Cap}_{\text{prohibited}} = \max(35\text{M},\ 0.07\,T),\qquad \text{Cap}_{\text{other}} = \max(15\text{M},\ 0.03\,T)$$
For SMEs and start-ups, the lower of the two amounts applies instead of the higher.

### Worked example (verified numerically)

| Turnover | Prohibited practice cap | Other breach cap |
|---|---|---|
| 2 billion EUR (large firm) | 140 million EUR (7% wins) | 60 million EUR |
| 100 million EUR, SME rule | 7 million EUR (lower of the two) | 3 million EUR |
| 5 million EUR, SME rule | 350,000 EUR | 150,000 EUR |

Timeline, as of Sept 2026:

| Date | What applies |
|---|---|
| 2 February 2025 | Prohibitions |
| 2 August 2025 | GPAI obligations |
| 2 August 2026 | Article 50 transparency |
| 2 December 2027 | Annex III high-risk (credit scoring), delayed by 487 days |
| 2 August 2028 | Annex I high-risk (AI in regulated products) |

From today (1 October 2026), a bank has 427 days before its credit scoring tools must comply. That sounds long, but documentation, data governance and testing for a model already in production take months.

### What a bank should do now
Inventory every AI use, classify each one, identify who is provider and who is deployer (a bank that substantially modifies a vendor model can become the provider), map gaps against the high-risk requirements, and reuse existing model risk management: validation, monitoring and documentation already cover a large part of the work.

### Common pitfalls
- Quoting 2 August 2026 as the high-risk deadline: that date was replaced by the omnibus.
- Thinking all AI in a bank is high-risk: an internal coding assistant is not; credit scoring of individuals is.
- Forgetting the deployer's own duties: buying a compliant tool does not end the bank's obligations.
- Confusing the AI Act with GDPR: GDPR (including the right not to be subject to purely automated decisions) applies in parallel.
- Calling fraud detection high-risk under 5(b): it is explicitly excluded.

### How to deliver it
Risk classes in one sentence, then "credit scoring of individuals is high-risk, Annex III 5(b)", the obligations split between provider and deployer, the chatbot under Article 50, and the dates with the 2026 delay. Mention the fines last, as an order of magnitude.
deep.cv-365:
### Context / why they ask this
"Investment recommendations under uncertainty" (Wavestone, an academic project with the school, report co-written) is a phrase an interviewer will poke at: what method? Decision analysis is also how traders and risk managers think: scenarios, probabilities, worst case, regret, value of information. Answer with the method; the numbers are illustrative, not from the project (see cv-114 for how to talk about the project itself). The cost side of each option is in cv-366.

### Key concepts
- **Payoff matrix**: value of each option in each scenario (state of the world).
- **Expected value (EV)**: probability-weighted average of the payoffs; needs probabilities.
- **Maximin**: pick the option whose worst payoff is the best; very prudent, ignores probabilities.
- **Maximax**: pick the best best case; optimistic.
- **Regret**: in a given scenario, the gap between the best payoff available and the one you got. **Minimax regret** picks the option whose largest regret is the smallest.
- **Hurwicz**: a weighted mix of best and worst case, with an optimism weight $\alpha$.
- **EVPI** (expected value of perfect information): how much better you would do on average if you learnt the scenario before choosing.

### Intuition
EV is the right answer if the decision is repeated many times or is small relative to the firm. When one bad scenario can hurt badly, or when the probabilities are guesses, decision makers also look at the worst case and at regret ("how stupid will I look if..."). Showing several criteria, and where they agree, is more honest than one number.

### The maths
For option $i$ and scenario $j$ with payoff $v_{ij}$ and probability $p_j$:
$$EV_i = \sum_j p_j v_{ij},\qquad r_{ij} = \max_k v_{kj} - v_{ij},\qquad EVPI = \sum_j p_j \max_i v_{ij} - \max_i EV_i.$$

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Illustrative NPV in k€, probabilities 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.2:

| Option | High | Moderate | Low | EV | Worst | Max regret | Std dev |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Build | 900 | 200 | −600 | 250 | −600 | 650 | 522 |
| Buy | 500 | 250 | −100 | 255 | −100 | 400 | 208 |
| Pilot | 400 | 150 | 50 | 205 | 50 | 500 | 133 |

Regrets: in "High" the best is 900, so regrets are 0, 400, 500; in "Moderate" the best is 250: 50, 0, 100; in "Low" the best is 50: 650, 150, 0.
- EV: Buy (255), just ahead of Build (250).
- Maximin: Pilot. Maximax: Build.
- Minimax regret: Buy (400).
- Hurwicz with $\alpha = 0.5$: Build 150, Buy 200, Pilot 225, so Pilot.
- With perfect information you would pick 900, 250 and 50: 0.3 × 900 + 0.5 × 250 + 0.2 × 50 = 405. EVPI = 405 − 255 = 150 k€.

Sensitivity: keep the low scenario at 0.2 and let $p$ be the probability of high adoption. Then $EV_{\text{Build}} = 700p + 40$ and $EV_{\text{Buy}} = 250p + 180$; Build wins only if $p > 140/450 \approx 0.311$. Since the base case is 0.3, the EV ranking is on a knife edge, which is exactly why the robust criteria matter. Buy is a good recommendation here: near-best EV, best minimax regret, a worst case of only −100, and less than half the standard deviation of Build.

### Common pitfalls
- Presenting EV alone when the probabilities are guesses: always show the sensitivity.
- Treating the pilot as a static option. Its real value is the option to scale or stop after learning; the EVPI of 150 k€ is an upper bound on what that learning is worth.
- Mixing units (cost in one column, NPV in another) or forgetting to discount.
- Counting the same risk twice: if the low scenario already includes a regulatory shock, do not add a separate penalty.
- Ignoring correlation with the rest of the firm: a −600 that comes when everything else is bad hurts more.

### How to deliver it
Draw the 3 × 3 table, give the EVs (250, 255, 205), then say "but the criteria disagree" and give maximin and minimax regret. Close with EVPI as the price of information and the 31% break-even. Say clearly that the figures are illustrative.
deep.cv-366:
### Context / why they ask this
"Investment recommendations" on "AI architectures" (Wavestone, an academic project, report co-written) suggest cost comparisons, and build versus buy or cloud versus on-premise is the classic one. The interviewer tests discounting, which you must master for any markets role, and whether you think about hidden costs and sensitivity. The numbers below are illustrative. For choosing between options under uncertain scenarios, see cv-365.

### Key concepts
- **TCO** (total cost of ownership): all costs over the life of the solution: purchase, installation, energy, hosting, maintenance, licences, staff, migration and exit costs.
- **Capex / opex**: capital expenditure (buy an asset now) versus operating expenditure (pay as you go).
- **Present value (PV)**: a cost paid in year $t$ is worth $C/(1+r)^t$ today; $r$ is the discount rate, often the firm's cost of capital.
- **Annuity factor**: PV of 1 paid at the end of each year for $n$ years.
- **Equivalent annual cost (EAC)**: PV divided by the annuity factor, to compare options with different lives.
- **Utilisation**: share of time the owned hardware does useful work. Cloud cost follows usage; on-premise cost is mostly fixed.
- **Egress fees and lock-in**: costs of moving data out of a cloud and of switching provider.

### Intuition
On-premise is a fixed cost paid upfront: cheap per unit if you use it a lot and for long, expensive if it sits idle or becomes obsolete. Cloud is a variable cost: you pay a premium per unit for flexibility, no upfront cash and no obsolescence risk. So the comparison comes down to three questions: how long, how much usage, and how uncertain is the usage.

### The maths
$$AF(n,r) = \sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{1}{(1+r)^t} = \frac{1-(1+r)^{-n}}{r}$$
$$PV_{\text{on-prem}} = I + c\cdot AF(n,r),\qquad PV_{\text{cloud}} = k\cdot AF(n,r)$$
They are equal when $AF(n,r) = I/(k-c)$. With $I = 300$, $c = 60$, $k = 150$: $AF = 300/90 \approx 3.333$, so $n = -\ln(1 - 0.08\cdot 3.333)/\ln 1.08 \approx 4.03$ years.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Costs in k€, $r = 8\%$, opex paid at the end of each year:

| Horizon | Annuity factor | On-premise | Cloud | Cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 year | 0.9259 | 355.6 | 138.9 | Cloud |
| 3 years | 2.5771 | 454.6 | 386.6 | Cloud |
| 4 years | 3.3121 | 498.7 | 496.8 | Cloud, barely |
| 5 years | 3.9927 | 539.6 | 598.9 | On-premise |

Sensitivities at 3 years:
- Discount rate: at 0% it is 480 versus 450, at 12% it is 444.1 versus 360.3. A higher rate makes the cloud more attractive, since its payments come later.
- Usage growth: if cloud spend grows 20% a year (150, 180, 216), its PV is 464.7, above the 454.6 of on-premise.
- Equivalent annual cost of on-premise: 454.6 / 2.5771 = 176.4 k€ a year, against 150 for cloud.
- Utilisation: if the 300 k€ buys 8 GPUs, 3 years give 210,240 GPU-hours. At full use, on-premise costs 2.16 € per GPU-hour; at 40% utilisation, 5.41 €. Idle hardware is the main way on-premise loses.

### Common pitfalls
- Comparing the cloud bill with the hardware price only, and forgetting power, cooling, staff, maintenance and the hardware refresh.
- Comparing options over different horizons without EAC.
- Forgetting cloud-specific costs: egress, premium support, reserved-capacity commitments.
- Ignoring obsolescence: AI hardware ages fast, so a 5-year life is optimistic.
- Ignoring non-cost factors: data location and confidentiality, regulatory requirements on outsourcing and concentration on a few cloud providers, and time to market.

### How to deliver it
State the method in one sentence (PV of all costs over the same horizon), give the 3-year numbers (454.6 versus 386.6), then show that the answer flips at about 4 years and with usage growth. Conclude: "below 3 to 4 years or with uncertain demand, rent; for a stable, heavy, long workload, buy."
deep.cv-367:
### Context / why they ask this
"Operational and financial risks of AI architectures" (Wavestone, academic project, report co-written) naturally includes model risk, and drift is the risk people quote first for machine learning. A risk or quant interviewer checks two things: that you know model risk is a managed risk type in banks, and that you can compute one monitoring metric. Stay generic about the project (see cv-033). The scorecard monitored here is the one in cv-361; operational risk in cv-363.

### Key concepts
- **Model**: a quantitative method that turns inputs into estimates (a PD, a price, a hedge ratio, a chatbot answer).
- **Model risk** (SR 11-7): adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs. Two sources: the model is wrong (errors, bad assumptions, bad data), or it is used outside its domain.
- **Model risk management (MRM)**: inventory of all models, tiering by materiality, independent validation before use, **effective challenge** (critical review by competent, independent people), ongoing monitoring, periodic revalidation. In the UK, PRA SS1/23 sets similar principles.
- **Data drift**: the input distribution changes (new customer mix, new product).
- **Concept drift**: the relation between inputs and outcome changes (same profile, but default rates rise in a recession).
- **PSI**: a distance between two distributions over the same bins; **CSI** is the same index computed variable by variable.

### Intuition
A model is a summary of the past. When the population or the economy changes, the summary goes stale. PSI is a cheap alarm that works immediately, because it only needs the scores, not the outcomes. Outcomes such as defaults take months to appear, so performance checks come later. For AI models from vendors there is one more source of drift: the provider can update the model under you.

### The maths
$$\text{PSI} = \sum_{i=1}^{B} (a_i - e_i)\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i} = KL(a\|e) + KL(e\|a)$$
Each term is non-negative (both factors have the same sign), so PSI is 0 only if the distributions match. It is the symmetrised Kullback-Leibler divergence. Usual reading: below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 watch, above 0.25 significant shift. Even with no real shift, sampling noise gives a PSI of roughly $(B-1)(1/n_a + 1/n_e)$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
5 score bands, 20% each at development; band 5 is the riskiest.

| Band | Development | Month 6 | Term | Month 12 | Term |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (safest) | 20% | 12% | 0.0409 | 8% | 0.1100 |
| 2 | 20% | 16% | 0.0089 | 12% | 0.0409 |
| 3 | 20% | 20% | 0.0000 | 18% | 0.0021 |
| 4 | 20% | 24% | 0.0073 | 24% | 0.0073 |
| 5 (riskiest) | 20% | 28% | 0.0269 | 38% | 0.1155 |
| PSI | | | 0.084 | | 0.276 |

Month 6: 0.084, stable but trending. Month 12: 0.276, above 0.25: the applicant population has moved towards risky scores. Next steps: CSI on each variable to find the cause, then check calibration (are observed default rates per band still in line with predicted PDs?) and the Gini as outcomes arrive.

Noise check: with 1,000 applicants in each sample and 5 bands, the formula gives about 4 × 0.002 = 0.008, and a simulation of 20,000 pairs of samples from the same distribution gives a mean of 0.008 and a 99% quantile of about 0.027. So 0.084 is unlikely to be noise, but on 100 applicants the noise level would be 10 times higher.

### Common pitfalls
- Reading a high PSI as "the model is wrong". It says the population changed; the model may still rank well.
- Reading a low PSI as "all is fine": concept drift can leave the score distribution unchanged while the default rate per band rises.
- Empty bins: $\ln 0$ breaks the formula; merge bins or floor shares at a small value.
- Comparing PSI values computed with different numbers of bins.
- Treating vendor AI models as outside MRM: they still need inventory, validation and monitoring.

### How to deliver it
Definition of model risk with SR 11-7, the MRM cycle in one sentence, data versus concept drift, then the PSI formula and one computed case: 0.084 then 0.276. Finish with the limit: "PSI is the smoke alarm, performance monitoring is the fire inspection."
deep.cv-368:
### Context / why they ask this
The Wavestone line (academic project, report co-written) lists security among the risks of AI architectures. Banks spend heavily on cyber security and ask the same question as for any investment: what does it buy? An interviewer checks that you can turn a qualitative risk map ("high", "medium") into a quantified decision. Keep the project link generic (see cv-033). Operational risk in general is in cv-363; cyber losses are one of its categories (external fraud, business disruption).

### Key concepts
- **Asset value (AV)**: what the asset is worth to the firm (data, systems, revenue it supports).
- **Exposure factor (EF)**: share of the asset value lost in one incident.
- **SLE** (single loss expectancy): $AV \times EF$.
- **ARO** (annualised rate of occurrence): expected incidents per year; 0.2 means one every 5 years.
- **ALE** (annualised loss expectancy): $SLE \times ARO$, the expected loss per year.
- **ROSI** (return on security investment): net benefit of a control relative to its cost.
- **FAIR** (Factor Analysis of Information Risk): an open standard that splits risk into loss event frequency (threat event frequency × vulnerability) and loss magnitude (primary loss, like response and replacement, plus secondary loss, like fines and lost clients), estimated as ranges.
- **AI-specific threats**: prompt injection, data poisoning, model theft, leaks of confidential data through the model's answers.

### Intuition
Risk = how often × how bad. A control can act on either: a filter on inputs reduces how often an attack succeeds, encryption and access limits reduce how bad a leak is. The single-number ALE is an average; for rare, severe events the average hides the year that hurts, so FAIR keeps the whole distribution.

### The maths
$$SLE = AV\times EF,\qquad ALE = SLE\times ARO,\qquad ROSI = \frac{ALE_{\text{before}} - ALE_{\text{after}} - C}{C}$$
FAIR: annual loss $S = \sum_{k=1}^{N} L_k$, $N \sim \text{Poisson}(LEF)$, each $L_k$ drawn from a range, for example a PERT distribution with minimum, most likely and maximum. With minimum $a$, mode $m$ and maximum $b$, the PERT mean is $(a+4m+b)/6$.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Illustrative figures.

| Item | Before control | After control |
|---|---|---|
| Asset value | 2,000,000 | 2,000,000 |
| Exposure factor | 25% | 25% |
| SLE | 500,000 | 500,000 |
| ARO | 0.2 | 0.05 |
| ALE | 100,000 | 25,000 |
| Control cost per year | | 40,000 |

ROSI = (100,000 − 25,000 − 40,000) / 40,000 = 0.875, so 87.5%. Break-even: the control is worth it as long as it costs less than the 75,000 EUR it saves.

FAIR version: frequency 0.2 a year, loss per event PERT with minimum 50,000, most likely 400,000 and maximum 1,350,000 EUR (mean exactly 500,000). A Monte Carlo with 1 million years gives:
- mean annual loss about 100,000 EUR (matches the ALE);
- probability of at least one event 18.1% (that is $1-e^{-0.2}$);
- 95% quantile about 690,000 EUR, 99% quantile about 1,050,000 EUR.

After the control (frequency 0.05): mean about 25,000 EUR, the 95% quantile drops to 0, but the 99% quantile is still about 720,000 EUR. The control cut the frequency, not the severity: in the bad year the loss is as large as before. That is an argument for adding a severity control too (encryption, segmentation, cyber insurance).

### Common pitfalls
- Presenting ALE as "what we will lose this year". Most years the loss is 0; some years it is several times the ALE.
- Double counting: two controls that each cut ARO by 75% do not cut it by 150%; apply them one after the other (0.2 → 0.05 → 0.0125).
- Forgetting secondary losses: GDPR fines (up to 4% of worldwide turnover), client compensation, lost business.
- False precision: ARO and EF are estimates; give ranges and say where they come from (incident data, industry reports, expert judgement).
- Ignoring that attackers adapt: a frequency estimate goes stale quickly.

### How to deliver it
Three formulas, one table, one ROSI: 500,000 SLE, 100,000 ALE, 25,000 after a 40,000 control, ROSI 87.5%. Then the FAIR upgrade in two sentences and the key insight: "this control cuts frequency, not severity; the 99% loss stays above 700,000."
deep.cv-369:
### Context / why they ask this
Business numbers on a CV are a classic trap: an interviewer asks "is 45 k€ revenue?" to see if you know the difference between what is signed, what is earned and what is collected. In a bank this matters everywhere: credit analysts look at cash conversion, equity research reads revenue recognition notes, and a company can be profitable and still run out of cash. Use only the CV facts about CNE (see cv-323); the figures below are illustrative.

### Key concepts
- **Booking (order intake)**: value of contracts signed in a period.
- **Backlog**: signed but not yet delivered, so not yet revenue.
- **Revenue** (turnover): recognised when the service is delivered, or progressively over time for a service delivered over months (IFRS 15 logic: revenue follows the transfer of the service to the client).
- **Invoice**: a payment request; it creates a **receivable** (money owed to you).
- **Accrued revenue / contract asset**: revenue earned but not yet invoiced. The opposite, invoiced but not yet earned, is **deferred revenue**.
- **Cash collected**: what actually reached the bank account.
- **DSO** (days sales outstanding): average time clients take to pay.
- **French payment terms** (Code de commerce, L441-10): 30 days after delivery by default; agreed terms at most 60 days from the invoice date or 45 days end of month; late payment interest at least 3 times the legal interest rate plus a fixed 40 EUR recovery fee.

### Intuition
Think of three buckets filled one after the other: signature fills "bookings", work fills "revenue", payment fills "cash". Time lags between them create working capital needs: you pay your team before the client pays you.

### The maths
$$\text{DSO} = \frac{\text{Receivables}}{\text{Revenue}}\times 365$$
$$\text{Backlog}_{\text{end}} = \text{Backlog}_{\text{start}} + \text{Bookings} - \text{Revenue recognised}$$
"45 days end of month" has two readings in practice: add 45 days then go to the end of that month, or go to the end of the month then add 45 days. The contract should say which.

### Worked example (verified numerically)
Mission of 12,000 EUR (excluding VAT) signed on 15 November 2025, delivered over three months, 30% invoiced at signature, 70% at delivery on 15 February 2026.

| At 31 December 2025 | Amount (EUR) |
|---|---|
| Bookings | 12,000 |
| Revenue recognised (50% done) | 6,000 |
| Backlog | 6,000 |
| Invoiced (deposit) | 3,600 |
| Accrued revenue (earned, not invoiced) | 2,400 |
| Cash, if the deposit is paid | 3,600 |

Final invoice of 8,400 EUR dated 15 February 2026:
- 30 days (default): due 17 March 2026.
- 60 days from invoice: 16 April 2026.
- 45 days end of month, first reading: 15 February + 45 days = 1 April, end of month 30 April 2026.
- 45 days end of month, second reading: 28 February + 45 days = 14 April 2026.

So full cash can come about five months after signature.

DSO: with 48,000 EUR of annual revenue and 8,000 EUR of receivables at year end, DSO = 8,000 / 48,000 × 365 ≈ 60.8 days, right at the legal maximum of 60 days for agreed terms.

### Common pitfalls
- Calling bookings "revenue" or "turnover" on a CV or in an interview.
- Mixing amounts before and after VAT: 12,000 EUR before 20% VAT is 14,400 EUR invoiced, and the VAT is not yours.
- Forgetting that a signed contract can be cancelled or cut back.
- Assuming that the agreed terms will be met: late payment is common, especially for small suppliers.
