Present value of a cash flow at $t$ is $CF/(1+r)^t$. Its sensitivity to $r$ is about $-t/(1+r)$: proportional to its date. A cash flow in 20 years loses about 20 times more value (in %) than one in 1 year when rates rise. A company whose value is mostly 10+ years away behaves like a long zero-coupon bond.

### The maths
Gordon: $P = \frac{CF_1}{r-g}$, so
$$\frac{dP}{P} = -\frac{dr}{r-g}$$
With $r - g = 4\%$, $dr = +1\%$: the first-order formula gives a fall of 1/4 (25%), but the exact fall is from $CF/0.04$ to $CF/0.05$, i.e. 20%; the difference is convexity. With $r - g = 8\%$ (low growth firm, say $r$ 10%, $g$ 2%), the fall is $1 - 8/9 \approx 11\%$.

### Worked example with numbers
Two companies, both with $r = 8\%$ and next year cash flow 10:
- Growth company, $g = 5\%$: $P = 10/0.03 = 333$. At $r = 9\%$: $10/0.04 = 250$, **−25%**.
- Mature company, $g = 1\%$: $P = 10/0.07 = 142.9$. At $r = 9\%$: $10/0.08 = 125$, **−12.5%**.
Same rate shock, twice the damage for the growth stock. This is the 2022 story: the jump in real yields crushed long-duration tech and unprofitable growth names far more than energy or banks.

### Nuances that make a strong answer
- **Why** rates rise matters: stronger growth expectations raise cash flow forecasts (partly offsetting); an inflation or term-premium shock with no growth is the worst case.
- The equity risk premium can move too (may compress in euphoric markets).
- Banks: NII rises with rates (at least initially), so they often outperform in rising-rate regimes, but bond portfolio losses and credit costs are the flip side.
- Highly leveraged firms are hit twice: higher discount rate and higher refinancing costs.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "Rates up, stocks down" with no mechanism.
- Ignoring the cash flow side of the equation.

### How to deliver it
Mechanism (WACC up), then the duration analogy, then a one-line number (the 20% example), then the nuance about the cause of the move. Mention 2022 as a real-world illustration.
deep.cf-013:
### Context / why they ask this
The entry point to all accounting questions. After this come "how are they linked" and "walk me through 10 of depreciation". Master the vocabulary here.

### Key concepts
- **Accrual accounting**: revenue booked when the good is delivered (even if the client pays in 60 days), expenses booked when incurred. Hence profit ≠ cash.
- **Income statement lines**: Revenue − COGS (cost of goods sold) = Gross profit; − SG&A (selling, general & admin) − R&D = EBITDA; − D&A = EBIT; − Interest = EBT (pre-tax profit); − Tax = **Net income**.
- **Balance sheet**: assets (cash, receivables, inventory, PP&E = property plant & equipment, intangibles, goodwill); liabilities (payables, accrued expenses, debt, deferred tax, pensions); equity (share capital, **retained earnings** = accumulated net income not distributed).
- **Cash flow statement (indirect method)**: CFO starts from net income, adds back non-cash items (D&A, impairments, stock comp), adjusts for working capital changes. CFI: capex, acquisitions, asset sales. CFF: debt, equity issuance, dividends, buybacks.

### Intuition
Think of a person: the income statement is the payslip minus expenses over a year (did I "earn" money?), the balance sheet is the list of what I own and owe on 31 December (house, savings, mortgage), and the cash flow statement is the bank account history (where did the money actually go?). Someone can have a great salary but no cash because clients have not paid yet or because they bought a house.

### The maths / identities
$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}$$
$$\Delta \text{Cash} = CFO + CFI + CFF$$
$$\text{Retained earnings}_{end} = RE_{begin} + NI - \text{Dividends}$$

### Worked example with numbers
Revenue 1,000, COGS 600, SG&A 200: EBITDA 200. D&A 50: EBIT 150. Interest 30: EBT 120. Tax 25%: 30. Net income 90.
CFO: 90 + 50 (D&A) − 20 (increase in receivables) = 120. CFI: capex −80. CFF: dividend −30. Change in cash = +10.

### Which statement if only one?
- **Cash flow statement** is the usual best answer: cash is harder to fake, shows sustainability, and you can partly rebuild the income statement from it.
- The balance sheet alone gives solvency but no performance; the income statement alone can hide cash problems (e.g. booking revenue that is never collected).
- For a **bank**, the balance sheet matters most (assets, capital, funding).

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Saying the balance sheet covers a period (it is a point in time).
- Thinking net income is cash.
- Forgetting that dividends are not an expense (they go through retained earnings and CFF, not the income statement).

### How to deliver it
One sentence per statement (what, period vs point in time, key output), then the "which one" answer. Keep it brisk: this is a warm-up.
deep.cf-014:
### Context / why they ask this
A classic that checks you see the statements as a system, not three separate documents. It sets up the "change one item" walkthroughs.

### Key concepts
- **PP&E**: property, plant & equipment. Next year PP&E = PP&E + capex − depreciation.
- **Working capital accounts**: accounts receivable (AR, customers owe you), inventory, accounts payable (AP, you owe suppliers).
- **Retained earnings**: RE + net income − dividends.
- **Roll-forwards**: each balance sheet item evolves by explicit flows (debt + issuance − repayment; equity + issuance − buybacks...).

### Intuition
The income statement tells you how much the owners got richer on paper. That gain has to go somewhere: it lands in equity (retained earnings). But it does not all land in cash, because some profits are stuck in receivables, and some expenses (depreciation) did not use cash. The cash flow statement is precisely the bridge from "paper richer" to "cash richer", and the end result has to match the cash line on the balance sheet. The balance sheet balances because every flow is recorded twice (double-entry).

### The maths: the links in one table
| Item | Income statement | Cash flow statement | Balance sheet |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net income | bottom line | top of CFO | + retained earnings |
| Depreciation | expense (↓ NI) | added back in CFO | ↓ PP&E |
| ↑ Receivables | revenue booked | − in CFO | ↑ AR |
| ↑ Payables | expense booked | + in CFO | ↑ AP |
| Capex | – | − in CFI | ↑ PP&E |
| New debt | – (interest later) | + in CFF | ↑ debt |
| Dividends | – | − in CFF | ↓ retained earnings |
| Net change in cash | – | sum of CFO+CFI+CFF | ↑ cash |

### Worked example with numbers
Start: cash 100, PP&E 500, debt 300, equity 300 (plus AR 0). During the year: NI 60 (after D&A 40), AR up 10, capex 50, debt repaid 20, dividend 15.
- CFO = 60 + 40 − 10 = 90; CFI = −50; CFF = −20 − 15 = −35. Δcash = +5 → cash 105.
- PP&E = 500 + 50 − 40 = 510; AR = 10. Assets = 105 + 10 + 510 = 625.
- Debt = 280; equity = 300 + 60 − 15 = 345. L + E = 625. Balanced.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Forgetting that the balance sheet change must be mirrored in the cash flow statement (sign conventions: asset up = cash down).
- Forgetting the tax effect in walkthroughs.

### How to deliver it
Start with "net income" (the two arrows from it), then "non-cash items and working capital", then "investing and financing", then "the change in cash hits the balance sheet". About 45 seconds. Offer an example if they want.
deep.cf-015:
### Context / why they ask this
The single most famous accounting question in banking interviews. It tests the three-statement links, the tax effect and the non-cash nature of depreciation. Say it cleanly, in the order IS, CFS, BS, with numbers, and end with "it balances".

### Key concepts
- **Depreciation**: allocation of the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life (a machine bought for 100 with a 10-year life: 10 per year). The cash left at purchase, recorded as capex.
- **Non-cash expense**: reduces accounting profit without any cash payment this period.
- **Tax shield**: expense × tax rate, the tax you save because the expense is deductible. This assumes book and tax depreciation move together (otherwise deferred taxes appear, a detail worth one sentence at most).
- **PP&E (net)**: gross cost minus accumulated depreciation.

### Intuition
Depreciation lowers profit on paper. Paper profit is what the taxman looks at, so you pay less tax: that is real cash saved. Nothing else about cash changes, because depreciation itself is not a payment. Hence: profit down, cash up (by the tax saving only).

### The maths
Let $\Delta D = 10$, $t = 25\%$:
$$\Delta NI = -\Delta D(1-t) = -7.5$$
$$\Delta \text{Cash} = \Delta NI + \Delta D = -7.5 + 10 = +2.5 = t \cdot \Delta D$$
$$\Delta \text{Assets} = +2.5 - 10 = -7.5 = \Delta \text{Equity}$$

### Worked example: the full table
| Statement | Line | Change |
|---|---|---|
| IS | Depreciation | +10 |
| IS | EBIT / pre-tax income | −10 |
| IS | Taxes | −2.5 |
| IS | Net income | −7.5 |
| CFS | Net income | −7.5 |
| CFS | + Depreciation | +10 |
| CFS | Net change in cash | +2.5 |
| BS | Cash | +2.5 |
| BS | PP&E | −10 |
| BS | Total assets | −7.5 |
| BS | Retained earnings (equity) | −7.5 |

### Variations they will throw at you
- **Amortisation of intangibles**: same mechanics as depreciation (if tax-deductible).
- **Impairment / write-down of 10** (asset loses value): same as depreciation if tax-deductible; goodwill impairment is often **not** tax-deductible, then NI falls by the full 10, cash is unchanged, goodwill −10, equity −10.
- **Stock-based compensation of 10**: expense on IS, NI −7.5 (if deductible), added back on CFS, cash +2.5, equity: retained earnings −7.5 but common stock/APIC +10, net +2.5. Balances with cash +2.5.
- **Without taxes**: NI −10, cash unchanged, PP&E −10, equity −10.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Saying cash goes down by 10 (confusing depreciation with a payment).
- Forgetting taxes.
- Saying liabilities change: taxes payable could change if the tax is not yet paid, but the standard answer assumes tax is paid in cash.
- Wrong sign on the balance sheet: PP&E goes **down**.

### How to deliver it
Walk IS → CFS → BS, state each number, and finish with "assets −7.5, equity −7.5, balances". Practise it out loud until it takes under 40 seconds. Then be ready for the variants.
deep.cf-016:
### Context / why they ask this
The natural next step after the depreciation question: now with financing, and across two periods. It checks you separate the balance sheet event (purchase) from the income statement effects (depreciation, interest) that come later.

### Key concepts
- **Capitalising** an expense: a long-lived asset is put on the balance sheet (PP&E) rather than expensed at once; the cost is spread through depreciation.
- **Interest expense**: cost of the debt, on the income statement, tax-deductible.
- **Principal repayment**: repaying the debt itself; a financing cash outflow, **never** on the income statement.

### Intuition
Buying an asset is just swapping one form of value for another (cash for machine), or here, taking a loan to get a machine: both sides of the balance sheet grow by 100, no profit or loss. Over time, the machine is "consumed" (depreciation) and the loan costs interest; those two are the expenses. Cash-wise, only interest (net of the tax saving) actually leaves: $-5 + 0.25 \times 15 = -1.25$.

### The maths
Year 1:
$$\Delta EBT = -(10 + 5) = -15, \quad \Delta Tax = -3.75, \quad \Delta NI = -11.25$$
$$\Delta Cash = -11.25 + 10 = -1.25 = -5 \text{ (interest)} + 3.75 \text{ (tax saved)}$$
$$\Delta Assets = -1.25 - 10 = -11.25 = \Delta Equity$$

### Worked example: table
| | At purchase | End of year 1 |
|---|---|---|
| IS: depreciation | 0 | +10 |
| IS: interest | 0 | +5 |
| IS: net income | 0 | −11.25 |
| CFS: CFO | 0 | −11.25 + 10 = −1.25 |
| CFS: CFI | −100 | 0 |
| CFS: CFF | +100 | 0 |
| BS: cash | 0 | −1.25 |
| BS: PP&E | +100 | 90 (−10 in the year) |
| BS: debt | +100 | 100 |
| BS: retained earnings | 0 | −11.25 |

### Variations
- **Repay 10 of principal at year end**: extra CFF −10, cash −11.25 in total, debt 90. Income statement unchanged.
- **Machine sold at year end for 95** (book value 90): gain on sale +5 on IS (pre-tax), NI +3.75; in CFS subtract the non-cash gain 5 from CFO and show 95 inflow in CFI.
- **Paid with cash instead of debt**: at purchase CFI −100, cash −100, PP&E +100. Year 1: only depreciation, NI −7.5, cash +2.5.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Expensing the 100 on the income statement at purchase.
- Putting principal repayment on the income statement.
- Forgetting interest is tax-deductible.

### How to deliver it
Split clearly: "At purchase... After one year...". Numbers in order. Say "it balances" at each stage.
deep.cf-017:
### Context / why they ask this
Working capital is where profit and cash diverge in real life, and it is behind many corporate collapses ("profitable but ran out of cash"). The question tests accrual accounting and CFS sign conventions.

### Key concepts
- **Accounts receivable (AR)**: amounts customers owe for goods delivered. Asset.
- **Inventory**: goods bought or produced but not yet sold. Asset. Expensed as **COGS** only when sold (matching principle).
- **Accounts payable (AP)**: amounts owed to suppliers. Liability.
- **Net working capital (operating)**: AR + inventory − AP (plus other operating items).
- **DSO / DIO / DPO**: days sales outstanding, days inventory, days payables; **cash conversion cycle** = DSO + DIO − DPO.

### Intuition
Accrual accounting says: you earned the revenue when you delivered, regardless of payment. The tax authority taxes that profit. So until the client pays, you are "rich on paper" and have actually spent cash (the tax). Inventory purchases are the opposite: cash has left but no expense yet; it is parked on the balance sheet until the sale.

Rule for CFS: **an increase in an operating asset uses cash (−), an increase in an operating liability provides cash (+)**.

### The maths
Sale on credit $S = 10$:
$$\Delta NI = S(1-t) = 7.5, \quad \Delta Cash = 7.5 - \Delta AR = 7.5 - 10 = -2.5$$
Inventory purchase: $\Delta NI = 0$, $\Delta Cash = -\Delta Inv = -10$.
Full sale of that inventory later for 15 on credit: revenue 15, COGS 10, pre-tax 5, NI 3.75; CFS: +3.75 − 15 (AR) + 10 (inventory decrease) = −1.25 cash (the tax on the margin); BS: inventory −10, AR +15, cash −1.25 → assets +3.75, RE +3.75.

### Worked example: table for the credit sale
| | IS | CFS | BS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | +10 | | |
| Tax | +2.5 | | |
| Net income | +7.5 | +7.5 | RE +7.5 |
| Δ AR | | −10 | AR +10 |
| Cash | | −2.5 | cash −2.5 |

### Real-world angle
Fast growth consumes working capital: revenue +50% means AR and inventory grow ~50%, draining cash. That is why growth firms need financing even when profitable, and why FCF, not earnings, drives value. Tricks to watch: aggressive revenue recognition inflates AR (channel stuffing), and supply-chain finance or factoring flatters operating cash flow.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Booking the inventory purchase as an expense.
- Sign errors in the CFS.
- Forgetting taxes, or saying cash is unchanged on the credit sale.

### How to deliver it
Same structure IS → CFS → BS, and the rule "asset up = cash down". End with the business lesson: "that's why a fast-growing company can be profitable and still run out of cash."
deep.cf-018:
### Context / why they ask this
EBITDA is everywhere in leveraged finance, M&A and credit sales. They test the definition, the rationale and the critique.

### Key concepts
- **EBIT**: operating profit. **EBITDA = EBIT + D&A**.
- **Non-GAAP measure**: not defined by IFRS/US GAAP, so its computation varies.
- **Adjusted EBITDA**: EBITDA excluding "one-off" items (restructuring, litigation, stock comp). Frequently abused, "EBITDA-C" jokes aside.
- **Leverage ratio**: net debt / EBITDA (e.g. 2x for investment grade typical, 5-7x in LBOs).
- **Interest coverage**: EBITDA / interest or EBIT / interest.

### Intuition
EBITDA answers "how much does the core business earn before the accounting of past investments, the choice of financing, and the tax jurisdiction?". That makes it a clean comparison of *operations*. But a business that must reinvest 80% of its EBITDA in new equipment every year (a telecom, a steelmaker) is not as good as one reinvesting 10% (software), even at equal EBITDA. Capex is precisely what D&A proxies over time, so ignoring D&A means ignoring capital intensity.

### The maths
$$EBITDA = Revenue - COGS - Opex \ (\text{excluding D\&A}) = EBIT + D\&A$$
$$\text{EBITDA margin} = EBITDA/Revenue$$
Relationship to cash: $UFCF = EBITDA - \text{taxes on EBIT} - Capex - \Delta NWC$.

### Worked example with numbers
Two companies, both with EBITDA 100:
- Software: capex 10, taxes 20, ΔNWC 0 → UFCF ≈ 70. Cash conversion 70%.
- Telecom: capex 60, taxes 8, ΔNWC 2 → UFCF ≈ 30. Cash conversion 30%.
At the same EV/EBITDA multiple they would be priced equally, which would be wrong: the software company deserves a higher multiple. That is why EBITDA-EBITDA comparisons only work within a sector.

Leverage: net debt 400 on EBITDA 100 = 4x net leverage, typical high-yield/leveraged loan territory.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Calling EBITDA "cash flow".
- Not knowing that IFRS 16 (leases) mechanically increased reported EBITDA, since lease payments moved from opex to depreciation + interest; comparisons across time/standards must adjust.
- Forgetting that EBITDA is what LBO debt sizing is based on, which is why adjustments are fought over.

### How to deliver it
Definition, two reasons (capital-structure neutral, cross-company comparability), then two criticisms (capex, adjustments). Buffett quote optional but memorable.
deep.cf-019:
### Context / why they ask this
A conceptual question that checks you understand accrual vs cash and liquidity vs solvency. Very relevant for credit sales and trading.

### Key concepts
- **Liquidity**: ability to meet short-term obligations with available cash and credit lines.
- **Solvency**: assets exceed liabilities in value; long-term ability to pay.
- **Maturity wall**: a large amount of debt maturing at the same time; refinancing risk.
- **Revolving credit facility (RCF)**: committed bank line a company can draw on; key liquidity buffer.
- **Cash burn / runway**: how fast a loss-making firm consumes cash, and how many months it has left.

### Intuition
Picture a builder who books a 1m profit on a project but will be paid in 12 months, while it must pay workers and suppliers now. Its payslips bounce long before the client pays. Now picture a start-up losing 50m a year but with 500m of VC money in the bank: 10 years of runway.

### Examples
- **Carillion (UK, 2018)**: reported profits on long-term contracts, but cash was not coming in, debt piled up, it collapsed.
- **Growth companies** like Amazon in the early 2000s had thin or negative profits but strong operating cash flow thanks to negative working capital (paid by customers before paying suppliers).
- **SVB (2023)** was a liquidity/confidence crisis on the funding side (covered in the rates deck).

### The maths
Operating cash flow bridge:
$$CFO = NI + D\&A + \text{other non-cash} - \Delta NWC$$
A firm with NI = +20, D&A = 10, ΔNWC = +60 has CFO = −30. Add capex of 20 and a debt maturity of 50: it needs 100 of external funding this year despite being profitable.

Conversely NI = −20 driven by a 50 impairment (non-cash): CFO = −20 + 50 + ... = positive.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Answering only "because of debt". Debt matters through the cash it requires (interest + principal) and refinancing risk.
- Confusing insolvency with illiquidity. Banks can be solvent but illiquid (a run), which is why central banks act as lender of last resort.

### How to deliver it
"Bankruptcy is about cash, not profit." Then three causes (working capital, capex, refinancing), then the converse (funding runway, non-cash charges). One real example if you have it.
deep.cf-020:
### Context / why they ask this
Fundamental for multiples, M&A and credit. Follow-ups test the bridge items (why subtract cash, why add minorities) and "does EV change if...".

### Key concepts
- **Diluted shares**: basic shares + dilutive securities (in-the-money options via the treasury stock method, convertibles if in the money).
- **Net debt**: gross debt (bonds, loans, often leases under IFRS 16) − cash and equivalents.
- **Preferred stock**: hybrid claim senior to common equity; not owned by common shareholders, so added.
- **Minority (non-controlling) interest**: when a parent owns e.g. 80% of a subsidiary, it consolidates 100% of the sub's EBITDA, but 20% of that belongs to others. Adding the minority stake to EV keeps numerator and denominator consistent.
- **Associates / equity investments**: stakes of 20-50% not consolidated; their earnings are not in EBITDA, so their value is **subtracted** from EV.

### Intuition
EV is the "takeover price" of the whole operating machine: buy all the shares, take over (repay) the debt and other claims, and pocket the cash. The cash you acquire offsets part of what you pay, so it is subtracted. Every bridge item follows one principle: **EV should include exactly the claims on the cash flows measured by the denominator (EBITDA, EBIT)**.

### The maths
$$EV = \underbrace{P \times N_{diluted}}_{\text{equity value}} + \text{Debt} + \text{Preferred} + \text{Minority interest} - \text{Cash} - \text{Non-operating investments}$$
Also, from a DCF: $EV = PV(UFCF)$ and equity value $= EV - \text{net debt} - \ldots$

### Worked example with numbers
Share price 20, 100m diluted shares: equity value 2,000. Debt 800, cash 300, minority interest 100, preferred 0, associates 50.
$$EV = 2000 + 800 + 100 - 300 - 50 = 2550$$
With EBITDA of 300, EV/EBITDA = 8.5x.

### Can equity value be greater than EV? Negative EV?
Yes: if the company has more cash than debt (net cash), EV < equity value. Tech firms with large cash piles are examples. EV can even be negative (cash > market cap + debt), which in theory means the market values the operating business negatively, often a sign of expected cash burn or trapped cash.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Using basic rather than diluted shares.
- Pairing EV with net income (P/E-type metrics) or equity value with EBITDA: mismatched.
- Subtracting all cash when some is operating cash needed to run the business or trapped abroad (a refinement).

### How to deliver it
Definitions, the formula, the house analogy, then the principle: "EV pairs with pre-interest metrics, equity value with post-interest metrics." Be ready for "why subtract cash".
deep.cf-021:
### Context / why they ask this
These questions check that you really understand the EV bridge rather than memorising a formula. They are also common in M&A-flavoured interviews and in equity sales when discussing buybacks and special dividends.

### Key concepts
- **Net debt** = debt − cash.
- **Ex-dividend date**: date from which the buyer of the share no longer receives the declared dividend; the price drops by roughly the dividend.
- **Recapitalisation (recap)**: changing the capital structure, e.g. borrowing to pay a dividend or buy back shares ("leveraged recap"). In an MM world it does not change EV.

### Intuition
Think of EV as the value of the "machine" (the operating business), and equity + net debt as two slices of that machine's value. Financial transactions (borrowing, paying dividends, buying back shares) resize the slices, not the machine. Operating transactions (buying a factory, making an acquisition) change the machine.

### The maths
$$EV = E + ND, \qquad ND = D - Cash$$
| Transaction | ΔD | ΔCash | ΔND | ΔE | ΔEV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Borrow 100, hold cash | +100 | +100 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Pay 100 dividend from cash | 0 | −100 | +100 | −100 | 0 |
| Borrow 100 and pay dividend | +100 | 0 | +100 | −100 | 0 |
| Buy back shares for 100 | 0 | −100 | +100 | −100 | 0 |
| Buy factory for 100 at NPV 0 | 0 | −100 | +100 | 0 | +100 |
| Issue 100 of new shares | 0 | +100 | −100 | +100 | 0 |

### Worked example with numbers
Company: 100 shares at 20, equity 2,000, debt 500, cash 200, EV 2,300. It pays a special dividend of 1 per share (100 total) from cash.
- After: cash 100, net debt 400, share price ≈ 19, equity 1,900, EV = 1,900 + 400 = 2,300. Unchanged.
- The shareholder had a 20 share; now has a 19 share and 1 of cash. No wealth created (before taxes).

### Real-world refinements (good to add)
- Debt adds a **tax shield**, which in theory raises firm value ($+tD$ in MM with taxes), and increases distress costs.
- Signalling: announcing a buyback can raise the share price if the market reads it as "management thinks the stock is cheap".
- Multiples change even if EV does not: after a debt-funded buyback, P/E, EPS and ROE move (see buyback card).

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- Saying "issuing debt increases EV because debt is added". Cash is also added.
- Saying the dividend reduces EV.

### How to deliver it
Go through each case with "net debt changes by X, equity by Y, so EV...". State the principle at the end: financing transactions don't change EV; operating investments do.
deep.cf-022:
### Context / why they ask this
Equity sales and trading talk in P/E all day ("the Stoxx 600 trades at about 15x forward earnings", as it did in August-September 2026; "US tech on 30x"). They check you can interpret the number and link it to growth, risk and rates.

### Key concepts
- **EPS (earnings per share)**: net income / diluted shares.
- **Trailing (LTM) vs forward P/E**: last twelve months' earnings vs next twelve months' consensus forecasts. Market commentary mostly uses forward.
- **Earnings yield**: E/P = 1/(P/E), comparable to bond yields; the gap vs real bond yields is a rough equity risk premium gauge.
- **PEG ratio**: P/E divided by growth rate (in %); P/E 20 with 20% growth gives PEG 1.
- **Payout ratio**: dividends / net income.

### Intuition
Paying 20x means you accept a 5% earnings yield today, which only makes sense if earnings grow or are very safe compared with bonds. Higher rates raise the required return, so for the same growth the market pays less: P/E falls. That is why multiples compress when yields rise.

### The maths
Gordon: $P_0 = \frac{D_1}{R_E - g}$ with $D_1 = b \cdot E_1$ ($b$ payout):
$$\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{b}{R_E - g} \qquad \text{(forward P/E)}$$
With sustainable growth $g = ROE \times (1-b)$, you can show that growth only increases value if $ROE > R_E$.

### Worked example with numbers
Payout 50%, $R_E = 9\%$, $g = 4\%$: forward P/E = 0.5/0.05 = **10x**. With $g = 6\%$: 0.5/0.03 = 16.7x. With $R_E = 10\%$, $g = 4\%$: 0.5/0.06 = 8.3x. Small changes in growth or discount rates move multiples a lot.
Company: price 50, EPS 2.5: P/E 20, earnings yield 5%.

### Why P/E can mislead
- **Leverage**: two firms with identical operations but different debt have different EPS and P/E (debt raises risk and changes earnings).
- **One-offs**: a big asset sale gain inflates earnings and depresses the P/E.
- **Accounting**: depreciation policy, tax rate differences across countries.
- **Cyclicals**: at the top of the cycle earnings are high so P/E looks low (value trap); at the bottom P/E looks very high. Hence "buy cyclicals on high P/Es, sell on low P/Es". Shiller CAPE smooths using 10-year average real earnings.
- **Negative earnings**: undefined.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "High P/E means expensive." Not necessarily: it may reflect growth or quality.
- Comparing P/Es across sectors with different growth and risk profiles.

### How to deliver it
Definition, interpretation (years of earnings, earnings yield), drivers (growth, risk/rates, payout), limits. The Gordon link is a nice differentiator for a maths profile.
deep.cf-023:
### Context / why they ask this
A top-5 technical question. The key word they want is "capital structure", followed by the consistency principle.

### Key concepts
- **Numerator-denominator consistency**: if the metric in the denominator is available to all investors (EBITDA, EBIT, revenue, UFCF), use EV; if it belongs only to shareholders (net income, FCFE, book equity), use equity value.
- **EV/EBIT**: accounts for D&A as a proxy for capex; better for capital-intensive comparisons.
- **EV/Sales**: for loss-making growth firms.
- **P/B (price to book)**: for banks and insurers.

### Intuition
Leverage changes who gets what, not what the business produces. EV/EBITDA looks at "what the business produces" and "what the whole business costs". P/E looks at "what shareholders get after lenders" and "what shareholders pay", so it bakes in each firm's financing choice.

### The maths: leverage effect on P/E
Two identical firms, EBITDA 100, D&A 20, EBIT 80, tax 25%, EV 800 (8x EBITDA).
- **Firm U** (no debt): NI = 80 × 0.75 = 60; equity 800; **P/E = 13.3x**.
- **Firm L** (debt 400 at 5%): interest 20, NI = 60 × 0.75 = 45; equity 400; **P/E = 8.9x**.
Same EV/EBITDA (8x), very different P/E. Note that L's P/E is lower because its earnings yield (11.25%) must compensate for the extra risk of levered equity. Whether leverage raises or lowers the P/E depends on the after-tax cost of debt versus the unlevered earnings yield: here after-tax cost of debt 3.75% < earnings yield 7.5%, so leverage raises EPS relative to price and lowers the P/E.

### When P/E is better
- **Financials**: debt/deposits are raw material; EBITDA is meaningless.
- When investors focus on EPS (equity research, short-term markets) and capital structures are similar.
- It captures taxes and interest, which are real costs to shareholders.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "EV/EBITDA is better because EBITDA is cash flow." It is not cash flow.
- Mixing: EV/net income or P/EBITDA (inconsistent).
- Forgetting minority/associate adjustments that keep EV consistent with consolidated EBITDA.

### How to deliver it
Three arguments: capital structure, accounting/tax neutrality, works when NI negative. Then one limitation (ignores capex, not for banks) and the consistency rule. The numerical example is a strong bonus if they want depth.
deep.cf-024:
### Context / why they ask this
A generalist classic that checks you know the toolbox and can compare methods. For S&T, trading comps logic is what equity sales and research use every day.

### Key concepts
- **Trading comparables (comps)**: peer group of listed companies with similar business, size, growth, geography. Compute their multiples on LTM and forward metrics, take median/range, apply to target.
- **Precedent transactions**: M&A deals in the sector; multiples reflect prices actually paid for control.
- **Control premium**: premium over market price paid to acquire control (ability to decide strategy, dividends, cash flows).
- **Synergies**: extra value from combining (cost savings, revenue cross-selling).
- **Sum-of-the-parts (SOTP)**: value each division separately and add; for conglomerates.
- **Football field**: bar chart showing value ranges from each method.

### Intuition
DCF asks "what is it worth given its cash flows?". Comps ask "what does the market pay for similar things today?". Precedents ask "what have buyers paid to own similar things outright?". LBO asks "what can a leveraged buyer afford?". The truth usually lies in the overlap.

### Pros and cons
| Method | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| DCF | Fundamental, captures specifics | Very assumption-sensitive, TV-heavy |
| Trading comps | Market-based, quick, current | Few true peers; market can be wrong; no control premium |
| Precedents | Real prices paid, includes control | Stale (different market conditions), few deals, deal-specific synergies |
| LBO | Sets financial buyer's max price | Depends on debt markets and return target |

### Worked example with numbers
Target EBITDA 100, net debt 200, 50 shares.
- Comps at 8x: EV 800, equity 600, **12.0/share**.
- Precedents at 10x: EV 1,000, equity 800, **16.0/share** (a 33% premium to comps).
- DCF: EV 900, **14.0/share**.
- LBO: sponsor targeting 20% IRR can pay 8.5x, EV 850, **13.0/share**.
Football field: 12-16, with a central range of 13-15.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "The DCF always gives the highest value." Not a rule.
- Using comps that differ in growth or margins without adjustment.
- Forgetting that a strategic buyer (with synergies) can typically pay more than a financial sponsor.

### How to deliver it
Name the three methods, one line each, then answer "which is highest" with the control premium argument. Mention the football field. 45 seconds.
deep.cf-025:
### Context / why they ask this
A test of judgment: do you understand *why* a multiple is used rather than applying EV/EBITDA everywhere. Useful for equity sales and research-facing roles.

### Key concepts
- **Book value (BV)**: accounting equity. **Tangible book (TBV)** = BV − goodwill − intangibles.
- **ROE**: net income / equity.
- **ARR**: annual recurring revenue (subscription businesses).
- **NAV**: net asset value, market value of assets minus liabilities.
- **FFO**: funds from operations for REITs.
- **EBITDAX**: EBITDA before exploration expenses (accounting treatment of exploration differs across firms).
- **RAB**: regulated asset base, on which regulators allow a return (utilities).

### Intuition
Pick the metric that (1) is positive and meaningful, (2) reflects the true economic driver, and (3) is comparable across the peer group. A bank's value comes from earning a return on its equity capital; a REIT from its properties; a start-up from its growth; an oil company from its reserves and the oil price.

### The maths: why P/B for banks
From the Gordon model with ROE and sustainable growth:
$$\frac{P}{B} = \frac{ROE - g}{R_E - g}$$
A bank earning ROE = cost of equity trades at book (P/B = 1). ROE 12%, $R_E$ 10%, g 2%: P/B = 10/8 = **1.25x**. ROE 8%: P/B = 6/8 = **0.75x**. This is why many European banks traded well below book in the low-rate 2010s (ROE below cost of equity) and re-rated as rates and ROEs rose.

### Worked example with numbers
Growth software firm: revenue 200 growing 40%, EBITDA margin −10%. Peers trade at 8x forward sales: EV ≈ 8 × 280 = 2,240. Rule of 40: 40% growth + (−10%) margin = 30 < 40, so maybe apply a discount.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- EV/EBITDA for a bank.
- P/E for a company with negative earnings.
- Ignoring cyclicality for commodity companies (normalised earnings).

### How to deliver it
Give the principle (meaningful, driver, comparable), then run through two or three sectors quickly. Expand on banks with P/B vs ROE, since it links to the bank cards and shows depth.
deep.cf-026:
### Context / why they ask this
MM is the foundation of corporate finance theory and a favourite with maths profiles. They check the proposition, the intuition (pie), the arbitrage argument, and the fact that real-world frictions are what make capital structure matter.

### Key concepts
- **Levered vs unlevered firm**: with debt vs all equity, identical operating assets.
- **Homemade leverage**: an investor replicates a levered firm's equity by buying unlevered shares partly with personal borrowing.
- **Tax shield**: taxes saved via interest deductibility, $t \times$ interest each year.
- **Financial distress costs**: direct (legal, administrators) and indirect (lost customers, suppliers asking for cash, underinvestment, fire sales).
- **Agency costs**: conflicts between shareholders, lenders and managers (e.g. risk-shifting when close to default; free cash flow wasted by managers, which debt disciplines).

### Intuition
A pizza is the same size whether you cut it into 2 or 8 slices. The firm's assets produce cash flows; debt and equity are just ways to cut them. Adding debt makes the equity slice riskier (it absorbs all variability on a smaller base), so shareholders demand more, precisely enough to keep the overall cost unchanged. Only when someone outside (the government via taxes, lawyers via bankruptcy) takes a slice does the capital structure change what investors get.

### The maths
**Prop I (no tax)**: $V_L = V_U$.
**Prop II (no tax)**: WACC = $\frac{E}{V}R_E + \frac{D}{V}R_D = R_U$ constant, so
$$R_E = R_U + (R_U - R_D)\frac{D}{E}$$
**With taxes**, perpetual debt $D$ at $R_D$: annual tax shield $t R_D D$, PV at $R_D$ = $tD$:
$$V_L = V_U + tD, \qquad R_E = R_U + (R_U - R_D)(1-t)\frac{D}{E}$$
**Trade-off**: $V_L = V_U + PV(\text{tax shields}) - PV(\text{distress costs})$, maximised at an interior leverage.

Arbitrage proof sketch (no tax): suppose $V_L > V_U$. Sell 1% of L's equity, borrow 1% of L's debt personally, buy 1% of U. Your payoff is identical to holding 1% of L's equity (1% of cash flows minus 1% of interest), but you pocketed the price difference. So $V_L = V_U$.

### Worked example with numbers
Unlevered cost of capital $R_U = 10\%$, cost of debt 5%, no tax.
- D/E = 0: $R_E = 10\%$, WACC 10%.
- D/E = 1: $R_E = 10\% + 5\% \times 1 = 15\%$; WACC = 0.5 × 15% + 0.5 × 5% = 10%.
- D/E = 3: $R_E = 25\%$; WACC = 0.25 × 25% + 0.75 × 5% = 10%.
With 25% tax, firm value 1,000 unlevered, it issues 400 of permanent debt to buy back shares: $V_L = 1000 + 0.25 \times 400 = 1100$. Shareholders capture the 100 of tax shield value.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "MM says debt doesn't matter, so it's useless." Its value is showing *where* capital structure matters: taxes, distress, agency, information.
- Saying WACC falls with debt because debt is cheaper, without the offsetting rise in $R_E$.

### How to deliver it
Prop I with pie analogy, Prop II formula, then "with taxes debt adds tD, with distress costs we get an optimum". The arbitrage argument in one sentence impresses a maths-heavy interviewer.
deep.cf-027:
### Context / why they ask this
Combines ratio mechanics with a judgment question. Relevant for DCM and credit sales (why corporates issue debt), and for bank analysis (leverage is the heart of banking).

### Key concepts
- **ROE** = net income / equity. **ROA** = net income / total assets (or, here, return on the operating assets before financing, e.g. NOPAT / invested capital, **ROIC**).
- **Financial leverage** = D/E or assets/equity.
- **Operating leverage**: high fixed costs relative to variable costs; amplifies EBIT volatility. Combined with financial leverage, it compounds risk.
- **Credit rating**: agency assessment (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) of default risk; IG (BBB−/Baa3 and above) vs high yield.
- **Covenants**: loan conditions (e.g. max net debt/EBITDA) whose breach gives lenders rights.

### Intuition
Borrow at 4% to invest in a business returning 8%: every euro of debt earns shareholders 4 cents on top. But if the business returns 2% in a bad year, each euro of debt costs them 2 cents. With enough debt, a bad year wipes out equity. Leverage is a magnifying glass on performance.

### The maths
With $r$ the after-tax return on invested capital and $r_D$ the after-tax cost of debt, invested capital $= D + E$:
$$NI = r(D+E) - r_D D \Rightarrow ROE = \frac{NI}{E} = r + (r - r_D)\frac{D}{E}$$
Volatility: if $r$ has standard deviation $\sigma_r$, $\sigma_{ROE} = \sigma_r(1 + D/E)$.

### Worked example with numbers
Invested capital 1,000, after-tax return 8%, after-tax cost of debt 4%.
| D/E | Debt | Equity | NI | ROE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 1000 | 80 | 8% |
| 1 | 500 | 500 | 80 − 20 = 60 | 12% |
| 3 | 750 | 250 | 80 − 30 = 50 | 20% |

Bad year, return 2%: D/E = 0 gives ROE 2%; D/E = 1 gives (20 − 20)/500 = 0%; D/E = 3 gives (20 − 30)/250 = **−4%**.

### Choosing the structure: factors
- **For debt**: tax shield, lower cost, discipline (Jensen's free cash flow argument), no dilution.
- **Against debt**: distress costs, covenants, rating downgrades, less flexibility for M&A or downturns, higher cost of equity.
- **Business profile**: stable cash flows and tangible collateral support more debt.
- **Market signals**: equity issuance is read negatively (pecking order), buybacks positively.
- **Market windows**: firms issue equity when their shares are richly valued and debt when spreads are tight (market timing).

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "More debt always increases ROE." Only if the return on capital exceeds the cost of debt, and at the cost of more risk.
- Ignoring that rating agencies and investors enforce limits in practice.

### How to deliver it
Formula with the 8% / 4% example, then "risk goes up too", then the trade-off list and "in practice companies target a rating". Tie to banks: "banks run at 15-20x leverage, which is why regulators impose capital ratios."
deep.cf-028:
### Context / why they ask this
Very common in equity sales/trading: buyback programmes and dividends move stocks and drive flows (buybacks are a big source of equity demand), and dividends matter for derivatives (dividend futures, forward pricing).

### Key concepts
- **Dividend**: cash paid per share. Key dates: announcement, **ex-dividend date** (buyers from this date don't get the dividend; the price drops by about the dividend), record date, payment date.
- **Dividend yield** = dividend per share / price. **Payout ratio** = dividends / net income.
- **Share buyback (repurchase)**: company buys its own shares on the market (or via tender offer / accelerated share repurchase with a bank), then cancels or holds them as treasury shares.
- **Special dividend**: one-off distribution.
- **Signalling**: management actions reveal private information to the market.

### Intuition
Imagine a company worth 1,000 with 100 shares at 10, holding 100 of spare cash.
- Dividend of 1/share: each shareholder gets 1 in cash; the company is worth 900; the share is worth 9. Wealth = 9 + 1 = 10.
- Buyback of 100: company buys 10 shares at 10; company worth 900 with 90 shares: still 10/share. Sellers got cash, holders kept shares worth 10.
Same total wealth. Differences are tax, signalling and flexibility.

### The maths
Dividend: $P_{ex} = P_{cum} - D$ (ignoring taxes).
Buyback at fair price $P$ with cash $X$: shares $N' = N - X/P$, value $V' = V - X$, price $V'/N' = (V - X)/(N - X/P) = P$ since $V = NP$.
If the buyback price is **above** fair value, remaining shareholders lose (wealth transfer to sellers); **below** fair value, they gain. Hence "buy back when undervalued".

### Worked example: EPS effect
Net income 100, 100 shares, price 20 (P/E 20, EPS 1). Buy back 10% (200) using cash earning 2% pre-tax, tax 25%: lost interest after tax = 200 × 2% × 0.75 = 3. New NI 97, shares 90, **EPS 1.078 (+7.8%)**. Accretive because the earnings yield of the shares bought (1/20 = 5%) exceeds the after-tax yield on cash (1.5%). But value per share is unchanged in theory (20): the higher EPS comes with higher leverage/risk, so P/E drifts down to about 18.6.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "Buybacks create value because EPS rises." EPS accretion ≠ value creation.
- Forgetting the ex-dividend price drop.
- Ignoring tax differences across investor types (a pension fund vs a taxable individual).

### How to deliver it
"Equivalent in theory, different in practice", then 3-4 practical differences (commitment/signal, flexibility, tax, EPS). End with the "base dividend plus buybacks" practice. Mention that buybacks are a large source of US equity demand, a market flow angle for S&T.
deep.cf-029:
### Context / why they ask this
ECM (equity capital markets) is core to equity sales: capital increases, rights issues, placements. They test that you understand that "dilution" is not automatically "value destruction", and the TERP arithmetic.

### Key concepts
- **Primary vs secondary offering**: primary = new shares issued, cash to the company (dilutive); secondary = existing holders sell, cash to them (not dilutive).
- **Rights issue**: pre-emptive offering to existing shareholders; rights are tradeable ("nil-paid rights"). Common in Europe, usually underwritten by banks.
- **Placement / accelerated bookbuild (ABB)**: shares sold quickly to institutional investors at a small discount, typically up to 10-20% of share capital without rights (limits vary by jurisdiction).
- **Pre-emption rights**: legal right of existing holders to maintain their percentage.
- **Treasury stock method**: dilution from options.

### Intuition
If new shares are sold at market price, the pie grows by exactly the value of the new slices: no one is richer or poorer. If sold at a discount to outsiders, the new holders get a bargain paid for by the old holders. A rights issue gives the bargain to the old holders themselves, so the discount can be large (30-40% is common for distressed issuers) without harming them, which makes the deal more certain to succeed.

### The maths
Before: $N$ shares at $P$. Rights issue of $n$ new shares per existing share at subscription price $S$:
$$TERP = \frac{P + nS}{1 + n}$$
Value of one right (attached to one new share): $TERP - S$. Per existing share: $n(TERP - S) = P - TERP$.

### Worked example with numbers
$N = 100$, $P = 20$, 1-for-4 ($n = 0.25$), $S = 12$:
- $TERP = (20 + 0.25 \times 12)/1.25 = 23/1.25 = 18.40$
- Right value per new share: 6.40; per existing share: $20 - 18.40 = 1.60 = 0.25 \times 6.40$.
- A holder of 4 shares (80): subscribes for 1 share paying 12 → owns 5 shares × 18.40 = 92 = 80 + 12. Unchanged. Or sells the right for 6.40 → owns 4 × 18.40 + 6.40 = 80. Unchanged. Or does nothing and lets the rights lapse: 73.60, loses 6.40 (banks usually sell unexercised rights in a "rump" placement to protect them).

Treasury stock method: 10m options with strike 10, share price 20: proceeds 100m buy back 5m shares, net dilution **5m shares**.

### Common pitfalls / bad answers
- "Dilution always hurts shareholders." Only when the price is below fair value or proceeds are invested poorly.
- Confusing secondary sales (no dilution) with primary issuance.

### How to deliver it
Definition, fair price vs discount distinction, then TERP with the numbers. Explain why rights issues can price at a deep discount. That shows you think like an ECM desk.
deep.cf-030:
### Context / why they ask this
This is a warm-up mental-maths question that checks three things at once: that you really understand discounting (not just a formula), that you can compute under pressure without a calculator, and that you notice the ambiguity of "net present value of 1 over 10 years" (one cash flow at year 10, or one cash flow every year?). The perpetual bond variant (asked on a French S&T assistant interview) tests whether you know the perpetuity shortcut and can link it to rate sensitivity. These formulas are also the building blocks of the DCF terminal value, the dividend discount model and bond pricing.

### Key concepts
- **Present value (PV)**: what a future cash flow is worth today, given you could invest money at rate $r$ in the meantime.
- **Discount factor**: $DF(t) = (1+r)^{-t}$, the price today of 1 paid at time $t$.
- **Annuity**: a fixed payment every period for $n$ periods (a mortgage, a bond's coupons, a lease).
- **Annuity due**: same, but payments at the start of each period (rent). Its value is the ordinary annuity times $(1+r)$.
- **Perpetuity**: an annuity that never stops. Real examples: British consols (redeemed in 2015), some perpetual bank bonds (AT1, which are callable, so not truly perpetual), preferred shares.
- **Growing perpetuity**: payments that grow at rate $g$ forever.

### Intuition
A perpetuity paying $C$ per year is worth $C/r$ because if you deposit $C/r$ at rate $r$, the interest is exactly $C$ every year and the capital is never touched: the deposit replicates the perpetuity. An annuity for $n$ years is a perpetuity starting today **minus** a perpetuity starting after year $n$: that is where the formula comes from, and why an annuity is always worth less than $C/r$.

### The maths
Geometric series with ratio $q = 1/(1+r)$:
$$PV_{\text{annuity}} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{C}{(1+r)^t} = \frac{C}{r}\left(1 - \frac{1}{(1+r)^n}\right)$$
Let $n \to \infty$: $PV_{\text{perp}} = C/r$. With growth, the ratio becomes $(1+g)/(1+r)$ and, provided $g < r$:
$$PV_{\text{growing perp}} = \frac{C_1}{r - g}$$
where $C_1$ is the first payment, one period from now. Duration of a perpetuity (Macaulay): $D = (1+r)/r$; modified duration $1/r$. So a 1 percentage point rise in rates from 5% to 6% cuts the value from 20,000 to 16,667, a 16.7% fall.

### Worked example with numbers
- Single cash flow: $1.1^{10} = 2.5937$, so $PV = 0.3855$. Mental trick: $\ln(1.1) \approx 0.0953$, so $1.1^{10} \approx e^{0.953} \approx 2.59$. Or the **rule of 72**: money doubles in about $72/10 = 7.2$ years at 10% (exact: 7.27), so in 10 years it multiplies by roughly $2^{10/7.2} \approx 2.6$.
- Annuity of 1 for 10 years at 10%: $\frac{1}{0.1}(1 - 0.3855) = 10 \times 0.6145 = 6.14$. Paid at the start of each year (annuity due): $6.14 \times 1.1 = 6.76$.
- Perpetual bond paying EUR 1,000: at 5%, $1000/0.05 = 20{,}000$; at 4%, $25{,}000$ (a 1pp fall in rates adds 25%).
- A 30-year annuity of EUR 1,000 at 5% is worth EUR 15,372: the payments beyond year 30 are worth only $20{,}000/1.05^{30} = 4{,}628$ today. This is why long annuities "look like" perpetuities.
- Growing perpetuity: first payment 100, growth 2%, rate 7%: $100/0.05 = 2{,}000$.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Answering "0.39" and stopping: mention the other reading.
- Using $C_0$ instead of $C_1$ in the growing perpetuity (off by a factor $1+g$).
- Forgetting that $g < r$ is required: if $g \ge r$ the sum diverges; in a DCF, a terminal growth close to the discount rate gives absurd values.
- Saying "a perpetuity is worth infinite money because it pays forever": the discount factors decay geometrically, so the series converges.

### How to deliver it
State the ambiguity in one sentence, give 0.39 and 6.14 with the mental steps (rule of 72 or $e^{0.95}$), then the perpetuity $C/r$ and one sentence on its huge rate sensitivity. If time allows, connect: "this is the terminal value in a DCF and the Gordon model for stocks".
deep.cf-031:
### Context / why they ask this
It is the simplest intrinsic valuation of a stock, and it connects to many other topics: the P/E and P/B formulas, the equity risk premium, why stocks fall when rates rise, and dividend futures and swaps traded on equity derivatives desks. Asking for the implied growth tests whether you can use a model "backwards", which is how markets actually use it: you observe the price and infer what is priced in.

### Key concepts
- **Dividend**: cash paid by a company to its shareholders out of profits, usually annual, semi-annual or quarterly.
- **Cost of equity ($r$ or $R_E$)**: the return shareholders require given the risk, typically from CAPM: risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium.
- **Payout ratio**: dividends / net income. **Retention ratio** $b = 1 -$ payout.
- **Sustainable growth**: $g = b \times ROE$: a company that retains a fraction $b$ of earnings and reinvests it at a return ROE grows its earnings at $b \cdot ROE$.
- **Dividend yield**: $D/P$.
- **Two-stage (multi-stage) DDM**: explicit dividends for a high-growth period, then a Gordon terminal value.

### Intuition
An investor buying a share and selling it in a year gets the dividend plus the resale price, but the resale price itself depends on the dividends after that, and so on: iterate and the share is worth the whole dividend stream. The Gordon formula is a growing perpetuity. The expected return decomposition $r = D/P + g$ is very intuitive: you earn the cash yield today, plus the growth of the whole stream (the price grows at $g$ in the model).

### The maths
$$P_0 = \sum_{t\ge1} \frac{D_1 (1+g)^{t-1}}{(1+r)^t} = \frac{D_1}{r-g}, \quad g<r$$
Sensitivity: $\frac{\partial \ln P}{\partial r} = -\frac{1}{r-g}$, a "duration" of $1/(r-g)$, 20 years here. So equities behave like very long-duration bonds, even more so for high-growth names where $r - g$ is small. Link to multiples: dividing by earnings $E_1$, $P_0/E_1 = \text{payout}/(r-g)$; and with $g = b \cdot ROE$, $P_0/B_0 = (ROE - g)/(r - g)$.

### Worked example with numbers
1. $D_1 = 3$, $g = 3\%$, $r = 8\%$: $P_0 = 3/0.05 = 60$.
2. If $r$ moves to 9%: $3/0.06 = 50$, a 16.7% fall for a 1pp move.
3. Implied return at price 50 with $D_1 = 2.5$, $g = 3\%$: $2.5/50 + 3\% = 8\%$.
4. Implied growth at price 60, $D_1 = 3$, $r = 9\%$: $9\% - 5\% = 4\%$.
5. Two-stage: current dividend $D_0 = 2$, growing 10% for 5 years, then 3% forever, $r = 9\%$. Dividends 2.20, 2.42, 2.66, 2.93, 3.22, with a PV of 10.28. $D_6 = 3.22 \times 1.03 = 3.32$, terminal value at year 5 $= 3.32/0.06 = 55.29$, PV $= 55.29/1.09^5 = 35.94$. Total value **46.22**, of which 78% comes from the terminal value: typical, and a reminder that the long-run assumptions dominate.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Using $D_0$ (last dividend paid) instead of $D_1$ (next dividend).
- Plugging in $g \ge r$: the formula breaks. Long-run $g$ should not exceed nominal GDP growth (roughly 3-4%).
- Applying it to a company that doesn't pay dividends or buys back shares instead. Fix: use total shareholder payout (dividends + buybacks) or switch to free cash flow to equity.
- Forgetting that dividends can be cut: in 2020 many European banks were told by the ECB to suspend dividends, which hit dividend futures hard.

### How to deliver it
State the formula, give 60, then immediately show the sensitivity (60 to 50 for +1pp) and the reverse-engineering (implied growth 4%). Finish with where it is used: utilities, banks, and the P/E and P/B formulas. For an equity derivatives desk, mention that dividend expectations are traded directly through dividend futures.
deep.cf-032:
### Context / why they ask this
This question (reported from a junior analyst interview on Quant StackExchange) tests cross-asset thinking: can you express equity valuations in the same language as bonds? Sales and traders often hear "equities are expensive versus bonds" or "TINA" (there is no alternative, when bond yields were near zero). It connects P/E, DCF, the equity risk premium and the stock-bond relationship.

### Key concepts
- **P/E**: price divided by earnings per share (trailing = last 12 months; forward = next 12 months, estimated).
- **Earnings yield**: $E/P = 1/(P/E)$.
- **Equity risk premium (ERP)**: extra expected return demanded by equity investors over the risk-free rate.
- **Fed model**: the popular (and criticised) rule that equities are cheap when their earnings yield is above the 10-year nominal yield.
- **Real yield**: nominal yield minus expected inflation, observed on inflation-linked bonds (TIPS in the US).
- **Payout ratio, ROE, sustainable growth**: see the DDM card; $g = (1 - \text{payout}) \times ROE$.

### Intuition
A bond at 4% pays exactly 4 per 100 forever (in nominal terms). A stock at 25x "pays" 4 of earnings per 100 today, but earnings grow, roughly with nominal GDP, so the equity investor's expected return is higher than the earnings yield when the company can reinvest profitably. Conversely, part of the earnings must be retained to finance that growth, which is why the earnings yield is not a cash yield. Rates enter through the discount rate: a higher risk-free rate raises $r$, and because $r - g$ is small, the P/E is very sensitive.

### The maths
From the Gordon model with payout ratio $p$: $P_0 = \frac{p E_1}{r-g} \Rightarrow \frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{p}{r-g}$. With $g = (1-p)\,ROE$: $\frac{P}{E} = \frac{1 - g/ROE}{r - g}$.
Special case where growth creates no value ($ROE = r$): $P/E = 1/r$, so the earnings yield equals the cost of equity. In that case $E/P = r = y + ERP$: the earnings yield is a direct estimate of expected return, which is what the Fed model implicitly assumes.
Expected return decomposition: $r \approx E/P$ (adjusted for growth that creates value), or $r = D/P + g$.

### Worked example with numbers
- 28x: earnings yield $= 1/28 = 3.57\%$.
- Implied $r - g$ with 70% payout: $0.70/28 = 2.5\%$. If $r = 8\%$ (say 4% risk-free + 4% ERP), implied perpetual growth is 5.5%, a demanding assumption versus nominal GDP.
- Rate shock: $ROE = 15\%$, $g = 4.5\%$ so payout $= 1 - 4.5/15 = 0.70$. With $r = 8\%$: $P/E = 0.70/0.035 = 20$. If yields rise by 1pp and $r$ goes to 9%: $P/E = 0.70/0.045 = 15.6$, a **22% fall** in the multiple, all else equal.
- Crude ERP gauge: earnings yield minus real 10-year yield. With an earnings yield of 4.5% and a real yield of 2%, the "excess earnings yield" is 2.5pp, low by historical standards.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Treating the earnings yield as a cash yield like a coupon: it is not paid out entirely.
- Comparing the earnings yield with the **nominal** yield without comment: earnings are a real-ish stream, so inflation muddies the Fed model. In the 1970s-80s high nominal yields and low P/Es moved together largely because of inflation.
- Forgetting that rates can rise for "good" reasons (stronger growth, which raises $g$) or "bad" reasons (inflation, term premium), with different equity outcomes.
- Using trailing earnings in a recession, when E is depressed and P/E looks artificially high.

### How to deliver it
One line: "invert the P/E, 28x is a 3.6% earnings yield". Then the formula $P/E = p/(r - g)$ and the implied growth. Then the sensitivity to rates and the real-vs-nominal caveat. That shows you can go from a quoted multiple to a macro view, exactly what a cross-asset salesperson does.
deep.cf-033:
### Context / why they ask this
The P/B question (CFI equity research list; eFinancialCareers France "questions qui tuent" for equities jobs) is the standard test for banks and insurers, where P/B is the key multiple. It checks that you connect a multiple to fundamentals (ROE vs cost of equity) rather than treating "cheap vs book" as a buy signal.

### Key concepts
- **Book value (BV)**: accounting equity = total assets - total liabilities. **Tangible book value (TBV)**: book minus goodwill and intangibles, preferred for banks because intangibles cannot absorb losses.
- **Return on equity (ROE)**: net income / average shareholders' equity. **ROTE**: on tangible equity.
- **Cost of equity (COE)**: required return, typically 9-12% for European banks.
- **Value trap**: a stock that looks cheap on multiples but stays cheap or falls because the fundamentals keep deteriorating.
- **Residual income (excess return) model**: value = book + PV of future (ROE - COE) × book.

### Intuition
Think of book value as the capital invested by shareholders. If that capital earns exactly what shareholders require, it is worth exactly 1x: nothing more, nothing less. If it earns more, each euro of book is a "better than market" investment and trades at a premium; if it earns less, investors would prefer to have the cash back, so it trades at a discount. Growth amplifies the effect in both directions: growing a business with ROE < COE is value destruction at scale.

### The maths
Using Gordon with $g = b \cdot ROE$ and $E_1 = ROE \cdot B_0$:
$$P_0 = \frac{(1-b)\,ROE\,B_0}{r-g} = \frac{(ROE - g)\,B_0}{r - g} \Rightarrow \frac{P_0}{B_0} = \frac{ROE - g}{r-g}$$
Also $P/B = P/E \times ROE$: two banks with the same P/E but different ROEs have very different P/Bs. Residual income form: $P_0 = B_0 + \sum_t \frac{(ROE_t - r) B_{t-1}}{(1+r)^t}$, which shows immediately that $P/B > 1 \iff$ ROE exceeds $r$ on average.

### Worked example with numbers
$r = 10\%$, $g = 3\%$:
- ROE 12%: $P/B = 9/7 = 1.29$x
- ROE 10%: $7/7 = 1.00$x
- ROE 8%: $5/7 = 0.71$x
- ROE 15%: $12/7 = 1.71$x
So a bank at 0.6x book with an 8% ROE is roughly fairly priced, not cheap; the upside comes only if ROE improves. Another reason for a discount: if the market thinks 10% of the book will be wiped out by future loan losses, a bank with book 100 has an "economic" book of 90, and 0.8x reported book is 0.89x economic book.

Buyback below book: a bank at 0.5x TBV buying back shares increases TBV per share for remaining holders (it pays 0.5 for each euro of book it retires), which is why cheap banks favoured buybacks in 2022-2025.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- "Below book means you can buy the assets for less than they're worth": only if book is a good estimate of liquidation or economic value, rarely true for banks under stress or companies with obsolete assets.
- Using P/B for asset-light companies (software, consulting), where book value is tiny and meaningless: P/B of 20x tells you little.
- Forgetting buybacks and goodwill write-offs distort book value (some companies have negative book equity after large buybacks, e.g. some US consumer brands).

### How to deliver it
Give the formula and the intuition in one line ("P/B above 1 if and only if ROE beats cost of equity"), a two-number example, then the two reasons for trading below book (low ROE, doubtful assets) and the value-trap warning. A concrete example (European banks in the 2010s, Japanese companies and the Tokyo Stock Exchange's 2023 push against sub-1x P/B listings) shows market awareness.
deep.cf-034:
### Context / why they ask this
It is the conceptual core of valuation and a favourite "think, don't recite" question. It explains why two companies with the same earnings and growth can deserve different multiples, why value investors focus on returns on capital, and why acquisitions at high prices often destroy value. For an S&T candidate it shows you understand what equity research and investors actually argue about.

### Key concepts
- **NOPAT**: net operating profit after tax = EBIT × (1 - tax rate). Operating profit as if the company had no debt.
- **Invested capital**: fixed assets + working capital (+ goodwill if you include acquisitions) = equity + net debt from the financing side.
- **ROIC** = NOPAT / invested capital.
- **Reinvestment rate** = net investment / NOPAT = $g/ROIC$: to grow at $g$ with return ROIC you must reinvest $g/ROIC$ of your profit.
- **Economic profit (EVA)** = (ROIC - WACC) × invested capital.

### Intuition
Picture a savings account paying 6% when your required return is 8%. Putting more money in grows your balance faster, but you are worse off every euro you add. A company is the same: growth requires investment, and investment is only worth it at returns above the hurdle rate. When ROIC = WACC, the present value of the new investment exactly equals its cost: growth adds nothing. The only good growth is profitable growth.

### The maths
Free cash flow = NOPAT - net investment = $NOPAT(1 - g/ROIC)$. Then Gordon:
$$V_0 = \frac{NOPAT_1\left(1 - \frac{g}{ROIC}\right)}{WACC - g}$$
Check: if $ROIC = WACC$, $V_0 = \frac{NOPAT_1 (WACC - g)/WACC}{WACC - g} = NOPAT_1/WACC$, independent of $g$. Taking $\partial V/\partial g$ gives a sign equal to the sign of $ROIC - WACC$. Equivalent decomposition: $V_0 = \text{invested capital} + PV(\text{economic profits})$.

### Worked example with numbers
NOPAT next year 100, WACC 8%.
| ROIC | g = 3% | g = 5% |
|---|---|---|
| 6% | 1,000 | 556 |
| 8% | 1,250 | 1,250 |
| 16% | 1,625 | 2,292 |

With 16% ROIC and 5% growth, the company reinvests $5/16 = 31\%$ of NOPAT and pays out 69; with 6% ROIC it must reinvest 83% of NOPAT to grow at 5%, leaving only 17 of free cash flow.
Implied EV/NOPAT multiples: 10x, 12.5x and 16.3x (at 3% growth): same profits, very different multiples.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- "More growth always means a higher valuation": only with ROIC > WACC.
- Comparing ROE with WACC, or ROIC with cost of equity: match the numerator and the denominator (operating returns vs WACC; equity returns vs cost of equity).
- Ignoring goodwill: an acquirer paying a large premium may have a great ROIC excluding goodwill but a poor one including it; the second is what matters for the acquirer's shareholders.
- Forgetting competition: high ROICs attract entrants and tend to mean-revert; a moat (brand, network effects, patents, scale) is what sustains them.

### How to deliver it
Start with the direct answer "only if ROIC > WACC", explain reinvestment, then give the three numbers (1,000 / 1,250 / 1,625). Link to multiples ("this is why two companies with the same growth trade on different P/Es") and to M&A ("paying a big premium lowers the return on the capital you deploy").
deep.cf-035:
### Context / why they ask this
A classic follow-up to "EV vs equity value" (CFI equity research list). It checks that you understand the bridge as a formula with signs, not a memorised sentence, and that you can reason about what an odd number means economically.

### Key concepts
- **Equity value (market capitalisation)**: share price × diluted shares outstanding. Value belonging to shareholders.
- **Enterprise value (EV)**: value of the operating business to all capital providers: $EV = \text{equity} + \text{debt} + \text{preferred} + \text{minority interests} - \text{cash} - \text{non-operating assets}$.
- **Net debt**: debt minus cash and equivalents. **Net cash** when negative.
- **Minority (non-controlling) interests**: the part of consolidated subsidiaries owned by outsiders; added because consolidated EBITDA includes 100% of those subsidiaries.
- **Trapped cash**: cash that cannot be freely distributed (held abroad with tax on repatriation, regulatory capital, customer money, collateral).
- **Cash burn**: negative free cash flow that will consume the cash pile.

### Intuition
EV is the price of buying the whole business "cash-free, debt-free": if you buy all the shares, you also take over the debt (so add it) and pocket the cash (so subtract it). A company that is sitting on a big pile of cash costs you less than its market cap, because the cash comes back to you. If the cash pile exceeds the purchase price of the shares, you are effectively being paid to take the business, which only makes sense if the business is expected to lose money or the cash isn't really free.

### The maths
$$EV = E + D + P + MI - C - \text{Investments}$$
$E > EV \iff C + \text{Investments} > D + P + MI$.
Negative EV means $E < C - D - \dots$: the market cap is below net cash. Multiples: EV/EBITDA becomes negative or meaningless; analysts then look at the business's cash burn relative to the cash pile ("cash runway" = net cash / annual burn).

### Worked example with numbers
1. Net cash company: market cap 500, debt 20, cash 120: EV = 400; equity exceeds EV by the net cash of 100. With EBITDA of 50, EV/EBITDA = 8x, while "market cap / EBITDA" of 10x would overstate how expensive it is.
2. Negative EV: a biotech with market cap 100, cash 180, debt 30: net cash 150, EV = -50. If it burns 60 a year, it has 2.5 years of runway; the market is pricing the pipeline at below zero, i.e. it expects the cash to be largely spent on trials that fail. An activist might push to liquidate and return the cash.
3. Missing claims: the same company has a 70 lawsuit provision and 40 of leases: "adjusted" EV = -50 + 70 + 40 = 60, positive after all.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Saying "EV is always larger than equity value because you add debt": forgets cash.
- Subtracting all cash for a bank or an insurer, where cash is operating (customer deposits), or for a retailer that needs a minimum operating cash balance.
- Forgetting leases (IFRS 16 puts them on the balance sheet), pensions deficits, or convertible bonds (debt or equity depending on moneyness) in the bridge.

### How to deliver it
"Yes, whenever the company has net cash", give the three-line example, then answer the negative EV part with two or three economic explanations. Finishing with "it can be a real opportunity if the cash is free and the business breaks even, that's what activists look for" shows judgement.
deep.cf-036:
### Context / why they ask this
Both questions come from the CFI equity research interview list. They test whether you know exactly what each multiple includes, and whether you can diagnose a discrepancy between multiples instead of reciting definitions. In S&T, salespeople quote both multiples to clients; understanding what drives a gap avoids naive "it's cheap on P/E" pitches.

### Key concepts
- **EBITDA**: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a proxy for operating cash flow before capex.
- **EBIT**: operating profit after D&A. EBIT ≈ EBITDA - D&A.
- **D&A**: accounting spreading of past capex (depreciation of tangible assets) and of acquired intangibles (amortisation).
- **Maintenance capex**: investment needed just to keep capacity constant; roughly approximated by D&A over the long run.
- **Associates / equity-method investments**: stakes of about 20-50%; their share of profit appears in net income, but not in EBITDA.
- **Earnings yield vs after-tax cost of debt**: the comparison that determines whether debt-financing raises EPS.

### Intuition
EV/EBITDA looks at the whole firm before capital intensity, financing and tax. P/E looks at equity after everything. A gap therefore points at one of the "missing layers": financing (debt cheaper than equity makes EPS look good), capital intensity (heavy D&A depresses net income), tax, or non-operating income. EBITDA is useful to compare operations across capital structures and tax regimes, but it silently assumes capex is free, which is wrong for telecoms, airlines, utilities and manufacturers.

### The maths
With EV fixed, adding debt $D$ at rate $k_d$ and tax $t$: net income falls by $k_d(1-t)D$, equity falls by $D$. The P/E falls if $k_d(1-t) < E/P$ (the after-tax cost of debt is below the earnings yield): classic leverage effect on EPS.
Link between multiples for an unlevered company: $P/E = \frac{EV/EBITDA}{(1 - \text{D\&A}/EBITDA)(1-t)}$.

### Worked example with numbers
EBITDA 100, D&A 20, EBIT 80, tax 25%.
- Unlevered, EV = equity = 900: NI = 60, EV/EBITDA 9x, P/E 15x.
- Same EV 900 but 600 of debt at 3%: interest 18, NI = (80 - 18) × 0.75 = 46.5, equity 300, P/E **6.5x** while EV/EBITDA stays 9x.
- Higher-multiple version: EV 1,200, debt 800 at 3%: interest 24, NI = 42, equity 400: EV/EBITDA **12x**, P/E **9.5x**.
- Capital intensity (no debt, EV 1,000, EV/EBITDA 10x for both): asset-light with D&A 10 has NI 67.5 and P/E 14.8x, EV/EBIT 11.1x; asset-heavy with D&A 50 has NI 37.5, P/E 26.7x, EV/EBIT 20x. On EBITDA they look identical; on EBIT the heavy one is almost twice as expensive, Buffett's point.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Saying high D&A explains a high EV/EBITDA and low P/E: it works the other way (high D&A lowers net income and raises the P/E).
- Forgetting that leverage also raises risk: a low P/E on a highly levered stock is often fair, because the cost of equity is higher.
- Treating EBITDA as cash flow: it ignores capex, working capital, taxes and interest.

### How to deliver it
Frame it: "the difference between the two multiples is D&A, interest, tax and non-operating items, so I look at each". Give the leverage case with numbers, then capital intensity and associates or one-offs. For Buffett: "depreciation is a real cost because capex is real", with the asset-heavy vs asset-light example.
deep.cf-037:
### Context / why they ask this
Three questions from the CFI equity research list that probe practical DCF judgement beyond "walk me through a DCF". Interviewers want to see that you know a DCF is only as good as its assumptions, and when another method is more appropriate.

### Key concepts
- **Explicit forecast period**: years for which you model revenue, margins, capex and working capital line by line.
- **Steady state**: growth at a sustainable long-run rate (at most nominal GDP), stable margins, reinvestment consistent with growth and ROIC.
- **Terminal value (TV)**: value at the end of the forecast of all later cash flows, by Gordon growth $FCF_{N+1}/(WACC - g)$ or by an exit multiple (EV/EBITDA × final-year EBITDA).
- **Mid-year convention**: discount factor $(1+WACC)^{-(t-0.5)}$ for year-$t$ cash flows.
- **Stub period**: a partial first year when the valuation date is mid-year.
- **Sum-of-the-parts (SOTP)**: valuing each division separately, useful for conglomerates.

### Intuition
Forecasting precision decays fast: next year's revenue can be estimated, year 12's cannot. So the method concentrates detailed work where information exists and uses a parsimonious steady-state assumption beyond. The mid-year convention is just a better approximation of reality: if a shop earns cash every day, on average it arrives in the middle of the year, so discounting it as if it arrived at year-end undervalues it by half a year of discounting.

### The maths
$$EV = \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{FCF_t}{(1+W)^{t-0.5}} + \frac{TV_N}{(1+W)^{N}} \ \text{(exit multiple)}$$
With a Gordon TV, the cash flows it represents also arrive mid-year, so consistent practice discounts it at $N - 0.5$ too; with an exit multiple (a price at a date), discount at $N$. Mid-year uplift on each flow: $(1+W)^{0.5}$.

### Worked example with numbers
FCF of 100 in year 1 growing 5% a year to 121.6 in year 5; WACC 9%; terminal growth 2%.
- PV of the explicit cash flows (end-year): **426.3**.
- TV at year 5: $121.55 \times 1.02/0.07 = 1{,}771$; PV $= 1{,}771/1.09^5 = 1{,}151$.
- EV = **1,577**, with the TV at **73%** of the total.
- Mid-year convention (applied to all flows including Gordon TV): EV = **1,647**, +4.4% $= 1.09^{0.5} - 1$.
- Sensitivity: terminal growth 2.5% instead of 2% raises EV to 1,672, **+6%**, more than the mid-year effect: the TV assumptions dominate, which is why analysts show a WACC × g sensitivity table.

### When not to use a DCF (and what to use)
- **Banks, insurers**: dividend discount model, residual income, P/TBV vs ROTE.
- **Early-stage / pre-profit**: comparables on revenue or users, venture method, scenario-weighted DCF at best.
- **Distressed**: liquidation value, recovery analysis.
- **Cyclical commodities**: normalised mid-cycle cash flows or NAV of reserves; a DCF on a spot price is misleading.
- **Very short horizon trading view**: relative value vs peers and catalysts matter more.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- A 10-year forecast that is really a spreadsheet extrapolation with no economic logic.
- Terminal growth above nominal GDP, or a TV where reinvestment is inconsistent with growth.
- Applying mid-year discounting to an exit-multiple TV.
- Claiming a DCF is "objective": it is precise but not necessarily accurate.

### How to deliver it
Answer each part in two sentences: steady state logic with the TV share, the mid-year definition with the 4.4% figure, and a list of three cases where you'd use something else and what. Good bridge: "In practice I'd triangulate DCF with comps and precedents."
deep.cf-038:
### Context / why they ask this
J.P. Morgan has asked this (reported by eFinancialCareers). It is a "non-finance" business case that tests whether you understand cash flow versus profit, can structure an answer, and can apply the three-statement logic to something concrete. There is no single right answer; they look for structure, realistic orders of magnitude and business sense (seasonality, perishability, working capital).

### Key concepts
- **Cash flow from operations (CFO)**: cash generated by the business itself = net income + non-cash charges (depreciation) - increase in working capital.
- **Cash flow from investing (CFI)**: purchases (capex) and sales of long-term assets.
- **Cash flow from financing (CFF)**: equity raised, debt borrowed or repaid, dividends.
- **Working capital**: inventory + receivables - payables. It absorbs cash when it grows.
- **Depreciation**: the accounting spreading of the truck's cost over its useful life (here 5 years, 12k/year). It reduces profit, not cash.
- **Break-even**: the sales level at which contribution margin covers fixed costs.
- **Seasonality**: predictable swings in activity over the year.

### Intuition
Profit tells you whether the truck is a good business on average; cash tells you whether the owner can pay the bank this month. The truck is cash-hungry at the start (capex), then cash-generative because customers pay on the spot while suppliers might give 30 days, so working capital can even be a small source of cash. The risks are operating leverage (wages and loan payments are fixed while sales depend on weather and footfall) and the capex cycle (engine, kitchen equipment).

### Worked example with numbers (EUR thousands, year 1)
Income statement: revenue 200, food 70, wages 60, fuel/permits/pitch 20, so **EBITDA 50**; depreciation 12, **EBIT 38**; interest on the 40 loan at 5%, 2, so EBT 36; tax 25%, 9: **net income 27**.
Cash flow statement:
- CFO: 27 + 12 (depreciation) - 3 (build-up of stock) + 2 (supplier credit) = **38**
- CFI: -60 (the truck)
- CFF: +20 owner equity + 40 loan - 8 loan repayment = **+52**
- Change in cash: 38 - 60 + 52 = **+30**
Balance sheet check at year end: cash 30, truck 60 - 12 = 48, inventory 3, total assets 81; payables 2, loan 32, equity 20 + 27 = 47, total 81. It balances.
Debt service: CFO 38 against interest + principal of 10 is comfortable (a debt service coverage ratio of about 3.8x); a bad summer halving EBITDA would still leave CFO around 15-20.

### What else to mention
- **Seasonality**: in winter cash could be negative for months; the owner needs a buffer or an overdraft.
- **Unit economics**: average ticket (say 10) × customers per day × days operated; food cost ratio around 30-35% of sales.
- **Maintenance capex**: over time, replace the equipment, roughly the level of depreciation.
- **Taxes and VAT**: VAT collected is not the owner's money, a timing effect on cash.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Listing revenue and costs without separating cash from profit, or forgetting the capex and its financing.
- Treating depreciation as a cash outflow.
- No numbers at all: even rough orders of magnitude show commercial sense.

### How to deliver it
Announce your structure ("I'll go through operating, investing and financing"), give rough numbers, then two insights: working capital is favourable because customers pay immediately, and the main risk is seasonality combined with fixed costs and loan payments. That shows you can do both accounting and business thinking.
deep.cf-039:
### Context / why they ask this
Bank of America has used this in S&T interviews (salesandtrading.org). It is a disguised "how do you value a company?" question. The interviewer wants to see that you can apply valuation principles to anything, structure your thinking, make reasonable assumptions and identify the key drivers, not that you know apple prices.

### Key concepts
- **Intrinsic value (DCF)**: PV of expected future cash flows at a risk-adjusted discount rate.
- **Relative value (comparables)**: price paid for similar assets, scaled by a common metric (per tree, per hectare, per tonne of yearly production).
- **Replacement cost**: cost to recreate the asset from scratch; a rational buyer won't pay more than this (Tobin's q logic).
- **Salvage / terminal value**: what's left at the end of life (timber).
- **Real option**: the right, not obligation, to change use later (cut and replant a better variety, sell the land to a developer).

### Intuition
A tree is a small business: capex (planting), a ramp-up period with negative cash flow, a mature productive phase, decline, and a terminal value. Its value is not the apples you see today but all the future apples, adjusted for time and risk. The market price of similar trees tells you what others pay; the replacement cost tells you the upper bound; the DCF tells you what it's worth to you with your assumptions. If DCF value is far above replacement cost, everyone would plant trees until apple prices fall: a nice competition argument.

### The maths
$$V = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{(\text{apples}_t \times p_t - \text{costs}_t)}{(1+r)^t} + \frac{\text{salvage}}{(1+r)^T}$$
With a constant net cash flow $C$ over $T$ years, the annuity formula: $V = \frac{C}{r}(1 - (1+r)^{-T})$.
