A portfolio manager long EUR 200mn of IG bonds (spread duration 5) fears a widening. He buys iTraxx Main protection on $200\times 5/4.6\approx$ EUR 217mn to match CS01. If spreads widen 20bp, the bonds lose about EUR 2mn and the CDS gains about the same (minus basis risk).

### Common pitfalls
- Giving a CDS index level you are not sure of: better to give the concept and the order of magnitude and say you would check.
- Confusing "spread tightening" (good for bond holders) with "tightening" of monetary policy.
- Forgetting that HY indices trade in price and IG in spread.
- Saying buying protection is "long credit": it is **short** credit risk.

### How to deliver it
"US IG about 85bp OAS, HY about 300, near the tights of the year despite the oil shock, because all-in yields attract buyers. For synthetic credit, Main is 125 European IG names, Crossover 75 high yield; I would check today's prints, but Crossover trades at roughly four to five times Main." Link to fd-035 (Treasury levels) and credit cards.
deep.fd-042:
### Context / why they ask this
Energy is the macro story of 2026: the oil and gas shock is why inflation rebounded and central banks hike again (card fd-034). Commodity desks obviously expect you to know the prices; macro, rates and FX interviewers ask because oil drives breakevens, terms of trade (EUR, JPY weak; NOK, CAD strong) and corporate margins. Knowing units and conversions shows you have actually looked at a screen.

### Key concepts
- **Brent**: North Sea light sweet crude, the global seaborne benchmark (ICE futures). **WTI**: West Texas Intermediate, US inland benchmark delivered at Cushing (NYMEX).
- **Front-month**: the nearest futures contract; on its expiry day the "continuous" price jumps to the next contract, which can look like a price move.
- **Backwardation / contango**: futures below / above spot. Tight markets are in backwardation (you pay up for oil now).
- **TTF**: Title Transfer Facility, the Dutch gas hub, the European gas benchmark, in EUR per megawatt-hour (MWh).
- **MMBtu**: million British thermal units, the US gas unit (Henry Hub). 1 MWh = 3.412 MMBtu.
- **EUA**: EU Allowance, the right to emit one tonne of CO2 under the EU Emissions Trading System, in EUR per tonne.
- **Crack spread**: refined product price minus crude, the refiner's margin.

### The levels (Yahoo futures data cross-checked with Trading Economics, closes)
| | 30 Sept 2026 | a year ago | 1y closing high | 1y low |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brent (front, USD/bbl) | 97.8 (29 Sept 102.6) | 67.0 | 118.4 (31 Mar); ~126 intraday (30 Apr) | 58.9 (16 Dec 2025) |
| WTI (front, USD/bbl) | 90.7 | 62.4 | 113.0 (7 Apr); ~119.5 intraday (9 Mar) | 55.3 (16 Dec 2025) |
| TTF (EUR/MWh) | ~70 (69.8 on 29 Sept; 68-72 on 30 Sept) | 31.4 | 82.6 (14 Sept) | 26.6 (10 Dec 2025) |
| EUA (EUR/t) | ~85 | | peak above 100 in Feb 2023 | |

EU gas storage about 71% full vs a 5-year average of about 87% for the date (Trading Economics). The Brent-WTI spread widened to about 13 dollars on 29 September (normally 3-5), a sign that seaborne crude near the Gulf carries the war premium; on 30 September the comparison is distorted because Brent had rolled to the December contract. That roll also creates a **fake 5% fall** in the continuous front-month series on 30 September: on the same contract Brent rose (December 96.2 to 97.7, +1.6%; November 102.6 to 103.3 at expiry). The 5-6 dollar gap between consecutive months is the backwardation (dated physical Brent was even higher, about 115 on 22 September, FRED).

### Intuition
Oil is priced at the margin by supply shocks: a disruption risk in the Strait of Hormuz (about a fifth of world oil flows) adds a risk premium, and the price falls fast on any peace headline, which is why daily moves of 3-5% are common (realized vol about 50% vs about 30% in normal years). Gas in Europe is a storage story: after losing Russian pipeline gas in 2022, Europe relies on LNG, competes with Asia for cargoes, and a low storage level going into winter puts a premium on TTF. Carbon depends on the EU cap and on the gas/coal switch: expensive gas pushes utilities to burn coal, raising demand for EUAs, while weak industry lowers it.

### The maths: conversions and pass-through
- **Oil in euros**: $97.78/1.1356\approx$ EUR 86.1 per barrel; per litre $86.1/158.99\approx$ EUR 0.54. Pump prices (roughly EUR 2 per litre in France; check the current level) are mostly taxes and refining margins, so a 10% crude move is only a few % at the pump.
- **Gas**: $70\ \text{EUR/MWh}\times 1.1356/3.412\approx$ **USD 23.3/MMBtu**, about 8 times the US Henry Hub spot price (about USD 2.9 on 22 September, FRED).
- **Year-on-year change**: Brent $97.8/67.0-1\approx +46\%$; TTF $70/31.4-1\approx +123\%$. Year-on-year energy inflation is 16.3% in the US CPI and 14.3% in euro-area HICP (August).
- **Inflation rule of thumb** (order of magnitude, varies by model): a 10% rise in oil prices adds roughly 0.2pp to euro-area headline inflation in the following year through fuel and heating, more with second-round effects.
- **Futures P&L**: a Brent contract is 1,000 barrels: long 100 contracts, a USD 5 drop (a common 5% day this year) = $-100\times 1{,}000\times 5=$ **-USD 500,000**.

### Worked example
An airline hedges 12 months of jet fuel. If it had bought Brent swaps at 67 a year ago, it would now be about 31 dollars a barrel in the money, offsetting most of the fuel bill increase. That is why corporate hedging desks were busy in 2026, and why a producer that hedged at 70 missed the upside.

### Common pitfalls
- Reading a contract roll as a price crash (check which month is the front): on 30 September 2026 the expiry of November Brent made the front month 'fall' 5% while every contract rose.
- Mixing USD/bbl and EUR/MWh, or MWh and MMBtu.
- Quoting a stale price: oil can move 5% in a day this year; say "about USD 100, it has been swinging between 95 and 105 this month".
- Confusing the EUA price (a regulatory right) with a tax: it is a market price for a capped quantity.

### How to deliver it
"Brent around 98 on the December contract (the 5% fall on screens today is the contract roll), still up about 45% on the year; TTF around 70 euros, storage only 71% full going into winter; carbon about 85. That is what pushed headline inflation to 3.2-3.4% while core stays at 2.4." Link to fd-031 (snapshot) and fd-044 (macro prints).
deep.fd-043:
### Context / why they ask this
Gold is the classic "what's your view on gold?" question: it tests whether you know that gold competes with real yields and the dollar, not with inflation alone. Copper is the growth/China/energy-transition question. For commodities or macro desks, knowing units (troy ounce, pound, tonne) matters.

### Key concepts
- **Troy ounce**: 31.1035 grams, the precious-metals unit.
- **Copper in USD/lb vs USD/t**: COMEX quotes cents or dollars per pound, LME per metric tonne; 1 tonne = 2,204.62 lb.
- **Real yield**: nominal yield minus expected inflation; the 10-year TIPS yield is the market measure (card fd-044).
- **Opportunity cost**: gold pays no coupon, so holding it costs the real rate you forgo.
- **Central-bank reserves**: emerging-market central banks (China, Poland, Turkey, India) have been large gold buyers since 2022, to diversify away from dollar assets after Russia's reserves were frozen.
- **Gold/silver ratio**: ounces of silver per ounce of gold.

### The levels (Yahoo futures, Trading Economics spot, 29-30 Sept 2026)
| | Now | a year ago | 1y high | 1y low |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gold (USD/oz) | ~4,185 spot / 4,220 futures | 3,873 | ~5,590-5,610 intraday (29 Jan); 5,318 close | 3,868 (2 Oct 2025) |
| Silver (USD/oz) | ~61 | 46 | ~121 intraday; 115 close (26 Jan) | 46 (2 Oct 2025) |
| Copper (USD/lb) | 6.56-6.63 | 4.80 | ~6.80 close (9 Sept), ~6.83-6.85 intraday (22 Sept) | 4.80 (30 Sept 2025) |

Copper at 6.56 USD/lb $\times 2{,}204.62\approx$ **USD 14,460 per tonne**. Gold per gram: $4{,}220/31.1035\approx$ USD 136, i.e. about USD 136,000 per kilo bar.

### Intuition
- **Gold's 2025-26 round trip**: gold ran from about 2,600 at the start of 2025 to a spike near 5,600 in January 2026 on central-bank buying, geopolitical fear and a speculative rush (silver doubled in weeks). Then the regime changed: the oil shock turned central banks hawkish, real yields rose to about 2.9% on the 10-year, the dollar firmed; gold lost about 25% and silver about 50%. The lesson: gold is not a simple inflation hedge; when inflation comes with rising **real** rates, gold can fall.
- **Copper at records**: supply is inelastic (new mines take 10+ years), ore grades fall, and demand from electrification, grids and data centres keeps growing; tariffs on US copper imports also distorted COMEX vs LME prices in 2025.

### The maths: a simple gold sensitivity
Empirically (2006-2021) a 100bp rise in the 10-year real yield was associated with a gold fall of roughly 15-25%. Treat it as a rough elasticity, not a law: the relationship broke down in 2022-2025 when central-bank buying dominated. Gold's carry: holding gold financed at SOFR 3.9% costs about 3.9% a year; the futures price therefore sits above spot by about the financing rate (futures 4,220 vs spot about 4,185, a gap consistent with a few months of carry).
**Futures size**: COMEX gold 100 oz (USD 1 = USD 100 per contract, notional about USD 422,000); COMEX copper 25,000 lb (USD 0.01 = USD 250).

### Worked example
A client holds USD 10mn of gold bought in January at 5,500. At 4,200 he is down $1-4{,}200/5{,}500\approx 23.6\%$, about USD 2.4mn. If he had bought a year ago at 3,873 he would be up about 9%. Same asset, opposite experience: the entry point matters, and it is a good talking point about volatility (gold realized vol about 30% over the past year, double its usual 15%).

### Common pitfalls
- Saying "gold is at record highs" in September 2026: it was in January; it is now 25% below.
- Forgetting the unit (ounce vs gram, pound vs tonne).
- Arguing gold only depends on inflation; the key variables are real yields, the dollar, central-bank demand and fear.
- Confusing COMEX and LME copper prices (they can differ when tariffs segment markets).

### How to deliver it
"Gold about 4,200, 25% off the January record as real yields went to 2.9% and the Fed turned hawkish; copper near records around 14,500 a tonne on electrification and supply constraints; silver halved. So precious metals price rates, copper prices growth and the energy transition." Link to fd-031 (snapshot) and fd-044 (real yields).
deep.fd-044:
### Context / why they ask this
Every markets interview includes "what's the macro picture?" and the Fed/ECB are data-dependent, so desks live by the release calendar (payrolls on the first Friday, CPI mid-month). The interviewer checks you know the last print, the consensus surprise, the next date, and the conventions that trip up beginners (annualised vs not, headline vs core, y/y vs m/m).

### Key concepts
- **GDP**: value of output. US: **SAAR** (seasonally adjusted annualised rate); euro area: q/q not annualised, plus y/y.
- **Nonfarm payrolls (NFP)**: monthly change in US jobs (establishment survey, BLS), released with the unemployment rate (household survey). Revisions are large.
- **Consensus**: median economist forecast; markets react to the **surprise** (actual minus consensus).
- **Breakeven payroll growth**: job creation needed to keep unemployment stable; it fell as immigration slowed (estimates in the tens of thousands rather than 100k+).
- **CPI / HICP**: consumer price index (US) / harmonised index (euro area). **Core**: excluding food and energy (volatile).
- **Breakeven inflation**: nominal Treasury yield minus TIPS (inflation-linked) yield of the same maturity: the inflation rate at which both pay the same.
- **Real yield**: TIPS yield, the return above inflation.

### The prints (latest as of 30 Sept 2026; BLS, BEA, Eurostat, cross-checked with Trading Economics)
| | US | Euro area |
|---|---|---|
| GDP (Q2) | +1.5% SAAR (Q1 2.1%), ~2.1% y/y | +0.6% q/q, +1.2% y/y |
| Unemployment | 4.1% (Aug) | 6.4% (Jul) |
| Jobs | NFP +162k Aug (cons. ~56k; Jul +23k) | |
| Headline inflation | CPI 3.4% y/y (Aug), +0.4% m/m | HICP 3.2% (Aug) |
| Core inflation | 2.4% y/y, +0.3% m/m | 2.4% (services 3.0%) |
| Energy | +16.3% y/y | +14.3% y/y |
| 10y breakeven / real | 2.35% / 2.90% | |
| Next releases | NFP 2 Oct, CPI 14 Oct | flash HICP early October |

Other: UK CPI 3.1%, Japan CPI about 1.9% (see fd-029).

### Intuition
Headline inflation is high because of **energy** (oil and gas shock, card fd-042) while **core** is close to target: central banks hike to prevent "second-round effects" (wages and expectations). Growth is positive but unspectacular. The August payrolls beat (162k vs 56k) mattered because the July print was very weak and the Fed hiked on 16 September partly because the labour market did not crack.

### The maths: conversions (python-checked)
- Quarterly to annualised: $(1+q)^4-1$: 0.6% q/q $\to 1.006^4-1=2.42\%$; conversely US 1.5% SAAR $\to 1.015^{1/4}-1=0.37\%$ q/q. So **Europe grew faster than the US in Q2** in comparable terms (2.4% vs 1.5% annualised), which surprises people who only read headlines.
- Monthly to annualised: $(1+m)^{12}-1$: core 0.3% m/m $\to 3.66\%$; headline 0.4% m/m $\to 4.9\%$. The Fed watches 3- and 6-month annualised core to see the trend before the y/y number moves.
- Fisher decomposition: $y_{nominal}\approx y_{real}+\pi^{e}$ (+ inflation risk premium): $2.90+2.35=5.25\%\approx$ the 5.26% 10-year.
- Base effects: y/y inflation can fall even if prices keep rising, when a big monthly jump from a year ago drops out of the 12-month window.

### Worked example: trading a release
Consensus for October NFP is, say, 60k. It prints 200k: markets price more Fed hikes, 2-year yields jump maybe 10-15bp, USD rallies, equities may fall on rates. A trader who is long 2-year Treasuries with DV01 USD 50,000 loses about USD 500,000-750,000. Desks prepare scenario tables before each release.

### Common pitfalls
- Comparing US annualised GDP with European q/q growth.
- Saying "inflation is 3.4%, so prices will rise 3.4% next year": it is backward-looking.
- Ignoring revisions (payrolls are revised by tens of thousands).
- Confusing breakeven inflation with realized CPI.

### How to deliver it
"US: growth about 1.5% annualised, unemployment 4.1%, payrolls beat at 162k, headline CPI 3.4% but core 2.4%, so it is an energy story; next payrolls Friday 2 October. Euro area: 0.6% q/q, HICP 3.2%, core 2.4%. The Fed and the ECB are hiking to stop second-round effects." Link to fd-034 (policy), fd-029 (inflation snapshot).
deep.fd-045:
### Context / why they ask this
Orders of magnitude separate someone who reads about markets from someone who understands flows. Interviewers ask "how big is the Treasury market?" or "what is QT?" to see if you can connect supply (deficits, issuance), central-bank balance sheets (QE/QT) and liquidity (reserves). Card fd-032 covers GDP and global stock/bond market sizes; this card focuses on the numbers behind **flows**.

### Key concepts
- **Debt held by the public vs intragovernmental**: the former is owed to investors (including the Fed), the latter to trust funds such as Social Security; only the former trades.
- **Marketable** Treasuries: bills (up to 1 year), notes (2-10 years), bonds (20-30 years), TIPS, FRNs.
- **QE / QT**: quantitative easing (central bank buys bonds, creating reserves) / tightening (lets them mature without reinvesting).
- **Reserves**: banks' deposits at the central bank; the "plumbing" liquidity. **TGA**: Treasury General Account, the government's cash at the Fed. **ON RRP**: overnight reverse repo facility where money funds park cash at the Fed.
- **BIS Triennial Survey**: every three years (April), the reference for market turnover.
- **FX swap**: spot plus opposite forward, mostly a funding tool; the largest FX instrument.

### The numbers
| Item | Size | Date / source |
|---|---|---|
| US total federal debt | USD 40.10trn | 28 Sept 2026, Debt to the Penny |
| held by the public | 32.39trn (~105% of 2025 GDP; ~100% of the Q2 2026 annualised GDP of 32.5trn) | same |
| intragovernmental | 7.72trn | same |
| Marketable Treasuries | 31.83trn: bills 7.25, notes 16.22, bonds 5.53, TIPS 2.15, FRN 0.68 | 31 Aug 2026, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt |
| Fed total assets | USD 6.748trn (~21-22% of GDP) | H.4.1, 23 Sept 2026 |
| of which UST / MBS | 4.558trn / 1.910trn | |
| Fed liabilities: reserves / currency / TGA / RRP | 2.930 / 2.431 / 0.947 / 0.321 trn | |
| Eurosystem total assets | EUR 5.897trn (~USD 6.7trn, ~37% of GDP) | week to 25 Sept 2026, ECB weekly statement |
| Bank of Japan total assets | JPY 644.7trn (~USD 4.1trn, ~100% of GDP) | August 2026 (via FRED) |
| FX turnover | USD 9.6trn/day (+28% vs 2022); FX swaps 4.0trn; spot + outright forwards about half | BIS Triennial, April 2025 |
| Currency shares (out of 200%) | USD 89%, EUR 28.9%, JPY 16.8%, GBP 10.2% | same |
| Trading centres | UK 38%; top 4 centres 75% | same |
| OTC interest-rate derivatives | USD 7.9trn/day (+59%); EUR 3.0trn (38%), USD 2.4trn (31%) | same |

### Intuition
- **Supply**: the US runs deficits around 6% of GDP, so the stock of Treasuries grows by roughly USD 2trn a year; bills are 23% of the stock because the Treasury funds cheaply at the short end. More supply at the long end pushes up term premium (card fd-035) and makes swap spreads negative (card fd-037).
- **QE/QT**: the Fed peaked near USD 9trn in 2022; QT brought it down to a trough of about 6.54trn in early December 2025 (FRED WALCL, 3 Dec), QT having ended on 1 December 2025, and the balance sheet has since edged back up to about 6.75trn as the Fed buys bills to keep reserves ample. The Eurosystem peaked near EUR 8.8trn and is now about 5.9trn as TLTRO loans were repaid and APP/PEPP bonds run off. The BoJ owns roughly half of the JGB market, which is why its exit is so delicate.
- **Plumbing**: reserves at about 2.9trn are close to what the Fed considers "ample"; the Fed stopped QT because, once the RRP facility had largely emptied, further runoff would have drained reserves directly and risked repo spikes like September 2019.
- **FX**: 9.6trn a day is about 20 times world GDP traded per year; most of it is swaps (funding), not speculation. The dollar's 89% share is the dollar's "vehicle currency" role: even EUR/JPY trades often go through USD.

### The maths (python-checked)
- Fed assets / US GDP: $6.748/30.8\approx 21.9\%$ on 2025 GDP (BEA; about 20.8% on the Q2 2026 annualised 32.5trn); Eurosystem: $5.897/15.8\approx 37\%$; BoJ: $644.7/\sim 620\approx 104\%$ (Japan's nominal GDP about JPY 600-630trn).
- Annual FX turnover vs world GDP: $9.6\times 250/118\approx 20$.
- Bill share: $7.25/31.83\approx 22.8\%$.
- BoJ in dollars: $644.7/157\approx$ USD 4.1trn; Eurosystem in dollars: $5.897\times 1.1356\approx$ USD 6.7trn.

### Worked example
Suppose a central bank runs off USD 25bn of Treasuries a month (the Fed's Treasury runoff cap from June 2024 to March 2025): over a year that is 300bn, about 1% of the marketable stock, which the Treasury must sell to private investors on top of the deficit. Ending QT removes that extra private supply. This is the kind of arithmetic a rates strategist does to explain term premium.

### Common pitfalls
- Confusing total debt (40.1trn) with debt held by the public (32.4trn) or marketable debt (31.8trn).
- Saying FX turnover is "speculation": most is dealer and funding activity (swaps).
- Forgetting currency shares sum to 200% (two currencies per trade).
- Giving central-bank balance sheets without the date; they change weekly.

### How to deliver it
"US debt passed 40 trillion, about 32 held by the public; the Fed is at 6.75 trillion after QT, the Eurosystem 5.9 trillion euros, the BoJ about 645 trillion yen, roughly Japan's GDP. FX trades 9.6 trillion a day, rates derivatives 7.9, with the euro now the biggest currency in rates derivatives." Link to fd-032 (other orders of magnitude).
deep.fd-046:
### Context / why they ask this
"How do you follow markets?" and "What did you read this morning?" are standard S&T questions. They test genuine interest (you cannot fake a daily routine), method (primary sources, structure), and whether your numbers are current. A candidate who knows ten numbers perfectly and connects them beats one who recites fifty.

### Key concepts
- **Level vs change**: the level (10y at 5.26%) tells you where; the change (+8bp on the day, +100bp on the year) tells you what the market is doing. Traders talk in changes.
- **Primary source**: the publisher of the data (FRED, Treasury, ECB, BLS, Eurostat) versus a news site that copies it.
- **Close vs intraday**: prices move all day; always anchor to a close (and say which: New York close for US assets, European close for European ones).
- **Economic calendar**: scheduled releases (payrolls, CPI, central-bank meetings) that move markets.
- **Trade idea**: a view expressed as an instrument, with entry level, target, stop and catalyst.

### The dashboard (template; fill in with fresh values)
| Block | Numbers | Free source |
|---|---|---|
| Central banks | Fed range, ECB DFR, BoE, BoJ; next meeting; pricing | federalreserve.gov, ecb.europa.eu, CME FedWatch |
| Rates | US 2y/10y/30y, Bund 2y/10y, OAT, BTP, gilt, JGB 10y; 2s10s; OAT-Bund | Treasury par curve, FRED (DGS2, DGS10), Trading Economics |
| Money markets | SOFR, €STR | FRED SOFR, ECB €STR |
| FX | EURUSD, USDJPY, GBPUSD, EURCHF, DXY | ECB reference rates, Yahoo Finance |
| Equities | S&P 500, Nasdaq, Euro Stoxx 50, CAC, DAX, Nikkei; S&P forward P/E | FRED SP500, FactSet Earnings Insight |
| Vol | VIX, V2X, MOVE | FRED VIXCLS, stoxx.com |
| Credit | US IG/HY OAS, Euro HY; iTraxx Main/Crossover | FRED BAML series; market wraps for iTraxx |
| Commodities | Brent, WTI, TTF, gold, copper | Yahoo futures, Trading Economics |
| Macro | last CPI/HICP, core, payrolls, unemployment, GDP; next dates | BLS, BEA, Eurostat |

### Intuition: why a routine beats cramming
Memory works through **stories and anchors**. If you know "the 10-year went from about 4.2% to 5.26% this year because of the oil shock and Fed hikes", you can rebuild the level. Anchors also let you sanity-check: if someone tells you EURUSD is 1.35, you know it is wrong because it has been in a 1.13-1.20 range. Updating daily means small changes each day, so the dashboard stays in your head without effort. Writing one sentence of "why" each evening builds the market narrative interviewers want.

### The maths: which precision is enough
Precision should match volatility. A 10-year yield moves about 6-7bp a day (MOVE about 107, card fd-040), so a number one week old can be 15-20bp off; quote to 5bp. EURUSD moves about 0.35% a day (about 40 pips): quote to the big figure plus one decimal (1.135). The S&P moves about 1% a day: quote to the nearest 50 points. Oil at 50% vol moves about 3% a day: quote "about 98, between 95 and 105 this month".
Useful free automation (what I did for this deck): FRED serves any series as CSV (`fredgraph.csv?id=DGS10`), the ECB data portal serves CSV through an API, Treasury publishes debt data through an API (fiscaldata). A 20-line Python script can refresh the dashboard every evening.

### Worked example: the interview morning
7:00 check overnight: Nikkei, USDJPY, Brent (did the Iran headline hold?), US futures. 7:15 read one wrap (FT/Reuters/Les Echos) and one bank note if available. 7:30 calendar: is there a CPI, payrolls or central-bank speaker today? 7:40 prepare the "market in 60 seconds" (card fd-048) and one trade idea, for example: "receive 2-year €STR swaps (OIS) at about 3.2% because the ECB hikes on an energy shock that will fade; catalyst: October HICP; risk: second-round wage effects; stop 20bp higher."

### Common pitfalls
- Quoting a number from a week-old article as current.
- Knowing levels but not the reason for moves.
- Mixing sources for the same number without noticing a 5-10bp difference (generic vs specific bond).
- Inventing a level when unsure: say "I have not checked it today, it was around X last week" or "I would check". Honesty beats a wrong precise number.
- Following only one asset class; S&T desks want cross-asset links.

### How to deliver it
"Every evening I update a dashboard of about twenty levels from FRED, the ECB and the Treasury, with the daily change and one line on why; I read the FT and a wrap in the morning and I keep one trade idea ready. Today, for instance, the 30-year Treasury is near 2002 highs, and the 5% Brent 'drop' on screens is only the November contract expiring." Then ask the interviewer what their desk is watching: it turns the answer into a conversation.
deep.fd-047:
### Context / why they ask this
Trading interviews quickly move from "where is X?" to "you are long 50mn 10-years and the market sells off 12bp, what is your P&L?". The interviewer wants mental arithmetic anchored on a few rules of thumb. These are the numbers traders actually use in their heads; exact risk systems come later.

### Key concepts
- **DV01 (PV01)**: price change for a 1bp change in yield, in currency per notional. $DV01\approx D_{mod}\times P\times 10^{-4}\times N/100$.
- **Modified duration**: % price change per 1% yield change.
- **Convexity**: curvature; makes gains on falling yields larger than losses on rising yields.
- **Carry**: income from holding the position (coupon minus financing cost). **Roll-down**: price gain as the bond ages and "rolls down" a positively sloped curve to a lower yield.
- **Pip / big figure**: 0.0001 / 0.01 in EURUSD (0.01 / 1.00 in USDJPY).
- **Vega**: option P&L per 1 vol point. **Gamma / theta**: convexity P&L vs time decay.
- **CS01**: P&L per 1bp change in credit spread.

### The maths (python-checked at September 2026 levels)
**Rates**
$$\Delta P\approx -D_{mod}P\,\Delta y+\tfrac12 C P(\Delta y)^2$$
10y UST par at 5.26%: $D_{mod}=7.70$, $C\approx 72$. For +100bp: $-7.70+\tfrac12\times 72\times 0.0001\times 100\approx -7.34$ points, exact -7.35; for -100bp: +8.07.
| Bond | Yield | DV01 per 10mn |
|---|---|---|
| UST 2y | 4.89% | USD 1,883 |
| UST 10y | 5.26% | USD 7,700 |
| UST 30y | 5.59% | USD 14,467 |
| Bund 10y | 3.58% | EUR 8,283 |
| Bund 30y | 3.92% | EUR 17,461 |
| 10y SOFR swap | 4.88% | ~USD 7,800 |

Hedge ratio 2s10s: $7{,}700/1{,}883\approx 4.1$.

**Carry and roll-down (10y UST, 1 year)**: carry $\approx 5.26\%-3.90\%=136$bp of price. Roll-down: interpolating between 5y (5.06%) and 10y (5.26%), the 9-year yields about 5.22%, so the bond gains about 0.28 points as it becomes a 9-year. Breakeven: $(1.36+0.28)/7.3\approx 22$bp; without roll, $136/7.7\approx 18$bp. If yields rise less than about 20bp in a year, the long position still makes money.

**FX**: P&L in quote currency $=N\times\Delta S$. EUR 10mn: 1 pip = USD 1,000, 1% = USD 113,560. USD 10mn in USDJPY: 1 pip (0.01) = JPY 100,000 (about USD 640). Forward points of about +162 pips on the 1-year EURUSD accrue at about 0.44 pip a day: that is the daily carry of a long USD/short EUR position.

**Equities**: notional $=$ level $\times$ multiplier. E-mini S&P 7,670 x 50 = USD 384k, 1% = USD 3,835; Euro Stoxx 50 future: 1% = EUR 630; DAX: EUR 6,340; CAC: EUR 800.

**Options** (1-month ATM S&P call, 16 vol, zero rates, Black-Scholes): price about 141 points; vega about 8.9 points per vol point ($\approx 0.4 S\sqrt{T}/100$); gamma about 0.0011 per point, so a 1% move (77 points) earns $\tfrac12\Gamma\Delta S^2\approx 3.3$ points; theta about -2.3 points per calendar day. Gamma and theta balance when the daily move equals $\sigma S/\sqrt{365}\approx 64$ points: that is the breakeven move of a delta-hedged long option.

**Rule of 16**: daily vol $=\sigma/\sqrt{252}\approx\sigma/16$. VIX 16 = 1%/day; MOVE 107 = about 6.7bp/day; EURUSD at 5.5% = about 0.35%/day.

**Credit**: CS01 $\approx N\times RD\times 10^{-4}$; 5-year CDS risky duration about 4.5, so EUR 10mn = EUR 4,500 per bp. Credit triangle: spread $\approx PD\times(1-R)$.

**Compounding**: rule of 72: at 5.26%, money doubles in about $72/5.26\approx 13.7$ years (exact $\ln 2/\ln 1.0526=13.5$).

### Worked example (a typical interview chain)
"You are long USD 50mn 10-year Treasuries, the market sells off 12bp after CPI." $50/10\times 7{,}700\times 12=$ **-USD 462,000**. "How do you hedge with 2-years?" Sell $4.1\times 50\approx$ USD 205mn 2-years. "Now you have a curve position: what do you gain if the curve steepens 5bp?" About $5\times 7{,}700\times 5=$ USD 192,500 lost if you are long 10s/short 2s (a flattener position loses on steepening).

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting that DV01 depends on the yield level and maturity (a Bund has more DV01 than a Treasury).
- Mixing up price points and bp.
- Using 365 instead of 252 in the rule of 16 (both conventions exist: say which).
- Calculating FX P&L in the wrong currency.
- Treating carry as free money: it is compensation for bearing duration risk.

### How to deliver it
Announce the rule, then compute out loud with round numbers: "10-year DV01 is about 7.7k per 10 million, so 50 million is 38.5k per bp, times 12 is about 460k." Speed and a sanity check matter more than decimals. Link to fd-035 (yields), fd-038 (FX), fd-040 (vol).
deep.fd-048:
### Context / why they ask this
"Walk me through the markets" is the most common open market question in S&T interviews, often the first after the CV. It tests whether you have a **coherent narrative** that links assets, not a list of prices. A great answer has one theme, three to five numbers, a causal chain, a tension or risk, and what comes next. It must fit in about a minute, then the interviewer digs where they want.

**How this card differs from mkt-075.** mkt-075 is the *content*: today's levels and the story to tell ("what's going on in markets?"). This card is the *method*: how to build the wrap from scratch in ten minutes, the five-box structure, how to re-order it for each desk, and how to update it when a number surprises. Learn mkt-075 for the numbers, this card so that you can rebuild any wrap on any day, including the day your numbers are stale.

### Key concepts
- **Macro regime**: the combination of growth and inflation (card fd-023): 2026 looks like "moderate growth, rising headline inflation from a supply shock", a mild stagflationary tilt.
- **Cross-asset**: how a shock propagates: oil to inflation to central banks to yields to FX to equities.
- **Term premium**: extra yield for long bonds; rising when inflation risk and supply rise.
- **Risk-on / risk-off**: investors buying or dumping risky assets together.
- **Catalyst**: a scheduled event (data, meeting) that can move the market.

### The structure (the "5 boxes")
1. **Theme** (one sentence): energy shock, inflation rebound, hawkish central banks.
2. **Rates and central banks**: Fed 3.75-4.00 after a hike on 16 Sept, ECB DFR 2.50, BoJ 1.25; US 10y about 5.25, 30y about 5.6; OAT-Bund about 110-120.
3. **FX**: dollar firm on rate differentials; EURUSD 1.135, USDJPY 157 (Japan intervened above 160).
4. **Risk assets**: S&P about 7,650 (7,651.54 at the 30 Sept close: +2% in Q3 but down in September), near the August record; VIX 16; HY about 300bp; gold 25% off its January record as real yields rose to 2.9%.
5. **What's next and the risk**: payrolls 2 Oct, CPI 14 Oct, FOMC 27-28 Oct (about 70% hike priced on 29 Sept, only about 35% at the 30 Sept close after Williams's 'no need for urgency' and the soft PCE), ECB 29 Oct (about 30% priced); the risk is a further bond sell-off hitting equity valuations, or a peace deal collapsing oil prices and reversing the whole trade. Note the first crack on 30 September: August PCE came in at 3.4% headline and **3.0% core** (after the BEA annual revision lowered July from 3.3% to 3.0% core), below the 3.3% expected; a wrap written the day before should now mention it.

### Intuition: the causal chain
Oil shock -> headline inflation up (energy +14-16% y/y) -> central banks fear second-round effects -> hikes and hawkish guidance -> front-end yields up; long-end yields up even more because of term premium (deficits, supply, inflation uncertainty) -> the dollar benefits from the widest rate gap (UST-Bund about 170bp) -> equities hold up because nominal earnings grow fast (FactSet: about +32% expected EPS growth for 2026) but valuation is stretched against bonds -> credit spreads stay tight because buyers want the high all-in yields. Once you have the chain, every number is a consequence you can reconstruct.

### The maths: the three checks that make the story coherent
- Real policy rate: Fed $3.875-3.4\approx +0.5\%$; ECB $2.50-3.2\approx -0.7\%$: the ECB is less restrictive, consistent with a weak euro.
- Fisher: $5.26\%\approx 2.90\%$ real $+2.35\%$ breakeven: the bond sell-off is mostly **real** yields, not inflation expectations, a sign of term premium and hawkish policy rather than loss of inflation credibility.
- Equity vs bond: earnings yield $1/19.2=5.2\%$ vs 10y 5.26%: zero nominal gap; about 2.3pp vs real yields.

### Worked example: the same story, four openings
The facts do not change between desks; the **order** and the **first number** do. Opening lines (20 seconds each), as of 30 September 2026:
- **Rates desk**: "The curve is bear-steepening: the Fed has hiked to 3.75-4%, but the 30-year at about 5.6% has sold off more than the 2-year because of term premium, deficits and supply; the move is in real yields (10-year TIPS near 2.9%), not in breakevens. In Europe, OAT-Bund is 110-120bp, France now yields more than Italy." Then FX and risk assets in one line each.
- **FX desk**: "The dollar is firm because the rate gap is the widest in years: UST-Bund about 170bp at 10 years. EURUSD is about 1.135, and USDJPY about 157 despite the BoJ at 1.25%, with the memory of the joint intervention near 164 in late July capping it."
- **Equity derivatives**: "Equities are calm while bonds are not: VIX about 16 and realized vol about 11 against a MOVE index about 107. The S&P is about 2% off its August record on strong earnings, but its earnings yield equals the 10-year, so the tail risk is a rates shock, which makes downside skew and cross-asset hedges interesting."
- **Commodities**: "Brent went back above 100 from 9 September on stalled Iran talks, after 79-94 in August; the curve is steeply backwardated, so when the November contract expired on 30 September screens dropped to about 98 on the December contract without any real sell-off. Gas and storage before winter are the next story in Europe."
Then give one trade idea consistent with your story, with its risk (card fd-046, and mkt-645 for a DV01-neutral steepener).

### The 10-minute refresh routine (morning of the interview)
1. **Last 48 hours**: read one market wrap (Reuters, Bloomberg, Les Echos, Yahoo) and note the one or two headlines that moved things (a CPI surprise, a central-bank speech, a geopolitical event).
2. **Fill the boxes** from a dashboard (fd-046): policy rates and next meetings; US 2y, 10y, 30y, Bund, OAT-Bund; EURUSD, USDJPY, dollar index; S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50, VIX; Brent (check the contract month) and gold. One number per box, rounded.
3. **Find the theme**: which number moved most over the week, in standard deviations rather than in points? That is usually your first sentence.
4. **Write the tension**: what in your boxes contradicts the theme (in 2026: 5% yields yet resilient equities).
5. **Calendar**: the next two or three scheduled catalysts, with dates.
6. **Say it aloud with a timer**, then once more re-ordered for the desk you are meeting.

### Common pitfalls
- A list of prices without a thread.
- Going over two minutes; the interviewer wants to interrupt.
- Stating views as facts ("the Fed will hike") instead of pricing plus view ("the market prices 70%, I think...").
- Stale narrative: check the last 48 hours before the interview (a peace deal or a surprise CPI can flip the story).
- Using numbers you are unsure of; round them ("about 5.25%").
- Taking a screen quote at face value around a futures expiry: the 30 September 2026 Brent 'drop' from about 103 to 98 was the November contract expiring, not news.
- Giving the same wrap to every desk: a rates interviewer who hears the S&P first concludes you do not know what the desk does.

### How to deliver it
Speak in the order theme -> rates -> FX -> risk assets -> next catalysts, with one number per asset, and finish with a question back ("what is your desk focused on?"). Rehearse it aloud with a timer and refresh the numbers each week from the dashboard (fd-046). Detail cards: fd-034 to fd-045; today's levels and the full story: mkt-075; live stories: mkt-630 to mkt-646.

### Context / why they ask this
"What is a bulge bracket bank?" is in eFinancialCareers' list of 70 terms you need for banking interviews. It's a basic industry-knowledge question, often asked as a warm-up or hidden inside "Why us and not X?". The interviewer checks that you know **where the bank you're applying to sits**, and that you understand why business models differ: capital, clients, revenue mix. For a Global Markets candidate the key point is **balance sheet**. Only banks that hold risk and fund inventory can run trading desks.

### Key concepts
- **Investment banking (IBD)**: advisory (M&A, restructuring) plus capital raising (ECM for equity, DCM for debt). It earns **fees**.
- **Global Markets / S&T**: sales and trading of securities and derivatives for clients. It earns **spreads** plus financing revenue (repo, prime brokerage) and needs **capital** because the bank holds positions.
- **Balance sheet**: here, the bank's ability to lend, hold inventory and take risk. It is limited by regulatory capital (CET1 ratio against risk-weighted assets, RWA) and by leverage ratios.
- **CIB**: corporate and investment bank, the wholesale division of a universal bank (e.g. BNP Paribas CIB).
- **League tables**: rankings of banks by fees or deal volume (Dealogic, LSEG). They are how "bulge bracket" is judged in practice.
- **Glass-Steagall**: a 1933 US law that separated commercial and investment banking. It was repealed in 1999. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley stayed pure investment banks until they became bank holding companies in 2008. The UK now uses **ring-fencing** (retail deposits kept separate within the group since 2019). France's 2013 banking law only isolates certain proprietary activities.
- **Non-bank market makers**: electronic trading firms that trade with their own capital, e.g. Citadel Securities, Jane Street, Optiver, Virtu. They are major liquidity providers in equities, options and increasingly in rates and FX.

### Intuition
Picture a spectrum from **pure brains** to **brains plus balance sheet**. A boutique sells judgement and relationships: its costs are mostly salaries, it needs almost no capital, and its revenue is volatile but high-margin. A universal bank sells judgement, execution and money together. It can lend to a company, advise on its acquisition, underwrite its bonds, hedge its FX and rates exposure and trade its stock. The deal flow from lending feeds the markets desks, and client flow gives traders information. The cost is capital: every position and every loan uses RWA, so returns on equity are lower and more regulated. Bulge bracket status is about **reach**: global coverage, top league-table positions, and big trading franchises in both FICC and equities.

### Worked example with numbers (illustrative, not real firms)
- **Boutique**: advises on a 2 bn EUR sale for a 0.5% fee, i.e. 10m EUR. Its capital need is close to zero, so almost all revenue goes to pay and profit.
- **Markets desk**: suppose a bank's markets business uses 100 bn EUR of RWA. At a 13% CET1 requirement that is 100 × 0.13 = **13 bn EUR of equity**. To earn a 12% return on that equity it needs about 1.56 bn EUR of net profit. That's why markets businesses care about **capital efficiency** (revenue per unit of RWA) and why they try to cross-sell financing and hedging to clients who also use the bank's lending.

### How the French banks fit in (useful for Paris interviews, as of 2026)
BNP Paribas, Société Générale, Crédit Agricole CIB and Natixis CIB are **universal banks' CIBs**. BNP Paribas is the largest markets player in the eurozone and among the global top 10. Société Générale is known historically for **equity derivatives and structured products**. Crédit Agricole CIB and Natixis are strong in rates, DCM and financing. They are not usually called "bulge bracket", but for Global Markets roles in Paris they are the main employers, alongside the Paris or London desks of US banks.

### Common pitfalls / what bad answers look like
- Treating "bulge bracket" as an official category. It's market slang, and the edges are debated.
- Saying elite boutiques have trading desks. They don't. If you're applying to Global Markets, a boutique is not an option for that role.
- Confusing "universal" with "big". Goldman Sachs is bulge bracket, but its retail and commercial business is small compared with JPMorgan's.
- Forgetting the non-bank market makers. In 2026 they compete with banks for flow and for graduates.
- Speaking badly of the bank you're *not* at. Compare business models, don't rank prestige.

### How to deliver it
One sentence per category with 2-3 names each, then the "so what": **balance sheet decides who can run S&T**, and universal banks use lending and client relationships to feed markets. End with where your target bank sits and why that matters to you, e.g. "BNP's universal model means corporate flow feeds rates and FX desks". Links: how banks make money in markets (fit-622), who is #1 in markets (fit-623), maturity transformation (fd-012), and the sell side against the buy side.

### Context / why they ask this
Commodity desks (and trading houses) throw unit-heavy arithmetic at candidates because the job is full of it. Traders quote in USD/bbl, USD/t, c/bu, USD/MMBtu or EUR/MWh, and clients ask "what is that per litre?". The interviewer tests speed, the habit of **checking units**, and whether you know the handful of conversion factors. The same skill is useful at any desk (DV01s, notionals per point).

### Key concepts
- **Barrel (bbl)**: 42 US gallons ≈ 159 litres.
- **bbl per tonne**: depends on density. About 7.33 for Brent-type light crude, about 6.3-6.7 for heavy crude, about 8.5 for gasoline. Lighter oil means more barrels per tonne.
- **Lot sizes**: ICE Brent and NYMEX WTI 1,000 bbl; LME copper 25 t; CBOT wheat and corn 5,000 bushels.
- **Bushel (bu)**: a volume unit for grains. By convention 1 t = 36.744 bu of wheat (60 lb/bu) and 39.368 bu of corn (56 lb/bu). CBOT prices are in **US cents per bushel**.
- **MMBtu**: million British thermal units. A barrel of crude holds roughly 5.8 MMBtu of energy, and one megawatt-hour is 3.412 MMBtu.
- **Crack spread**: refining margin. 3-2-1 means 3 barrels of crude make 2 of gasoline and 1 of distillate (diesel/heating oil). Product futures (RBOB, ULSD) are quoted in USD per gallon.
- **Contango test**: storage pays if M1-M2 > storage + financing + insurance per barrel-month.

### Worked drills (all checked)
1. **Percentage**: (95.68 − 92.00)/92.00 = 0.0400 → +4.0%.
2. **Barrels in a VLCC**: 270,000 × 7.33 = 1,979,100 bbl; heavy: 270,000 × 6.29 = 1,698,300 bbl.
3. **Cargo value**: 2m bbl × 78.50 = 157m USD; a 0.25 differential = 0.5m USD.
4. **Futures P&L**: 500 × 1,000 × 0.40 = 200,000 USD. Copper: 40 × 25 × 150 = 150,000 USD.
5. **Copper move**: 9,850 → 9,260 = −590, and −590/9,850 = **−5.99%**. On 320 lots: 320 × 25 × 590 = **4.72m USD**.
6. **Financing a cargo**: 190m × 6% × 30/360 = **950,000 USD**, i.e. 0.475 USD/bbl on 2m bbl (937k on an ACT/365 basis).
7. **Freight per barrel**: time charter 45,000 USD/day × 60 days = 2.7m USD; / 2m bbl = **1.35 USD/bbl** (before bunker fuel). Worldscale: flat rate 18.00 USD/t at WS 65 → 11.70 USD/t → / 7.33 ≈ **1.60 USD/bbl**.
8. **3-2-1 crack**: 102.90 and 109.20 USD/bbl for the products, (205.80 + 109.20 − 225.00)/3 = **30.00**.
9. **Storage check**: contango 1.00; carrying costs are 0.45 (storage) + 0.40 (financing, 0.5% × 80) + 0.02 (insurance) = 0.87 < 1.00, so storing pays **0.13 USD/bbl**, i.e. 130,000 USD on 1m bbl.
10. **Blending cost**: (600k × 82.00 + 400k × 79.50)/1m = **81.00**.
11. **Energy conversions**: Brent 87/5.8 = **15.0 USD/MMBtu**; TTF 35 EUR/MWh × 1.08/3.412 ≈ **11.08 USD/MMBtu**.
12. **Quick fire**: 17 × 23 = 391 (20² − 3²); 1/7 = 0.142857; 4.5% of 220m = 9.9m; 0.6% of 1.98m bbl = 11,880 bbl.

### The maths (shortcuts)
- Percentages: $\Delta/P$, then check by multiplying back.
- $(a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2$ for products around a round number: $17\times23 = 20^2-3^2$.
- Unit chains: write units on every factor (USD/gal × gal/bbl = USD/bbl) and cancel.

### Common pitfalls
- Mixing cents and dollars for grains (650 c/bu is 6.50 USD/bu).
- Forgetting the ×42 when combining product prices per gallon with crude per barrel.
- Using a single bbl/t for all crudes (density matters).
- Quoting a P&L without the sign or the unit.

### How to deliver it
Say the formula in words ("lots times lot size times move"), give the number, check it one way. Round only at the end. If you don't know a conversion factor, say what you would assume ("about 7.3 barrels per tonne for light crude") rather than freezing. Link to bt-070 (timed arithmetic tests) and fd-042 (energy price levels and conversions).
deep.fd-130:
### Context / why they ask this
"How do you follow markets?" tests genuine interest and method. Anyone can say "I read the FT"; a candidate who shows a structured weekly routine, with levels and a feedback loop, stands out. It also prepares every other market-view question (mkt-749 to mkt-758): the one-pager is where those answers come from. Related: fd-046 (learning levels), fd-048 (60-second wrap), fd-131 (how to phrase a view).

### Key concepts
- **Market wrap**: a short summary of what moved and why.
- **What is priced**: market-implied expectations (e.g. futures price about 70% chance of a Fed hike in October, fd-034); your view only has value relative to it.
- **Catalyst**: a scheduled event that can move prices (data releases, central bank meetings, auctions, budgets, rating reviews).
- **Trade journal / view log**: a dated record of views and outcomes to learn from mistakes and avoid hindsight bias.

### The template (one page)
| Box | Content | Example (week of 28 Sept 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Theme | one sentence | Oil-driven inflation rebound, hawkish central banks, long-end sell-off |
| 10 numbers | level and weekly change | UST 10y 5.26%; Bund 3.58%; gilt 5.42%; EURUSD 1.135; Brent Dec about 98; gold about 4,200; S&P about 7,684; VIX about 16; US HY about 302bp |
| What changed | 2-3 moves + cause | 30y UST about 5.62% intraday, highest since 2002; softer PCE (core 3.0%) pulled yields off highs |
| Priced | OIS/futures | about 70% for a Fed hike on 28 Oct; ECB hike about 60% for 29 Oct |
| Calendar | next 2 weeks | payrolls and HICP flash 2 Oct, OPEC+ 4 Oct, US CPI 14 Oct |
| View + trade | direction, level, stop, invalidation | 2s10s steepener; wrong if wages accelerate |

### Weekly and daily process
- **Daily (5-10 min)**: headlines, the ten numbers, one chart. Note anything surprising.
- **Weekly (30-45 min, e.g. Sunday)**: fill the page; read one central-bank statement or minutes and one in-depth article; update the calendar.
- **Monthly**: re-read four weekly pages: which views worked, which reasoning failed.
Sources: central-bank websites (Fed, ECB, BoE statements, minutes), statistical agencies (BLS, BEA, Eurostat, ONS, Insee), treasury.gov for the US curve, FRED for spreads and real yields, and a financial newspaper (FT, Les Echos, Bloomberg, Reuters). For interviews, a bank's own research pages are useful to know the house view.

### Worked example: learning from the log
Suppose your 1 September view was "Fed on hold, 10-year back to 4.9%". By 29 September the Fed had hiked and the 10-year was 5.26%. The log shows the mistake: you underweighted the oil pass-through to core inflation and the term premium. A 36bp move on a 10-year with duration about 7.7 would be about $7.7 \times 0.36\% \approx 2.8\%$ of loss on a long: a concrete way to feel why stops matter. In an interview, saying "I was wrong on X, here is what I learnt" is very credible.

### Common pitfalls
- Collecting headlines without a view.
- Only following one market: interviewers ask cross-asset questions.
- No numbers or stale numbers.
- Never checking past views, which leads to overconfidence.

### How to deliver it
Describe the routine in 30 seconds (daily numbers, weekly one-pager, monthly review), cite two or three sources, give this week's theme in one sentence, and offer to share your current view. Tailor the box you lead with to the desk.
deep.fd-131:
### Context / why they ask this
Interviewers often push back on your view on purpose: "Everyone says that", "What if you're wrong?". They test whether you can hold a position with arguments, update when given new information, and communicate uncertainty like a professional. On a desk, sales present views to clients and traders commit risk: both need calibrated language. Related: mkt-609 (pitch under pushback), fd-130 (weekly routine), mkt-749 (rates framework).

### Key concepts
- **Base case**: the most likely scenario; not the only one.
- **Conditional view**: "if X, then Y"; makes the logic explicit.
- **Falsifiable / invalidation level**: the data or price that would prove you wrong (e.g. the stop in a trade).
- **Calibration**: your stated probabilities match how often things happen; "60%" should be wrong 40% of the time.
- **What is priced**: market expectations; a view is interesting only if it differs from them or has a reason why the market is right.
- **Conviction**: how strongly you hold a view; it should drive position size.

### Templates
- **Direction + horizon + reason + risk**: "Over [horizon], I expect [market] to [move], because [reason vs priced]. The main risk is [X]; I'd reconsider if [data/level]."
- **Probabilistic**: "I put about [60]% on [base], [25]% on [upside], [15]% on [downside]."
- **Relative**: "I'm more confident about the curve than the level: steepener rather than outright."
- **Update gracefully**: "That's a fair point: if [the counterargument] holds, my target is too ambitious; I'd keep the direction but cut size."

### Worked example: translating conviction into numbers
Suppose you give 60% to the 10-year falling 30bp and 40% to rising 30bp over three months. Expected change $= 0.6 \times (-30) + 0.4 \times (+30) = -6$bp. On a 10-year with DV01 about USD 7,700 per USD 10m, the expected gain is about $6 \times 7{,}700 \approx$ USD 46k, against a standard deviation of roughly $\sqrt{0.6 \times 24^2 + 0.4 \times 36^2} \approx 29.4$bp, about USD 226k. The edge is small relative to the risk: a "60% view" justifies a small position, not a big bet. Saying this in an interview shows you understand that conviction and sizing go together.
(Deviations from the mean: $-30 - (-6) = -24$ and $+30 - (-6) = +36$.)

### Good vs bad phrasings
| Bad | Why | Better |
|---|---|---|
| "Rates will go down." | no horizon, no reason, no risk | "Over six months I expect the 2-year to fall about 30bp because the market prices more hikes than the data justify; the risk is wages." |
| "It's hard to say, it could go either way." | no view | "It's close, but I lean towards X at about 55-60%, mainly because of Y." |
| "The ECB will definitely hike." | overconfident | "My base case is one more hike, about 60%, given 3.2% inflation, but weak growth argues for a pause." |
| "Everyone knows gold goes up in a war." | cliché, wrong in 2026 | "Gold fell during the war because real yields rose; the rate effect dominated." |

### Common pitfalls
- Changing your view at the first pushback: acknowledge, weigh, then keep or adjust with a reason.
- Refusing to update when the interviewer gives a real fact you missed.
- Hiding behind jargon.
- Fake precision ("the 10-year will be 4.87% in December").

### How to deliver it
Speak slowly, start with the direction, attach the reason and the risk, and use numbers for probabilities and levels. When challenged, repeat the counterargument in your own words, then answer it. Saying "I might be wrong, and here is how I'd know" sounds more professional than certainty.
deep.str-001:
### Context / why they ask this
This is almost always the first question in a structuring interview, especially at French banks (SocGen, BNP Paribas, Natixis, CACIB) where structured products are a core franchise. The interviewer checks that you know **why you want this seat and not another one**. A vague answer ("structurers create complex products") is a red flag; a good answer shows you understand the **flow of a trade** from client idea to hedge.

### Key concepts
- **Structured product / structured note**: a security (usually a bond issued by the bank) whose payoff is linked to an underlying (index, stock, rate, credit) through embedded derivatives.
- **Term sheet**: the short document describing the payoff, dates, underlying, barriers, issuer. The legally binding version is the *final terms* under a base prospectus.
- **Hedge / risk recycling**: after selling a product, the bank holds the opposite exposure. The trader hedges the delta (with stock/futures) and manages residual risks (vol, correlation, dividends). "Recycling" means selling products that offset risks already in the book.
- **Margin / P&L day one**: the difference between the price the client pays and the fair value of what the bank delivers.
- **Flow vs exotic**: flow products are standard, liquid (vanilla options, swaps); exotics are bespoke (autocallables, cliquets, worst-ofs) and are where structurers operate.

### Intuition: the chain of a trade
1. **Client need** (via sales): view on market, yield target, risk tolerance, maturity, regulatory constraints (retail vs institutional), currency, wrapper (note, swap, assurance-vie fund).
2. **Structuring**: build candidate payoffs, price them, compare. Tune parameters (barrier level, coupon, maturity, underlying) until the product is attractive for the client *and* fits the bank's margin target.
3. **Validation**: the trader agrees to take the risk at that price (and may push back if it adds risk the book already has too much of: e.g. more short correlation). Legal/compliance checks target market and documentation.
4. **Execution and hedging**: the bank issues the note, the trader hedges. The structurer often handles the lifecycle (fixings, autocall events, secondary market buyback prices).

### Comparison
| Role | Main question they answer | Core skills |
|---|---|---|
| Sales | Who needs what, and can I sell it? | Relationship, market narrative |
| Structurer | What payoff answers the need, at what price? | Payoff design, pricing intuition, communication |
| Trader | How do I hedge this and make money on the book? | Risk management, market sense |
| Quant | Is the model correct and fast? | Stochastic calculus, numerics, code |

Structurers split into **investor/solution structuring** (products for clients: notes, funds) and sometimes **cross-asset / QIS** (systematic indices), **corporate / hedging structuring** (hedges for corporates), or **financing structuring** (repo, collateral trades).

### Why the role suits a maths profile
You need to decompose any payoff into building blocks (zero-coupon bond + vanillas + digitals + barriers), know the sign of each sensitivity by intuition, and explain it simply to sales. Much of it is "pricing intuition": *if I lower the barrier, does the coupon go up or down, and by how much?*

### Common pitfalls
- Saying the structurer "takes risk": no, the **trading desk** holds the risk. The structurer designs.
- Ignoring the hedging side: a product that sells well but cannot be hedged (illiquid underlying, no vol market) will be refused.
- Describing only the maths: this is a client-facing job; communication counts.

### How to deliver it
Tell the trade story in 4 steps (need, design, validation, hedge) and end with why it fits you: "I like the mix of quantitative pricing and designing something concrete for a client." Be ready to name a product you find interesting (autocallables are the default in France) and explain it.
deep.str-002:
### Context / why they ask this
Decomposition is the core skill of structuring. The interviewer wants to see that you can take any payoff and write it as a portfolio of simple instruments you know how to price. Everything else (margin, sensitivities, hedging) follows from the decomposition.

### Key concepts
- **Zero-coupon bond (ZCB)**: pays 100 at maturity $T$, nothing before. Price today $100\,e^{-(r+s)T}$ where $r$ is the risk-free rate and $s$ the **issuer's funding/credit spread**.
- **Notional**: the amount invested (e.g. 100 or €1,000 per note).
- **Option budget**: what is left after buying the ZCB and taking the margin: $\text{budget} = 100 - \text{ZCB} - \text{margin}$.
- **Capital protection / capital guarantee**: the investor gets at least X% back at maturity (if the issuer does not default).
- **Yield enhancement**: the investor sells optionality (typically a put) to earn a coupon above market rates.
- **Wrapper**: the legal form: EMTN note, certificate, warrant, OTC swap, fund unit in an assurance-vie contract.

### Intuition
The client hands over 100. The bank must guarantee something at maturity: the cheapest way is to set aside the PV of that guarantee (the ZCB). Whatever is left is "free money" to buy upside. Two families:
1. **Protected (participation) products**: ZCB + long call (or call spread, Asian call...). Client can't lose capital, gets a share of upside.
2. **Yield products**: ZCB + coupon, minus a put sold by the client (reverse convertible, autocallable). The client takes equity downside risk in exchange for a high coupon.

### The maths
Capital-protected note at 100% protection with participation $p$ on an index $S$:
$$\text{Payoff}_T = 100 + p\cdot 100\cdot\max\left(\frac{S_T}{S_0}-1,0\right)$$
$$\text{Price} = 100\,e^{-(r+s)T} + p\cdot C_{ATM}(\%) + \text{margin} = 100$$
so $p = \dfrac{100 - 100e^{-(r+s)T} - \text{margin}}{C_{ATM}}$.

Reverse convertible with coupon $c$, strike 100%:
$$\text{Payoff}_T = 100(1+c) - 100\max\left(1-\frac{S_T}{S_0},0\right)$$
$$= \text{ZCB paying } 100(1+c) \;-\; \text{ATM put}.$$

### Worked example with numbers
5-year note, $r = 3\%$, issuer spread $s = 1\%$ (continuous), margin 1.5%:
- ZCB $= 100e^{-0.04\times5} = 81.87$
- Budget $= 100 - 81.87 - 1.5 = 16.63$
- 5y ATM call on an index (vol 18%, dividend yield 3%) ≈ 13.73% of notional (Black-Scholes)
- Participation $= 16.63 / 13.73 \approx 121\%$.

So the client gets 100% capital back plus 121% of the index rise.

### Pitfalls
- Forgetting the **issuer spread**: the ZCB is priced on the bank's own funding curve, not risk-free. That is a real source of budget (and of risk for the client).
- Forgetting the **margin**.
- Mixing up who is long/short the option: in yield products, the *client* is short the put.

### How to deliver it
Draw the box: "100 = ZCB + options + margin". Then say which family the product belongs to and whether the client is long or short optionality. That instantly tells you most sensitivities: long options → likes vol; short put → dislikes vol.
deep.str-003:
### Context / why they ask this
Interviewers want to see commercial sense: a structurer's job is to make the product attractive **and** profitable. They also test whether you understand that "margin" is not a hidden trick but a price for structuring, hedging, capital and distribution.

### Key concepts
- **Fair value / theoretical value**: the model price of the payoff using market inputs (vol surface, rates, dividends, correlation) and the issuer's funding curve.
- **Issue price**: usually 100% of nominal.
- **Day-one P&L**: issue price minus fair value (minus hedging reserves).
- **Retrocession / distribution fee**: part of the margin paid to the distributor (private bank, insurer, CGP i.e. *conseiller en gestion de patrimoine*). Often ~0.5-1% per year of maturity, paid upfront.
- **Funding spread**: the spread over risk-free the bank pays when it borrows. A note issued by the bank *is* borrowing.
- **Reserves / model reserves**: amounts held back from day-one P&L for parameters that cannot be hedged (correlation, long-dated vol), released over time.

### Intuition
Think of the bank as a manufacturer:
- Raw materials: ZCB + options, at fair value.
- Selling price: 100.
- Gross margin: 100 − fair value, shared with the shop (distributor).

Plus a financial side: the bank gets cash for 5-10 years. If its marginal cost of funding (e.g. issuing a senior bond) is €STR + 80bp and the note effectively funds it at €STR + 60bp, the treasury gains 20bp per year.

### Worked example with numbers
5y autocall, notional €50m sold through a private bank network.
- Fair value 96.5% → total margin 3.5% = €1.75m.
- Distributor retrocession, paid upfront, say 2% = €1.0m.
- Desk keeps 1.5% = €0.75m, part of which is reserved (e.g. 0.3% correlation/dividend reserve) and released as the product matures or autocalls.

Order of magnitude: yearly margins on retail products are often quoted in the 0.5-1.5% per year range all-in, depending on complexity and distribution channel (a PRIIPs KID must disclose total costs, so this is visible).

### The maths
$$\text{Margin} = 100 - \left[\text{PV}_{\text{issuer curve}}(\text{bond leg}) + \text{Value}(\text{options})\right]$$
The bond leg discounted at $r+s$: a larger issuer spread $s$ makes the bond cheaper, leaving more room for options or margin. That's why banks with higher funding spreads can offer more attractive-looking coupons: the client is being paid for credit risk.

### Pitfalls
- Saying "the bank bets against the client": the bank hedges; its P&L comes from margin and risk management, not from the client losing.
- Forgetting distribution: in France most retail notes go through networks (private banks, insurers, CGPs) who take a big share.
- Ignoring **unhedgeable parameters**: correlation and dividend risk remain in the book; that's where losses come from.

### How to deliver it
List "margin, funding, risk management (plus secondary)", give one number (2-3% upfront on a 5-year retail note), and mention that unhedgeable parameters are the flip side. Linking to 2020 (dividend cancellations) shows market awareness.
deep.str-004:
### Context / why they ask this
A classic trap: candidates talk only about the equity payoff and forget that the note is a bond. Interviewers (and regulators) care a lot about this after Lehman: thousands of retail investors held "capital-protected" Lehman notes that paid cents on the euro.

### Key concepts
- **Unsecured senior debt**: a bond with no collateral; in a default, holders become creditors and recover a fraction (**recovery rate**, often 30-40%).
- **Credit spread / funding spread**: extra yield over risk-free investors demand to lend to that issuer. Visible in the bank's bond yields or CDS.
- **CDS (credit default swap)**: insurance against default; its premium is the market price of credit risk.
- **Bail-in (EU BRRD)**: under European resolution rules, senior unsecured debt, including structured notes, can be written down or converted to equity if the bank fails. This is disclosed in prospectuses and KIDs.
- **Issuance vehicle**: many notes are issued by an offshore/Luxembourg/Dutch entity (e.g. "SG Issuer", "BNP Paribas Issuance B.V.") with a **guarantee** from the parent; the credit risk is the parent's.
- **Collateralised notes**: some issuers post collateral into a segregated pool for the benefit of noteholders (e.g. "COSI"-type structures in Switzerland, or secured notes), reducing credit risk at a cost.

### Intuition
The client lends 100 to the bank for $T$ years. The bank promises a payoff. Two independent questions: (1) what is the payoff worth if the bank is alive? (2) what is the probability the bank is alive? The ZCB leg carries (2).

### The maths
Price of the bond leg with a flat hazard rate $\lambda$ and recovery $R$: approximately spread $s \approx \lambda(1-R)$, and
$$\text{ZCB} = 100\,e^{-(r+s)T}.$$
Sensitivity of the note to spread (credit "DV01"): $\partial \text{ZCB}/\partial s = -T\cdot \text{ZCB}$.

### Worked example with numbers
5y 100% protected note, $r=3\%$.
- Issuer A, spread 0.5%: ZCB $=100e^{-0.035\times5}=83.95$ → budget before margin 16.05.
- Issuer B, spread 1.5%: ZCB $=100e^{-0.045\times5}=79.85$ → budget 20.15.

Issuer B can offer about 25% more option budget (20.15 vs 16.05), which looks like a better product but is partly compensation for credit risk.

Mark-to-market: note held one day after issue, issuer A's spread widens by 50bp. Bond-leg value falls by about $5 \times 0.005 \times 83.95 \approx 2.1$ points. The client sees the note down ~2% with the equity index unchanged.

### Pitfalls
- Saying "capital guaranteed" without "subject to issuer credit risk": compliance would reject that, and so would an interviewer.
- Forgetting that the **issuer benefits** from its own spread: the higher the spread, the more budget; this is why lower-rated issuers are more aggressive on coupons.
- Confusing this with the **credit-linked note** where credit risk of a *third party* is the underlying (see CLN card).

### How to deliver it
"It's the bank's senior unsecured debt: default and bail-in risk, priced via the funding spread in the ZCB. Wider spread = bigger option budget = better-looking terms, and a drop in note value if spreads widen after issue." Mention Lehman 2008 as the canonical example.
deep.str-005:
### Context / why they ask this
It is *the* canonical structuring question: it combines bond pricing, option pricing and product design. Expect them to follow up with "what happens if rates go down" and "what if vol goes up" (separate cards).

### Key concepts
- **Participation rate $p$**: the fraction of the underlying's performance paid to the investor. $p=121\%$ means +10% on the index gives +12.1% on the note.
- **Capital protection level**: the floor at maturity, e.g. 100% or 90% of notional.
- **Option budget**: $100 - \text{ZCB} - \text{margin}$.
- **ATM call** (at-the-money): strike = initial level $S_0$. Here priced in % of notional.
- **Dividend yield $q$**: dividends lower the forward $F = S_0e^{(r-q)T}$ and so cheapen calls. Index calls on a price index (not total return) are cheaper when dividends are high.

### The maths
$$\text{Payoff} = 100\left[k + p\max\left(\frac{S_T}{S_0}-1, 0\right)\right],\qquad k = \text{protection level}$$
$$p = \frac{100 - k\cdot 100e^{-(r+s)T} - m}{C_{ATM}}$$
with $C_{ATM}$ the Black-Scholes price of a call with strike $S_0$ in % of notional:
$$C = S_0e^{-qT}N(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_2).$$

### Worked example with numbers
Inputs: $T=5$, $r=3\%$, issuer spread $s=1\%$, margin $m=1.5$, index vol $\sigma=18\%$, $q=3\%$.
1. ZCB $= 100e^{-0.20} = 81.87$
2. Budget $= 100 - 81.87 - 1.5 = 16.63$
3. $C_{ATM}$ (5y, 18% vol, $r=q=3\%$) $= 13.73$
4. $p = 16.63/13.73 = 121\%$

Now cap the upside at +50% (buy the 100% call, sell the 150% call): call spread cost 10.29, so $p = 16.63/10.29 \approx 162\%$ but max gain $= 1.62 \times 50\% = 81\%$.

Now 90% protection: ZCB $=0.9\times 81.87 = 73.68$, budget $=24.82$, $p = 24.82/13.73 \approx 181\%$.

### Intuition
Protection is bought with time value of money: the longer the maturity and higher the rates, the cheaper the ZCB, and the more is left for upside. The call is priced like any option: more vol, more expensive; more dividends, cheaper (lower forward).

### Pitfalls
- Using risk-free rates without the issuer spread.
- Forgetting the margin (interviewers will ask "and where's your fee?").
- Saying participation is capped at 100%: it can exceed 100% whenever the budget exceeds the call price.
- Forgetting that the payoff is only protected **at maturity**: the mark-to-market in between can be below 100 (rates up, vol down, spread widening).

### How to deliver it
Say the formula in words ("budget over call price"), do the numbers quickly (ZCB 82, budget ~17, call ~14, participation ~120%), then list levers to improve it. Show you know the product is only protected at maturity and subject to issuer credit.
deep.str-006:
### Context / why they ask this
The single most classic structuring question. They want (1) the right direction, (2) the mechanism through the ZCB, (3) bonus: the second-order effect via the call, and (4) market awareness (low rates killed capital protection).

### Key concepts
- **ZCB price**: $B = e^{-(r+s)T}$. $\partial B / \partial r = -T B$: the bond's duration is $T$.
- **Rho of a call**: $\rho_C = KTe^{-rT}N(d_2) > 0$ holding spot fixed; with dividends/forward, higher $r$ → higher forward → higher call value.
- **Forward**: $F = S_0e^{(r-q)T}$.

### Intuition
Capital protection is financed by interest: you lend 82 today and it grows to 100 in 5 years at 4%. If rates are 1% (plus 1% spread = 2%), 82 only grows to about 90.6; you need 90.5 today to reach 100. The investor's "free budget" for upside is the interest they give up. No interest, no budget.

The call effect: with lower rates, the risk-neutral drift is lower, so the underlying is expected to rise less → call cheaper. That helps, but the ZCB effect is first order in the notional (100 × T × Δr), while the call effect is first order in a much smaller number (the call's rho).

### Worked example with numbers
$T=5$, spread 1%, margin 1.5, vol 18%, $q=3\%$.

| | $r=3\%$ | $r=1\%$ |
|---|---|---|
| ZCB | 81.87 | 90.48 |
| Budget | 16.63 | 8.02 |
| ATM call | 13.73 | 10.36 |
| Participation | **121%** | **77%** |

A 2% rate drop cut the budget by half, and the call only by 25%.

### The maths (sensitivity)
$$p(r) = \frac{100 - 100e^{-(r+s)T} - m}{C(r)}$$
$$\frac{\partial p}{\partial r} = \frac{100Te^{-(r+s)T}}{C} - \frac{p\,\rho_C}{C}$$
The first term (ZCB) is positive and large; the second (call rho, positive) reduces it. With the numbers: $100 \times 5 \times 0.819 / 13.73 \approx 29.8$ per unit of rate (so +0.30 participation per +1% rate from the ZCB term alone), partly offset by the call rho.

### Market context (as of 2026)
During 2015-2021, EUR rates were at or below zero: a 5-year 100% protected note had almost no budget. Structurers responded with: longer maturities (8-10 years), partial protection (90-95%), capped/Asian calls, and above all **yield products** (autocallables) where the client sells optionality. After ECB hikes in 2022-2023, capital-protected notes returned in force in French assurance-vie. As of Sept 2026, after two more ECB hikes (deposit rate 2.50%) and an oil-shock sell-off, 5-year EUR swaps are around 3.6-3.7%, so the protection budget is large again.

### Pitfalls
- Saying "participation goes up because calls are cheaper": direction wrong, and misses the dominant effect.
- Forgetting the time dimension: the effect scales with maturity $T$ (ZCB duration).
- Forgetting the issuer spread can move too: a spread widening has the same sign as a rate rise for the budget.

### How to deliver it
One sentence answer first ("it goes down, because the zero-coupon gets more expensive"), then the small offset from the call, then one number and the market story. That structure (direction → mechanism → second-order → context) is exactly what interviewers look for.
deep.str-007:
### Context / why they ask this
The natural pair of the "rates down" question. It tests whether you know **who is long vol** in the product. Rule: the client of a protected product is long optionality → hurt by expensive vol at issuance. The call spread twist tests deeper understanding.

### Key concepts
- **Vega**: sensitivity of an option price to implied vol. Vanilla calls and puts have positive vega, maximal near ATM and for long maturities (grows like $\sqrt{T}$).
- **Call spread**: long call strike $K_1$, short call strike $K_2 > K_1$. Payoff capped at $K_2 - K_1$.
- **Implied vol at issuance vs later**: the participation is fixed at issuance with the vol then. After issue, a vol rise *increases* the note's value for the client (long vega).

### Intuition
More vol = more chance of large moves = options worth more. The client wants to buy a call; the price of the call went up; with the same budget they get less participation. For a call spread, the client is long vol at $K_1$ and short vol at $K_2$: the two partly cancel. When spot is near $K_1$, the spread is still slightly long vega; if spot is near or above the cap $K_2$, the spread becomes short vega, because more vol now mostly raises the chance of falling back below the cap.

### The maths
$$\nu_{\text{spread}} = \nu(K_1) - \nu(K_2),\quad \nu(K) = S_0e^{-qT}\sqrt{T}\,\varphi(d_1(K)).$$
With the skew (lower strikes have higher implied vol in equity), the short high-strike call is priced at a lower vol than the long ATM call, which makes spreads a bit more expensive than in a flat-vol world; a vol-surface-consistent pricer is needed.

### Worked example with numbers
$T=5$, $r=3\%$, spread 1%, margin 1.5 → budget 16.63.

| vol | ATM call | participation | 100/150 spread | capped participation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18% | 13.73 | 121% | 10.29 | 162% |
| 25% | 18.95 | 88% | 11.06 | 150% |

Vol +7 points: uncapped participation −33 points; capped only −12.

### Design implication
In a high-vol environment, to keep an attractive headline participation: cap it, use **Asian averaging** of the final level (averaging reduces effective vol by roughly $1/\sqrt{3}$ for continuous arithmetic averaging over the whole life), use a lower-vol underlying (broad index, **risk-control / vol-target index**), or a **decrement index**. These are exactly the tools French structurers use.

### Pitfalls
- Thinking the ZCB changes with vol (it doesn't).
- Confusing issuance (participation fixed) with lifetime MTM (client long vega, benefits from a vol rise).
- Saying a call spread has zero vega: it's reduced, not zero, and its sign depends on spot vs strikes.

### How to deliver it
"Client is long a call → long vega → higher vol makes it expensive → lower participation. With a cap, the client also sells vol, so the effect is much smaller." Then pivot: "That's why when vol is high, you sell the client yield products instead: there, the client is short vol and high vol means a high coupon.\"
deep.str-008:
### Context / why they ask this
This is a "design" question: there is no single answer, and the interviewer wants a **structured list of levers** with the **trade-off** each implies. It shows you think like a structurer: every improvement is paid for by giving up something the client values less.

### Key concepts
- **Asian option**: payoff on the *average* of the underlying over several dates (e.g. monthly over the last year, or over the whole life), rather than the final level. The average is less volatile than the terminal value, so the option is cheaper.
- **Call spread / cap**: the client's upside is capped; the bank sells back the high-strike call.
- **Shark fin**: an up-and-out call: upside participation until a barrier; if the barrier is touched, the client gets a fixed rebate instead.
- **Decrement index**: an index that subtracts a fixed dividend (e.g. 50 index points or 5% per year) from a total-return index. Popular in France (see separate card). It has a lower forward, so calls are cheaper and puts dearer.
- **Vol-target / risk-control index**: dynamically allocates between equity and cash to target, e.g., 10% vol.

### Intuition
Budget = what the client "pays" with interest; option price = cost of the upside. Structuring = finding the upside the client *values most per euro*. Clients typically overvalue certainty (protection), and undervalue extreme upside, so capping is often cheap from their point of view.

### Worked example with numbers
Base: 5y, $r=3\%$, spread 1%, margin 1.5 → budget 16.63; vol 18%, $q=3\%$.
- Vanilla ATM call 13.73 → $p = 121\%$ (in the low-rate case this is where you'd see 60-77%).
- Cap at +50% (100/150 call spread): 10.29 → $p = 162\%$.
- Asian over the whole life: rough approximation with effective vol $\sigma/\sqrt3 \approx 10.4\%$ → call ≈ 8.0 → $p \approx 208\%$ (the exact arithmetic-average price differs a bit, but the order of magnitude is right: averaging roughly halves the call cost).
- 90% protection: budget 24.82 → $p = 181\%$ on the vanilla call.

### The maths behind Asian cheapness
For continuous geometric averaging of a GBM over $[0,T]$, $\ln G = \frac1T\int_0^T \ln S_t\,dt$ is normal with variance $\sigma^2T/3$. So the average behaves like a terminal value with vol $\sigma/\sqrt{3}$ (and a lower drift). Averaging only over the last year of five reduces vol much less.

### Pitfalls
- Listing levers without trade-offs: the interviewer wants "cap → gives up large rallies, fine if the client is mildly bullish".
- Proposing to cut the margin first: that's the last resort, the desk won't love it.
- Forgetting **path**: Asian averaging also hurts if the market rallies late in the life (the average lags).

### How to deliver it
Organise: "two sides: increase the budget (maturity, protection level, issuer spread, margin) or reduce the option cost (cap, averaging, barrier, underlying)". Then pick one based on the client's view and quantify quickly. Ending with "I'd ask sales what the client expects the market to do" is exactly the right structuring reflex.
deep.str-009:
### Context / why they ask this
It tests barrier intuition (knock-out logic) in a product context, and whether you understand why barrier features cheapen options and where hedging becomes difficult.

### Key concepts
- **Up-and-out call (UOC)**: call with strike $K$ that ceases to exist if $S_t \ge H$ at any monitoring time ($H > K$).
- **Rebate**: fixed amount paid if knocked out (at KO time or at maturity).
- **Continuous vs discrete monitoring**: continuous = any time during the life (usually on closing prices, sometimes intraday); discrete = only on specified dates.
- **Gamma**: rate of change of delta. Near a knock-out barrier the option value collapses from roughly $H-K$ to the rebate, so delta and gamma explode.

### The maths
Payoff at maturity:
$$100\left[1 + p\max\left(\frac{S_T}{S_0}-1,0\right)\mathbf 1_{\{\max_{t\le T}S_t < H\}} + R\,\mathbf 1_{\{\max_{t\le T} S_t \ge H\}}\right].$$
In-out parity: $\text{UOC} + \text{UIC} = \text{Call}$, so $\text{UOC} = \text{Call} - \text{UIC}$ and it is always cheaper than the vanilla.

### Worked example with numbers
3-year note, $r=3\%$, issuer spread 1%, margin 1.5, vol 18%, $q=3\%$.
- ZCB $=100e^{-0.12}=88.69$ → budget $9.81$.
- Vanilla ATM 3y call: 11.32 → $p = 87\%$ only.
- UOC strike 100, barrier 130, daily monitoring (Monte Carlo): about 1.31, and the probability of knocking out is ~34%.
- 100% participation with a 20% rebate paid at maturity if knocked out: $1.31 + 20\times0.34\times e^{-0.09} \approx 1.31 + 6.2 = 7.5$ < 9.81 → affordable, with room for more rebate or margin.

The client's max gain is +30% (just below the barrier), a guaranteed 100 otherwise, and +20% if the market rallies strongly (rebate).

### Intuition on hedging
Just below the barrier, the UOC is worth about $p\times30$; just above, it's worth the rebate. A small move up destroys most of the value: delta is very negative near $H$ (despite being a call). The trader must be short the stock near the barrier: when spot approaches, dealers sell, which can itself push spot towards the barrier. Desks usually **price with a shifted barrier** (e.g. as if at 128 instead of 130) to build a cushion (see barrier hedging card).

### Pitfalls
