| 8% | 15% | 4.50 | −6.9% | 70% | 1.6% |
| 8% | 20% | 1.94 | −9.1% | 37% | 0.7% |
| 10% | 20% | 4.83 | −9.1% | 64% | 1.7% |
| 12% | 20% | 9.08 | −9.1% | 84% | 3.2% |
| 12% | 25% | 5.24 | −11.3% | 60% | 1.8% |

Fair $X$ at 20% vol: **10.8%** (average coupon 2.25%/year, positive in 73% of years).
The value falls by almost half from 15% to 20% vol: strongly short vol.

### Intuition
The minimum of 12 monthly returns with monthly vol $\sigma/\sqrt{12}\approx5.8\%$ is about $-1.6$ to $-1.7$ monthly standard deviations ≈ −9%: that's the "expected cost" eating the fixed rate. The client is selling the bank 12 monthly out-of-the-money forward-start puts each year, and the bank pays a high headline rate for them.

### Risks the bank keeps
Long forward vol and forward skew (the mirror of the client), gap risk on a crash month, model risk (forward skew as for cliquets). The bank's long vol can be recycled against short-vol positions elsewhere.

### How to pitch it to a client
"Up to 10.8% per year with 100% capital protection; each month the market falls, the coupon is reduced by that fall, only the worst month counts." A structurer must add: "in a year with one bad month of −10%, the coupon is under 1%". Under MiFID II the performance scenarios in the KID must show that.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying the client is long vol (because it's "option-like"): he is short the downside.
- Using annual return instead of worst monthly.
- Confusing Napoleon with reverse cliquet (reverse cliquet subtracts the **sum** of negative returns, Napoleon only the **worst** one).

### How to deliver it
Payoff in one line, "worst-of across time → short vol", one number contrasting headline 10.8% with average 2.3%.
deep.str-034:
### Context / why they ask this
Range accruals are a core rates structured product (callable range accruals were huge in Asia and Europe), and they also exist on FX and equity. The interviewer checks the digital decomposition, the vol sign, and realism about accrual probabilities growing worse with time.

### Key concepts
- **Fixing**: the published daily value of the reference rate (e.g. 3M Euribor).
- **Normal (Bachelier) vol**: rates vol in basis points per year; a 1-year move of 80 bp is one standard deviation.
- **Digital range**: pays 1 if the fixing is in $[L,U]$ = digital above $L$ minus digital above $U$.
- **Callable range accrual**: the issuer can call the note (usually when it's favorable to the issuer), giving more coupon to the client.

### The maths
$$\text{Coupon}=c\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{d=1}^N \mathbf 1_{L\le X_d\le U},\qquad V\approx c\sum_d \frac{P(0,T_{pay})}{N}\,\mathbb Q^{T}\big(L\le X_d\le U\big).$$
Normal model, forward $f$ flat, vol $\sigma_N$:
$$\mathbb Q(L\le X_t\le U)=N\Big(\tfrac{U-f}{\sigma_N\sqrt t}\Big)-N\Big(\tfrac{L-f}{\sigma_N\sqrt t}\Big).$$
(Exact pricing uses the right forward measure and convexity for payment delays; smile makes each digital a call spread, so skew matters.)

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, illustrative levels)
These are 2025-style levels. As of Sept 2026, after two ECB hikes (deposit rate 2.50%), 3-month Euribor is about 2.6% (2.62% on 29 Sept) and forwards price further hikes, so a 0%-2.5% range would already be breached: today the range would be recentred around the forward, e.g. 1.5%-3.5%.
$f=2.0\%$, $\sigma_N=0.80\%$, range [0%, 2.5%]:
- Probability in range for a fixing at $t=2$: $N(0.5/1.13)-N(-2/1.13)\approx63\%$.
- Average over each year: **83%** (y1), **68%** (y2), **60%** (y3); 3-year average 70%.
- Budget: funding rate ~2% + 0.8% issuer spread − 0.5%/y margin = 2.3%/y of coupon value. Range accrual coupon: $2.3\%/0.70\approx\mathbf{3.27\%}$ per year of accrual (discounting differences ignored).
Scenario: rates stay at 2%: client receives 3.27% every year vs 2.3% fixed. Rates spike to 3%: 0 until they come back.

### Intuition
The client sells a strip of **strangles-like** exposures (digitals outside the range). The range is set around the forward so that early fixings are very likely in, but uncertainty grows with $\sqrt t$, so later years accrue less. Tighter range / longer maturity → higher $c$.

### Risks the bank keeps
Bank long the digitals outside the range: long vol, digital/pin risk near the boundaries on each fixing, skew, and for callable versions **Bermudan call** risk (model with a term-structure model like Hull-White or LMM, correlation between rates). Funding: the issuer benefits if it can call when rates fall.

### How to pitch it to a client
"You earn 3.27% a year, accrued for every day 3-month Euribor stays between 0% and 2.5%. If you think the ECB will keep Euribor near where the forwards are, the range should be respected; if it is breached, you earn nothing for those days but keep your capital." Target: treasurers or private clients with a stable-rates view. Mention the risk clearly: a rate move outside the range for months means low income.

### Common pitfalls
- Forgetting accrual probabilities decline with time.
- Saying the client is long vol.
- Ignoring that in a callable version the issuer calls when the note is valuable to the client (it's the client selling a Bermudan option).

### How to deliver it
"Coupon × days in range / total days; each day is a digital range; client short vol." Then the numbers, then who buys it.
deep.str-035:
### Context / why they ask this
Callable notes are the most common rates structured product: private banks, insurers and corporate treasuries buy "multi-callable" fixed-rate notes every day, and issuers (SocGen, BNP, Natixis, CACIB) use them as cheap funding. The interviewer wants: (1) who owns the option, (2) which option it is (a Bermudan swaption, not a vanilla), (3) why it increases the coupon, and (4) what the client really risks.

### Key concepts
- **Bullet note**: repays 100% at a fixed maturity, no early redemption.
- **Call date / non-call period (NC)**: dates on which the issuer may redeem at par; "5NC1" = 5-year maturity, not callable during the first year, then callable (here annually).
- **Bermudan option**: can be exercised on a discrete set of dates (between European and American).
- **Receiver swaption**: the right to enter a swap receiving the fixed rate. When rates fall, receiving an above-market fixed rate is valuable.
- **Normal (Bachelier) volatility**: rate vol quoted in basis points per year (80 bp = one-standard-deviation yearly move of 0.80%).
- **Negative convexity**: price rises less than a bullet's when rates fall (capped near par because the note will be called), falls as much when rates rise.
- **Funding / issuer spread**: the extra yield the issuer pays over swaps because of its credit risk (see the issuer credit card).

### Intuition
The issuer borrows at a fixed coupon but keeps the right to repay. If rates fall, it repays at par and borrows again at the lower rate: that is the same economic benefit as holding a receiver swaption. Nothing is free, so the issuer pays the investor for that right through a higher coupon. The investor is effectively saying: "I accept to be taken out of a good investment in exchange for a higher yield today."

Why a **swaption** and not a bond option: the issuer swaps its fixed coupon into floating (Euribor + spread) with its own trading desk. Calling the note cancels the remaining fixed flows, so the desk holds a right to cancel a swap in which it pays fixed = a Bermudan receiver swaption on the remaining schedule (a "cancellable swap").

### The maths
Value to the investor:
$$V_{callable}=V_{bullet}(c)-\text{Berm}(c),$$
where Berm is the value of the issuer's option to redeem at par. At each call date $t_i$ the issuer (who minimises its liability) calls if the continuation value exceeds par:
$$V(t_i)=\min\big(100,\;V^{cont}(t_i)\big)+c\cdot 100 .$$
The structurer solves for the coupon $c$ such that
$$V_{callable}(c)=100-\text{margin},$$
discounting at the issuer's funding curve (swap rate + issuer spread). A Bermudan needs a term-structure model: Hull-White (one factor, normal rates) is the desk standard for pricing callables, calibrated to the co-terminal European swaptions (the 1y-into-4y, 2y-into-3y, 3y-into-2y, 4y-into-1y for a 5NC1). LMM or two-factor models are used when correlation between rates matters.

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python)
Assumptions: flat 2.5% (continuous) euro swap curve, issuer spread 60 bp, one-factor Ho-Lee binomial tree (normal rates, monthly steps), normal vol 80 bp, annual coupons, 5 years, bank margin 1.5 points upfront.
- **Bullet**: coupon that makes the price 98.5 = **2.82%**. (At par it would be 3.15%, so the margin costs 33 bp a year.)
- **5NC1 annual callable**: coupon that makes the price 98.5 = **3.18%**.
- At the 3.18% coupon: bullet worth 100.12, callable worth 98.50, so the **Bermudan is worth about 1.62 points**.
- Vol sensitivity of the callable coupon: 50 bp normal vol gives 2.98%, 80 bp gives 3.18%, 120 bp gives 3.47%. More vol = more valuable option = higher coupon.
Scenarios for the client: rates fall 1% after year 1 → called at par in year 1, must reinvest at about 1.5-2%; rates rise → keeps a 3.18% note that is now below market, trades below par, and runs to maturity.

### Risks the bank keeps
The issuer's desk is long the Bermudan and swaps the note. It hedges vega with European swaptions, but keeps: **model risk** (the exercise decision depends on the rates model's correlation between forward rates, which Europeans don't pin down), **smile risk**, a residual **exercise boundary** risk, and a big **gamma/vega concentration** when the whole street issues callables at the same strikes (in Asia and Europe the flows from callable issuance push long-dated swaption vol down: desks are structurally long vega and need to recycle it to hedge funds or insurers). There's also funding: calling is a funding decision too, and the treasury may not call even if economically optimal (clients then call it a "bank that doesn't call" — rare, reputational).

### How to pitch it to a client
"Instead of 2.8% on a 5-year bullet from the same issuer, you earn 3.2% a year. In exchange, we can repay you at par each year from year 1. If rates stay where they are or go up, you keep the higher coupon; if rates fall, you get your capital back early and you'll have earned an above-market coupon until then." Right client: a yield buyer who doesn't expect rates to fall sharply and doesn't need a fixed maturity (insurer with liquidity, private bank client in a "carry" portfolio).

### Common pitfalls
- Saying the investor holds the option. The **issuer** holds it; the investor is short.
- Saying it's an American or European option: it's Bermudan.
- Forgetting reinvestment risk: the note is called precisely when reinvestment rates are low.
- Pricing the call with a bond option on a single forward rate: the exercise depends on the whole remaining swap.

### How to deliver it
Three sentences: "Fixed coupon, issuer can redeem at par; the investor has sold a Bermudan receiver swaption; the premium lifts the coupon." Then the example numbers (2.8% vs 3.2%), the vol sensitivity, and the client risk (reinvestment, negative convexity).
deep.str-036:
### Context / why they ask this
Steepeners were one of the flagship rates structured notes of the 2000s and returned when curves were flat or inverted (2023-2024). They test whether the candidate understands forward curves, spread options, correlation and leverage, and whether they can explain why "the curve is flat, it can only steepen" is a view and not a free lunch.

### Key concepts
- **Swap rate / CMS rate**: the fixed rate of a par swap. A CMS10 coupon pays the 10-year swap rate observed at each fixing, i.e. a "constant maturity" rate that keeps rolling.
- **2s10s spread**: 10-year swap rate minus 2-year swap rate: the **slope** of the curve. Steepening = spread widens.
- **Forward spread**: the spread implied today for a future date by the forward curve. It is typically lower than the spot spread because long forward rates converge.
- **Leverage (gearing)** $L$: multiplier applied to the spread.
- **Spread option**: an option on the difference of two rates. Its vol is $\sigma_S^2=\sigma_{10}^2+\sigma_2^2-2\rho\sigma_{10}\sigma_2$ (normal vols), so it depends on **correlation** $\rho$.
- **CMS convexity adjustment**: paying a swap rate at a single date (instead of over the swap's life) creates a convexity bias; the expected CMS rate is above the forward swap rate, more so for long tenors and long maturities. It is priced by replicating with swaptions across strikes (static replication).

### The maths
Coupon in year $t$ (fixed at $t-1$, paid at $t$):
$$c_t=\min\big(\max(L\,S_{t-1},0),\,\text{cap}\big)=L\big[(S)^+-(S-\text{cap}/L)^+\big],$$
a **call spread on the CMS spread** with strikes 0 and cap/L. With $S_{t-1}\sim\mathcal N(F_{t-1},\sigma_S^2 (t-1))$:
$$\mathbb E[c_t]=\mathbb E\big[\min(\max(L S,0),\text{cap})\big],\qquad PV=\sum_t P(0,t)\,\mathbb E[c_t].$$
The structurer chooses $L$ so that the PV of all coupons equals the **coupon budget** = PV of (swap rate + issuer spread − margin).

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, illustrative)
Flat 2.5% curve for discounting, 10-year note, issuer spread 60 bp, margin 30 bp a year → budget ≈ **2.83% a year** (PV ≈ 24.7% of notional over 10 years).
Structure: year 1 fixed 5%; years 2-10: $\min(\max(L\,(\text{CMS}_{10}-\text{CMS}_2),0),8\%)$.
Forward 2s10s: 85 bp for the first floating fixing, falling 5 bp a year to 45 bp; normal spread vol 45 bp per year.
- Solving the budget gives **L ≈ 3.2**.
- Intrinsic coupons on the forwards: 2.72% (year 2) down to 1.44% (year 10); expected coupons including the floor's optionality: 2.74% down to 2.42%. The floor at zero is worth about 3.6 points of notional (at L=3).
- Client scenarios at L=3.2: spread stays at 90 bp → 2.9% a year; widens to 150 bp → 4.8%; to 250 bp → capped 8%; curve flat or inverted → 0% (and capital back at maturity).
The pitch relies on the gap between the spot spread (90 bp) and the forward (45-85 bp): a client who expects "no change" beats the forwards.

### Intuition
The client sells the forward curve's flattening. If the slope just stays constant ("curve doesn't roll down"), he gains. Leverage turns a small spread (tens of basis points) into a coupon comparable to fixed-rate alternatives. Correlation: if the 2-year and 10-year rates move together (high $\rho$), the spread barely moves, the option is cheap; the client, being long spread options, is **long spread vol = short correlation**.

### Risks the bank keeps
The desk is short the CMS spread options: short long-dated **spread vol**, long **correlation** between CMS rates (it loses if correlation drops and the spread becomes more volatile), **CMS convexity** and **smile** risk from the static replication, and **caps/floors** near zero where rates skew matters. Correlation is not directly hedgeable with liquid instruments; desks recycle it via spread options traded with other dealers or hedge funds. In 2008 and again in 2022 (inversions), large books of steepeners moved sharply: clients' notes fell well below par (zero coupons for years), which is a mark-to-market and reputational issue.

### How to pitch it to a client
"The market prices a flattening of the euro curve; we think the slope stays around 90 bp. This note pays 5% in year one, then 3.2 times the 10-year minus 2-year swap spread, floored at 0 and capped at 8%. If the curve simply stays as it is, you earn around 2.9% a year, and more if it steepens, with your capital protected at maturity by the issuer." Mention clearly: zero coupon if the curve inverts, long maturity, mark-to-market volatility.

### Common pitfalls
- Using the spot spread instead of the forward spread to value coupons.
- Forgetting the floor is an option the client owns (it costs budget).
- Ignoring correlation: a steepener is a spread option, not two separate CMS options.
- Ignoring CMS convexity for long tenors.

### How to deliver it
"Coupon = leverage × (10y − 2y swap rate), floored and capped: zero-coupon plus CMS spread call spreads. The client bets the slope beats the forwards; leverage around 3x makes the coupon competitive; the bank is short spread vol and long correlation." Then one scenario.
deep.str-037:
### Context / why they ask this
Snowballs (and their cousins "snowbear", "ratchet floaters") are the classic example of a **path-dependent** rates payoff. Quant and structuring interviewers use them to see if the candidate can write the recursion, understand why a closed form fails, and explain the Greeks' signs. In equity, the word "snowball" is also used in Asia for an autocall with accumulated coupons; don't mix them up, but say you know both exist.

### Key concepts
- **Euribor**: the euro interbank reference rate for a term (3M, 6M, 12M).
- **Path dependence**: the payoff depends on the whole history of the underlying, not only on its value at one date.
- **Floor at zero**: the coupon cannot be negative.
- **Put on a rate**: pays $\max(K-\text{rate},0)$; gains when rates fall.
- **Issuer call**: the issuer's right to redeem at par (see callable notes).

### The maths
$$c_1\ \text{fixed},\qquad c_t=\big(c_{t-1}+k-E_t\big)^+,\quad t=2,\dots,T,$$
where $E_t$ is the Euribor fixing for period $t$. Unrolling without the floor: $c_t=c_1+(t-1)k-\sum_{s=2}^t E_s$, a coupon that decreases with the **sum** of past fixings (an Asian-type put). With the floor, each coupon is a put on $E_t$ struck at the random level $c_{t-1}+k$. The value is
$$V=\sum_{t=1}^T P(0,t)\,\mathbb E^{Q}[c_t]\ (+\ \text{zero-coupon redemption}),$$
computed by Monte Carlo under Hull-White or LMM. The structurer picks $k$ (or $c_1$) such that PV(coupons) = coupon budget.

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, 400,000 paths)
Assumptions: 6-year note, discount rate 2.2%, Euribor forward flat at 2.0%, normal vol 80 bp a year (Brownian model $E_t=2\%+0.8\%\,W_{t-1}$), issuer spread 60 bp, margin 35 bp a year → budget ≈ **2.47% a year** (PV ≈ 13.8% of notional).
First coupon 4%. Solving the budget: **k ≈ 1.02%**.
- Expected coupons by year: 4.00%, 3.02%, 2.15%, 1.79%, 1.78%, 1.95%.
- Probability the coupon is zero: 0% in years 1-2, 13% in year 3, 36% in year 4, 49% in year 5, 54% in year 6.
Deterministic paths (coupons in years 1 to 6):
- Euribor flat 2%: 4.00, 3.02, 2.03, 1.05, 0.06, 0.
- Euribor flat 1%: 4.00, 4.02, 4.03, 4.05, 4.06, 4.08.
- Euribor flat 3%: 4.00, 2.02, 0.03, 0, 0, 0.
Sensitivities: forward at 1.5% → PV 18.3%; at 2.5% → 10.3% (client long duration, very rate sensitive). Vol 50 bp → 11.9%; vol 110 bp → 15.7%: the client is **long vol** because the zero floor protects him from paying back when rates spike, while low-rate paths compound.

### Intuition
A snowball is a leveraged bet on low rates with memory. The first high coupon is the "hook". The coupon's variance grows over time and the zero floor truncates bad paths, which is why vol helps the client. Compare with a range accrual, where the client is short vol.

### Risks the bank keeps
The desk is short the path-dependent puts: short rate vol, long rates (it loses when rates fall), exposure to the **vol term structure and to forward-rate correlations** (because the payoff depends on sums of fixings across time). When callable, the desk is also long the Bermudan; the combination is priced with Monte Carlo plus least-squares regression (Longstaff-Schwartz) for the exercise decision. Model risk is significant, hedging uses swaps (delta), caps/floors and swaptions (vega).

### How to pitch it to a client
"You get 4% in year one. After that, your coupon is last year's coupon plus 1.02% minus Euribor, never below zero. If Euribor stays below about 1%, your coupon stays around 4% or grows; if rates rise, the coupon shrinks quickly." Target: a client with a firm "rates stay low / ECB cuts" view. Say clearly that a rate spike can mean zero coupons for the remaining years.

### Common pitfalls
- Pricing it as a strip of independent caplets/floorlets: the strike is random and path dependent.
- Saying the client is short vol (it's the floor that makes him long vol).
- Forgetting the issuer call in real term sheets.

### How to deliver it
Write the recursion, unroll it (Asian-type), say "Monte Carlo under Hull-White or LMM", give the sign of rates and vol exposure, one path example.
deep.str-038:
### Context / why they ask this
CLNs are the main credit structured product for private banks and institutional clients, and banks also use them for **risk transfer** (synthetic securitisation, selling credit risk of their loan books). Credit structuring desks at BNP, SocGen, Natixis and CACIB issue them daily. The interviewer checks the CDS link, the coupon arithmetic, the default mechanics and the double credit exposure.

### Key concepts
- **CDS (credit default swap)**: insurance on a reference entity. The protection buyer pays a running spread (e.g. 150 bp a year); the seller pays $(1-R)$ times notional if a credit event occurs.
- **Recovery rate $R$**: the fraction of face value recovered after default (determined by the ISDA auction for CDS).
- **Credit event**: defined by ISDA (bankruptcy, failure to pay, restructuring for some contracts, obligation acceleration, repudiation for sovereigns). The **Determinations Committee** decides whether one occurred.
- **Hazard rate $\lambda$**: instantaneous default intensity; credit triangle $\lambda\approx s/(1-R)$.
- **Funded vs unfunded**: a CDS is unfunded (no cash upfront); a CLN is funded (investor pays 100, so the protection buyer has no counterparty risk on the investor).
- **Wrong-way risk**: exposure increases when the counterparty's credit worsens; here when the issuer and the reference entity default together.

### Construction (the bank's side)
1. The investor pays 100 to the issuing bank.
2. The bank's credit desk **buys CDS protection** on the reference entity from the investor, embedded in the note: the note is the bank's funding + a sold CDS.
3. The desk hedges by **selling** the same protection in the CDS market (or keeps it if it wants to hedge its own loan exposure to the entity, a risk-transfer CLN).
4. On a credit event, the bank stops paying coupons and redeems the note at $R\times100$ (cash settlement from the auction) or delivers a defaulted bond (physical settlement).

### The maths
Fixed coupon approximation:
$$c\approx \text{swap}_T+s_{\text{issuer}}+s_{\text{CDS}}-\text{margin per year}.$$
Survival and default probabilities with a constant hazard:
$$\lambda=\frac{s}{1-R},\qquad \mathbb Q(\tau>T)=e^{-\lambda T}.$$
Value of the note to the investor: coupons weighted by survival + recovery on default:
$$V=\sum_i c\,P(0,t_i)e^{-\lambda t_i}+100\,P(0,T)e^{-\lambda T}+R\cdot 100\int_0^T P(0,t)\lambda e^{-\lambda t}dt,$$
(discounted also at the issuer's spread for issuer risk).

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python)
5-year CLN on a BBB corporate. CDS 150 bp, $R=40\%$, 5-year swap 2.3%, issuer spread 70 bp, margin 40 bp a year.
- Coupon: $2.3\%+0.7\%+1.5\%-0.4\%=\mathbf{4.1\%}$ a year, versus 3.0% (2.3 + 0.7) on a plain note of the issuer.
- Hazard: $\lambda=1.5\%/0.6=2.5\%$ a year. Survival over 5 years $e^{-0.125}=88.2\%$, so **11.8%** risk-neutral default probability. (Real-world probabilities are lower; the spread also contains a risk premium and liquidity premium, which is exactly what the investor is paid to carry.)
- Default in year 3 with recovery 40%: the investor received two coupons (8.2) and gets 40 back: total 48.2 for 100 invested.

### Variants
- **Basket CLN / first-to-default CLN** (next card), **tranche CLN** on an index (iTraxx), **leveraged CLN** (notional of CDS larger than note), **zero-recovery CLN** (fixed recovery at 0, higher coupon), **fixed vs floating** coupon.
- Bank balance-sheet **Significant Risk Transfer** (SRT) CLNs: the bank buys protection on a portfolio of its own loans to free up regulatory capital.

### Risks the bank keeps
If back-to-back hedged with a CDS, the desk keeps: **basis** between the CLN terms and the market CDS (different maturities, restructuring clauses), **recovery** and settlement mechanics, the **funding** benefit/cost, **counterparty risk** on the CDS hedge (collateralised), and **jump-to-default** mismatch if the hedge is not exact. On a basket, correlation risk.

### How to pitch it to a client
"You like the credit of company X and would buy its bond, but its 5-year bonds are illiquid or don't exist in euros. This note gives you 4.1% a year for 5 years, 110 bp above a plain note from us. You're paid for bearing the default risk of X: if X defaults, the note stops and you receive the recovery value, historically around 40% for senior unsecured." Must mention: double exposure (issuer + reference entity), mark-to-market moves with X's spread, liquidity.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying the investor **buys** protection. He **sells** protection (he's long credit risk).
- Forgetting the issuer's own credit risk.
- Confusing risk-neutral default probabilities with historical ones.
- Mixing up credit event and rating downgrade (a downgrade is not a credit event).

### How to deliver it
"A CLN is a bank note plus a sold CDS: coupon ≈ funding + CDS spread; on a credit event it redeems at recovery." Then the 4.1% example and the double credit risk.
deep.str-039:
### Context / why they ask this
FtD baskets were sold to private banks as CLNs ("5 names you know, 7% coupon"), and they are the textbook example of correlation products in credit (with CDO tranches). They connect directly to worst-of equity structures. Interviewers ask the correlation limits (sum of spreads vs max spread) because it can be derived without any model.

### Key concepts
- **nth-to-default (NtD)**: pays on the n-th default of the basket; FtD is n = 1.
- **Default correlation**: tendency of defaults to cluster. Modelled with a **copula**: each name's default time is linked to a latent variable, and the latent variables are correlated.
- **Gaussian one-factor copula**: $X_i=\sqrt\rho\,Z+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i$, name $i$ defaults before $t$ if $N(X_i)\le 1-e^{-\lambda_i t}$. $Z$ is the common factor (economy), $\varepsilon_i$ is idiosyncratic. This is the "Li model" (2000) used for CDOs before 2008.
- **Hazard rate** and survival: $\lambda=s/(1-R)$, $\mathbb Q(\tau>t)=e^{-\lambda t}$.

### The model-free limits
- **Independence**: probability of no default up to $t$ = $\prod_i e^{-\lambda_i t}=e^{-(\sum\lambda_i)t}$. The first default time is exponential with intensity $\sum_i\lambda_i$, so the FtD spread is $(1-R)\sum_i\lambda_i=\sum_i s_i$ (same recoveries): **sum of spreads**.
- **Perfect correlation (comonotonic)**: all names default in the order of their riskiness; the first default is that of the riskiest name, so the FtD spread = **max spread**.
Hence $\max_i s_i\le s_{FtD}\le\sum_i s_i$ (for positive correlation).

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, 400,000 simulations)
5 names, 100 bp each, $R=40\%$, $\lambda=1.67\%$, 5 years. Single-name 5-year default probability: 8.0%.

| Correlation | P(at least one default in 5y) | FtD spread | P(two or more defaults) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0% | 34.1% | 500 bp | 5.4% |
| 30% | 28.7% | 406 bp | 8.5% |
| 60% | 22.2% | 302 bp | 10.0% |
| 90% | 14.3% | 185 bp | 9.8% |
| ≈100% | 8.6% | ≈ 100 bp | 8.2% |

(Spread approximated as the flat hazard implied by the FtD probability times $1-R$.) Notice the probability of two or more defaults: it rises with correlation first, then falls, which is why the second-to-default has a non-monotone correlation profile.

### Intuition
Selling FtD protection = holding a portfolio where you lose on the weakest link. Correlation makes names behave as one: fewer independent chances to have a default, so the FtD is safer and cheaper. Exactly like a worst-of equity put the investor is short: investor long correlation (see the worst-of card). The equity/credit analogy is a great answer to deliver.

### Structuring an FtD CLN
Note pays funding + FtD spread − margin. With the numbers above at 30% correlation: 5-year swap 2.3% + issuer 70 bp + 406 bp − margin 60 bp ≈ **6.5%** a year on 5 well-known investment grade names, which is why it sells. On the first credit event, the note redeems at the recovery of the defaulted name (e.g. 40%) and stops.

### Risks the bank keeps
The desk buys FtD protection from the client and hedges by selling single-name CDS on each name, with notional = the FtD's sensitivity to each name (the "delta" in a copula model), rebalanced as spreads move. It keeps: **correlation risk** (it's short correlation after selling the CLN, since the client is long correlation), **jump-to-default** risk (after a default, the hedges on the remaining names must be unwound instantly: big P&L jump), **spread convexity**, and **model risk** (Gaussian copula has no fat-tailed common factor; 2005 and 2008 showed correlation can move violently). Recovery assumptions also matter.

### How to pitch it to a client
"You get 6.5% a year for 5 years on five investment-grade names you know. You bear the risk that any one of them defaults; historically investment-grade 5-year default rates are well below the risk-neutral probability of 29% priced here, so you're paid a large premium for that tail risk." Always stress: one default among five names is enough to lose about 60% of capital.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying correlation increases the FtD spread. It **decreases** it.
- Forgetting the bounds max ≤ FtD ≤ sum.
- Confusing asset correlation in the copula with default-event correlation (the latter is much smaller).

### How to deliver it
"FtD = pay on the first default. Bounds: sum of spreads at zero correlation, max spread at perfect correlation. The seller is long correlation, like a worst-of investor." Then the five-name table and the jump-to-default risk.
deep.str-040:
### Context / why they ask this
FX structured hedging for corporates is the main business of corporate structuring teams (CACIB and Natixis corporate solutions, BNP and SocGen FX structuring). TARFs are the most famous and controversial product: attractive strike, short vol, path dependent, capped upside. Regulators (e.g. the Hong Kong SFC and several European ones) required suitability checks after losses. The interviewer checks that you can explain where the "better strike" comes from and who takes which risk.

### Key concepts
- **EURUSD quote**: number of USD per 1 EUR. A European exporter paid in USD wants to **buy EUR / sell USD**; a **lower** strike is better for him.
- **Forward**: $F=S_0e^{(r_{USD}-r_{EUR})T}$; with USD rates above EUR rates, forwards are above spot (EUR at a forward premium).
- **Big figure**: 0.01 in EURUSD (1.17 → 1.18 = 1 big figure = 100 pips).
- **Target**: cap on the cumulative gain (sum of $(S_i-K)^+$); once reached, the trade terminates (with full, capped or no final-fixing payment depending on the term sheet; here capped).
- **Leverage**: on losing fixings the client deals a multiple (1.5x or 2x) of the notional.
- **Knock-out**: early termination.

### The maths
Per EUR of monthly notional, payoff to the client at fixing $i$ (in USD):
$$\pi_i=\mathbf 1_{\{\text{alive}\}}\Big[\min\big((S_i-K)^+,\;G-A_{i-1}\big)-L\,(K-S_i)^+\Big],\qquad A_i=A_{i-1}+(S_i-K)^+\wedge(G-A_{i-1}),$$
alive while $A_{i-1}<G$ (target $G$, leverage $L$). Zero-cost strike: $K$ such that $\mathbb E^Q[\sum_i P(0,t_i)\pi_i]=0$ (minus the bank's margin, i.e. in practice the strike is set slightly worse). Path dependent → Monte Carlo (with local or stochastic vol for the smile).

Decomposition: without target, it's a strip of long calls on EURUSD at K (1x) and short puts at K (2x): a **leveraged forward**, cheaper than a forward because the client sells extra puts. The **target** is a knock-out on the calls he owns, triggered by accumulated gains: he sells that too. Both give him a better strike.

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, 200,000 paths, GBM)
EURUSD spot 1.17, USD rate 3.75%, EUR rate 2.0% (illustrative), vol 7%, 12 monthly fixings, target 0.10 (10 big figures), leverage 2x. These are round illustrative levels, not live quotes: as of 30 Sept 2026 EURUSD is about 1.135, SOFR about 3.9% and €STR about 2.44%, so rescale the strikes before quoting; the mechanics and the ordering of the structures do not change.
- Forwards: 1.1717 (1 month) to 1.1907 (12 months); DF-weighted average **1.1811** = the strike of a plain forward strip.
- Zero-cost TARF strike: **1.1291**, i.e. about **5.2 big figures better** than the strip.
- Expected number of fixings before knock-out: **4.3**; probability of knocking out before the end: **88%**.
- Flat scenarios (undiscounted, USD per 1 EUR of monthly notional): EURUSD at 1.30 → gain 0.10 capped at the first fixing, then gone; at 1.10 → loss of 0.70 over 12 fixings (2 × 2.9 figures × 12); at 1.05 → loss of 1.90.
- Tail: 5% quantile of the PV −0.67, 1% quantile −1.44 per EUR of monthly notional. On 1m EUR a month, that's −1.44m USD in a 1-in-100 scenario, for a "zero-cost hedge".
- Vol: at the same strike, the client's value is +0.065 at 5% vol and −0.128 at 10% vol: **client short vol**.

### Intuition
The client sells upside (the target caps what he can gain) and sells extra downside (leverage), and in exchange improves the strike. When EURUSD trends up, he knocks out quickly: good rate but only on 3-4 months of flows, then he's unhedged at higher levels. When EURUSD trends down, he's locked in for the full year at 2x volume, over-hedged (he may not even have enough USD receivables: "speculation" in accounting terms). Heads you win a little, tails you lose a lot.

### Risks the bank keeps
The desk is long vol, long the tail, and holds a **path-dependent** position with **discontinuous delta** near the target (like a barrier), **smile and skew** dependence (risk reversals matter), **correlation between spot and vol**, **gap risk** on sudden moves (CHF 2015). Also **client credit risk**: a corporate with large mark-to-market losses on a TARF may not be able to pay (the bank needs credit lines, collateral), plus **conduct risk**: mis-selling claims if the hedge exceeded real flows.

### How to pitch it to a client (responsibly)
"A forward locks 1.181 for the year. This structure lets you buy EUR at 1.129 on each monthly fixing until you've accumulated 10 figures of gains. In exchange, when EURUSD is below 1.129, you buy twice your monthly amount at 1.129. It suits a view that EURUSD will stay range-bound to slightly higher, and only for flows you're certain to have twice over." Always show a stress scenario (e.g. EURUSD −10%), the maximum volume, and compare with a vanilla forward and a participating forward.

### Common pitfalls
- Calling it "zero cost" without explaining the sold options.
- Saying the better strike comes from "the bank's margin being low".
- Forgetting leverage creates over-hedging and accounting issues (IFRS 9 hedge accounting may not apply).
- Mixing up the direction of EURUSD for an exporter.

### How to deliver it
"Strip of forwards at an improved strike; knocks out when accumulated gains hit a target; leverage on losing fixings. The client sells vol and tail risk to improve the strike." Then the numbers (5 big figures better, 4 fixings expected), the stress scenario, and the suitability point.
deep.str-041:
### Context / why they ask this
Flow products (turbos, warrants, certificates) are a big business for French banks: BNP Paribas and SocGen are among the largest issuers of listed leverage products in Europe. Structuring and trading candidates for "flow" or "listed products" desks get this question. It also tests barrier option intuition: why does a knock-out call with barrier at the strike cost almost exactly intrinsic value?

### Key concepts
- **Warrant**: a securitised (listed) option issued by a bank, usually with a **parity** (ratio): e.g. 100 warrants for one index unit.
- **Turbo / knock-out warrant**: barrier option whose knock-out barrier equals (classic turbo) or is set above (non-BEST turbo infini / mini-future with a stop-loss, which pays a residual value) the strike; "BEST" = Barrier Equal STrike.
- **Leverage (gearing)**: percentage change of the product per 1% of the underlying. Turbo: $S/(S-K)$. Warrant: elasticity $\Delta\cdot S/C$.
- **Parity**: number of turbos per underlying unit.
- **Open-end / "infini"**: no maturity; the financing level (strike) is adjusted daily.
- **Residual value**: for mini-futures, when the stop-loss barrier is hit, the issuer unwinds its hedge and pays whatever is left above the strike.
- **Gap risk**: the underlying jumps through the barrier overnight; the issuer's hedge can't be unwound at the barrier.

### The maths
Down-and-out call with barrier $H=K$, zero rates and dividends: by the reflection principle
$$C_{DO}(S)=S-K\quad(S>K).$$
Intuition: the position "long stock, short $K$ in cash, closed as soon as $S=K$" replicates it exactly and costs $S-K$, no option value because the payoff is linear while alive and zero at the barrier. With $r\neq q$, the price is close to $S-Ke^{-(r-q)\cdot\text{something}}$: the carry (financing of $K$ minus dividends) enters the price. For open-end turbos the issuer simply updates
$$K_{t+dt}=K_t\,(1+(r+\text{fee})\,dt)-\text{dividends (on ex-date)},$$
so the price stays $\approx(S_t-K_t)/\text{parity}$.

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python)
CAC 40 at 8,000, turbo call strike = barrier 7,200, parity 100.
- Price ≈ (8,000 − 7,200)/100 = **8.00 EUR**; leverage 8,000/800 = **10**.
- Closed-form down-and-out call, 1 year, $r=2\%$, $\sigma=20\%$: with $q=2\%$: 784.2 index points (7.84 EUR); with $q=3\%$: 736.4. So carry, not vol, drives the difference to intrinsic value.
- Index −5% to 7,600: turbo worth 4.00, **−50%**.
- Open-end financing: at 2% rate + 2% fee, the strike rises by 7,200 × 4% = 288 points a year (0.79 points a day). The investor pays this whether the index moves or not.
- Compare a 1-year ATM **warrant** (strike 8,000, vol 18%, $r=2\%$, $q=3\%$): 5.21 EUR, delta 0.50, elasticity 7.6. Deep ITM warrant struck at 7,200: 9.57 EUR, of which 1.57 is time value, elasticity 5.9. The warrant needs vol and time, the turbo doesn't.

### Intuition
A turbo is a margin account in a wrapper: you're long the index, financed by a loan equal to the strike, with an automatic stop-loss at the strike. The issuer lends you the money, charges interest, and cuts the position when your equity is gone. You can't lose more than what you paid (unlike a margin account or CFD), the price of that "negative balance protection" is the gap risk the bank bears.

### Risks the bank keeps
- **Gap risk**: overnight jump below the barrier (earnings, a crash, a weekend); the bank must unwind its delta hedge at a worse price than the strike and absorbs the difference. That's why barriers of mini-futures are set above strikes and why issuers charge a fee.
- **Barrier/discontinuity** risk: millions of small turbos with barriers clustered at round numbers; the bank hedges delta dynamically and knock-out events create sell (for calls) or buy flows near barriers.
- **Warrants**: the issuer is short vol on the warrants it sold and hedges with listed options; it earns bid-offer and the vol spread.
- **Market-making obligation**: the issuer is the liquidity provider on the exchange (quotes all day), so operational and pricing-latency risks.
- **Conduct**: ESMA data show most retail leverage product investors lose money; distribution rules (MiFID II appropriateness, PRIIPs KIDs) apply.

### How to pitch it
"A turbo gives you 10x exposure to the CAC 40 for 8 EUR, with a maximum loss of 8 EUR. Its price moves one-for-one with the index divided by 100: no volatility or time value to understand. The price of simplicity: a daily financing cost and the knock-out if the index touches 7,200." For hedging, a turbo put can protect a portfolio for a known cost.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying turbos are "options with vol". The barrier-at-strike kills the vol dependence.
- Forgetting financing costs on open-end turbos.
- Saying the investor can lose more than the premium (he can't; the bank bears gap risk).

### How to deliver it
"Warrant = listed vanilla, depends on vol and time; turbo = knock-out with barrier at strike, priced at intrinsic value plus carry; leverage S/(S−K); bank earns financing and bears gap risk." Then the CAC example.
deep.str-042:
### Context / why they ask this
Structurers don't just design payoffs; they choose the wrapper, which determines the documentation, regulation, taxation, credit risk and target market. In France, the question "how does an autocall reach a retail client?" almost always leads to assurance-vie and CGP (independent advisers). Knowing this shows commercial sense.

### Key concepts
- **EMTN (Euro Medium Term Note) programme**: a framework allowing an issuer to issue many notes quickly using a single approved **base prospectus**; each issue only needs short **final terms** (the term sheet in legal form).
- **Issuing vehicle**: many banks issue from subsidiaries guaranteed by the parent (for example SG Issuer, BNP Paribas Issuance B.V., Natixis Structured Issuance, Crédit Agricole CIB Financial Solutions), for tax and operational reasons; the credit risk is the guarantor's.
- **Public offer vs private placement**: under the EU Prospectus Regulation, a public offer to retail needs an approved prospectus (plus a PRIIPs KID); private placements (e.g. to qualified investors, fewer than 150 non-qualified persons per member state, or a 100k EUR minimum) are exempt from the prospectus.
- **UCITS**: EU regulated fund; a **formula fund** (fonds à formule) delivers a predefined payoff via a total return swap with a bank, with counterparty exposure limited (10% of NAV for a credit institution) and collateralised.
- **Assurance-vie**: French life-insurance savings contract; **fonds euros** (capital guaranteed by the insurer) vs **unités de compte (UC)** (market risk borne by the client). Structured notes are referenced as UCs. Tax: favourable treatment after 8 years and in inheritance (rules change, check current law).
- **PEA / compte-titres**: other French accounts; most structured notes are not PEA-eligible (not equities), so they go into a compte-titres or assurance-vie.
- **CGP (conseiller en gestion de patrimoine)**: independent financial advisers, a major distribution channel for autocalls, often via platforms and "enveloppes" of insurers.

### Why the wrapper matters (comparison)
| Wrapper | Credit risk | Liquidity | Typical client | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EMTN note | Issuer | Issuer's secondary market | Private banks, CGP, insurers' UC | Fast, flexible, cheapest to issue |
| Listed certificate | Issuer | Exchange, issuer as market maker | Self-directed retail | Standardised, smaller tickets |
| UCITS formula fund | Swap counterparty, limited and collateralised | Daily NAV | Bank networks, retail | More costly, protected by UCITS rules |
| OTC swap / option | Bilateral, collateralised (CSA) | Unwind with counterparty | Institutions | Needs ISDA, can be tailored fully |
| Structured deposit | Bank deposit (deposit guarantee scheme up to 100k EUR) | Low | Retail | Rare in France |

### Worked example with numbers (fee layering, verified in Python)
A client invests 100,000 EUR in a Phoenix autocall paying 7% a year, held as a UC in assurance-vie: entry fee 1%, UC management fee 0.85% a year.
- Invested: 99,000 EUR.
- The note autocalls after 2 years: redeems 100% + 2 × 7% = 112,860 EUR.
- UC fees over 2 years: ≈ 2 × 0.85% × 99,000 = 1,683 EUR → 111,177 EUR.
- Net annualised return: **5.4%**, versus a gross 6.8% annualised for the note itself (and the note's 7% coupon already embeds the bank's structuring margin and the distributor's retrocession, typically around 1% a year of expected life, which is what the AMF/ACPR studies of 2026 scrutinise).
The lesson for a structurer: the distributor and the wrapper consume part of the coupon, so the payoff must be designed with the **total cost** and the PRIIPs cost disclosure in mind.

### How the choice is made
- **French retail through insurers**: EMTN (or fund) referenced as UC in assurance-vie contracts; often a "fenêtre de commercialisation" (subscription period of a few weeks) with a fixed strike date; subscriptions from 1,000 EUR.
- **Private bank**: EMTN, private placement, tailor-made (client's chosen underlyings, 250k-5m EUR tickets), sometimes the private bank asks for a multi-issuer competition to pick the best coupon (and diversify credit).
- **Institutions**: a note if they can't trade derivatives (some insurers, pension funds), a swap with collateral if they can, or a fund for regulatory reasons (Solvency II look-through).
- **Corporate treasury**: OTC derivatives or structured deposits/notes on money market.

### Risks the bank keeps
Issuing notes gives the bank **funding** (it borrows the 100), so the treasury's appetite and funding value matter (see the margin and issuer-credit cards). With funds, the bank doesn't get funding and must post collateral, so coupons are a bit lower. Operational risk (documentation errors in final terms), **legal and conduct risk** (target market mismatch), and **secondary market** commitments (the bank usually provides daily prices and buyback liquidity).

### How to deliver it
"Same payoff, different wrappers: note, certificate, fund, swap, deposit. The choice depends on client type, regulation, credit risk tolerance and tax. In France, most retail structured products reach clients as UC in assurance-vie via CGP and bank networks." Give one fee-layering number to show commercial awareness.

### Common pitfalls
- Confusing the payoff with the wrapper.
- Saying assurance-vie protects the structured product's capital (only the fonds euros is guaranteed by the insurer; a UC carries the note's full risk, including the issuer's credit risk).
- Forgetting that a note = funding for the bank, a fund/swap is not.
deep.str-043:
### Context / why they ask this
Structurers sit on the "manufacturer" side of the regulation: they fill in the target-market fields sent to distributors (the EMT, European MiFID Template), they present new products to the **new product committee**, and they write the scenario analysis. French regulators (AMF, ACPR) are especially active on structured products (Feb 2026 AMF communiqué on marketing materials, June 2026 AMF/ACPR study on distribution, fees and performance of structured products). A candidate who can talk about this sounds like someone who can be trusted with retail products.

### Key concepts
- **MiFID II**: EU directive (and MiFIR regulation) governing investment services since January 2018. Product governance rules: Articles 16(3) and 24(2) of the directive, detailed by Delegated Directive 2017/593 and ESMA's product governance guidelines (updated in 2023, notably to include sustainability objectives).
- **Manufacturer / distributor**: the one who creates the product vs the one who sells or advises. Both have obligations; information flows both ways (the distributor reports sales outside the target market and complaints).
- **Target market (positive/negative)**: the group of end clients for whom the product is designed, and those for whom it is not.
- **Suitability** (advice or portfolio management): the adviser checks that a product fits a specific client's knowledge, financial situation and objectives. **Appropriateness** (non-advised sale of a complex product): checks knowledge and experience only.
- **Complex product**: structured notes are generally complex under MiFID II (embedded derivatives), so they can't be sold on an execution-only basis without an appropriateness test.
- **Inducements / retrocessions**: fees paid by the manufacturer to distributors; allowed under conditions (quality enhancement, disclosure) and scrutinised; the EU Retail Investment Strategy aims at stricter "value for money" rules and a tighter inducement test (as of Sept 2026: political agreement 18 Dec 2025, endorsed by Council COREPER on 5 June 2026 and Parliament's ECON committee on 23 June 2026, final plenary/Council votes expected Q4 2026, then transposition; check the latest status).
- **SRI**: the PRIIPs summary risk indicator (1-7), used as a proxy for risk tolerance (next card).

### What the structurer actually does (product approval)
1. **Identify the need**: e.g. "retail income investors want 5-7% yield with some downside buffer."
2. **Design and test**: payoff, underlying, maturity; **scenario analysis**: stressed markets, the probability and size of capital losses, early-redemption probabilities, what happens if the issuer defaults.
3. **Cost review**: structuring margin, distributor fees, total costs (PRIIPs), check that the costs don't erode the expected return so much that the product has no value for the target market.
4. **Target market grid** (the EMT fields): client type, knowledge (informed/advanced), ability to bear loss ("no capital guarantee, can lose all capital"), risk tolerance (SRI), objectives (growth, income, hedging), horizon, sustainability preferences, distribution strategy (advised only? execution-only allowed?).
5. **Committee sign-off**: legal, compliance, risk, trading (can we hedge it?), treasury (funding), operations.
6. **Post-launch review**: monitoring of sales outside the target market, product performance vs what was expected, market events (e.g. a barrier becoming close), complaints.

### Worked example with numbers (scenario analysis, verified in Python)
8-year Phoenix autocall on the Euro Stoxx 50: annual observations, autocall at 100% from year 1, coupon paid if the index ≥ 70%, capital protected at maturity if the index ≥ 60%. Flat 18% vol, 2.3% rate, 3% dividends, issuer spread 60 bp, 3 points of margin: fair coupon **6.4%** a year (no skew; with skew it would be somewhat different).
Risk-neutral scenario analysis (200,000 paths):
- Expected life: **3.6 years** (most scenarios autocall early).
- Probability of capital loss at maturity: **16%**; average redemption in those scenarios: **44%** of capital; probability of losing more than half: **11%**.
Target-market consequences: not for clients needing capital protection or liquidity before 8 years; client must understand autocall (uncertain maturity), barrier, issuer credit risk; income objective; horizon up to 8 years; SRI probably 4-6 depending on the model (to check with the KID engine). Negative target market: clients with low loss tolerance, short horizon, or no knowledge of barrier products. Distribution: advised sales or portfolio management; execution-only only after appropriateness.

### Risks the bank keeps (conduct side)
**Mis-selling risk**: claims and fines if products are sold outside the target market or with misleading materials (the AMF has sanctioned distributors and requires marketing documents to show the key risks as prominently as the coupon). **Reputational** risk when a whole vintage hits its barriers (2008, 2020). **Documentation** risk: the target market must match the prospectus, the KID and the marketing brochure.

### How to deliver it
"Manufacturer obligations: product approval, target market on the five ESMA criteria, scenario analysis, cost review, distribution strategy, periodic review. Distributor refines and checks suitability." Then a concrete target market for a product you know, with one scenario-analysis number (probability of loss and average loss). Mention the French regulators' current focus on structured products to show you follow the market.

### Common pitfalls
- Confusing target market (a product-level exercise) and suitability (a client-level test).
- Thinking a professional-only product has no governance obligations (lighter, but still applies).
- Forgetting the negative target market and the review after launch.
deep.str-044:
### Context / why they ask this
Every retail structured note needs a KID; the structuring team produces or validates the inputs (fair value, costs, scenarios) and must understand why the SRI or the scenarios look the way they do, because a product with an SRI of 6 may fall outside its target market, and "moderate scenario" numbers end up in sales conversations. PRIIPs is also a regular topic of criticism (backward-looking scenarios), so it's a good discussion point.

### Key concepts
- **PRIIP**: Packaged Retail and Insurance-based Investment Product: structured notes, funds, unit-linked insurance, derivatives sold to retail. Regulation (EU) 1286/2014, applicable since 2018 (to UCITS since 2023); technical rules in Delegated Regulation 2017/653, amended by 2021/2268 (new scenario and cost methodology from 2023).
- **Recommended holding period (RHP)**: for a structured note usually the maturity (with a warning that it may redeem early).
- **SRI**: 1 (lowest risk) to 7, combining the **MRM** (market risk measure, classes 1-7) and the **CRM** (credit risk measure, from the issuer's credit quality). A good credit (CRM 1-2) doesn't change the MRM; weaker credit pushes the SRI up.
- **VEV (VaR-equivalent volatility)**: the volatility of a lognormal asset that would have the same 97.5% VaR as the product. MRM classes by VEV: <0.5% → 1; 0.5-5% → 2; 5-12% → 3; 12-20% → 4; 20-30% → 5; 30-80% → 6; >80% → 7.
- **Category 3 PRIIP**: non-linear products (structured notes); simulated with at least 10,000 bootstrap paths of the underlying's historical returns (5 years of data, typically).
- **Fair value**: the model price of the note at issue, using the bank's pricing models; **entry cost = issue price − fair value**.
- **RIY / annual cost impact**: the reduction in annualised return due to total costs.

### The maths
VaR in log-return space: let $\text{VaR}_{97.5}$ be the 2.5% quantile of the simulated redemption value relative to the price. Then
$$\text{VEV}=\frac{\sqrt{3.842-2\ln \text{VaR}_{97.5}}-1.96}{\sqrt{T}} .$$
Where it comes from: for a lognormal asset with vol $\sigma$ and risk-neutral drift, $\ln(\text{VaR})=-\sigma^2T/2-1.96\sigma\sqrt T$; solving this quadratic in $\sigma\sqrt T$ gives the formula ($3.842=1.96^2$).
Cost impact for an upfront cost $c$ over $T$ years with gross annual return $g$:
$$\text{RIY}=g-\Big[(1+g)^T(1-c)\Big]^{1/T}+1 .$$

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python)
VEV for a 5-year product as a function of its 2.5% worst-case value:
- VaR at 90% of price: VEV 2.4% → MRM 2.
- 75%: VEV 6.3% → MRM 3.
- 60%: VEV 11.0% → MRM 3.
- 45%: VEV 16.6% → MRM 4.
Costs: fair value 97, issue price 100 → entry cost 3%. With a 5% gross annual return over 5 years, the net return is 4.36%: **annual cost impact 0.64%**. The KID also shows the cost in EUR on a 10,000 EUR investment (here 300 EUR entry if held to term, plus any exit cost if sold early: the bid-offer and the issuer's secondary spread).
Performance scenarios since 2023 for category 3: the favourable, moderate and unfavourable scenarios are the 90th, 50th and 10th percentiles of the simulated distribution at the RHP; the stress scenario uses a stressed volatility on the lower tail. Early redemption scenarios are shown with their date.

### Intuition and criticism
The SRI is a quantile-based risk measure: an autocall with a 60% barrier has a thin but fat tail (most outcomes are "coupon and early redemption", a few are big losses), so the VaR captures the tail and the SRI is often 4-5, like equity funds. Scenario criticism: bootstrapping the last 5 years of returns after a bull market gives very rosy moderate scenarios; the 2023 reform improved this but the scenarios are still model outputs, not forecasts. Structurers must never use them as a promise in marketing.

### Risks the bank keeps
Regulatory and conduct risk: wrong KIDs (cost understatement, stale scenarios) lead to sanctions; the KID must be updated when the risk profile changes materially (e.g. when the underlying falls close to the barrier, the SRI can jump). Operational: KIDs are produced by engines for thousands of products and languages; the structurer is responsible for the payoff description.

### How to deliver it
"Three pages: what it is, risk (SRI 1-7 = market risk from a 97.5% VaR converted to a VEV, plus issuer credit), scenarios (percentiles of simulated outcomes), costs (issue price minus fair value, shown as an annual impact)." One number: "a 3% upfront cost on a 5-year note is about 0.6% a year."

### Common pitfalls
- Thinking the SRI is based on historical volatility of the note (it's a simulated VaR at the holding period for structured products).
- Forgetting the credit component.
- Presenting the moderate scenario as an expected return.
deep.str-045:
### Context / why they ask this
"Draw the payoff of an Asian option" is a classic Goldman Sachs structuring question, and averaging is one of the main levers to improve the terms of capital-protected notes. The interviewer wants the payoff, the intuition for why it's cheaper, a rough pricing method, and the client trade-off.

### Key concepts
- **Arithmetic average** $\bar S=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n S_{t_i}$; **geometric average** $(\prod S_{t_i})^{1/n}$ (always ≤ arithmetic, has a closed form under Black-Scholes because a product of lognormals is lognormal).
- **Average-price (average-rate) option**: payoff on $\bar S - K$. **Average-strike option**: payoff on $S_T-\bar S$.
- **Averaging-out**: average over the last months before maturity. **Averaging-in**: the initial level is the average over the first months.
- **Participation**: the fraction of the index performance paid to the client (see str-005).

### The maths
Continuous geometric average over $[0,T]$ in Black-Scholes: $\ln G$ is normal with variance $\sigma^2T/3$, so the Asian behaves like an option with volatility $\sigma_A=\sigma/\sqrt3$ and an adjusted drift ($b_A=\tfrac12(r-q-\sigma^2/6)$). Why $1/3$: $\operatorname{Var}\big(\frac1T\int_0^T W_t\,dt\big)=\frac{T}{3}$. For discrete arithmetic averages there is no closed form: desks use Monte Carlo with the geometric Asian as a **control variate**, or moment matching (Turnbull-Wakeman, Levy approximations).
Capital-protected note budget:
$$\text{budget}=100-100\,e^{-(r+s)T}-\text{margin},\qquad \text{participation}=\frac{\text{budget}}{\text{option price}} .$$

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, 200,000 paths)
5 years, $S_0=100$, vol 18%, $r=2.5\%$, $q=3\%$, issuer spread 60 bp, margin 2 points.
- Zero-coupon: $100e^{-0.031\times5}=85.64$ → budget $=100-85.64-2=\mathbf{12.36}$.
- Vanilla ATM call: 12.84 → participation **96%**.
- Asian call on 20 quarterly observations (whole life): 7.81 → **158%**.
- Asian on the last 12 monthly observations: 12.06 → **102%**.
The full-life average cuts the effective vol from 18% to about $18\%/\sqrt3\approx10.4\%$: that is the whole effect here. (The drift also matters: the average is an average of forwards; with $r<q$ the forward curve slopes down, so the average of forwards is slightly *above* the final forward, which makes the Asian a bit more expensive, but the vol reduction dominates by far.)

### Intuition
The average is a smoother variable: extreme final values are diluted. The call on a smoother variable has less optionality, so it's cheaper. Payoff drawing: with averaging-out, a sharp rally in the last months is only partially captured; a crash in the last months is partially avoided. Averaging-in: if the market falls in the first months, the client gets a lower strike (good), if it rallies, a higher strike (bad).

### Risks the bank keeps
Asians are among the easiest exotics to hedge: vega is lower, gamma decreases as the average "locks in" (each fixing removes randomness), there's no barrier discontinuity. The desk keeps: **forward/dividend risk** over the averaging window (dividend futures hedges), some **vol term-structure** risk (the forward-start part of the average depends on forward vols), and fixing risk on each observation date (it trades at the close to hedge, like any fixing). Averaging also reduces the incentive or impact of manipulation around a single fixing, a reason commodity and FX corporates like it.

### How to pitch it to a client
"We protect 100% of your capital at 5 years and pay you 158% of the average quarterly performance of the Euro Stoxx 50, rather than 96% of the final performance. You're less dependent on the level at a single date; you give up some of the upside if the index rallies only at the very end." For commodity or FX corporates: "your costs are an average of monthly purchases, so hedge the average, it's cheaper and matches your exposure."

### Common pitfalls
- Saying the Asian is cheaper "because it's path dependent". It's cheaper because the average has **lower variance**.
- Forgetting that averaging-in can make the option more expensive than claimed if the strike is set late (vol exposure during the averaging-in window).
- Using the $\sigma/\sqrt3$ rule for averages that don't start at time 0 (last-year averaging: the reduction applies only to the last year's variance, so the price is close to a vanilla, as the 102% example shows).

### How to deliver it
Draw the payoff, say "average lowers variance, roughly vol over root 3 for a full-life average", give the participation comparison, then the client trade-off and one sentence on hedging (easy, lock-in).
deep.str-046:
### Context / why they ask this
Accumulators are an iconic private-banking product (Hong Kong, Singapore, Switzerland), also used on FX and gold. They illustrate the "short put, long capped call" structure with leverage, knock-outs and why suitability matters. For a structurer at a French bank's private-banking or cross-asset solutions desk, they're a standard product.

### Key concepts
- **Strike at a discount**: the client buys below the current price, an attractive headline.
- **Knock-out (KO)**: when the stock closes above the KO level, the contract ends (sometimes with guaranteed days for the first weeks).
- **Leverage / gearing**: the quantity doubles when the stock is below the strike.
- **Settlement**: shares bought daily are usually settled weekly or monthly.
- **Decumulator**: the client sells shares at a premium strike, KO below, double quantity above.

### The maths
Per unit of daily quantity, with fixings $t_1,\dots,t_n$, strike $K$, KO level $B$ and leverage $L$:
$$\text{PV}=\sum_{i=1}^n P(0,t_i)\,\mathbb E\Big[\mathbf 1_{\{\max_{j\le i}S_{t_j}<B\}}\big((S_{t_i}-K)^+-L\,(K-S_{t_i})^+\big)\Big].$$
Each day is a **knock-out forward with asymmetric notional**: a KO call at $K$ (client long) and $L$ KO puts at $K$ (client short). The zero-cost strike solves PV = 0 (the bank's margin is included by setting the strike a bit higher). Path dependent (KO) → Monte Carlo or PDE.

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, 100,000 paths)
Stock 100, vol 30%, $r=2.3\%$, dividend yield 2%, 252 daily fixings, KO at 105 on closing prices, leverage 2.
- Zero-cost strike: **81.96**, i.e. an 18% "discount".
- Expected number of accumulation days: **75** out of 252; probability of KO within the first month: **48%**.
- Expected shares bought: ≈ 100 per unit of daily quantity (because of doubling in bad paths and early KO in good paths).
- Scenario "stock at 104 all year" (no KO): client buys 252 shares/unit at 82: gain ≈ 5,550 per unit, but this path is rare because 104 is close to the KO.
- Scenario "stock falls to 70 and stays": buys 2 × 252 = 504 shares/unit at 82: **loss ≈ 6,030 per unit**. With 1,000 shares a day: 504,000 shares, 41.3m EUR paid for shares worth 35.3m EUR.
- Tail of the PV per unit: 5% quantile −3,615, 1% quantile −7,796.

### Intuition
The client sells a lot of downside (two puts per day) and receives an upside that is cut off early by the KO. In calm or rising markets, the product dies quickly with small gains; in falling markets, it runs all year with doubled quantities. The discount looks like a free gift; it's really the premium of the puts the client sells.

### Risks the bank keeps
The bank is long the puts and short the KO calls: **long vol** overall, **short gamma near the KO** barrier, **skew** sensitivity (the client's short puts are priced on the skew), **gap risk** and **concentration** (many clients accumulating the same popular stock: the bank, long puts, hedges by holding stock and buys more as the stock falls, which is long gamma and supports the price; but near the KO level it is short gamma and the hedge flips abruptly when contracts knock out). Major risk: **client credit**. When the stock falls, clients face huge commitments and margin calls; the private bank must lend against the shares (Lombard loans), and client defaults become correlated with the market. Also **conduct/suitability** risk: in 2008, Hong Kong regulators and courts dealt with many accumulator mis-selling complaints.

### How to pitch it (and to whom)
"You want to build a position in stock X, which you'd buy anyway below 85. This contract lets you buy it daily at 82, 18% below today's price. If the stock rises above 105, the contract stops. If it falls below 82, you buy twice as many shares at 82." Suitable only for a client who really wants the stock at that price, in double size, with the financial capacity to take delivery. Always show the doubled maximum quantity and a -30% scenario.

### Common pitfalls
- Presenting the discount as the bank's generosity.
- Forgetting the leverage doubles the quantity, not just the loss per share.
- Saying the client is long vol (he is short vol: more vol makes the short puts more valuable to the bank).

### How to deliver it
"Daily buying at a discounted strike, KO above, double quantity below: long KO calls, short two puts per day. Gains capped, losses leveraged, hence 'I kill you later'." Then the numbers: 82 strike, 75 days expected, -6m EUR scenario.
deep.str-047:
### Context / why they ask this
CPPI was huge in the 2000s (fund-linked protected products, guaranteed funds sold in bank networks), and it's still used on hedge funds, fund baskets, and for insurers' guaranteed products. It tests dynamic strategies, convexity and the difference between selling an option and selling gap risk. Quant and structuring interviews often ask to write the CPPI rule and explain the multiplier.

### Key concepts
- **Floor** $F_t=G\,P(t,T)$: the amount that, invested in a zero-coupon, guarantees $G$ at $T$.
- **Cushion** $C_t=V_t-F_t$.
- **Multiplier** $m$: exposure $E_t=m\,C_t$ (capped at a maximum leverage, e.g. 100% or 150% of $V$).
- **Cash-lock (monetisation)**: when the cushion goes to (near) zero, the whole portfolio sits in the zero-coupon until maturity, no upside anymore.
- **Gap risk**: the risk that the risky asset jumps down more than $1/m$ before the manager can rebalance, making $V<F$.
- **OBPI**: zero-coupon + call; the bank sells the call and delta-hedges it.
- **Ratchet / lock-in**: raising the floor after good performance (TIPP variant).

### The maths
Continuous-time CPPI with the risky asset following GBM $dS/S=\mu dt+\sigma dW$ and the floor growing at $r$: $dC=dV-dF=mC\frac{dS}{S}+(V-mC)r\,dt-rF\,dt$, so
$$\frac{dC}{C}=m\frac{dS}{S}+(1-m)r\,dt\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_T=C_0\Big(\frac{S_T}{S_0}\Big)^m\exp\Big[(1-m)\big(r+\tfrac{m\sigma^2}{2}\big)T\Big].$$
The cushion is a **power** $m$ of the asset (a convex payoff, like a long option), and in continuous time without jumps it never reaches zero: no gap risk. With jumps or discrete rebalancing, a fall of more than $1/m$ between rebalancings wipes out the cushion: the probability of that event is what the bank sells.
OBPI: $V_T=G+\text{participation}\cdot(S_T-S_0)^+$ with participation $=(V_0-G P(0,T))/\text{Call}$.

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python, 100,000 paths)
8 years, 100% guarantee, rate 2.5%, risky asset vol 18% plus rare 20% jumps (0.2% probability per week), weekly rebalancing, $m=4$, exposure capped at 100%, cash-lock when the cushion falls below 2% of the floor; no fees.
- **OBPI**: zero-coupon at the bank's 3.0% funding: 78.66; ATM 8-year call on a total-return asset: 28.69 → participation **74%**.
- Risk-neutral drift (pricing view): CPPI mean final value 122, median 102; **63% of paths cash-locked**; probability of ending below the floor (gap events) ≈ 0.2%, minimum 97.5. OBPI: mean 127, median 104.
- Real-world drift of rate + 4% (client's view): CPPI mean 150, median 106, **44% cash-locked**, 90th percentile 259; OBPI mean 156, median 134, 90th percentile 243.
Reading: CPPI's distribution is very skewed: many paths end near the guarantee (locked), a few end very high (leverage of the cushion in bull markets). OBPI has a more balanced distribution.

### Intuition
CPPI is "buying a call by delta-hedging it yourself with a simple rule": exposure grows after gains and shrinks after losses (buy high, sell low), which creates convexity like a long option. The multiplier trades off upside leverage against the probability of cash-lock and the gap risk. OBPI buys the convexity upfront at implied vol; CPPI "pays" for it through realised path (whipsaws cost money when the market oscillates).

### Risks the bank keeps
- **Gap risk** on the guarantee: the bank sells a deep out-of-the-money put on the strategy (triggered only by jumps larger than $1/m$). It's hard to hedge (deep OTM puts, variance of jumps) and was a big issue in 2008 for leveraged CPPIs on hedge funds and CPDOs (credit CPPI-like products).
- **Liquidity risk** of the underlying: funds with monthly liquidity or gates can't be rebalanced in time (the Madoff and 2008 fund-of-funds episodes).
- **Model and operational risk**: the rules must be executed mechanically; any delay increases gap risk.
For OBPI: the classic vega/gamma risk of a sold call, hedgeable on liquid indices.

### How to pitch it to a client
"This 8-year fund-linked note guarantees 100% of your capital and invests dynamically in the fund: the more the fund performs, the more you're exposed. If markets fall significantly, the strategy protects your capital by moving to bonds." Say clearly that after a large fall the product may stay in bonds until maturity (cash-lock), and compare with an OBPI when options on the underlying exist.

### Common pitfalls
- Saying CPPI has no cost: it pays for protection through path (selling after falls) and through the gap premium.
- Forgetting cash-lock.
- Confusing the multiplier with leverage of the whole portfolio.

### How to deliver it
Write $E=m(V-F)$, explain floor/cushion/multiplier, gap risk at $1/m$, cash-lock; then compare with OBPI (static, option-based) and state when each is preferred: OBPI on liquid indices, CPPI on funds or custom underlyings without an options market.
deep.str-048:
### Context / why they ask this
In the low-rate years (2012-2021), option budgets were small, so structurers moved to vol-target and custom (QIS, "quantitative investment strategies") indices: the index sponsor is often the bank itself. They're still common in insurance products (fixed indexed annuities in the US, capital-protected notes in Europe). Interviewers ask "why use a vol-target index?" to test understanding of what drives option prices.

### Key concepts
- **Realised vol estimator**: e.g. the max of 20-day and 60-day historical vol (the max makes it react fast to spikes).
- **Exposure / leverage cap**: typically 0%-150%.
- **Excess return (ER) vs total return (TR) index**: ER subtracts the cash rate (the index is financed), making its forward ≈ spot, so calls are cheaper; TR includes the cash return.
- **Decrement**: a fixed deduction (e.g. 3-5% a year or points) that lowers the forward further (see str-029).
- **QIS**: a systematic strategy index created by a bank (momentum, carry, multi-asset risk parity...), used as underlying.

### The maths
Index return: $\frac{dI_t}{I_t}=w_t\frac{dS_t}{S_t}+(1-w_t)r\,dt$ (TR version), with $w_t=\min\big(\frac{\sigma^*}{\hat\sigma_t},w_{max}\big)$. If $\hat\sigma_t$ equals the true instantaneous vol, the index vol is exactly $\sigma^*$, so in the ideal case the index is a Black-Scholes asset with constant vol $\sigma^*$, independent of the market's vol regime: that's why desks can price and hedge options on it at a vol close to $\sigma^*$ (with an adjustment for estimation lag, which requires a stochastic-vol or jump model).

### Worked example with numbers (verified in Python)
Participation of an 8-year 100%-protected note: zero-coupon at 3.1% funding: 78.0; margin 3 → option budget ≈ 19.0.
- ATM call on a 10% vol index: 21.7 → participation **87%**.
- On an 18% vol index: 28.7 → **66%**.
- On a 25% vol index: 35.1 → **54%**.
Exposure rule with a 10% target: realised vol 8% → 125%; 15% → 67%; 20% → 50%; 35% → 29%; 50% → 20%.
Simulation of a regime-switching market (15% calm / 35% stress, 5 years, 20-day lookback): the underlying's realised vol is 18.1%, the vol-target index's 10.7%. Distribution of 5-year log-returns (zero-drift pricing view): underlying 5th/50th/95th percentiles −75%, −8%, +58%; vol-target index −44%, −4%, +35%: the tails are compressed.

### Intuition
The index sells when vol rises (usually when markets fall, because of the leverage effect) and buys when vol falls. It's a "trend-follower light": good in slow crashes (2008), bad in fast V-shaped markets (March 2020: de-risked at the bottom, missed the rebound). The client buys a cheap option on a smoothed asset: high participation × lower underlying performance. Compare apples to apples: 87% of a 10%-vol index is not better than 66% of the Euro Stoxx 50 if the index grows much less.

### Risks the bank keeps
- **Vol-of-vol and lag**: the realised vol estimator reacts with delay; a sudden spike (a crash day) happens at full exposure: the index's short-term vol can exceed the target. Priced with stochastic-vol/jump models.
- **Gap risk** between rebalancings (usually daily, with a lag).
- **Rebalancing costs** and **crowding**: many vol-target products and funds de-lever together after spikes, adding selling pressure (discussed after Feb 2018 and March 2020).
- Index governance and **conflicts of interest** when the bank is sponsor, calculation agent and issuer: must be managed and disclosed (EU Benchmarks Regulation).
The bank has less vega and skew exposure than on a vanilla index, which is why it can quote better terms.

### How to pitch it to a client
"This note protects 100% of your capital over 8 years and pays 87% of the performance of an index that invests in European equities while targeting 10% volatility: it automatically reduces exposure when markets become turbulent." Be clear: the index can underperform the equity market a lot, especially with a decrement or ER construction; show backtests with and without the decrement, and point out they're backtests.

### Common pitfalls
- Comparing participations on different underlyings as if they were equivalent.
- Forgetting the ER/decrement effect on the forward.
- Claiming the index can't lose much: it can, just more slowly.

### How to deliver it
"Exposure = target vol / realised vol; realised vol of the index ~ target; so options are cheaper and participation higher. The client pays through a de-risked, often decremented underlying; the bank faces vol-of-vol and gap risk." Then the 87% vs 66% numbers.
deep.str-049:
### Context / why they ask this
This is the typical "case" question in structuring interviews (SocGen, BNP, Natixis and CACIB assessment centres): the client gives a coupon target, a view and a risk tolerance; you must ask the right questions, choose a payoff, know the direction and rough size of each lever, and check consistency with the client's constraints (MiFID target market). There's no single right answer; the process is what is assessed.

### Step 1: ask questions (show you think like a structurer)
- **Horizon and liquidity**: can the money be locked for 8-10 years? Is early redemption (autocall) fine?
- **Loss tolerance**: "only if the market crashes" → a capital barrier around 50-60%, no worst-of on single stocks.
- **View**: moderately bullish → an autocall suits "flat to moderately up"; a strongly bullish client would prefer participation.
- **Underlying preference**: index vs stocks, ESG constraints, decrement acceptable?
- **Currency, issuer rating, wrapper** (EMTN, assurance-vie), ticket size.

### Step 2: choose the base payoff
Phoenix autocall: annual observations; if the index ≥ 100% of initial, redeem at 100% + coupon; the coupon is paid each year the index is ≥ the coupon barrier; at maturity, capital repaid if the index ≥ capital barrier, else the client gets the index performance. It matches "moderately bullish, wants income, accepts loss only in a crash".

### Step 3: size it and pull the levers (verified in Python, 150,000 paths)
Assumptions: flat vol 18% for the Euro Stoxx 50, rate 2.3%, dividends 3%, issuer spread 60 bp, margin 3 points, annual observations, no skew (so absolute levels are indicative; directions and orders of magnitude are what matter).

| Structure | Coupon | Expected life | P(capital loss) | Avg redemption if loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ESX 8y, coupon barrier 70%, capital barrier 60% | **6.42%** | 3.6y | 16.4% | 44% |
| same, barriers 60/50 | 4.63% | 3.6y | 11.0% | 38% |
| same, barriers 80/70 | 9.13% | 3.6y | 20.9% | 48% |
| 70/60 with memory | 5.74% | 3.6y | 16.4% | 44% |
| 70/60 with autocall step-down 5%/year | 6.10% | 3.1y | 13.0% | 42% |
| Decrement index (5% synthetic dividend) | 8.62% | 4.1y | 23.9% | 42% |
| Worst-of 3 stocks (vols 25-30%, correlation 0.6) | 19.1% | 5.3y | 42.8% | 33% |
| Worst-of 3 stocks, barriers 60/50 | 13.2% | 5.3y | 37.1% | 30% |
| ESX 10y, 70/60 | 6.80% | 4.2y | 17.3% | 41% |
| ESX 5y, 70/60 | 5.22% | 2.7y | 12.6% | 49% |

Reading the levers:
- **Barriers** (the client sells a down-and-in put and digitals): higher barriers = more coupon, more risk.
- **Maturity**: longer = more coupon (more time value sold, more coupon dates).
- **Underlying**: higher vol, lower correlation (worst-of) or higher dividend (decrement) = more coupon; each raises the risk.
- **Features the client values** (memory, step-down) cost coupon.
- Others not in the table: lower autocall trigger early; quarterly observations; a lower-rated issuer (higher funding spread); reducing the bank's or distributor's margin; a non-call period; currency (a USD version pays more when USD rates are higher, but adds FX risk unless quanto).

### Step 4: recommend and check consistency
"Target 7%, crash-only losses": a 10-year Euro Stoxx 50 Phoenix 70/60 at about 6.8% (or 7% with a slightly lower margin or quarterly observations), or a decrement version around 8.6% if the client accepts the decrement's drag and a higher loss probability. I'd refuse the worst-of: its 43% loss probability contradicts "only if the market crashes". Also stress the **issuer credit** (diversify issuers for big tickets) and check skew: with a real skew, the client's short down-and-in put is worth more, so the actual coupon will differ from the flat-vol figure and must be re-priced on the desk's model.

### Risks the bank keeps
Same as any autocall (see str-017): short vol convexity near barriers, long dividends/decrement dynamics, correlation on worst-ofs, forward-skew and model risk. For the client: early redemption risk (reinvestment), coupon loss, capital loss below the barrier, issuer default.

### How to pitch it to the client
"We can offer about 7% a year on the Euro Stoxx 50 for up to 10 years. Every year where the index is above 70% of its starting level, you get 7%. If it's above its starting level on an anniversary, you're repaid early with the coupon. You only lose capital if at maturity the index is down more than 40%; in our simulations that happens in about 17% of scenarios, and then you lose on average about 59%." Always give both the upside story and the loss scenario.
